speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To the Congress of the United States: A quarter century ago the Congress decided that it could no longer consider the financial programs of the various departments on a piecemeal basis.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Instead it has called on the President to present a comprehensive Executive Budget.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Congress has shown its satisfaction with that method by extending the budget system and tightening its controls.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The bigger and more complex the Federal Program, the more necessary it is for the Chief Executive to submit a single budget for action by the Congress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At the same time, it is clear that the budgetary program and the general program of the Government are actually inseparable.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The President bears the responsibility for recommending to the Congress a comprehensive set of proposals on all Government activities and their financing.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In formulating policies, as in preparing budgetary estimates, the Nation and the Congress have the right to expect the President to adjust and coordinate the views of the various departments and agencies to form a unified program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And that program requires consideration in connection with the Budget, which is the annual work program of the Government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Since our programs for this period which combines war liquidation with reconversion to a peacetime economy are inevitably large and numerous it is imperative that they be planned and executed with the utmost efficiency and the utmost economy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have cut the war program to the maximum extent consistent with national security.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have held our peacetime programs to the level necessary to our national well-being and the attainment of our postwar objectives.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Where increased programs have been recommended, the increases have been held as low as is consistent with these goals.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I can assure the Congress of the necessity of these programs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I can further assure the Congress that the program as a whole is well within our capacity to finance it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: All the programs I have recommended for action are included in the Budget figures.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For these reasons I have chosen to combine the customary Message on the State of the Union with the annual Budget Message, and to include in the Budget not only estimates for functions authorized by the Congress, but also for those which I recommend for its action.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I am also transmitting herewith the Fifth Quarterly Report of the Director of War Mobilization and Reconversion.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is a comprehensive discussion of the present state of the reconversion program and of the immediate and long-range needs and recommendations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This constitutes, then, as complete a report as I find it possible to prepare now.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It constitutes a program of government in relation to the Nation's needs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: With the growing responsibility of modern government to foster economic expansion and to promote conditions that assure full and steady employment opportunities, it has become necessary to formulate and determine the Government program in the light of national economic conditions as a whole.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In both the executive and the legislative branches we must make arrangements which will permit us to formulate the Government program in that light.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Such an approach has become imperative if the American political and economic system is to succeed under the conditions of economic instability and uncertainty which we have to face.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Government needs to assure business, labor, and agriculture that Government policies will take due account of the requirements of a full employment economy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The lack of that assurance would, I believe, aggravate the economic instability.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: With the passage of a full employment bill which I confidently anticipate for the very near future, the executive and legislative branches of government will be empowered to devote their best talents and resources in subsequent years to preparing and acting on such a program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This new year of 1945 can be the greatest year of achievement in human history.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: 1945 can see the final ending of the Nazi Fascist reign of terror in Europe.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: 1945 can see the closing in of the forces of retribution about the center of the malignant power of imperialistic Japan.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Most important of all-1945 can and must see the substantial beginning of the organization of world peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: All those hopes, and more, were fulfilled in the year 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It was the greatest year of achievement in human history.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It saw the end of the Nazi-Fascist terror in Europe, and also the end of the malignant power of Japan.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And it saw the substantial beginning of world organization for peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These momentous events became realities because of the steadfast purpose of the United Nations and of the forces that fought for freedom under their flags.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The plain fact is that civilization was saved in 1945 by the United Nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our own part in this accomplishment was not the product of any single service.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Those who fought on land, those who fought on the sea, and those who fought in the air deserve equal credit.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They were supported by other millions in the armed forces who through no fault of their own could not go overseas and who rendered indispensable service in this country.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They were supported by millions in all levels of government, including many volunteers, whose devoted public service furnished basic organization and leadership.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They were also supported by the millions of Americans in private life-men and women in industry, in commerce, on the farms, and in all manner of activity on the home front-who contributed their brains and their brawn in arming, equipping, and feeding them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The country was brought through four years of peril by an effort that was truly national in character.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Everlasting tribute and gratitude will be paid by all Americans to those brave men who did not come back, who will never come back-the 330,000 who died that the Nation might live and progress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: All Americans will also remain deeply conscious of the obligation owed to that larger number of soldiers, sailors, and marines who suffered wounds and sickness in their service.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They may be certain that their sacrifice will never be forgotten or their needs neglected.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The beginning of the year 1946 finds the United States strong and deservedly confident.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have a record of enormous achievements as a democratic society in solving problems and meeting opportunities as they developed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We find ourselves possessed of immeasurable advantages-vast and varied natural resources;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: great plants, institutions, and other facilities;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: unsurpassed technological and managerial skills;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: an alert, resourceful, and able citizenry.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have in the United States Government rich resources in information, perspective, and facilities for doing whatever may be found necessary to do in giving support and form to the widespread and diversified efforts of all our people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And for the immediate future the business prospects are generally so favorable that there is danger of such feverish and opportunistic activity that our grave postwar problems may be neglected.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We need to act now with full regard for pitfalls;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: we need to act with foresight and balance.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should not be lulled by the immediate alluring prospects into forgetting the fundamental complexity of modern affairs, the catastrophe that can come in this complexity, or the values that can be wrested from it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But the long-range difficulties we face should no more lead to despair than our immediate business prospects should lead to the optimism which comes from the present short-range prospect.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On the foundation of our victory we can build a lasting peace, with greater freedom and security for mankind in our country and throughout the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We will more certainly do this if we are constantly aware of the fact that we face crucial issues and prepare now to meet them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To achieve success will require both boldness in setting our sights and caution in steering our way on an uncharted course.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But we have no luxury of choice.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must move ahead.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: No return to the past is possible.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our Nation has always been a land of great opportunities for those people of the world who sought to become part of us.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Now we have become a land of great responsibilities to all the people of all the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must squarely recognize and face the fact of those responsibilities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Advances in science, in communication, in transportation, have compressed the world into a community.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The economic and political health of each member of the world community bears directly on the economic and political health of each other member.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The evolution of centuries has brought us to a new era in world history in which manifold relationships between nations must be formalized and developed in new and intricate ways.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The United Nations Organization now being established represents a minimum essential beginning.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It must be developed rapidly and steadily.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Its work must be amplified to fill in the whole pattern that has been outlined.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Economic collaboration, for example, already charted, now must be carried on as carefully and as comprehensively as the political and security measures.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is important that the nations come together as States in the Assembly and in the Security Council and in the other specialized assemblies and councils that have been and will be arranged.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But this is not enough.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our ultimate security requires m ore than a process of consultation and compromise.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It requires that we begin now to develop the United Nations Organization as the representative of the world as one society.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The United Nations Organization, if we have the will adequately to staff it and to make it work as it should, will provide a great voice to speak constantly and responsibly in terms of world collaboration and world well-being.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There are many new responsibilities for us as we enter into this new international era.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The whole power and will and wisdom of our Government and of our people should be focused to contribute to and to influence international action.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is intricate, continuing business.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Many concessions and adjustments will be required.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The spectacular progress of science in recent years makes these necessities more vivid and urgent.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That progress has speeded internal development and has changed world relationships so fast that we must realize the fact of a new era.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is an era in which affairs have become complex and rich in promise.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Delicate and intricate relationships, involving us all in countless ways, must be carefully considered.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On the domestic scene, as well as on the international scene, we must lay a new and better foundation for cooperation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We face a great peacetime venture;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: the challenging venture of a free enterprise economy making full and effective use of its rich resources and technical advances.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is a venture in which business, agriculture, and labor have vastly greater opportunities than heretofore.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But they all also have vastly greater responsibilities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: that was tried after the last war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The general objective, on the contrary, is to move forward to find the way in time of peace to the full utilization and development of our physical and human resources that were demonstrated so effectively in the war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To accomplish this, it is not intended that the Federal Government should do things that can be done as well for the Nation by private enterprise, or by State and local governments.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On the contrary, the war has demonstrated how effectively we can organize our productive system and develop the potential abilities of our people by aiding the efforts of private enterprise.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As we move toward one common objective there will be many and urgent problems to meet.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Industrial peace between management and labor will have to be achieved-through the process of collective bargaining-with Government assistance but not Government compulsion.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is a problem which is the concern not only of management, labor, and the Government, but also the concern of every one of us.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Private capital and private management are entitled to adequate reward for efficiency, but business must recognize that its reward results from the employment of the resources of the Nation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Business is a public trust and must adhere to national standards in the conduct of its affairs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These standards include as a minimum the establishment of fair wages and fair employment practices.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Labor also has its own new peacetime responsibilities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Under our collective bargaining system, which must become progressively more secure, labor attains increasing political as well as economic power, and this, as with all power, means increased responsibility.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The lives of millions of veterans and war workers will be greatly affected by the success or failure of our program of war liquidation and reconversion.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Their transition to peacetime pursuits will be determined by our efforts to break the bottlenecks in key items of productions, to make surplus property immediately available where it is needed, to maintain an effective national employment service, and many other reconversion policies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our obligations to the people who won the war will not be paid if we fail to prevent inflation and to maintain employment opportunities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: While our peacetime prosperity will be based on the private enterprise system, Government can and must assist in many ways.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is the Government's responsibility to see that our economic system remains competitive, that new businesses have adequate opportunities, and that our national resources are restored and improved.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Government must realize the effect of its operations on the whole economy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is the responsibility of Government to gear its total program to the achievement of full production and full employment.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our basic objective-toward which all others lead-is to improve the welfare of the American people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In addition to economic prosperity, this means that we need social security in the fullest sense of the term;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: the people must be protected from the fear of want during old age, sickness, and unemployment.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Opportunities for a good education and adequate medical care must be generally available.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Every family should have a decent home.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The new economic bill of rights to which I have referred on previous occasions is a charter of economic freedom which seeks to assure that all who will may work toward their own security and the general advancement;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: that we become a well housed people, a well-nourished people, an educated people, a people socially and economically secure, an alert and responsible people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These and other problems which may face us can be met by the cooperation of all of us in furthering a positive and well balanced Government program-a program which will further national and international well-being.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: II. THE FEDERAL PROGRAM INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS / 1. FOREIGN POLICY: The year 1945 brought with it the final defeat of our enemies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There lies before us now the work of building a just and enduring peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our most immediate task toward that end is to deprive our enemies completely and forever of their power to start another war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Of even greater importance to the preservation of international peace is the need to preserve the wartime agreement of the United Nations and to direct it into the ways of peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Long before our enemies surrendered, the foundations had been laid on which to continue this unity in the peace to come.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Atlantic meeting in 1941 and the conferences at Casablanca, Quebec, Moscow, Cairo, Tehran, and Dumbarton Oaks each added a stone to the structure.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Early in 1945, at Yalta, the three major powers broadened and solidified this base of understanding.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There fundamental decisions were reached concerning the occupation and control of Germany.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There also a formula was arrived at for the interim government of the areas in Europe which were rapidly being wrested from Nazi control.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This formula was based on the policy of the United States that people be permitted to choose their own form of government by their own freely expressed choice without interference from any foreign source.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At Potsdam, in July 1945, Marshal Stalin, Prime Ministers Churchill and Attlee, and I met to exchange views primarily with respect to Germany.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As a result, agreements were reached which outlined broadly the policy to be executed by the Allied Control Council.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At Potsdam there was also established a Council of Foreign Ministers which convened for the first time in London in September.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Council is about to resume its primary assignment of drawing up treaties of peace with Italy, Rumania, Bulgaria, Hungary, and Finland.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In addition to these meetings, and in accordance with the agreement at Yalta, the Foreign Ministers of Great Britain, the Soviet Union, and the United States conferred together in San Francisco last spring, in Potsdam in July, in London in September, and in Moscow in December.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These meetings have been useful in promoting understanding and agreement among the three governments.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Simply to name all the international meetings and conferences is to suggest the size and complexity of the undertaking to prevent international war in which the United States has now enlisted for the duration of history.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is encouraging to know that the common effort of the United Nations to learn to live together did not cease with the surrender of our enemies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: When difficulties arise among us, the United States does not propose to remove them by sacrificing its ideals or its vital interests.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Neither do we propose, however, to ignore the ideals and vital interests of our friends.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Last February and March an Inter-American Conference on Problems of War and Peace was held in Mexico City.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Among the many significant accomplishments of that Conference was an understanding that an attack by any country against any one of the sovereign American republics would be considered an act of aggression against all of them;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: and that if such an attack were made or threatened, the American republics would decide jointly, through consultations in which each republic has equal representation, what measures they would take for their mutual protection.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This agreement stipulates that its execution shall be in full accord with the Charter of the United Nations Organization.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The first meeting of the General Assembly of the United Nations now in progress in London marks the real beginning of our bold adventure toward the preservation of world peace, to which is bound the dearest hope of men.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have solemnly dedicated ourselves and all our will to the success of the United Nations Organization.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For this reason we have sought to insure that in the peacemaking the smaller nations shall have a voice as well as the larger states.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The agreement reached at Moscow last month preserves this opportunity in the making of peace with Italy, Rumania, Bulgaria, Hungary, and Finland.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The United States intends to preserve it when the treaties with Germany and Japan are drawn.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It will be the continuing policy of the United States to use all its influence to foster, support, and develop the United Nations Organization in its purpose of preventing international war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If peace is to endure it must rest upon justice no less than upon power.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The question is how justice among nations is best achieved.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We know from day-to-day experience that the chance for a just solution is immeasurably increased when everyone directly interested is given a voice.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That does not mean that each must enjoy an equal voice, but it does mean that each must be heard.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Last November, Prime Minister Attlee, Prime Minister MacKenzie King, and I announced our proposal that a commission be established within the framework of the United Nations to explore the problems of effective international control of atomic energy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Soviet Union, France, and China have joined us in the purpose of introducing in the General Assembly a resolution for the establishment of such a commission.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our earnest wish is that the work of this commission go forward carefully and thoroughly, but with the greatest dispatch.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I have great hope for the development of mutually effective safeguards which will permit the fullest international control of this new atomic force.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I believe it possible that effective means can be developed through the United Nations Organization to prohibit, outlaw, and prevent the use of atomic energy for destructive purposes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The power which the United States demonstrated during the war is the fact that underlies every phase of our relations with other countries.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We cannot escape the responsibility which it thrusts upon us.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: What we think, plan, say, and do is of profound significance to the future of every corner of the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The great and dominant objective of United States foreign policy is to build and preserve a just peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The peace we seek is not peace for twenty years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is permanent peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At a time when massive changes are occurring with lightning speed throughout the world, it is often difficult to perceive how this central objective is best served in one isolated complex situation or another.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Despite this very real difficulty, there are certain basic propositions to which the United States adheres and to which we shall continue to adhere.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: One proposition is that lasting peace requires genuine understanding and active cooperation among the most powerful nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Another is that even the support of the strongest nations cannot guarantee a peace unless it is infused with the quality of justice for all nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On October 27, 1945, I made, in New York City, the following public statement of my understanding of the fundamental foreign policy of the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I believe that policy to be in accord with the opinion of the Congress and of the people of the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I believe that that policy carries out our fundamental objectives.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: 1. We seek no territorial expansion or selfish advantage.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have no plans for aggression against any other state, large or small.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have no objective which need clash with the peaceful aims of any other nation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: 2. We believe in the eventual return of sovereign rights and self government to all peoples who have been deprived of them by force.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: 3. We shall approve no territorial changes in any friendly part of the world unless they accord with the freely expressed wishes of the people concerned.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: 4. We believe that all peoples who are prepared for self-government should be permitted to choose their own form of government by their own freely expressed choice, without interference from any foreign source.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is true in Europe, in Asia, in Africa, as well as in the Western Hemisphere.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: 5. By the combined and cooperative action of our war allies, we shall help the defeated enemy states establish peaceful democratic governments of their own free choice.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And we shall try to attain a world in which nazism, fascism, and military aggression cannot exist.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: 6. We shall refuse to recognize any government imposed upon any nation by the force of any foreign power.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In some cases it may be impossible to prevent forceful imposition of such a government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But the United States will not recognize any such government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: 7. We believe that all nations should have the freedom of the seas and equal rights to the navigation of boundary rivers and waterways and of rivers and waterways which pass through more than one country.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: 8. We believe that all states which are accepted in the society of nations should have access on equal terms to the trade and the raw materials of the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: 9. We believe that the sovereign states of the Western Hemisphere, without interference from outside the Western Hemisphere, must work together as good neighbors in the solution of their common problems.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: 10. We believe that full economic collaboration between all nations, great and small, is essential to the improvement of living conditions all over the world, and to the establishment of freedom from fear and freedom from want.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: 11. We shall continue to strive to promote freedom of expression and freedom of religion throughout the peace-loving areas of the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: 12. We are convinced that the preservation of peace between nations requires a United Nations Organization composed of all the peace-loving nations of the world who are willing jointly to use force, if necessary, to insure peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is our foreign policy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We may not always fully succeed in our objectives.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There may be instances where the attainment of those objectives is delayed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But we will not give our full sanction and approval to actions which fly in the face of these ideals.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The world has a great stake in the political and economic future of Germany.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Allied Control Council has now been in operation there for a substantial period of time.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It has not met with unqualified success.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The accommodation of varying views of four governments in the day-to-day civil administration of occupied territory is a challenging task.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In my judgment, however, the Council has made encouraging progress in the face of most serious difficulties.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is my purpose at the earliest practicable date to transfer from military to civilian personnel the execution of United States participation in the government of occupied territory in Europe.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are determined that effective control shall be maintained in Germany until we are satisfied that the German people have regained the right to a place of honor and respect.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On the other side of the world, a method of international cooperation has recently been agreed upon for the treatment of Japan.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In this pattern of control, the United States, with the full approval of its partners, has retained primary authority and primary responsibility.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It will continue to do so until the Japanese people, by their own freely expressed choice, choose their own form of government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our basic policy in the Far East is to encourage the development of a strong, independent, united, and democratic China.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That has been the traditional policy of the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At Moscow the United States, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, and Great Britain agreed to further this development by supporting the efforts of the national government and nongovernmental Chinese political elements in bringing about cessation of civil strife and in broadening the basis of representation in the Government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is the policy which General Marshall is so ably executing today.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is the purpose of the Government of the United States to proceed as rapidly as is practicable toward the restoration of the sovereignty of Korea and the establishment of a democratic government by the free choice of the people of Korea.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At the threshold of every problem which confronts us today in international affairs is the appalling devastation, hunger, sickness, and pervasive human misery that mark so many areas of the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: By joining and participating in the work of the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration the United States has directly recognized and assumed an obligation to give such relief assistance as is practicable to millions of innocent and helpless victims of the war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Congress has earned the gratitude of the world by generous financial contributions to the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have taken the lead, modest though it is, in facilitating under our existing immigration quotas the admission to the United States of refugees and displaced persons from Europe.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have joined with Great Britain in the organization of a commission to study the problem of Palestine.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Commission is already at work and its recommendations will be made at an early date.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The members of the United Nations have paid us the high compliment of choosing the United States as the site of the United Nations headquarters.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We shall be host in spirit as well as in fact, for nowhere does there abide a fiercer determination that this peace shall live than in the hearts of the American people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is the hope of all Americans that in time future historians will speak not of World War I and World War II, but of the first and last world wars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: II. THE FEDERAL PROGRAM INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS / 2. FOREIGN ECONOMIC POLICY: The foreign economic policy of the United States is designed to promote our own prosperity, and at the same time to aid in the restoration and expansion of world markets and to contribute thereby to world peace and world security.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We shall continue our efforts to provide relief from the devastation of war, to alleviate the sufferings of displaced persons, to assist in reconstruction and development, and to promote the expansion of world trade.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have already joined the International Monetary Fund and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have expanded the Export-Import Bank and provided it with additional capital.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Congress has renewed the Trade Agreements Act which provides the necessary framework within which to negotiate a reduction of trade barriers on a reciprocal basis.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It has given our support to the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In accordance with the intentions of the Congress, lend-lease, except as to continuing military lend-lease in China, was terminated upon the surrender of Japan.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The first of the lend-lease settlement agreements has been completed with the United Kingdom.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Negotiations with other lend-lease countries are in progress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In negotiating these agreements, we intend to seek settlements which will not encumber world trade through war debts of a character that proved to be so detrimental to the stability of the world economy after the last war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have taken steps to dispose of the goods which on VJ-day were in the lend-lease pipe line to the various lend-lease countries and to allow them long-term credit for the purpose where necessary.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are also making arrangements under which those countries may use the lend-lease inventories in their possession and enable the United Kingdom to avoid discriminatory trade arrangements of the type which destroyed freedom of trade during the 1930's.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I consider the progress to ward multilateral trade which will be achieved by this agreement to be in itself sufficient warrant for the credit.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The view of this Government is that, in the longer run, our economic prosperity and the prosperity of the whole world are best served by the elimination of artificial barriers to international trade, whether in the form of unreasonable tariffs or tariff preferences or commercial quotas or embargoes or the restrictive practices of cartels.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The United States Government has issued proposals for the expansion of world trade and employment to which the Government of the United Kingdom has given its support on every important issue.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These proposals are intended to form the basis for a trade and employment conference to be held in the middle of this year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If that conference is a success, I feel confident that the way will have been adequately prepared for an expanded and prosperous world trade.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We shall also continue negotiations looking to the full and equitable development of facilities for transportation and communications among nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The vast majority of the nations of the world have chosen to work together to achieve, on a cooperative basis, world security and world prosperity.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The effort cannot succeed without full cooperation of the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To play our part, we must not only resolutely carry out the foreign policies we have adopted but also follow a domestic policy which will maintain full production and employment in the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A serious depression here can disrupt the whole fabric of the world economy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: II. THE FEDERAL PROGRAM INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS / 3. OCCUPIED COUNTRIES: The major tasks of our Military Establishment in Europe following VE-day, and in the Pacific since the surrender of Japan, have been those of occupation and military government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In addition we have given much needed aid to the peoples of the liberated countries.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The end of the war in Europe found Germany in a chaotic condition.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Organized government had ceased to exist, transportation systems had been wrecked, cities and industrial facilities had been bombed into ruins.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In addition to the tasks of occupation we had to assume all of the functions of government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Great progress has been made in the repatriation of displaced persons and of prisoners of war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Of the total of 3,500,000 displaced persons found in the United States zone only 460,000 now remain.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The extensive complications involved by the requirement of dealing with three other governments engaged in occupation and with the governments of liberated countries require intensive work and energetic cooperation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The influx of some 2 million German refugees into our zone of occupation is a pressing problem, making exacting demands upon an already overstrained internal economy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Improvements in the European economy during 1945 have made it possible for our military authorities to relinquish to the governments of all liberated areas, or to the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration, the responsibility for the provision of food and other civilian relief supplies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Army's responsibilities in Europe extend now only to our zones of occupation in Germany and Austria and to two small areas in northern Italy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: By contrast with Germany, in Japan we have occupied a Country still possessing an organized and Operating governmental system.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Although severely damaged, the Japanese industrial and transportation systems have been able to insure at least a survival existence for the population.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The repatriation of Japanese military and civilian personnel from overseas is proceeding as rapidly as shipping and other means permit.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In order to insure that neither Germany nor Japan will again be in a position to wage aggressive warfare, the armament making potential of these countries is being dismantled and fundamental changes in their social and political structures are being effected.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Democratic systems are being fostered to the end that the voice of the common man may be heard in the councils of his government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For the first time in history the legal culpability of war makers is being determined.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The trials now in progress in Nurnberg- those soon to begin in Tokyo- bring before the bar of international justice those individuals who are charged with the responsibility for the sufferings of the past six years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have high hope that this public portrayal of the guilt of these evildoers will bring wholesale and permanent revulsion on the part of the masses of our former enemies against war, militarism, aggression, and notions of race superiority.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: II. THE FEDERAL PROGRAM INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS / 4. DEMOBILIZATION OF OUR ARMED FORCES: The cessation of active campaigning does not mean that we can completely disband our fighting forces.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For their sake and for the sake of their loved ones at home, I wish that we could.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But we still have the task of clinching the victories we have won- making certain that Germany and Japan can never again wage aggressive warfare, that they will not again have the means to bring on another world war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The performance of that task requires that, together with our allies, we occupy the hostile areas, complete the disarmament of our enemies, and take the necessary measures to see to it that they do not rearm.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As quickly as possible, we are bringing about the reduction of our armed services to the size required for these tasks of occupation and disarmament.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Army and the Navy are following both length-of-service and point systems as far as possible in releasing men and women from the service.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The points are based chiefly on length and character of service, and on the existence of dependents.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Over 5 million from the Army have already passed through the separation centers.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Navy, including the Marine Corps and the Coast Guard, has discharged over one and a half million.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Of the 12 million men and women serving in the Army and Navy at the time of the surrender of Germany, one-half have already been released.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The greater part of these had to be brought back to this country from distant parts of the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Of course there are cases of individual hardship in retention of personnel in the service.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There will be in the future.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: No system of such size can operate to perfection.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But the systems are founded on fairness and justice, and they are working at full speed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We shall try to avoid mistakes, injustices, and hardship as far as humanly possible.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have already reached the point where shipping is no longer the bottleneck in the return of troops from the European theater.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The governing factor now has become the requirement for troops in sufficient strength to carry out their missions.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In a few months the same situation will exist in the Pacific.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: By the end of June, 9 out of 10 who were serving in the armed forces on V-day will have been released.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Demobilization will continue thereafter, but at a slower rate, determined by our military responsibilities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our national safety and the security of the world will require substantial armed forces, particularly in overseas service.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At the same time it is imperative that we relieve those who have already done their duty, and that we relieve them as fast as we can.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To do that, the Army and the Navy are conducting recruiting drives with considerable success.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Army has obtained nearly 400,000 volunteers in the past four months, and the Navy has obtained 80,000.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Eighty percent of these volunteers for the regular service have come from those already with the colors.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Congress has made it possible to offer valuable inducements to those who are eligible for enlistment.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Every effort will be made to enlist the required number of young men.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The War and Navy Departments now estimate that by a year from now we still will need a strength of about 2 million including officers, for the armed forces-Army, Navy, and Air.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I have reviewed their estimates and believe that the safety of the Nation will require the maintenance of an armed strength of this size for the calendar year that is before us.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In case the campaign for volunteers does not produce that number, it will be necessary by additional legislation to extend the Selective Service Act beyond May 16, the date of expiration under existing law.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is the only way we can get the men and bring back our veterans.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There is no other way.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Action along this line should not be postponed beyond March, in order to avoid uncertainty and disruption.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: II. THE FEDERAL PROGRAM DOMESTIC AFFAIRS. / 1. THE ECONOMIC OUTLOOK: Prophets of doom predicted that the United States could not escape a runaway inflation during the war and an economic collapse after the war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These predictions have not been borne out.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On the contrary, the record of economic stabilization during the war and during the period of reconversion has been an outstanding accomplishment.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We know, however, that nothing is as dangerous as overconfidence, in war or in peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have had to fight hard to hold the line.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have made strenuous efforts to speed reconversion.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But neither the danger of a postwar inflation nor of a subsequent collapse in production and employment is yet overcome.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must base our policies not on unreasoning optimism or pessimism but upon a candid recognition of our objectives and upon a careful analysis of foreseeable trends.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Any precise appraisal of the economic outlook at this time is particularly difficult.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The period of demobilization and reconversion is fraught with uncertainties.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There are also serious gaps in our statistical information.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Certain tendencies are, however, fairly clear and recognition of them should serve as background for the consideration of next year's Federal Program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In general, the outlook for business is good, and it is likely to continue to be good--provided we control inflation and achieve peace in management- labor relations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Civilian production and employment can be expected to increase throughout the next year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This does not mean, however, that continuing full employment is assured.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is probable that demobilization of the armed forces will proceed faster than the increase in civilian employment opportunities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Even if substantial further withdrawals from the labor market occur, unemployment will increase temporarily.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The extent to which this unemployment will persist depends largely on the speed of industrial expansion and the effectiveness of the policies of the Federal Government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Along with extraordinary demand there are still at this time many critical shortages resulting from the war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These extraordinary demands and shortages may lead to a speculative boom, especially in the price of securities, real estate, and inventories.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Therefore, our chief worry still is inflation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: While we control this inflationary pressure we must look forward to the time when this extraordinary demand will subside.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It will be years before we catch up with the demand for housing.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The extraordinary demand for other durable goods, for the replenishment of inventories, and for exports may be satisfied earlier.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: No backlog of demand can exist very long in the face of our tremendous productive capacity.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must expect again to face the problem of shrinking demand and consequent slackening in sales, production, and employment.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This possibility of a deflationary spiral in the future will exist unless we now plan and adopt an effective full employment program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: II. THE FEDERAL PROGRAM DOMESTIC AFFAIRS. / 2. GENERAL POLICIES--IMMEDIATE AND LONG-RANGE: During the war, production for civilian use was limited by war needs and available manpower.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Economic stabilization required measures to spread limited supplies equitably by rationing, price controls, increased taxes, savings bond campaigns, and credit controls.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Now, with the surrender of our enemies, economic stabilization requires that policies be directed toward promoting an increase in supplies at low unit prices.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must encourage the development of resources and enterprises in all parts of the country, particularly in underdeveloped areas.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For example, the establishment of new peacetime industries in the Western States and in the South would, in my judgment, add to existing production and markets rather than merely bring about a shifting of production.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I am asking the Secretaries of Agriculture, Commerce, and Labor to explore jointly methods for stimulating new industries, particularly in areas with surplus agricultural labor.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must also aid small businessmen and particularly veterans who are competent to start their own businesses.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The establishment and development of efficient small business ventures, I believe, will not take away from, but rather will add to, the total business of all enterprises.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Even with maximum encouragement of production, we cannot hope to remove scarcities within a short time.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The most serious deficiencies will persist in the fields of residential housing, building materials, and consumers' durable goods.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The critical situation makes continued rent control, price control, and priorities, allocations, and inventory controls absolutely essential.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Continued control of consumer credit will help to reduce the pressure on prices of durable goods and will also prolong the period during which the backlog demand will be effective.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: While we are meeting these immediate needs we must look forward to a long-range program of security and increased standard of living.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The best protection of purchasing power is a policy of full production and full employment opportunities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Obviously, an employed worker is a better customer than an unemployed worker.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There always will be, however, some frictional unemployment.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the present period of transition we must deal with such temporary unemployment as results from the fact that demobilization will proceed faster than reconversion or industrial expansion.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Such temporary unemployment is probably unavoidable in a period of rapid change.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The unemployed worker is a victim of conditions beyond his control.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: He should be enabled to maintain a reasonable standard of living for himself and his family.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The most serious difficulty in the path of reconversion and expansion is the establishment of a fair wage structure.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The ability of labor and management to work together, and the wage and price policies which they develop, are social and economic issues of first importance.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Both labor and management have a special interest.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Labor's interest is very direct and personal because working conditions, wages, and prices affect the very life and happiness of the worker and his family.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Management has a no less direct interest because on management rests the responsibility for conducting a growing and prosperous business.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But management and labor have identical interests in the long run.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Good wages mean good markets.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Good business means more jobs and better wages.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In this age of cooperation and in our highly organized economy the problems of one very soon become the problems of all.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Better human relationships are an urgent need to which organized labor and management should address themselves.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: No government policy can make men understand each other, agree, and get along unless they conduct themselves in a way to foster mutual respect and good will.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Government can, however, help to develop machinery which, with the backing of public opinion, will assist labor and management to resolve their disagreements in a peaceful manner and reduce the number and duration of strikes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: All of us realize that productivity--increased output per man--is in the long run the basis of our standard of living.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Management especially must realize that if labor is to work wholeheartedly for an increase in production, workers must be given a just share of increased output in higher wages.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Most industries and most companies have adequate leeway within which to grant substantial wage increases.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These increases will have a direct effect in increasing consumer demand to the high levels needed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Substantial wage increases are good business for business because they assure a large market for their products;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: substantial wage increases are good business for labor because they increase labor's standard of living;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: substantial wage increases are good business for the country as a whole because capacity production means an active, healthy, friendly citizenry enjoying the benefits of democracy under our free enterprise system.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Labor and management in many industries have been operating successfully under the Government's wage-price policy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Upward revisions of wage scales have been made in thousands of establishments throughout the Nation since VJ-day.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is estimated that about 6 million workers, or more than 20 percent of all employees in nonagricultural and nongovernmental establishments, have received wage increases since August 18, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The amounts of increases given by individual employers concentrate between 10 and 15 percent, but range from less than 5 percent to over 30 percent.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The United States Conciliation Service since VJ-day has settled over 3,000 disputes affecting over 1,300,000 workers without a strike threat and has assisted in settling about 1,300 disputes where strikes were threatened which involved about 500,000 workers.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Only workers directly involved, and not those in related industries who might have been indirectly affected, are included in these estimates.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Many of these adjustments have occurred in key industries and would have seemed to us major crises if they had not been settled peaceably.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Within the framework of the wage-price policy there has been definite success, and it is to be expected that this success will continue in a vast majority of the cases arising in the months ahead.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: However, everyone who realizes the extreme need for a swift and orderly reconversion must feel a deep concern about the number of major strikes now in progress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If long continued, these strikes could put a heavy brake on our program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I have already made recommendations to the Congress as to the procedure best adapted to meeting the threat of work stoppages in Nation-wide industries without sacrificing the fundamental rights of labor to bargain collectively and ultimately to strike in support of their position.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we manage our economy properly, the future will see us on a level of production half again as high as anything we have ever accomplished in peacetime.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Business can in the future pay higher wages and sell for lower prices than ever before.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is not true now for all companies, nor will it ever be true for all, but for business generally it is true.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: on prices.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Production and more production was the byword during the war and still is during the transition from war to peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: However, when deferred demand slackens, we shall once again face the deflationary dangers which beset this and other countries during the 1930's.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Prosperity can be assured only by a high level of demand supported by high current income;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: it cannot be sustained by deferred needs and use of accumulated savings.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we take the right steps in time we can certainly avoid the disastrous excesses of runaway booms and headlong depressions.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must not let a year or two of prosperity lull us into a false feeling of security and a repetition of the mistakes of the 1920's that culminated in the crash of 1929.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the year ahead the Government will be called upon to act in many important fields of economic policy from taxation and foreign trade to social security and housing.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In every case there will be alternatives.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must choose the alternatives which will best measure up to our need for maintaining production and employment in the future.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must never lose sight of our long-term objectives: the broadening of markets--the maintenance of steadily rising demand.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This demand can come from only three sources: consumers, businesses, or government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In this country the job of production and distribution is in the hands of businessmen, farmers, workers, and professional people -- in the hands of our citizens.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We want to keep it that way.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: However, it is the Government's responsibility to help business, labor, and farmers do their jobs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There is no question in my mind that the Government, acting on behalf of all the people, must assume the ultimate responsibility for the economic health of the Nation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There is no other agency that can.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: No other organization has the scope or the authority, nor is any other agency accountable, to all the people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This does not mean that the Government has the sole responsibility, nor that it can do the job alone, nor that it can do the job directly.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: All of the policies of the Federal Government must be geared to the objective of sustained full production and full employment--to raise consumer purchasing power and to encourage business investment.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The programs we adopt this year and from now on will determine our ability to achieve our objectives.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must continue to pay particular attention to our fiscal, monetary, and tax policy, programs to aid business--especially small business--and transportation, labor-management relations and wage-price policy, social security and health, education, the farm program, public works, housing and resource development, and economic foreign policy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For example, the kinds of tax measures we have at different times--whether we raise our revenue in a way to encourage consumer spending and business investment or to discourage it--have a vital bearing on this question.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is affected also by regular notions on consumer credit and by the money market, which is strongly influenced by the rate of interest on Government securities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is affected by almost every step we take.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In short, the way we handle the proper functions of government, the way we time the exercise of our traditional and legitimate governmental functions, has a vital bearing on the economic health of the Nation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These policies are discussed in greater detail in the accompanying Fifth Quarterly Report of the Director of War Mobilization and Reconversion.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: II. THE FEDERAL PROGRAM DOMESTIC AFFAIRS. / 3. LEGISLATION HERETOFORE RECOMMENDED AND STILL PENDING: To attain some of these objectives and to meet the other needs of the United States in the reconversion and postwar period, I have from time to time made various recommendations to the Congress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In making these recommendations I have indicated the reasons why I deemed them essential for progress at home and abroad.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A few--a very few--of these recommendations have been enacted into law by the Congress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Most of them have not.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I here reiterate some of them, and discuss others later in this Message.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I urge upon the Congress early consideration of them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Some are more urgent than others, but all are necessary.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (I) Legislation to authorize the President to create fact-finding boards for the prevention of stoppages of work in Nationwide industries after collective bargaining and conciliation and voluntary arbitration have failed--as recommended by me on December 3, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (2) Enactment of a satisfactory full employment bill such as the Senate bill now in conference between the Senate and the House--as recommended by me on September 6, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (3) Legislation to supplement the unemployment insurance benefits for unemployed workers now provided by the different States--as recommended by me on May 28,1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (4) Adoption of a permanent Fair Employment Practice Act--as recommended by me on September 6, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (5) Legislation substantially raising the amount of minimum wages now provided by law--as recommended by me on September 6, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (6) Legislation providing for a comprehensive program for scientific research--as recommended by me on September 6, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (7) Legislation enacting a health and medical care program--as recommended by me on November 19, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (8) Legislation adopting the program of universal training--as recommended by me on October 23, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (9) Legislation providing an adequate salary scale for all Government employees in all branches of the Government--as recommended by me on September 6, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (10) Legislation making provision for succession to the Presidency in the event of the death or incapacity or disqualification of the President and Vice President--as recommended by me on June 19, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (11) Legislation for the unification of the armed services--as recommended by me on December 19, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (12) Legislation for the domestic use and control of atomic energy--as recommended by me on October 3, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (13) Retention of the United States Employment Service in the Federal Government for a period at least up to June 30, 1947--as recommended by me on September 6, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (14) Legislation to increase unemployment allowances for veterans in line with increases for civilians--as recommended by me on September 6, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (15) Social security coverage for veterans for their period of military service--as recommended by me on September 6, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (16) Extension of crop insurance--as recommended by me on September 6, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (17) Legislation permitting the sale of ships by the Maritime Commission at home and abroad--as recommended by me on September 6, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I further recommend that this legislation include adequate authority for chartering vessels both here and abroad.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (18) Legislation to take care of the stock piling of materials in which the United States is naturally deficient--as recommended by me on September 6, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (19) Enactment of Federal airport legislation--as recommended by me on September 6, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (20) Legislation repealing the Johnson Act on foreign loans--as recommended by me on September 6, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (21) Legislation for the development of the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence River Basin--as recommended by me on October 3, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: II. THE FEDERAL PROGRAM DOMESTIC AFFAIRS. / 4. POLICIES IN SPECIFIC FIELDS./ (a) Extension of Price Control Act: Today inflation is our greatest immediate domestic problem.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: So far the fight against inflation has been waged successfully.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: order and in the face of the greatest pressures which this country has ever seen, the cost of living index has risen only three percent.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Wholesale prices in this same period have been held to an increase of two and one-half percent.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This record has been made possible by the vigorous efforts of the agencies responsible for this program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But their efforts would have been fruitless if they had not had the solid support of the great masses of our people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Congress is to be congratulated for its role in providing the legislation under which this work has been carried out.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On VJ-day it was clear to all thinking people that the danger of inflation was by no means over.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Many of us can remember vividly our disastrous experience following World War I.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Then the very restricted wartime controls were lifted too quickly, and as a result prices and rents moved more rapidly upward.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the year and a half following the armistice, rents, food, and clothing shot to higher and still higher levels.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: When the inevitable crash occurred less than two years after the end of the war, business bankruptcies were widespread.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Profits were wiped out.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Inventory losses amounted to billions of dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Farm income dropped by one-half.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Factory pay rolls dropped 40 percent, and nearly one fifth of all our industrial workers were walking the streets in search of jobs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This was a grim greeting, indeed, to offer our veterans who had just returned from overseas.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: When I addressed the Congress in September, I emphasized that we must continue to hold the price line until the production of goods caught up with the tremendous demands.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Since then we have seen demonstrated the strength of the inflationary pressures which we have to face.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Retail sales in the closing months of 1945 ran 12 percent above the previous peak for that season, which came in 1944.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Prices throughout the entire economy have been pressing hard against the price ceilings.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The prices of real estate, which cannot now be controlled under the law, are rising rapidly.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Commercial rents are not included in the present price control law and, where they are not controlled by State law, have been increasing, causing difficulties to many businessmen.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It will be impossible to maintain a high purchasing power or an expanding production unless we can keep prices at levels which can be met by the vast majority of our people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Full production is the greatest weapon against inflation, but until we can produce enough goods to meet the threat of inflation the Government will have to exercise its wartime control over prices.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I am sure that the people of the United States are disturbed by the demands made by several business groups with regard to price and rent control.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I am particularly disturbed at the effect such thinking may have on production and employment.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If manufacturers continue to hold back goods and decline to submit bids when invited--as I am informed some are doing--in anticipation of higher prices which would follow the end of price controls, we shall inevitably slow down production and create needless unemployment.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On the other hand, there are the vast majority of American businessmen who are not holding back goods, but who need certainty about the Government pricing policy in order to fix their own long-range pricing policies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Businessmen are entitled therefore to a clear statement of the policy of the Government on the subject.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Tenants and housewives, farmers and workers--consumers in general--have an equal right.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are all anxious to eliminate unnecessary controls just as rapidly as we can do so.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The steps that we have already taken in many directions toward that end are a clear indication of our policy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The present Price Control Act expires on June 30, 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we expect to maintain a steady economy we shall have to maintain price and rent control for many months to come.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The inflationary pressures on prices and rents, with relatively few exceptions, are now at an all time peak.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Unless the Price Control Act is renewed there will be no limit to which our price levels would soar.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our country would face a national disaster.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We cannot wait to renew the act until immediately before it expires.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Inflation results from psychological as well as economic conditions.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The country has a clear right to know where the Congress stands on this all-important problem.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Any uncertainty now as to whether the act will be extended give rise to price speculation, to witholding of goods from the market in anticipation of rising prices, and to delays in achieving maximum production.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I do not doubt that the Congress will be beset by many groups who will urge that the legislation that I have proposed should either be eliminated or modified to the point where it is nearly useless.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Congress has a clear responsibility to meet this challenge with courage and determination.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I have every confidence that it will do so.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I strongly urge that the Congress now resolve all doubts and as soon as possible adopt legislation continuing rent and price control in effect for a full year from June 30, 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: II. THE FEDERAL PROGRAM DOMESTIC AFFAIRS. / 4. POLICIES IN SPECIFIC FIELDS./ (b) Food subsidies:  If the price line is to be held, if our people are to be protected against the inflationary dangers which confront us, we must do more than extend the Price Control Act.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In September we were hopeful that the inflationary pressures would by this time have begun to diminish.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We were particularly hopeful on food.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Indeed, it was estimated that food prices at retail would drop from 3 to 5 per cent in the first six months following the end of the war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In anticipation of this decline in food prices, it was our belief that food subsidies could be removed gradually during the winter and spring months, and eliminated almost completely by June 30 of this year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It was our feeling that the food subsidies could be dropped without an increase to the consumer in the present level of food prices or in the over-all cost of living.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As matters stand today, however, food prices are pressing hard against the ceilings.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The expected decline in food prices has not occurred, nor is it likely to occur for many months to come.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This brings me to the reluctant conclusion that food subsidies must be continued beyond June 30, 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we fail to take this necessary step, meat prices on July 1 will be from 3 to 5 cents higher than their average present levels;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: butter will be at least 12 cents a pound higher, in addition to the 5 cents a pound increase of last fall;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: milk will increase from 1 to 2 cents a quart;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: bread will increase about 1 cent a loaf;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: sugar will increase over 1 cent a pound; cheese, in addition to the increase of 4 cents now planned for the latter part of this month, will go up an additional 8 cents.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In terms of percentages we may find the cost-of-living index for food increased by more than 8 percent, which in turn would result in more than a 3-percent increase in the cost of living.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If prices of food were allowed to increase by these amounts, I must make it clear to the Congress that, in my opinion, it would become extremely difficult for us to control the forces of inflation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: None of us likes subsidies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our farmers, in particular, have always been opposed to them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But I believe our farmers are as deeply conscious as any group in the land of the havoc which inflation can create.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Certainly in the past eighteen months there has been no group which has fought any harder in support of the Government's price control program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I am confident that, if the facts are placed before them and if they see clearly the evils between which we are forced to choose, they will understand the reasons why subsidies must be continued.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The legislation continuing the use of food subsidies into the new fiscal year should be tied down specifically to certain standards.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A very proper requirement, in my opinion, would be that subsidies be removed as soon as it is indicated that the cost of living will decline below the present levels.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
