text: II. THE FEDERAL PROGRAM DOMESTIC AFFAIRS. / 4. POLICIES IN SPECIFIC FIELDS./ (c) Extension of War Powers Act: The Second War Powers Act has recently been extended by the Congress for six months instead of for a year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It will now expire, unless further extended, on June 30, 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This act is the basis for priority and inventory controls governing the use of scarce materials, as well as for other powers essential to orderly reconversion.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I think that this Administration has given adequate proof of the fact that it desires to eliminate wartime controls as quickly and as expeditiously as possible.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: However, we know that there will continue to be shortages of certain materials caused by the war even after June 30, 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is important that businessmen know now that materials in short supply are going to be controlled and distributed fairly as long as these war-born shortages continue.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I, therefore, urge the Congress soon to extend the Second War Powers Act.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We cannot afford to wait until just before the act expires next June.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To wait would cause the controls to break down in a short time, and would hamper our production and employment program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: II. THE FEDERAL PROGRAM DOMESTIC AFFAIRS. / 4. POLICIES IN SPECIFIC FIELDS./(d) Small business and competition:  A rising birth rate for small business, and a favorable environment for its growth, are not only economic necessities but also important practical demonstrations of opportunity in a democratic free society.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A great many veterans and workers with new skills and experience will want to start in for themselves.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The opportunity must be afforded them to do so.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They are the small businessmen of the future.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Actually when we talk about small business we are talking about almost all of the Nation's individual businesses.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Nine out of every ten concerns fall into this category, and 45 percent of all workers are employed by them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Between 30 and 40 percent of the total value of all business transactions are handled by small business.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is obvious national policy to foster the sound development of small business.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It helps to maintain high levels of employment and national income and consumption of the goods and services that the Nation can produce.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It encourages the competition that keeps our free enterprise economy vigorous and expanding.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Small business, because of its flexibility, assists in the rapid exploitation of scientific and technological discoveries.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Investment in small business can absorb a large volume of savings that might otherwise not be tapped.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Government should encourage and is encouraging small-business initiative and originality to stimulate progress through competition.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the war, the Smaller War Plants Corporation assisted small concerns to make a maximum contribution to victory.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The work of the Smaller War Plants Corporation is being carried on in peacetime by the Federal Loan Agency and the Department of Commerce.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The fundamental approach to the job of encouraging small concerns must be based on: 1. Arrangements for making private and public financial resources available on reasonable terms.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: 2. Provision of technical advice and assistance to business as a whole on production, research, and management problems.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This will help equalize competitive relationships between large and small companies, for many of the small companies cannot afford expensive technical research, accounting, and tax advice.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: 3. Elimination of trade practices and agreements which reduce competition and discriminate against new or small enterprises.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We speak a great deal about the free enterprise economy of our country.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is competition that keeps it free.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is competition that keeps it growing and developing.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The truth is that we need far more competition in the future than we have had in t he immediate past.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: By strangling competition, monopolistic activity prevents or deters investment in new or expanded production facilities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This lessens the opportunity for employment and chokes off new outlets for idle savings.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Monopoly maintains prices at artificially high levels and reduces consumption which, with lower prices, would rise and support larger production and higher employment.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Monopoly, not being subject to competitive pressure, is slow to take advantage of technical advances which would lower prices or improve quality.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: All three of these monopolistic activities very directly lower the standard of living--through higher prices and lower quality of product--which free competition would improve.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Federal Government must protect legitimate business and consumers from predatory and monopolistic practices by the vigilant enforcement of regulatory legislation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The program will be designed to have a maximum impact upon monopolistic bottlenecks and unfair competitive practices hindering expansion in employment.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the war, enforcement of antimonopoly laws was suspended in a number of fields.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Government must now take major steps not only to maintain enforcement of antitrust laws but to encourage new and competing enterprises in every way.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The deferred demand of the war years and the large accumulations of liquid assets provide ample incentive for expansion.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Equalizing of business opportunity, under full and free competition, must be a prime responsibility in the reconversion period and in the years that follow.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Many leading businessmen have recognized the importance of such action both to themselves and to the economy as a whole.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But we must do more than break up trusts and monopolies after they have begun to strangle competition.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must take positive action to foster new, expanding enterprises.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: By legislation and by administration we must take specific steps to discourage the formation or the strengthening of competition-restricting business.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must have an over-all antimonopoly policy which can be applied by all agencies of the Government in exercising the functions assigned to them--a policy designed to encourage the formation and growth of new and freely competitive enterprises.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Among the many departments and agencies which have parts in the program affecting business and competition, the Department of Commerce has a particularly important role.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is why I have recommended a substantial increase in appropriations for the next fiscal year for this Department.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In its assistance to industry, the Department of Commerce will concentrate its efforts on these primary objectives: Promotion of a large and well-balanced foreign trade; provision of improved technical assistance and management aids, especially for small enterprises; and strengthening of basic statistics on business operations, both by industries and by regions.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To make new inventions and discoveries available more promptly to all businesses, small and large, the Department proposes to expand its own research activities, promote research by universities, improve Patent Office procedures, and develop a greatly expanded system of field offices readily accessible to the businesses they serve.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Many gaps exist in the private financial mechanism, especially in the provision of long-term funds for small and medium-sized enterprises.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the peacetime economy the Reconstruction Finance Corporation will take the leadership in assuring adequate financing for small enterprises which cannot secure funds from other sources.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Most of the funds should and will be provided by private lenders; but the Reconstruction Finance Corporation will share any unusual risks through guarantees of private loans, with direct loans only when private capital is unwilling to participate on a reasonable basis.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: II. THE FEDERAL PROGRAM DOMESTIC AFFAIRS. / 4. POLICIES IN SPECIFIC FIELDS./(e) Minimum wage: Full employment and full production may be achieved only by maintaining a level of consumer income far higher than that of the prewar period.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A high level of consumer income will maintain the market for the output of our mills, farms, and factories, which we have demonstrated during the war years that we can produce.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: One of the basic steps which the Congress can take to establish a high level of consumer income is to amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to raise substandard wages to a decent mini mum and to extend similar protection to additional workers who are not covered by the present act.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Substandard wages are bad for business and for the farmer.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Substandard wages provide only a substandard market for the goods and services produced by American industry and agriculture.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At the present time the Fair Labor Standards Act prescribes a minimum wage of 40 cents an hour for those workers who are covered by the act.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The present minimum wage represents an annual income of about $800 to those continuously employed for 50 weeks--clearly a wholly inadequate budget for an American family.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I am in full accord with the proposal now pending in the Congress that the statutory minimum be raised immediately to 65 cents an hour, with further increases to 70 cents after one year and t o 75 cents after two years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I also favor the proposal that the industry committee procedure be used to set rates higher than 65 cents per hour during the two-year interval before the 75-cent basic wage would otherwise become applicable.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The proposed minimum wage of 65 cents an hour would assure the worker an annual income of about $1,300 a year in steady employment.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This amount is clearly a modest goal.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: After considering cost-of living increases in recent years, it is little more than a 10-cent increase over the present legal minimum.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In fact, if any large number of workers earn less than this amount, we will find it impossible to maintain the levels of purchasing power needed to sustain the stable prosperity which we desire.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Raising the minimum to 75 cents an hour will provide the wage earner with an annual income of $1,500 if he is fully employed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The proposed higher minimum wage levels are feasible without involving serious price adjustments or serious geographic dislocations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Today about 20 percent of our manufacturing wage earners--or about 2 million-- earn less than 65 cents an hour.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Because wages in most industries have risen during the war, this is about the same as the proportion--17 percent--who were earning less than 40 cents an hour in 1941.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I also recommend that minimum wage protection be extended to several groups of workers not now covered.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The need for a decent standard of living is by no means limited to those workers who happen to be covered by the act as it now stands.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is particularly vital at this period of readjustment in the national economy and readjustment in employment of labor to extend minimum wage protection as far as possible.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Lifting the basic minimum wage is necessary, it is justified as a matter of simple equity to workers, and it will prove not only feasible but also directly beneficial to the Nation's employers.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: II. THE FEDERAL PROGRAM DOMESTIC AFFAIRS. / 4. POLICIES IN SPECIFIC FIELDS./(f) Agricultural programs:  The farmers of America generally are entering the crop year of 1946 in better financial condition than ever before.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Farm mortgage debt is the lowest in 30 years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Farmers' savings are the largest in history.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our agricultural plant is in much better condition than after World War I.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Farm machinery and supplies are expected to be available in larger volume, and farm labor problems will be less acute.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The demand for farm products will continue strong during the next year or two because domestic purchases will be supplemented by a high level of exports and foreign relief shipments.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is currently estimated that from 7 to 10 percent of the total United States food supply may be exported in the calendar year 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Farm prices are expected to remain at least at their present levels in the immediate future, and for at least the next 12 months they are expected to yield a net farm income double the 1935-39 average and higher than in any year prior to 1943.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We can look to the future of agriculture with greater confidence than in many a year in the past.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Agriculture itself is moving confidently ahead, planning for another year of big production, taking definite and positive steps to lead the way toward an economy of abundance.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Agricultural production goals for 1946 call for somewhat greater acreage than actually was planted in 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Agriculture is prepared to demonstrate that it can make a peacetime contribution as great as its contribution toward the winning of the war .

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In spite of supplying our armed forces and our allies during the war with a fifth to a fourth of our total food output, farmers were still able to provide our civilians with 8 percent more food per capita than the average for the five years preceding the war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Since the surrender of Japan, civilian food consumption has risen still further.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: By the end of 1945 the amount of the increase in food consumption was estimated to be as high as 15 percent over the prewar average.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The record shows that the people of this country want and need more food and that they will buy more food if only they have the jobs and the purchasing power.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The first essential therefore in providing fully for the welfare of agriculture is to maintain full employment and a high level of purchasing power throughout the Nation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For the period immediately ahead we shall still have the problem of supplying enough food.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we are to do our part in aiding the war-stricken and starving countries some of the food desires of our own people will not be completely satisfied, at least until these nations have had an opportunity to harvest another crop.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the next few months the need for food in the world will be more serious than at any time during the war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And, despite the large shipments we have already made, and despite what we shall send, there remain great needs abroad.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Beyond the relief feeding period, there will still be substantial foreign outlets for our farm commodities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The chief dependence of the farmer, however, as always, must be upon the buying power of our own people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The first obligation of the Government to agriculture for the reconversion period is to make good on its price-support commitments.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This we intend to do, with realistic consideration for the sound patterns of production that will contribute most to the long-time welfare of agriculture and the whole Nation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The period during which prices are supported will provide an opportunity for farmers individually to strengthen their position in changing over from a wartime to a peacetime basis of production.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It will provide an opportunity for the Congress to review the needs of agriculture and make changes in national legislation where experience has shown changes to be needed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In this connection, the Congress will wish to consider legislation to take the place of the 1937 Sugar Act which expires at the end of this year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During this period we must do a thorough job of basic planning to the end that agriculture shall be able to contribute its full share toward a healthy national economy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our long-range agricultural policies should have two main objectives: First, to assure the people on the farms a fair share of the national income;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: and, second, to encourage an agricultural production pattern that is best fitted to the Nation's needs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To accomplish this second objective we shall have to take into consideration changes that have taken place and will continue to take place in the production of farm commodities--changes that affect costs and efficiency and volume.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: What we seek ultimately is a high level of food production and consumption that will provide good nutrition for everyone.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This cannot be accomplished by agriculture alone.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We can be certain of our capacity to produce food, but we have often failed to distribute it as well as we should and to see that our people can afford to buy it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The way to get good nutrition for the whole Nation is to provide employment opportunities and purchasing power for all groups that will enable them to buy full diets at market prices.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Wherever purchasing power fails to reach this level we should see that they have some means of getting adequate food at prices in line with their ability to buy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Therefore, we should have available supplementary programs that will enable all our people to have enough of the right kind of food.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For example, one of the best possible contributions toward building a stronger, healthier Nation would be a permanent school-lunch program on a scale adequate to assure every school child a good lunch at noon.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Congress, of course, has recognized this need for a continuing school-lunch program and legislation to that effect has been introduced and hearings held.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The plan contemplates the attainment of this objective with a minimum of Federal expenditures.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I hope that the legislation will be enacted in time for a permanent program to start with the beginning of the school year next fall.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have the technical knowledge and the productive capacity to provide plenty of good food for every man, woman, and child in the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is time we made that possibility a reality.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: II. THE FEDERAL PROGRAM DOMESTIC AFFAIRS. / 4. POLICIES IN SPECIFIC FIELDS./(g) Resource development:  The strength of our Nation and the welfare of the people rest upon the natural resources of the country.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have learned that proper conservation of our lands, including our forests and minerals, and wise management of our waters will add immensely to our national wealth.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The first step in the Government's conservation program must be to find out just what are our basic resources, and how they should be used.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We need to take, as soon as possible, an inventory of the lands, the minerals, and the forests of the Nation .

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the war it was necessary to curtail some of our long-range plans for development of our natural resources, and to emphasize programs vital to the prosecution of the war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Work was suspended on a number of flood control and reclamation projects and on the development of our national forests and parks.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This work must now be resumed, and new projects must be undertaken to provide essential services and to assist in the process of economic development.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The rivers of America offer a great opportunity to our generation in the management of the national wealth.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: By a wise use of Federal funds, most of which will be repaid into the Treasury, the scourge of floods and drought can be curbed, water can be brought to arid lands, navigation can be extended, and cheap power can be brought alike to the farms and to the industries of our land.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Through the use of the waters of the Columbia River, for example, we are creating a rich agricultural area as large as the State of Delaware.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At the same time, we are producing power at Grand Coulee and at Bonneville which played a mighty part in w inning the war and which will found a great peacetime industry in the Northwest.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Tennessee Valley Authority will resume its peacetime program of promoting full use of the resources of the Valley.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We shall continue our plans for the development of the Missouri Valley, the Arkansas Valley, and the Central Valley of California.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Congress has shown itself alive to the practical requirements for a beneficial use of our water resources by providing that preference in the sale of power be given to farmers' cooperatives and public agencies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The public power program thus authorized must continue to be made effective by building the necessary generating and transmission facilities to furnish the maximum of firm power needed at the wholesale markets, which are often distant from the dam sites.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These great developmental projects will open the frontiers of agriculture, industry, and commerce.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The employment opportunities thus offered will also go far to ease the transition from war to peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: II. THE FEDERAL PROGRAM DOMESTIC AFFAIRS. / 4. POLICIES IN SPECIFIC FIELDS./(h) Public works: During the war even urgently needed Federal, State, and local construction projects were deferred in order to release resources for war production.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In resuming public works construction, it is desirable to proceed only at a moderate rate, since demand for private construction will be abnormally high for some time.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our public works program should be timed to reach its peak after demand for private construction has begun to taper off.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Meanwhile, however, plans should be prepared if we are to act promptly when the present extraordinary private demand begins to run out.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Congress made money available to Federal agencies for their public works planning in the fiscal year 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I strongly recommend that this policy be continued and extended in the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: State and local governments have an essential role to play in a national public works program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In my message of September 6, 1945, I recommended that the Congress vote such grants to State and local governments as will insure that each level of government makes its proper contribution to a balanced public construction program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Specifically, the Federal Government should aid State and local governments in planning their own public works programs, in undertaking projects related to Federal programs of regional development, and in constructing such public works as are necessary to carry out the various policies of the Federal Government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Early in 1945 the Congress made available advances to State and local governments for planning public works projects, and recently made additional provision to continue these advances through the fiscal year 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I believe that further appropriations will be needed for the same purpose for the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Congress has already made provision for highway programs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is now considering legislation which would expand Federal grants and loans in several other fields, including construction of airports, hospital and health centers, housing, water pollution control facilities, and educational plant facilities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I hope that early action will be taken to authorize these Federal programs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: With respect to public works of strictly local importance, State and local governments should proceed without Federal assistance except in planning.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This rule should be subject to review when and if the prospect of highly adverse general economic developments warrants it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: All loans and grants for public works should be planned and administered in such a way that they are brought into accord with the other elements of the Federal Program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our long-run objective is to achieve a program of direct Federal and Federally assisted public works which is planned in advance and synchronized with business conditions.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In this way it can make its greatest contribution to general economic stability.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: II. THE FEDERAL PROGRAM DOMESTIC AFFAIRS. / 4. POLICIES IN SPECIFIC FIELDS./ (i) National housing program:  Last September I stated in my message to the Congress that housing was high on the list of matters calling for decisive action.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Since then the housing shortage in countless communities, affecting millions of families, has magnified this call to action.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Today we face both an immediate emergency and a major postwar problem.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Since VJ-day the wartime housing shortage has been growing steadily worse and pressure on real estate values has increased.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Returning veterans often cannot find a satisfactory place for their families to live, and many who buy have to pay exorbitant prices.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Rapid demobilization inevitably means further overcrowding.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A realistic and practical attack on the emergency will require aggressive action by local governments, with Federal aid, to exploit all opportunities and to give the veterans as far as possible first chance at vacancies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It will require continuation of rent control in shortage areas as well as legislation to permit control of sales prices.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It will require maximum conversion of temporary war units for veterans' housing and their transportation to communities with the most pressing needs;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: the Congress has already appropriated funds for this purpose.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The inflation in the price of housing is growing daily.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As a result of the housing shortage, it is inevitable that the present dangers of inflation in home values will continue unless the Congress takes action in the immediate future.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Legislation is now pending in the Congress which would provide for ceiling prices for old and new houses.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The authority to fix such ceilings is essential.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: With such authority, our veterans and other prospective home owners would be protected against a skyrocketing of home prices.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The country would be protected from the extension of the present inflation in home values which, if allowed to continue, will threaten not only the stabilization program but our opportunities for attaining a sustained high level of home construction.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Such measures are necessary stopgaps--but only stopgaps.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This emergency action, taken alone, is good--but not enough.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The housing shortage did not start with the war or with demobilization;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: it began years before that and has steadily accumulated.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The speed with which the Congress establishes the foundation for a permanent, long-range housing program will determine how effectively we grasp the immense opportunity to achieve our goal of decent housing and to make housing a major instrument of continuing prosperity and full employment in the years ahead.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It will determine whether we move forward to a stable and healthy housing enterprise and toward providing a decent home for every American family.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Production is the only fully effective answer.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To get the wheels turning, I have appointed an emergency housing expediter.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I have approved establishment of priorities designed to assure an ample share of scarce materials to builders of houses for which veterans will have preference.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Additional price and wage adjustments will be made where necessary, and other steps will be taken to stimulate greater production of bottleneck items.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I recommend consideration of every sound method for expansion in facilities for insurance of privately financed housing by the Federal Housing Administration and resumption of previously authorized low-rent public housing projects suspended during the war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In order to meet as many demands of the emergency situation as possible, a program of emergency measures is now being formulated for action.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These will include steps in addition to those already taken.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As quickly as this program can be formulated, announcement will be made.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Last September I also outlined to the Congress the basic principles for the kind of decisive, permanent legislation necessary for a long-range housing program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These principles place paramount the fact that housing construction and financing for the overwhelming majority of our citizens should be done by private enterprise.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They contemplate also that we afford governmental encouragement to privately financed house construction for families of moderate income, through extension of the successful system of insurance of housing investment;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: that research be undertaken to develop better and cheaper methods of building homes;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: that communities be assisted in appraising their housing needs;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: that we commence a program of Federal aid, with fair local participation, to stimulate and promote the rebuilding and redevelopment of slums and blighted areas--with maximum use of private capital.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is equally essential that we use public funds to assist families of low income who could not otherwise enjoy adequate housing, and that we quicken our rate of progress in rural housing.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Legislation now under consideration by the Congress provides for a comprehensive attack jointly by private enterprise, state and local authorities, and the federal government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This legisation would make permanent the National Housing Agency and give it authority and funds for much needed technical and economic research.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It would provide additional stimulus for privately financed housing construction.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This stimulus consists of establishing a new system of yield insurance to encourage large-scale investment in rental housing and broadening the insuring powers of the Federal Housing Administration and the lending powers of the Federal savings and loan associations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Where private industry cannot build, the Government must step in to do the job.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The bill would encourage expansion in housing available for the lowest income groups by continuing to provide direct subsidies for low-rent housing and rural housing.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It would facilitate land assembly for urban redevelopment by loans and contributions to local public agencies where the localities do their share.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Prompt enactment of permanent housing legislation along these lines will not interfere with the emergency action already under way.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On the contrary, it would lift us out of a potentially perpetual state of housing emergency.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It would offer the best hope and prospect to millions of veterans and other American families that the American system can offer more to them than temporary makeshifts.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I have said before that the people of the United States can be the best housed people in the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I repeat that assertion, and I welcome the cooperation of the Congress in achieving that goal.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: II. THE FEDERAL PROGRAM DOMESTIC AFFAIRS. / 4. POLICIES IN SPECIFIC FIELDS./ (j) Social security and health:  Our Social Security System has just celebrated its tenth anniversary.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the past decade this program has supported the welfare and morale of a large part of our people by removing some of the hazards and hardships of the aged, the unemployed, and widows and dependent children.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But, looking back over 10 years' experience and ahead to the future, we cannot fail to see defects and serious inadequacies in our system as it now exists.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Benefits are in many cases inadequate;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: a great many persons are excluded from coverage;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: and provision has not been made for social insurance to cover the cost of medical care and the earnings lost by the sick and the disabled.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the field of old-age security, there seems to be no adequate reason for excluding such groups as the self-employed, agricultural and domestic workers, and employees of non-profit organizations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Since many of these groups earn wages too low to permit significant savings for old age, they are in special need of the assured income that can be provided by old-age insurance.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must take urgent measures for the readjustment period ahead.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Congress for some time has been considering legislation designed to supplement at Federal expense, during the immediate reconversion period, compensation payments to the unemployed .

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Again I urge the Congress to enact legislation liberalizing unemployment compensation benefits and extending the coverage.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Providing for the sustained consumption by the unemployed persons and their families is more than a welfare policy;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: it is sound economic policy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A sustained high level of consumer purchases is a basic ingredient of a prosperous economy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the war, nearly 5 million men were rejected for military service because of physical or mental defects which in many cases might have been prevented or corrected.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is shocking evidence that large sections of the population are at substandard levels of health.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The need for a program that will give everyone opportunity for medical care is obvious.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Nor can there be any serious doubt of the Government's responsibility for helping in this human and social problem.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The comprehensive health program which I recommended on November 19, 1945, will require substantial additions to the Social Security System and, in conjunction with other changes that need to be made, will require further consideration of the financial basis for social security.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The system of prepaid medical care which I have recommended is expected eventually to require amounts equivalent to 4 percent of earnings up to $3,600 a year, which is about the average of present expenditures by individuals for medical care.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The pooling of medical costs, under a plan which permits each individual to make a free choice of doctor and hospital, would assure that individuals receive adequate treatment and hospitalization when they are faced with emergencies for which they cannot budget individually.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In addition, I recommended insurance benefits to replace part of the earnings lost through temporary sickness and permanent disability.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Even without these proposed major additions, it would now be time to undertake a thorough reconsideration of our social security laws.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The structure should be expanded and liberalized.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Provision should be made for extending coverage credit to veterans for the period of their service in the armed forces.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the financial provisions we must reconcile the actuarial needs of social security, including health insurance, with the requirements of a revenue system that is designed to promote a high level of consumption and full employment.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: II. THE FEDERAL PROGRAM DOMESTIC AFFAIRS. / 4. POLICIES IN SPECIFIC FIELDS./ (k) Education:  Although the major responsibility for financing education rests with the States, some assistance has long been given by the Federal Government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Further assistance is desirable and essential.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There are many areas and some whole States where good schools cannot be provided without imposing an undue local tax burden on the citizens.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is essential to provide adequate elementary and secondary schools everywhere, and additional educational opportunities for large numbers of people beyond the secondary level.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Accordingly, I repeat the proposal of last year's Budget Message that the Federal Government provide financial aid to assist the States in assuring more nearly equal opportunities for a good education.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The proposed Federal grants for current educational expenditures should be made for the purpose of improving the educational system where improvement is most needed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They should not be used to replace existing non-Federal expenditures, or even to restore merely the situation which existed before the war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the future we expect incomes considerably higher than before the war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Higher incomes should make it possible for State and local governments and for individuals to support higher and more nearly adequate expenditures for education.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But inequality among the States will still remain, and Federal help will still be needed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As a part of our total public works program, consideration should be given to the need for providing adequate buildings for schools and other educational institutions.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In view of current arrears in the construction of educational facilities, I believe that legislation to authorize grants for educational facilities, to be matched by similar expenditures by State and local authorities, should receive the favorable consideration of the Congress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Federal Government has not sought, and will not seek, to dominate education in the States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It should continue its historic role of leadership and advice and, for the purpose of equalizing educational opportunity, it should extend further financial support to the cause of education in areas where this is desirable.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: II. THE FEDERAL PROGRAM DOMESTIC AFFAIRS. / 4. POLICIES IN SPECIFIC FIELDS./ (l) Federal Government personnel:  The rapid reconversion of the Federal Government from war to peace is reflected in the demobilization of its civilian personnel.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The number of these employees in continental United States has been reduced by more than 500,000 from the total of approximately 2,900,000 employed in the final months of the war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I expect that by next June we shall have made a further reduction of equal magnitude and that there will be continuing reductions during the next fiscal year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Of the special wartime agencies now remaining, only a few are expected to continue actively into the next fiscal year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At the same time that we have curtailed the number of employees, we have shortened the workweek by one-sixth or more throughout the Government and have restored holidays.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The process of readjustment has been complicated and costs have been increased by a heavy turn-over in the remaining personnel-particularly by the loss of some of our best administrators.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Thousands of war veterans have been reinstated or newly employed in the civil service.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Many civilians have been transferred from war agencies to their former peacetime agencies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Recruitment standards, which had to be relaxed during the war, are now being tightened.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The elimination last autumn of overtime work for nearly all Federal employees meant a sharp cut in their incomes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For salaried workers, the blow was softened but by no means offset by the increased rates of pay which had become effective July 1.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Further adjustments to compensate for increased living costs are required.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Moreover, we have long needed a general upward revision of Federal Government salary scales at all levels in all branches-legislative, judicial, and executive.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Too many in Government have had to sacrifice too much in economic advantage to serve the Nation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Adequate salaries will result in economies and improved efficiency in the conduct of Government business-gains that will far outweigh the immediate costs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I hope the Congress will expedite action on salary legislation for all Federal employees in all branches of the Government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The only exception I would make is in the case of workers whose pay rates are established by wage boards;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: a blanket adjustment would destroy the system by which their wages are kept aligned with prevailing rates in particular localities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The wage boards should he sensitive now, as they were during the war, to changes in local prevailing wage rates and should make adjustments accordingIy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I hope also that the Congress may see fit to enact legislation for the adequate protection of the health and safety of Federal employees, for their coverage under a system of unemployment compensation, and for their return at Government expense to their homes after separation from wartime service.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: II. THE FEDERAL PROGRAM DOMESTIC AFFAIRS. / 4. POLICIES IN SPECIFIC FIELDS./ (m) Territories, insular possessions, and the District of Columbia:  The major governments of the world face few problems as important and as perplexing as those relating to dependent peoples.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This Government is committed to the democratic principle that it is for the dependent peoples themselves to decide what their status shall be.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To this end I asked the Congress last October to provide a means by which the people of Puerto Rico might choose their form of government and ultimate status with respect to the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I urge, too, that the Congress promptly accede to the wishes of the people of Hawaii that the Territory be admitted to statehood in our Union, and that similar action be taken with respect to Alaska as soon as it is certain that this is the desire of the people of that great Territory.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The people of the Virgin Islands should be given an increasing measure of self-government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have already determined that the Philippine Islands are to be independent on July 4, 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The ravages of war and enemy occupation, however, have placed a heavy responsibility upon the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I urge that the Congress complete, as promptly and as generously as may be possible, legislation which will aid economic rehabilitation for the Philippines.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This will be not only a just acknowledgment of the loyalty of the people of the Philippines, but it will help to avoid the economic chaos which otherwise will he their heritage from our common war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Perhaps no event in the long centuries of colonialism gives more hope for the pattern of the future than the independence of the Philippines.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The District of Columbia, because of its special relation to the Federal Government, has been treated since 1800 as a dependent area.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should move toward a greater measure of local self-government consistent with the constitutional status of the District.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should take adequate steps to assure that citizens of the United States are not denied their franchise merely because they reside at the Nation's Capital.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: III. THE BUDGET FOR THE FEDERAL PROGRAM FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1947/ SUMMARY OF THE BUDGET:  For the first time since the fiscal year 1930 the Budget for the next fiscal year will require no increase in the national debt.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Expenditures of all kinds, authorized and recommended, in the next year are estimated at just above 35.8 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Net receipts are estimated at 31.5 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The estimated difference of 4.3 billion dollars will be met by a reduction in the very substantial balance which will be in the Treasury during the next fiscal year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: other activities in a following table, is still due to repercussions of the war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: other activities include more than 2 billion dollars for aids to agriculture and net outlays for the Commodity Credit Corporation--almost double the expenditures for the same purposes in prewar years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This increase is due mainly to expenditures for purposes of price stabilization and price support resulting from the war food production program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Other increases in this category are due to the fact that certain wartime agencies now in the process of liquidation are included in this group of activities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If all expenditures for those activities which are directly or indirectly related to the war are excluded, the residual expenditures are below those for corresponding activities in prewar years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In making this comparison account should be taken of the fact that, while prewar expenditures were affected by direct relief and work relief for the unemployed, the postwar budgets are affected by the considerable increase in pay rates and other increases in costs and prices.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To elaborate, the Budget, as I have remarked above, reflects on both sides of the ledger the Government's program as recommended by the Executive.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It includes estimates not only of expenditures and receipts for which legislative authority already exists, but also of expenditures and receipts for which authorization is recommended.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Budget total for the next fiscal year, the year that ends on June 30, 1947, is estimated at just above 35.8 billion dollars--about a third of the budgets for global war, although nearly four times the prewar budgets.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This estimate is based on the assumption that a rapid liquidation of the war program will be associated with rapid reconversion and expansion of peacetime production.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The total includes net outlays of Government corporations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The estimated expenditures in the next and current fiscal year compare as follows with those of a year of global war and a prewar year: Total Budget expenditures Fiscal year: (in millions) 1947,$35,860, 1946, 67,229, 1945, 100,031, 1940, 9,252.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Although allowances for occupation, demobilization, and defense are drastically reduced in the fiscal year 1947, they will still amount to 42 percent of the total Budget.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: expenditures account for a further 30 percent of the total.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The total of all other programs, which was drastically cut during the war, is increasing again as liquidation of the war program proceeds and renewed emphasis is placed on the peacetime objectives of the Government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On the other side of the ledger, net receipts are estimated at 31.5 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This estimate assumes that all existing taxes will continue all through the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Included are the extraordinary receipts from the disposal of surplus property.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As a result, estimated expenditures will exceed estimated receipts by 4.3 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This amount can be provided by a reduction in the cash balance in the Treasury.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Thus, after a long period of increasing public debt resulting from depression budgets and war budgets, it is anticipated that no increase in the Federal debt will he required next year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The current fiscal year, 1946, is a year of transition.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: When the year opened, in July 1945, we were still fighting a major war, and Federal expenditures were running at an annual rate of about 100 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: By June 1946 that rate will be more than cut in half.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Budget total for the current fiscal year is now estimated at 67.2 billion dollars, of which more than two-thirds provides for war and war liquidation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Since net receipts are estimated at 38.6 billion dollars, there will be an excess of expenditures of 28.6 billion dollars for the current fiscal year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For all programs discussed in this Message I estimate the total of Budget appropriations and authorizations (including re-appropriations and permanent appropriations) at 30,982 million dollars for the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Of this amount, present permanent appropriations are expected to provide 5,755 million dollars, principally for interest.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This leaves 24,224 million dollars to be made available through new appropriations, exclusive of appropriations to liquidate contract authorizations;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: 900 million dollars in new contract authorizations;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: and 103 million dollars through the re-appropriation of un-liquidated balances of previous appropriations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The appropriations needed to liquidate contract authorizations are estimated at 1,113 million dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the Budget for the year ahead only over-all estimates are included at this time for the major war agencies and for net outlays of Government corporations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Detailed recommendations will be transmitted in the spring for the war agencies;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: and the business-type budgets of Government corporations will likewise be transmitted in accordance with the recently adopted Government Corporation Control Act.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Similarly, only overall estimates are provided for new programs recommended in this Message;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: detailed recommendations will be transmitted after authorizing legislation has been enacted.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It should be recognized that many of the estimates for new programs recommended in this Message are initial year figures.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These figures will be affected by the date the legislation is enacted and by the time needed for getting a program under way.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: New programs, such as that for a national research agency, will require larger amounts in later years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The estimates exclude major elements of the proposed national health program since the greater part of these will be covered by expenditures from trust funds.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Budget total includes expenditures for capital outlay as well as for current operations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: An estimated 1,740 million dollars will be expended in the fiscal year 1947 for direct Federal public works and for loans and grants for public works.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: III. THE BUDGET FOR THE FEDERAL PROGRAM FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1947/ THE ECONOMIC IMPACT OF THE LIQUIDATION OF THE WAR PROGRAM: Government programs are of such importance in the development of production and employment opportunities-domestic and international--that it has become essential to formulate and consider the Federal Budget in the light of the Nation's budget as a whole.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The relationship between the receipts, expenditures, and savings of consumers, business, and government is shown in the accompanying table.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Considering the whole Nation, total expenditures must equal the total receipts, because what any individual or group spends becomes receipts of other individuals or groups.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Such equality can be achieved on either a high level of incomes or on a low or depression level of incomes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Tremendous orders for munitions during the war shifted production and employment into high gear.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Total goods produced and services rendered for private as well as for Government purposes--the Nation's budget--reached about 200 billion dollars in the calendar year 1944.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Federal, State, and local government expenditures represented half of this total.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Corresponding estimates for the past 3 months depict the national economy in the process of demobilization and reconversion.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The wartime annual rate of Federal expenditures has been reduced by 32 billion dollars, while the Nation's budget total has dropped only half as much.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The drop in total value of production and services has been less drastic because increasing private activities have absorbed in large measure the manpower and materials released from war production and war services.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The largest increase in private activities has occurred in business investments, which include residential and other construction, producers' durable equipment, accumulation of inventories, and net exports.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Under conditions of global war, expenditures for private construction and equipment were held to a minimum and inventories were depleted.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: With the beginning of reconversion these developments have been reversed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Residential construction and outlays for plant and equipment are on the increase;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: inventories, too, are being replenished.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: International transactions (excluding landless and international relief which are included under war expenditures) showed an import surplus under conditions of global war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the past 3 months private exports have be en slightly in excess of imports, for the first time since 1941.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Consumers' budgets show a significant change.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: pay of war workers is, to a large extent, offset for the time being by the mustering-out payments received by war veterans and by unemployment compensation received by the unemployed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On the expenditure side, however, consumers budgets, restricted during the war, have increased substantially as a result of the fact that scarce goods are beginning to appear on the market and wartime restraints are disappearing.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Thus, consumers' current savings are declining substantially from the extraordinarily high wartime rate and some wartime savings are beginning to be used for long-delayed purchases.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Unemployment has increased less than was expected during this first period of demobilization and reconversion.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is true that 6 million men and women have been discharged from the armed forces since May 1945 and more than 5 million have been laid off from war work.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On the other hand, more than a million civilians have been enlisted in the armed forces, a considerable number of war veterans have not immediately sought jobs, and many war workers, especially women, have withdrawn from the labor force.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In addition, many industries, and especially service trades which were undermanned during the war, are beginning now, for the first time in years, to recruit an adequate labor force.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The reduced workweek has also contributed to the absorption of those released from war service and war work.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In general, the drastic cut in war programs has thrown the economy into lower gear; it has not thrown it out of gear.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our economic machine demonstrates remarkable resiliency, although there are many difficulties that must still be overcome.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The rapid termination of war contracts, prompt clearance of unneeded Government-owned equipment from private plants, and other reconversion policies have greatly speeded up the beginning of peacetime work in reconverted plants.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Although the first great shock of demobilization and war-work termination has thus been met better than many observers expected, specific industries and specific regions show much unevenness in the progress of reconversion.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Quarterly Report of the Director of War Mobilization and Reconversion analyzes the difficulties in recruiting personnel and obtaining materials that hamper reconversion in certain industries and proposes policies to deal with these situations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The lack of adequate housing is one of the main factors checking the flow of workers into areas where job opportunities exist.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: III. THE BUDGET FOR THE FEDERAL PROGRAM FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1947/ FEDERAL REVENUE, BORROWING, AND THE PUBLIC DEBT./ I. FINANCIAL REQUIREMENTS AND TAX POLICY:  Recommendations for tax legislation should be considered not only in the light of the financial requirements of the ensuing year, but also in the light of future years financial requirements and a full consideration of economic conditions.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Expenditures are estimated at nearly 36 billion dollars in the fiscal year 1947;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: they can hardly he expected to be reduced to less than 25 billion dollars in subsequent years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Net receipts in the fiscal year 1947 are estimated at 31.5 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Included in this estimate are 2 billion dollars of receipts from disposal and rental of surplus property and 190 million dollars of receipts from renegotiation of wartime contracts.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These sources of receipts will disappear in future years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Tax collections for the fiscal year 1947 also will not yet fully reflect the reduction in corporate tax liabilities provided in the Revenue Act of 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If the extraordinary receipts from the disposal of surplus property and renegotiation of contracts be disregarded, and if the tax reductions adopted in the Revenue Act of 1945 were fully effective, present tax rates would yield about 27 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These estimates for the fiscal year 1947 are based on the assumption of generally favorable business conditions but not on an income reflecting full employment and the high productivity that we hope to achieve.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In future years the present tax system, in conjunction with a full employment level of national income, could be expected to yield more than 30 billion dollars, which is substantially above the anticipated peacetime level of expenditures.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In view of the still extraordinarily large expenditures in the coming year and continuing inflationary pressures, I am making no recommendation for tax reduction at this time.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have already had a substantial reduction in taxes from wartime peaks.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Revenue Act of 1945 was a major tax-reduction measure.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It decreased the total tax load by more than one-sixth, an amount substantially in excess of the reductions proposed by the Secretary of the Treasury to congressional tax committees in October 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These proposed reductions were designed to encourage reconversion and peacetime business expansion.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The possibility of further tax reductions must depend on the budgetary situation and the economic situation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The level of anticipated expenditures for the fiscal year 1947 and the volume of outstanding public debt require the maintenance of large revenues.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Moreover, inflationary pressures still appear dangerously powerful, and ill-advised tax reduction would operate to strengthen them still further.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: My decision not to recommend additional tax reductions at this time is made in the light of existing economic conditions and prospects.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: III. THE BUDGET FOR THE FEDERAL PROGRAM FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1947/ FEDERAL REVENUE, BORROWING, AND THE PUBLIC DEBT./ 2. BORROWING AND THE PUBLIC DEBT:  The successful conclusion of the Victory loan marked the end of war borrowing and the beginning of the transition to postwar debt management.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Because of the success of the Victory loan, I am happy to report that the Treasury will not need to borrow any new money from the public during the remainder of the present fiscal year except through regular sales of savings bonds and savings notes .

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Furthermore, a part of the large cash balance now in the Treasury will be used for debt redemption so that the public debt which now amounts to about 278 billion dollars will decrease by several billion dollars during the next 18 months.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The present statutory debt limit of 300 billion dollars will provide an ample margin for all of the public-debt transactions through the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The net effect of the excess of expenditures and debt redemption on the Treasury cash balance, as compared with selected previous years, is shown in the following table:

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Although the public debt is expected to decline, a substantial volume of refinancing will be required, because of the large volume of maturing obligations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Redemptions of savings bonds also have been running high in recent months and are expected to remain large for some time.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The issuance of Savings bonds will be continued.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These bonds represent a convenient method of investment for small savers, and also an anti-inflationary method of refinancing.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Government agencies and trust funds are expected to buy about 2.5 billion dollars of Government securities during the next 6 months, and 2.8 billion dollars more during the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Through these and other debt operations, the distribution of the Federal debt among the various types of public and private owners will change, even though the total is expected to decline.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The interest policies followed in the refinancing operations will have a major impact not only on the provision for interest payments in future budgets, but also on the level of interest rates prevailing in private financing.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The average rate of interest on the debt is now a little under 2 percent.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Low interest rates will be an important force in promoting the full production and full employment in the postwar period for which we are all striving.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Close wartime cooperation between the Treasury Department and the Federal Reserve System has made it possible to finance the most expensive war in history at low and stable rates of interest.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This cooperation will continue.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: No less important than the level of interest rates paid on the debt is the distribution of its ownership.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Of the total debt, more than half represents direct savings of individuals or investments of funds received from individual Savings by life insurance companies, mutual Savings banks, Savings and loan associations, private or Government trust funds, and other agencies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Most of the remaining debt-more than 100 billion dollars--is held by the commercial banks and the Federal Reserve banks.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Heavy purchases by the banks were necessary to provide adequate funds to finance war expenditures.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A considerable portion of these obligations are short-term in character and hence will require refinancing in the coming months and years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Since they have been purchased out of newly created bank funds, continuance of the present low rates of interest is entirely appropriate.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To do otherwise would merely increase bank profits at the expense of the taxpayer.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The 275-billion-dollar debt poses a problem that requires careful consideration in the determination of financial and economic policies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have learned that the problem, serious as it is, can be managed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Its management will require determined action to keep our Federal Budget in order and to relate our fiscal policies to the requirements of an expanding economy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The more successful we are in achieving full production and full employment the easier it will he to manage the debt and pay for the debt service.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Large though the debt is, it is within our economic capacity.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The interest charges on it amount to but a small proportion of our national income.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Government is determined, by a resolute policy of economic stabilization, to protect the interests of the millions of American citizens who have invested in its securities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the past 6 months the net revenue receipts of the Federal Government have been about 20 billion dollars, almost as much as during the closing 6 months of 1944 when the country was still engaged in all-out warfare.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The high level of these receipts reflects the smoothness of the reconversion and particularly the strength of consumer demand.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But the receipts so far collected, it must be remembered, do not reflect any of the tax reductions made by the Revenue Act of 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These reductions will not have their full effect on the revenue collected until the fiscal year 1948.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is good to move toward a balanced budget and a start on the retirement of the debt at a time when demand for goods is strong and the business outlook is good.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These conditions prevail today.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Business is good and there are still powerful forces working in the direction of inflation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is not the time for tax reduction.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: III. THE BUDGET FOR THE FEDERAL PROGRAM FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1947/ RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SPECIFIC FEDERAL ACIVITIES./ I. WAR LIQUIDATION AND NATIONAL DEFENSE./ (a) War expenditures:  The fiscal year 1947 will see a continuance of war liquidation and occupation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During this period we shall also lay the foundation for our peacetime system of national defense.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the fiscal year that ended on June 30, 1945, almost wholly a period of global war-fare, war expenditures amounted to 90.5 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For the fiscal year 1946, war expenditures were originally estimated at 70 billion dollar.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That estimate was made a year ago while we were still engaged in global warfare.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: After victory over Japan this estimate was revised to 50.5 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Further cut-backs and accelerated demobilization have made possible an additional reduction in the rate of war spending.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the first 6 months 32.9 billion dollars were spent.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is now estimated that 16.1 billion dollars will be spent during the second 6 months, or a total of 49 billion dollars during the whole fiscal year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For the fiscal year 1947 it is estimated, tentatively, that expenditures for war liquidation, for occupation, and for national defense will be reduced to 15 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The War and Navy Departments are expected to spend 13 billion dollars; expenditures of other agencies, such as the United States Maritime Commission, the War Shipping Administration, and the Office of Price Administration, and payments to the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration are estimated at 3 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Allowing for estimated net receipts of 1 billion dollars arising from war activities of the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, the estimated total of war expenditures is 15 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At this time only a tentative break-down of the total estimate for war and defense activities can be indicated.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: An expenditure of 15 billion dollars for war liquidation, occupation, and national defense is a large sum for a year which begins 10 months after fighting has ended.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is 10 times our expenditures for defense before the war; it amounts to about 10 percent of our expected national income.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This estimate reflects the immense job that is involved in winding up a global war effort and stresses the great responsibility that victory has placed upon this country.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The large expenditures needed for our national defense emphasize the great scope for effective organization in furthering economy and efficiency.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To this end I have recently recommended to the Congress adoption of legislation combining the War and Navy Departments into a single Department of National Defense.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A large part of these expenditures is still to be attributed to the costs of the war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Assuming, somewhat arbitrarily, that about one-half of the 15-billion-dollar outlay for the fiscal year 1947 is for war liquidation, aggregate expenditures by this Government for the second World War are now estimated at 347 billion dollars through June 30, 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Of this, about 9 billion dollars will have been recovered through renegotiation and sale of surplus property by June 30, 1947;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: this has been reflected in the estimates of receipts.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Demobilization and strength of armed forces - Demobilization of our armed forces is proceeding rapidly.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At the time of victory in Europe, about 12.3 million men and women were in the armed forces;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: 7.6 million were overseas.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: By the end of December 1945 our armed forces had been reduced to below 7 million.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: By June 30, 1946, they will number about 2.9 million, of whom 1.8 million will be individuals enlisted and inducted after VE-day.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Mustering-out pay is a large item of our war liquidation expense;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: it will total 2.5 billion dollars in the fiscal year 1946, and about 500 million dollars in the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the fiscal year 1947 the strength of our armed forces will still be above the ultimate peacetime level.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As I have said, War and Navy Department requirements indicate a strength of about 2 million in the armed forces a year from now.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is necessary to enable us to do our share in the occupation of enemy territories and in the preservation of peace in a troubled world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Expenditures for pay, subsistence, travel, and miscellaneous expenses of the armed forces, excluding mustering-out pay, are estimated at 5 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Contract settlement and surplus property disposal- The winding up of war procurement is the second most important liquidation job.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: By the end of November a total of 301,000 prime contracts involving commitments of 64 billion dollars had been terminated.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Of this total, 67,000 contracts with commitments of 35 billion dollars remained to be settled.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Termination payments on these contracts are estimated at about 3.5 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is expected that more than half of these terminated contracts will be settled during the current fiscal year, leaving payments of about 1.5 billion dollars for the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Another important aspect of war supply liquidation is the disposal of surplus property.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Munitions, ships, plants, installations, and supplies, originally costing 50 billion dollars or more, will ultimately be declared surplus.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The sale value of this property will be far less than original cost and disposal expenses are estimated at 10 to 15 cents on each dollar realized.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Disposal units within existing agencies have been organized to liquidate surplus property under the direction of the Surplus Property Administration.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Overseas disposal activities have been centralized in the State Department to permit this program to he carried on in line with over-all foreign policy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
