text: Thus far only about 13 billion dollars of the ultimate surplus, including 5 billion dollars of un-salable aircraft, has been declared.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Of this amount, 2.3 billion dollars have been disposed of, in sales yielding 600 million dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The tremendous job of handling surplus stocks will continue to affect Federal expenditures and receipts for several years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The speed and effectiveness of surplus disposal operations will be of great importance for the domestic economy as well as for foreign economic policies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: War supplies, maintenance, and relief- Adequate provision for the national defense requires that we keep abreast of scientific and technical advances.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The tentative estimates for the fiscal year 1947 make allowance for military research, limited procurement of weapons in the developmental state, and some regular procurement of munitions which were developed but not mass-produced when the war ended.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Expenditures for procurement and construction will constitute one-third or less of total defense outlays, compared to a ratio of two-thirds during the war years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The estimates also provide for the maintenance of our war-expanded naval and merchant fleets, military installations, and stocks of military equipment and supplies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our naval combatant fleet is three times its pre-Pearl Harbor tonnage.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our Merchant Marine is five times its prewar size.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The War Department has billions of dollars worth of equipment and supplies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Considerable maintenance and repair expense is necessary for the equipment which we desire to retain in active status or in war reserve.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Expenses will be incurred for winnowing the stocks of surpluses, for preparing lay-up facilities for the reserve fleets, and for storage of reserve equipment and supplies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Military expenditures in the current fiscal year include 650 million dollars for civilian supplies for the prevention of starvation and disease in occupied areas.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Expenditures on this account will continue in the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The war expenditures also cover the expenses of civilian administration in occupied areas.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the war, 15 cents of each dollar of our war expenditures was for lend-lease aid.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: With lend-lease terminated, I expect the direct operations under this program to be substantially completed in the current fiscal year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The expenditures estimated for the fiscal year 1947 under this program are mainly inter-agency reimbursements for past transactions.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Relief and rehabilitation expenditures are increasing.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is imperative that we give all necessary aid within our means to the people who have borne the ravages of war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I estimate that in the fiscal year 1946 expenditures for the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration will total 1.3 billion dollars and in the following year 1.2 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Insofar as possible, procurement for this purpose will be from war surpluses.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: III. THE BUDGET FOR THE FEDERAL PROGRAM FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1947/ RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SPECIFIC FEDERAL ACIVITIES./ I. WAR LIQUIDATION AND NATIONAL DEFENSE./(b) Authorizations for war and national defense: During the war, authorizations and appropriations had to be enacted well in advance of obligation and spending to afford ample time for planning of production by the procurement services and by industry.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Thus our cummulative war program authorized in the period between July 1, 1940, and July I, 1945, was 431 billion dollars, including net war commitments of Government corporations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Expenditures against those authorizations totaled 290 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This left 141 billion dollars in un-obligated authorizations and un-liquidated obligations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: With the end of fighting, it became necessary to adjust war authorizations to the requirements of war liquidation and continuing national defense.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Intensive review of the war authorizations by both the executive and the legislative branches has been continued since VJ-day.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As a result, the authorized war program is being brought more nearly into line with expenditures.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Rescissions and authorizations through the fiscal year 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Readjusting the war program, as The Congress well knows, is not an easy task.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Authorizations must not be too tight, lest we hamper necessary operations;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: they must not be too ample, lest we lose control of spending.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Last September, I transmitted to the Congress recommendations on the basis of which the Congress voted H.R. 4407 to repeal 50.3 billion dollars of appropriations and authorizations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I found it necessary to veto this bill because it was used as a vehicle for legislation that would impair the reemployment program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: However, in order to preserve the fine work of the Congress on the rescissions, I asked the Director of the Bureau of the Budget to place the exact amounts indicated for repeal in a nonexpendable reserve, and to advise the departments and agencies accordingly.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This has been done.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In accord with Public Law 132 of the Seventy-ninth Congress, I have transmitted recommendations for additional rescissions for the current fiscal year of appropriations amounting to 5.8 billion dollars and of contract authorizations totaling 420 million dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The net reduction in authority to obligate will be 5.0 billion dollars, because, of the appropriations, 1.2 billion dollars will have to be restored in subsequent years to liquidate contract authorizations still on the books.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The appropriations recommended for repeal include 2,827 million dollars for the Navy Department, 1,421 million dollars for the War Department, 850 million dollars for lend-lease, 384 million dollars for the War Shipping Administration, and 260 million dollars for the United States Maritime Commission.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The contract authorizations proposed for repeal are for the Maritime Commission.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In addition, there are unused tonnage authorizations for construction of naval vessels now valued at 5.4 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In September 1945, I suggested that this authority be reviewed by the appropriate committees of the Congress, and the Congress has moved to bar construction under these authorizations during the remainder of the fiscal year 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I propose to continue this prohibition in the Navy budget estimates for the fiscal year 1947 and now renew my recommendation that legislation be enacted at the earliest time to clear the statute books of these authorizations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The amounts indicated for repeal in H.R. 4407 and the further rescissions which I have recommended, excluding duplications and deferred cash payments on existing authorizations, represent a cut in the authorized war program of 60.8 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The war authorizations will also be reduced 3.7 billion dollars by carrying receipts of revolving accounts to surplus, by lapses, and by cancellation and repayment of commitments of the Government war corporations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On the other hand, supplemental appropriations of 600 million dollars will be required for the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the net, it is estimated that the cumulative authorized war and national defense program will amount to 368 billion dollars on June 30, 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Expenditures of 49 billion dollars during the fiscal year 1946 will have pushed cumulative expenditures to 339 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The unexpended balances will be down to 28 billion dollars on June 30,1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: New authorizations for national defense and war liquidation in the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The expenditures of 15 billion dollars for national defense and war liquidation in the fiscal year 1947 will be partly for payment of contractual obligations incurred in the past, and partly for the payment of new obligations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The unexpended balances on June 30, 1946, will be scattered among hundreds of separate appropriations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Thus, while some appropriation accounts will have unused balances, others will require additional appropriations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is estimated that authorizations to incur new obligations of 11,772 million dollars will be needed during the fiscal year 1947, mainly for the War and Navy Departments.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Of the required authorizations, 11,365 million dollars will be in new appropriations, 400 million dollars in new contract authority, and 7 million dollars in re-appropriations of un-obligated balances.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In addition, appropriations of 825 million dollars will be needed to liquidate obligations under existing contract authorizations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Taking into account the tentative authorizations and expenditures estimated for the fiscal year 1947, and offsets of 3 billion dollars in war commitments of Government corporations, the cumulative authorized war and national defense program on June 30, 1947, will be 376 billion dollars; total expenditures, 354 billion dollars;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: and unexpended balances, 22 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The 22 billion dollars of unexpended balances tentatively indicated as of June 30, 1947, comprise both un-obligated authorizations and un-liquidated obligations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Most of the un-liquidated obligations result from transactions booked during the war years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A large part of the 22 billion dollars would never be spent even if not repealed, for the appropriations will lapse in due course.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For example, several billion dollars of these un-liquidated obligations represent unsettled inter- and intra-departmental agency accounts for war procurement.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Legislation is being requested to facilitate the adjustment of some of these inter-agency accounts.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Another 6 billion dollars is set aside for contract termination payments.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If contract settlement costs continue in line with recent experience, it is likely that part of the 6 billion dollars will remain unspent.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On the other hand, some of the 22 billion dollars would be available for obligation and expenditure unless impounded.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In certain appropriations, such as those for long cycle procurement, considerable carryover of un-liquidated obligations into future years is to be expected and is necessary.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: However, substantial further rescissions can and should he made when the war liquidation program tapers off and budgetary requirements for national defense are clarified.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As I have said, I shall continue to review the war authorizations and from time to time recommend excess balances for repeal.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As in recent years, detailed recommendations concerning most appropriations for the national defense program are postponed until the spring.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In connection with the war activities of the United States Maritime Commission and certain other agencies, however, I now make specific recommendations for the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: No additional authorizations or appropriations will be necessary for the Maritime Commission since sufficient balances will he left after the above mentioned rescissions to carry out the program now contemplated for the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: III. THE BUDGET FOR THE FEDERAL PROGRAM FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1947/ RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SPECIFIC FEDERAL ACIVITIES./ 2. AFTERMATH OF WAR:  Nearly one-third--11 billion dollars --of estimated Federal expenditures in the fiscal year 1947 will be for purposes that are largely inherited from the war-payments to veterans, interest on the Federal debt, and refunds of taxes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: III. THE BUDGET FOR THE FEDERAL PROGRAM FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1947/ RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SPECIFIC FEDERAL ACIVITIES./ 2. AFTERMATH OF WAR./ (a) For veterans:  Veterans' pensions and benefits has become one of the largest single categories in the Federal Budget.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I am recommending for this purpose total appropriations of 4,787 million dollars for the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Expenditures in the fiscal year are estimated, under present legislation, at 4,208 million dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These expenditures will help our veterans through their readjustment period and provide lasting care for those who were disabled.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Congress has provided unemployment allowances for veterans during their readjustment period.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Expenditure of 850 million dollars for this purpose is anticipated for the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In addition, readjustment allowances for self-employed veterans are expected to cost 340 million dollars in the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On May 28, 1945, in asking the Congress to raise the ceiling on benefits for civilian unemployed to not less than 25 dollars a week during the immediate reconversion period, I suggested that the Congress also consider liberalizing veterans' allowances.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Elsewhere in this Message I reiterate my recommendation with respect to emergency unemployment compensation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I also recommend increasing veterans' unemployment allowances from 20 dollars to 25 dollars a week.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This would involve additional expenditures estimated at approximately 220 million dollars for the fiscal year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Included in the 1947 Budget is an expenditure of 535 million dollars for veterans' education under provisions of the Servicemen's Readjustment Act.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This amount includes both tuition expenses and maintenance allowances.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is expected that half a million veterans will be enrolled in our schools and colleges during the year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The ultimate benefit which veterans receive from the loan guarantee provisions of the Servicemen's Readjustment Act depends largely on the success of our stabilization program in restraining building costs and real estate values.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Under the revised procedure contained in recent amendments, the administrative workload will be minimized by the almost complete transfer of authority for approving the guarantees to private lending agencies and private appraisers designated by the Veterans Administration.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This authority carries with it the responsibility for restricting the guarantees to loans on reasonably valued properties.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Costs of the program, other than for administration, are estimated at 21 million dollars in the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Pensions for veterans will require expenditures estimated at 1,748 million dollars for the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Two-thirds of this amount will be received by veterans of the war which we have just won.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This figure includes 55 million dollars of increased pensions for student-veterans in our vocational rehabilitation program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In addition, 170 million dollars will he expended in transfers to the National Service Life Insurance Fund from general and special accounts.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Expenditures under the appropriation for salaries and expenses of the Veterans Administration are estimated at 528 million dollars in the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This includes 260 million dollars for medical care and the operation of some 103,000 hospital and domiciliary beds.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A separate appropriation for hospital and domiciliary facilities, additional to the total for veterans' pensions and benefits, covers construction that will provide some 13,000 hospital beds as part of the 500-million dollar hospital construction program already authorized by the Congress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The estimated expenditures of 130 million dollars for this purpose are classified in the Budget as part of the general public works program for the next fiscal year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: III. THE BUDGET FOR THE FEDERAL PROGRAM FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1947/ RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SPECIFIC FEDERAL ACIVITIES./ 2. AFTERMATH OF WAR./ (b) For interest: Interest payments on the public debt are estimated at 5 billion dollars in the fiscal year 1947, an increase of 250 million dollars from the revised estimate for the current fiscal year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This increase reflects chiefly payment of interest on additions to the debt this year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Assuming continuance of present interest rates, the Government's interest bill is now reaching the probable postwar level.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: III. THE BUDGET FOR THE FEDERAL PROGRAM FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1947/ RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SPECIFIC FEDERAL ACIVITIES./ 2. AFTERMATH OF WAR./ (c) For refunds:  An estimated total of 1,585 million dollars of refunds will he paid to individuals and corporations during the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Slightly over half of this amount, or 80 million dollars, will be accessory to the simplified pay-as-you-go method of tax collection, and will be the result of over-withholding and over-declaration of expected income.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Most of the remainder will arise from loss and excess-profits credit carry backs, recomputed amortization on war plants, and special relief from the excess profits tax.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: character, and by the succeeding year will reflect almost entirely the normal operation of loss carry-backs and current tax collection.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: III. THE BUDGET FOR THE FEDERAL PROGRAM FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1947/ RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SPECIFIC FEDERAL ACIVITIES./ 3. AGRICULTURAL PROGRAMS:  The agricultural programs contemplated for the fiscal year 1947 are those which are essential for the provision of an adequate supply of food and other agricultural commodities with a fair return to American farmers.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To support these objectives, expenditures by the Department of Agriculture estimated at 784 million dollars from general and special accounts will be required in the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This compares with estimated expenditures of 676 million dollars in 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These figures exclude expenditures by the Department of Agriculture on account of lend-lease, the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration, and other war expenditures.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: 35 million dollars for general public works, and 196 million dollars for other services of the Department.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Net outlays for the price stabilization, price support, and other programs of the Commodity Credit Corporation are expected to increase from about 750 million dollars in the fiscal year 1946 to about 1,500 million dollars in 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Cash advances made on loans by the Farm Security Administration and the Rural Electrification Administration are expected to amount to 266 million dollars in the fiscal year 1946 and 351 million dollars in 1947;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: and after receipts from principal and interest are taken in to account, net loan expenditures of these two agencies will amount to 120 and 209 million dollars in the two fiscal years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To provide for the expenditures from general and special accounts, I recommend for the fiscal year 1947 appropriations of 721 million dollars (including the existing permanent appropriation of an amount equal to 30 percent of estimated annual customs receipts) and a re-appropriation of 88 million dollars of prior-year balances from customs receipts.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In addition there is a recommended authorization of 367.5 million dollars for borrowing from the Reconstruction Finance Corporation for the loan programs of the Farm Security Administration and the Rural Electrification Administration.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is expected that the operations of the Commodity Credit Corporation will be financed during the coming year through the 500 million dollars of lend-lease funds which the Congress has earmarked for price support purposes, a supplemental appropriation to restore impaired capital of the Corporation, and the borrowing authority of the Corporation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Some detailed recommendations follow for major agricultural programs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: - the so-called AAA program-for the fiscal year 1947, compared with 356 million dollars in the current year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This reduction of 86 million dollars is in large part accounted for by elimination of the wartime flax production incentive project and other nonrecurring items;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: the proposed reduction in normal activities is less than 33 million dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For the past several years, this program has consisted largely of payments to farmers for application of fertilizer and other approved soil management practices.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I am convinced that farmers generally are now fully alert to the benefits, both immediate and long-term, which they derive from the practices encouraged by this program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I believe, therefore, that this subsidization should continue to be reduced.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Rural electrification-It is proposed that the loan authorization for the Rural Electrification Administration for the fiscal year 1947 he increased from 200 million dollars to 250 million dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the war period, REA was limited by the scarcity of materials and manpower.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But that situation is rapidly changing, and the REA program, which was materially stepped up for the fiscal year 1946, can he increased still more.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is my belief that a feasible and practical rural electrification program should be carried forward as rapidly as possible.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This will involve total loans of approximately 1,800 million dollars over the next 10 years, much of which will be repaid during that period.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Other programs--It is recommended that the continuing forest land-acquisition program be resumed at the rate of 3 million dollars annually, which is about the minimum rate at which this program can be economically carried on.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The lands involved in this program can contribute fully to the national welfare only when brought into the national forest system for protection and development.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Such programs as those of the Farm Security Administration and the Farm Credit Administration are estimated to be continued during the fiscal year 1947 at about the same level as in the fiscal year 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Recent action by the Congress has permitted some expansion of the school-lunch program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I hope it will be continued and expanded.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The budgets of the Federal Crop Insurance Corporation and the Federal Farm Mortgage Corporation will be transmitted in the spring under the terms of the Government Corporation Control Act.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: III. THE BUDGET FOR THE FEDERAL PROGRAM FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1947/ RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SPECIFIC FEDERAL ACIVITIES./ 4. TRANSPORTATION:  Transportation is one of the major fields for both public and private investment.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our facilities for transportation and communication must be constantly improved to serve better the convenience of the public and to facilitate the sound growth and development of the whole economy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Federal capital outlays for transportation facilities are expected to approximate 519 million dollars in the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: State and local governments may spend 400 million dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Private investment, over half of it by railways, may approach 1,150 million dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Congress has already taken steps for the resumption of work on improvement of rivers and harbors and on the construction of new Federal-aid highways.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Much needed work on airports can begin when the Congress enacts legislation now in conference between the two Houses.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Federal expenditure estimates for the fiscal year 1947 include 53 million dollars for new construction in rivers, harbors, and the Panama Canal and 291 million dollars for highways and grade-crossing elimination, assuming that the States expend some 275 million dollars on the Federal-aid system.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Additional expenditures for highways totaling 36 million dollars are anticipated by the Forest Service, National Park Service, and the Territory of Alaska.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Civil airways and airports will involve expenditures of 35 million dollars under existing authority.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Additional Federal expenditures exceeding 20 million dollars (to be matched by States and municipalities) may be made during the fiscal year 1947 under the airport legislation now in conference between the two Houses of the Congress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The United States now controls almost two-thirds of the world's merchant shipping, most of it Government-owned, compared with little more than one-seventh of the world's tonnage in 1939.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This places a heavy responsibility upon the Nation to prove for speedy and efficient world commerce as a contribution to general economic recovery.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The estimates for the United States Maritime Commission and War Shipping Administration provide for the transition of shipping operation from a war to a peace basis;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: the sale, chartering, or lay-up of much of the war-built fleet;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: and for a program of s hip construction of some 84 million dollars in the fiscal year 1947 to round out the merchant fleet for peacetime use.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Federal aids, subsidies, and regulatory controls for transportation should follow the general principle of benefiting the national economy as a whole.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They should seek to improve the transportation system and increase its efficiency with resulting lower rates and superior service.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Differential treatment which benefits one type of transportation to the detriment of another should be avoided save when it is demonstrated clearly to be in the public interest.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: III. THE BUDGET FOR THE FEDERAL PROGRAM FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1947/ RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SPECIFIC FEDERAL ACIVITIES./ 5. RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT: Total capital outlays for resource development are estimated at 653 million dollars in the fiscal year 1947 as compared with 452 million dollars in 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The reclamation and flood control projects which I am recommending for the fiscal year 1947 will involve capital outlays of approximately 319 million dollars as compared with 245 million dollars in the fiscal year 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These expenditures cover programs of the Corps of Engineers, the Bureau of Reclamation, the Bureau of Indian Affairs, the Department of Agriculture, and the International Boundary and Water Commission, United States and Mexico.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A number of these projects are multiple-purpose projects, providing not only for reclamation and irrigation of barren land and flood control, but also for the production of power needed for industrial development of the areas.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Expenditures for power transmission and distribution facilities by the Bonneville Power Administration are expected to increase from 12 million dollars in the fiscal year 1946 to 15 million dollars in the next fiscal year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In addition, the Southwestern Power Administration will undertake a new program involving expenditures of about 16 million dollars in the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Rural Electrification Administration will require expenditures during the current fiscal year estimated at 156 million dollars; in the fiscal year 1947, at 241 million dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The TVA program includes completion of major multiple-purpose projects-navigation, flood control, and power facilities--and additions to chemical plants and related facilities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Expenditures for these capital improvement programs are estimated at 30 million dollars in the fiscal year 1946 and 39 million dollars in the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Expenditures for the construction of roads and other developmental works in the national forests, parks, and other public lands, and for capital outlays for fish and wildlife development will increase from below 9 million dollars in the fiscal year 1946 to 24 million dollars in fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: III. THE BUDGET FOR THE FEDERAL PROGRAM FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1947/ RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SPECIFIC FEDERAL ACIVITIES./ 6. Social Security and Health: Benefit payments out of the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund during 1947 are estimated at 407 million dollars, while withdrawals by the States from the Unemployment Trust Fund for compensation payments are expected to total 1 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These disbursements are financed out of Social Security contributions.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The appropriations from general and special accounts for the social security program, which cover Federal administrative expenses and grants to States for assistance programs, are estimated at 593 million dollars for the fiscal year 1947, an increase of 57 million dollars over the current year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The increase anticipates greater administrative workload and higher grants to match increasing State payments.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The social security program does not include all the Federal health services under existing legislation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For the other health services classified under general government and national defense, appropriations are estimated at 102 million dollars for the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Some expansion in peacetime medical research and other programs of the Public Health Service is provided for in the appropriation estimates for these purposes totaling approximately 87 million dollars for the fiscal year 1947 which are submitted under provisions of existing law.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Part of this will be provided through the social security appropriations, the remainder through other appropriations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: About 28 million dollars is recommended for maternity care and health services for children under existing law, mainly under the emergency provision for the wives and infants of servicemen.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: While we should avoid duplication of maternity and child health services which will be provided through the proposed general system of prepaid medical care, legislation is needed to supplement such services.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For medical education, I have recommended legislation authorizing grants-in-aid to public and nonprofit institutions.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The existing sources of support for medical schools require supplementation to sustain the expansion that is needed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Hospitals, sanitation works, and additional facilities at medical schools will be required for an adequate national health program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Legislation is now pending in the Congress to authorize grants for the construction of hospitals and health centers and grants and loans for water-pollution control.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I hope the Congress will act favorably on generous authorizing legislation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: III. THE BUDGET FOR THE FEDERAL PROGRAM FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1947/ RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SPECIFIC FEDERAL ACIVITIES./ 7. RESEARCH AND EDUCATION:  The Budget provides for continuation and desirable expansion of the research activities that are carried on throughout the Federal establishment and through previously authorized grants to the States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Additional appropriations will he required for the proposed central Federal research agency which I recommended last September 6.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That agency will coordinate existing research activities and administer funds for new research activities wherever they are needed;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: it will not itself conduct research.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The plan contemplates expenditures through the new research agency of approximately 40 million dollars for the first year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These amounts are small in relation to the important contribution they can make to the national income, the welfare of our people, and the common defense.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Expenditures must be limited for the time being by the capacity of research agencies to make wise use of funds.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The maintenance of our position as a nation, however, will require more emphasis on research expenditures in the future than in the past.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Educational expenditures will require a significant share of the national income in the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: State, local, and private expenditures for the current support of elementary, secondary, and higher education are expected to be substantially above 3 billion dollars in that year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These non-Federal expenditures will be supplemented by Federal expenditures estimated at 625 million dollars in the present Budget.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Of this amount, the estimate for veterans' education, as previously mentioned, is 535 million dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Other amounts include 21 million dollars for the support of vocational education in public schools, 5 million dollars for the land-grant colleges, 50 million dollars for the present school lunch and milk program, 1 million dollars for the Office of Education, and approximately 13 million dollars for various other items.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In view of the major policy issues which are still under study by the Congress and the Administration, no specific amount has been determined for the Federal grants, previously recommended in this Message, which would assist the States generally in assuring more nearly equal opportunities for a good education.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Notwithstanding the urgent need for additional school and college buildings, careful planning will be required for the expenditures to be made under the proposed legislation to aid the States in providing educational facilities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A major share of the grants for the first year would he for surveys and plans.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: III. THE BUDGET FOR THE FEDERAL PROGRAM FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1947/ RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SPECIFIC FEDERAL ACIVITIES./ 8. INTERNATIONAL-FINANCIAL PROGRAMS: I have already outlined the broad objectives of our foreign economic policy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the present section I shall indicate the Federal outlays which the execution of these programs may require in the fiscal years 1946 and 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (a) On the termination of lend-lease, the lend-lease countries were required to pay for goods in the lend-lease pipe line either in cash or by borrowing from the United States or by supplying goods and services to the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Credits for this purpose have already been extended to the Soviet Union, France, the Netherlands, and Belgium amounting to 675 million dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The settlement credit of 650 million dollars to the United Kingdom includes an amount preliminarily fixed at 118 million dollars which represents the excess of purchases by the United Kingdom from the pipe line over goods and services supplied by the United Kingdom to the United States since VJ-day and the balance of various claims by one government against the other.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Credits are also being negotiated with lend-lease countries to finance the disposition of lend-lease inventories and installations and property declared to be surplus.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For instance, 532 million dollars of the settlement credit to the United Kingdom is for this purpose.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These credits will involve no new expenditures by this Government, since they merely provide for deferred repayment by other governments for goods and services which have been financed from war appropriations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (b) Expenditures from the appropriations to United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration, which were discussed under war expenditures above, are estimated to be 1.3 billion dollars in the fiscal year 1946 and 1.2 billion dollars in the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (c) To assist other countries in the restoration of their economies the Export-Import Bank has already negotiated loans in the fiscal year 1946 amounting in total to about 1,010 million dollars and an additional 195 million dollars will probably be committed shortly.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Bank is also granting loans to carry out its original purpose of directly expanding the foreign trade of the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In this connection the Bank has established a fund of too million dollars to finance the export of cotton from the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Export-Import Bank has thus loaned or committed approximately 1,300 million dollars during the current fiscal year and it is expected that demands on its resources will increase in the last 6 months of the fiscal year 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Requests for loans are constantly being received by the Bank from countries desiring to secure goods and services in this country for the reconstruction or development of their economies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On July 31, 1945, the lending authority of the Export-Import Bank was increased to a total of 3,500 million dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I anticipate that during the period covered by this.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Budget the Bank will reach this limit.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The bulk of the expenditures from the loans already granted will fall in the fiscal year 1946 while the bulk of the expenditures from loans yet to be negotiated will fall in the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In view of the urgent need for the Bank's credit, I may find it necessary to request a further increase in its lending authority at a later date.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (d) The proposed line of credit of 3,750 million dollars to the United Kingdom will be available up to the end of 1951 and will be used to assist the United Kingdom in financing the deficit in its balance of payments during the transition period.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The rate at which the United Kingdom will draw on the credit will depend on the rapidity with which it can reconvert its economy and adapt its trade to the postwar world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The anticipated rate of expenditure is likely to be heaviest during the next 2 years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: (e) Since the Bretton Woods Agreements have now been approved by the required number of countries, both the International Monetary Fund and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development will commence operations during 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The organization of these institutions will undoubtedly take some time, and it is unlikely that their operations will reach any appreciable scale before the beginning of the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Of the 2,750 million dollars required for the Fund, 1,800 million dollars will be provided in cash or notes from the exchange stabilization fund established under the Gold Reserve Act of 1934.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The remaining 950 million dollars will be paid initially in the form of non-interest-bearing notes issued by the Secretary of the Treasury.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is not anticipated that the Fund will require in cash any of the 950 million dollars during the fiscal years 1946 and 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Consequently, no cash withdrawals from the Treasury will be required in connection with the Fund in these years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The subscription to the Bank amounts to 3,175 million dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Of this total, 2 percent must be paid immediately and the Bank is required to call a further 8 percent of the subscription during its first year of operations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The balance of the subscription is payable when required by the Bank either for direct lending or to make good its guarantees.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is likely that the United States will be required to pay little if any more than the initial 10 percent before the end of the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I anticipate that net expenditures of the Export-Import Bank and expenditures arising from the British credit and the Bretton Woods Agreements will amount to 2,614 million dollars, including the non-cash item of 950 million dollars for the Fund, in the fiscal year 1946, and 2,754 million dollars in the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: III. THE BUDGET FOR THE FEDERAL PROGRAM FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1947/ RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SPECIFIC FEDERAL ACIVITIES./ 9. GENERAL GOVERNMENT:  The responsibilities of the Government, in both domestic and international affairs, have increased greatly in the past decade.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Consequently, the Government is larger than it was before the war, and its general operating costs are higher.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We cannot shrink the Government to prewar dimensions unless we slough off these new responsibilities--and we cannot do that without paying an excessive price in terms of our national welfare.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We can, however, enhance its operating efficiency through improved organization.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I expect to make such improvements under the authority of the Reorganization Act of 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The appropriations which I am recommending for general government for the fiscal year 1947 are 1,604 million dollars under existing legislation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is an increase of 458 million dollars over the total of enacted appropriations for the current fiscal year, but a substantial part of this increase is due to the fact that the appropriations for the fiscal year 1946 were made prior to the general increase of employees' salaries last July 1, for which allowance is made in the anticipated supplemental appropriations for 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The recommended total for 1947 for general government, like the estimates for national defense and other specific programs, does not allow for the further salary increases for Government employees which, I hope, will be authorized by pending legislation, but the tentative lump-sum estimates under proposed legislation contemplate that such salary increases will be effective almost at once.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Expenditures for general government in the fiscal year 1947 are expected to continue the slowly rising trend which began in 1943.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This category includes a great variety of items-not merely the overhead costs of the Government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It includes all the expenditures of the Cabinet departments, other than for national defense, aids to agriculture, general public works, and the social security program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It includes also expenditures of the legislative branch, the Judiciary;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: and many of the independent agencies of the executive branch.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Consequently, the estimated increase in 1947 in the total of general government expenditures reflects a variety of influences.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Now included in general government are certain activities formerly classified under national defense.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Some of these, such as certain functions of the former Foreign Economic Administration and the War Manpower Commission, are still needed during the period of reconversion;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: others are in the process of liquidation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A few wartime activities, for example, the international information and foreign intelligence services and some of the wartime programs for controlling disease and crime, have become part of our regular government establishment.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Expenditures for these former wartime functions explain about 40 percent of the increase in expenditures for general government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Other increases are for civil aeronautics promotion, the business and manufacturing censuses, and other expanded business services of the Department of Commerce which have been referred to above;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: the Forest and Soil Conservation Services and other activities of the Department of Agriculture;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: certain conservation activities of the Department of the Interior;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: and the collection of internal revenue in the Treasury Department.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The necessity for reestablishing postal services curtailed during the war and advances in the rates of pay for postal employees have increased substantially the estimated expenditures for postal service for both the current and the next fiscal year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is not expected that this increase will cause expenditures to exceed postal revenues in either year, although an excess of expenditures may occur in the fiscal year 1947 if salaries are increased further.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Expenditures for our share of the administrative budgets of the United Nations and other permanent international bodies will increase sharply in the fiscal year 1947, yet will remain a small part of our total Budget.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The budget for the United Nation s has not yet been determined;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: an estimate for our contribution will be submitted later.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our contributions to the Food and Agriculture Organization, the International Labor Office, the Pan American Union, and other similar international agencies will aggregate about 3 million dollars for the fiscal year 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The administrative expenses of the International Monetary Fund and the International Bank will be met from their general funds.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have won a great war- we, the nations of plain people who hate war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the test of that war we found a strength of unity that brought us through - a strength that crushed the power of those who sought by force to deny our faith in the dignity of man.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During this trial the voices of disunity among us were silent or were subdued to an occasional whine that warned us that they were still among us.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Those voices are beginning to cry aloud again.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must learn constantly to turn deaf ears to them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They are voices which foster fear and suspicion and intolerance and hate.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: live and let live.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They have become busy again, trying to set race against race, creed against creed, farmer against city dweller, worker against employer, people against their own governments.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They seek only to do us mischief.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They must not prevail.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It should be impossible for any man to contemplate without a sense of personal humility the tremendous events of the 12 months since the last annual Message, the great tasks that confront us, the new and huge problems of the coming months and years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Yet these very things justify the deepest confidence in the future of this Nation of free men and women.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The plain people of this country found the courage and the strength, the self-discipline, and the mutual respect to fight and to win, with the help of our allies, under God.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I doubt if the tasks of the future are more difficult.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But if they are, then I say that our strength and our knowledge and our understanding will be equal to those tasks.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Mr. President, Mr. Speaker, Members of the Congress of the United States: It looks like a good many of you have moved over to the left since I was here last.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I come before you today to report on the State of the Union and, in the words of the Constitution, to recommend such measures as I judge necessary and expedient.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I come also to welcome you as you take up your duties and to discuss with you the manner in which you and I should fulfill our obligations to the American people during the next 2 years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The power to mold the future of this Nation lies in our hands-yours and mine, and they are joined together by the Constitution.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If in this year, and in the next, we can find the right course to take as each issue arises, and if, in spite of all difficulties, we have the courage and the resolution to take that course, then we shall achieve a state of well-being for our people without precedent in history.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And if we continue to work with the other nations of the world earnestly, patiently, and wisely, we can-granting a will for peace on the part of our neighbors make a lasting peace for the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But, if we are to realize these ends, the Congress and the President, during the next 2 years, must work together.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is not unusual in our history that the majority of the Congress represents a party in opposition to the President's party.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I am the twentieth President of the United States who, at some time during his term of office, has found his own party to be in the minority in one or both Houses of Congress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The first one was George Washington.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Wilson was number eighteen, and Hoover was number nineteen.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I realize that on some matters the Congress and the President may have honest differences of opinion.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Partisan differences, however, did not cause material disagreements as to the conduct of the war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Nor, in the conduct of our international relations, during and since the war, have such partisan differences been material.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On some domestic issues we may, and probably shall, disagree.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That in itself is not to be feared.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is inherent in our form of Government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But there are ways of disagreeing;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: men who differ can still work together sincerely for the common good.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We shall be risking the Nation's safety and destroying our opportunities for progress if we do not settle any disagreements in this spirit, without thought of partisan advantage.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As the year 1947 begins, the state of our national economy presents great opportunities for all.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have virtually full employment, our national production of goods and services is 50 percent higher than in any year prior to the war emergency.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The national income in 1946 was higher than in any peace-time year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our food production is greater than it has ever been.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the last 5 years our productive facilities have been expanded in almost every field.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The American standard of living is higher now than ever before, and when the housing shortage can be overcome it will be even higher.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the past few months we have removed at a rapid rate the emergency controls that the Federal Government had to exercise during the war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The remaining controls will be retained only as long as they are needed to protect the public.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Private enterprise must be given the greatest possible freedom to continue the expansion of our economy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In my proclamation of December 31, 1946, I announced the termination of hostilities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This automatically ended certain temporary legislation and certain executive powers.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: termination of the war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I shall submit to the Congress recommendations for the repeal of certain of the statutes which by their terms continue for the duration of the emergency.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I shall at the same time recommend that others within this classification be extended until the state of war has been ended by treaty or by legislative action.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As to those statutes which continue until the State of war has been terminated, I urge that the Congress promptly consider each statute individually, and repeal such emergency legislation where it is advisable.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Now that nearly all wartime controls have been removed, the operation of our industrial system depends to a greater extent on the decisions of businessmen, farmers, and workers.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These decisions must be wisely made with genuine concern for public welfare.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The welfare of businessmen, farmers, and workers depends upon the economic well-being of those who buy their products.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: An important present source of danger to our economy is the possibility that prices might be raised to such an extent that the consuming public could not purchase the tremendous volume of goods and services which will be produced during 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We all know that recent price increases have denied to many of our workers much of the value of recent wage increases.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Farmers have found that a large part of their increased income has been absorbed by increased prices.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: While some of our people have received raises in income which exceed price increases, the great majority have not.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Those persons who live on modest fixed incomes-retired persons living on pensions, for example-and workers whose incomes are relatively inflexible, such as teachers and other civil servants-have suffered hardship.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the effort to bring about a sound and equitable price structure, each group of our population has its own responsibilities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is up to industry not only to hold the line on existing prices, but to make reductions whenever profits justify such action.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is up to labor to refrain from pressing for unjustified wage increases that will force increases in the price level.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And it is up to Government to do everything in its power to encourage high- volume production, for that is what makes possible good wages, low prices, and reasonable profits.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In a few days there will be submitted to the Congress the Economic Report of the President, and also the Budget Message.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Those messages will contain many recommendations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Today I shall outline five major economic policies which I believe the Government should pursue during 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These policies are designed to meet our immediate needs and, at the same time, to provide for the long-range welfare of our free enterprise system: First, the promotion of greater harmony between labor and management.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Second, restriction of monopoly and unfair business practices;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: assistance to small business;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: and the promotion of the free competitive system of private enterprise.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Third, continuation of an aggressive program of home construction.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Fourth, the balancing of the budget in the next fiscal year and the achieving of a substantial surplus to be applied to the reduction of the public debt.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Fifth, protection of a fair level of return to farmers in post-war agriculture.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: LABOR AND MANAGEMENT: The year just past-like the year after the First World War-was marred by labor management strife.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Despite this outbreak of economic warfare in 1946, we are today producing goods and services in record volume.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Nevertheless, it is essential to improve the methods for reaching agreement between labor and management and to reduce the number of strikes and lockouts.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must not, however, adopt punitive legislation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must not, in order to punish a few labor leaders, pass vindictive laws which will restrict the proper rights of the rank and file of labor.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must not, under the stress of emotion, endanger our American freedoms by taking ill-considered action which will lead to results not anticipated or desired.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must remember, in reviewing the record of disputes in 1946, that management shares with labor the responsibility for failure to reach agreements which would have averted strikes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For that reason, we must realize that industrial peace cannot be achieved merely by laws directed against labor unions.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the last decade and a half, we have established a national labor policy in this country based upon free collective bargaining as the process for determining wages and working conditions.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is still the national policy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And it should continue to be the national policy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But as yet, not all of us have learned what it means to bargain freely and fairly.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Nor have all of us learned to carry the mutual responsibilities that accompany the right to bargain.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There have been abuses and harmful practices which limit the effectiveness of our system of collective bargaining.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Furthermore, we have lacked sufficient governmental machinery to aid labor and management in resolving their differences.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Certain labor-management problems need attention at once and certain others, by reason of their complexity, need exhaustive investigation and study.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should enact legislation to correct certain abuses and to provide additional governmental assistance in bargaining.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But we should also concern ourselves with the basic causes of labor-management difficulties.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the light of these considerations, I propose to you and urge your cooperation in effecting the following four-point program to reduce industrial strife: Point number one is the early enactment of legislation to prevent certain unjustifiable practices.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: First, under this point, are jurisdictional strikes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In such strikes the public and the employer are innocent bystanders who are injured by a collision between rival unions.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This type of dispute hurts production, industry, and the public-and labor itself.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I consider jurisdictional strikes indefensible.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The National Labor Relations Act provides procedures for determining which union represents employees of a particular employer.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In some jurisdictional disputes, however, minority unions strike to compel employers to deal with them despite a legal duty to bargain with the majority union.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Strikes to compel an employer to violate the law are inexcusable.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Legislation to prevent such strikes is clearly desirable.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Another form of inter-union disagreement is the jurisdictional strike involving the question of which labor union is entitled to perform a particular task.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: When rival unions are unable to settle such disputes themselves, provision must be made for peaceful and binding determination of the issues.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A second unjustifiable practice is the secondary boycott, when used to further jurisdictional disputes or to compel employers to violate the National Labor Relations Act.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Not all secondary boycotts are unjustified.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must judge them on the basis of their objectives.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For example, boycotts intended to protect wage rates and working conditions should be distinguished from those in furtherance of jurisdictional disputes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The structure of industry sometimes requires unions, as a matter of self-preservation, to extend the conflict beyond a particular employer.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There should be no blanket prohibition against boycotts.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The appropriate goal is legislation which prohibits secondary boycotts in pursuance of unjustifiable objectives, but does not impair the union's right to preserve its own existence and the gains made in genuine collective bargaining.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A third practice that should be corrected is the use of economic force, by either labor or management, to decide issues arising out of the interpretation of existing contracts.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Collective bargaining agreements, like other contracts, should he faithfully adhered to by both parties.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the most enlightened union-management relationships, disputes over the interpretation of contract terms are settled peaceably by negotiation or arbitration.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Legislation should be enacted to provide machinery whereby unsettled disputes concerning the interpretation of an existing agreement may be referred by either party to final and binding arbitration.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Point number two is the extension of facilities within the Department of Labor for assisting collective bargaining.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: One of our difficulties in avoiding labor strife arises from a lack of order in the collective bargaining process.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The parties often do not have a clear understanding of their responsibility for settling disputes through their own negotiations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We constantly see instances where labor or management resorts to economic force without exhausting the possibilities for agreement through the bargaining process.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Neither the parties nor the Government have a definite yardstick for determining when and how Government assistance should be invoked.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There is need for integrated governmental machinery to provide the successive steps of mediation, voluntary arbitration, and-ultimately in appropriate cases-ascertainment of the facts of the dispute and the reporting of the facts to the public.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Such machinery would facilitate and expedite the settlement of disputes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Point number three is the broadening of our program of social legislation to alleviate the causes of workers' insecurity.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On June 11, 1946, in my message vetoing the Case Bill, I made a comprehensive statement of my views concerning labor-management relations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I said then, and I repeat now, that the solution of labor-management difficulties is to be found not only in legislation dealing directly with labor relations, but also in a program designed to remove the causes of insecurity felt by many workers in our industrial society.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In this connection, for example, the Congress should consider the extension and broadening of our social security system, better housing, a comprehensive national health program, and provision for a fair minimum wage.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Point number four is the appointment of a Temporary Joint Commission to inquire into the entire field of labor-management relations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I recommend that the Congress provide for the appointment of a Temporary Joint Commission to undertake this broad study.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The President, the Congress, and management and labor have a continuing responsibility to cooperate in seeking and finding the solution of these problems.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I therefore recommend that the Commission be composed as follows: twelve to be chosen by the Congress from members of both parties in the House and the Senate, and eight representing the public, management and labor, to be appointed by the President.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Commission should be charged with investigating and making recommendations upon certain major subjects, among others: First, the special and unique problem of nationwide strikes in vital industries affecting the public interest.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In particular, the Commission should examine into the question of how to settle or prevent such strikes without endangering our general democratic freedoms.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Upon a proper solution of this problem may depend the whole industrial future of the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The paralyzing effects of a nationwide strike in such industries as transportation, coal, oil, steel, or communications can result in national disaster.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have been able to avoid such disaster, in recent years, only by the use of extraordinary war powers.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: All those powers will soon be gone.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In their place there must be created an adequate system and effective machinery in these vital fields.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This problem will require careful study and a bold approach, but an approach consistent with the preservation of the rights of our people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The need is pressing.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Commission should give this its earliest attention.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Second, the best methods and procedures for carrying out the collective bargaining process.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This should include the responsibilities of labor and management to negotiate freely and fairly with each other, and to refrain from strikes or lockouts until all possibilities of negotiation have been exhausted.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Third, the underlying causes of labor management disputes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Some of the subjects presented here for investigation involve long-range study.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Others can be considered immediately by the Commission and its recommendations can be submitted to the Congress in the near future.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I recommend that this Commission make its first report, including specific legislative recommendations, not later than March 15, 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: RESTRICTION OF MONOPOLY AND PROMOTION OF PRIVATE ENTERPRISE: The second major policy I desire to lay before you has to do with the growing concentration of economic power and the threat to free competitive private enterprise.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In 1941 the Temporary National Economic Committee completed a comprehensive investigation into the workings of the national economy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Committee's study showed that, despite a half century of anti-trust law enforcement, one of the gravest threats to our welfare lay in the increasing concentration of power in the hands of a small number of giant organizations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the war, this long-standing tendency toward economic concentration was accelerated.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As a consequence, we now find that to a greater extent than ever before, whole industries are dominated by one or a few large organizations which can restrict production in the interest of higher profits and thus reduce employment and purchasing power.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In an effort to assure full opportunity and free competition to business we will vigorously enforce the anti-trust laws.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There is much the Congress can do to cooperate and assist in this program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To strengthen and enforce the laws that regulate business practices is not enough.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Enforcement must be supplemented by positive measures of aid to new enterprises.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Government assistance, research programs, and credit powers should be designed and used to promote the growth of new firms and new industries.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Assistance to small business is particularly important at this time when thousands of veterans who are potential business and industrial leaders are beginning their careers.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should also give special attention to the decentralization of industry and the development of areas that are now under-industrialized.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: HOUSING: The third major policy is also of great Importance to the national economy-an aggressive program to encourage home construction.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The first Federal program to relieve the veterans' housing shortage was announced in February 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In 1946 one million family housing units have been put under construction and more than 665,000 units have already been completed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The rate of expansion in construction has broken all records.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the coming year the number of dwelling units built will approach, if not surpass, the top construction year of 1926.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The primary responsibility to deliver housing at reasonable prices that veterans can afford rests with private industry and with labor.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Government will continue to expedite the flow of key building materials, to limit nonresidential construction, and to give financial support where it will do the most good.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Measures to stimulate rental housing and new types of housing construction will receive special emphasis.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To reach our long-range goal of adequate housing for all our people, comprehensive housing legislation is urgently required, similar to the non-partisan bill passed by the Senate last year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At a minimum, such legislation should open the way for rebuilding the blighted areas of our cities and should establish positive incentives for the investment of billions of dollars of private capital in large-scale rental housing projects.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It should provide for improvement of housing in rural areas and for the construction, over a 4-year period, of half a million units of public low-rental housing.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It should authorize a single peacetime Federal housing agency to assure efficient use of our resources on the vast housing front.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: FISCAL AFFAIRS: The fourth major policy has to do with the balancing of the budget.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: in a prosperous period such as the present one, the budget of the Federal Government should be balanced.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Prudent management of public finance requires that we begin the process of reducing the public debt.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The budget which I shall submit to you this week has a small margin of surplus.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the Budget Message I am making recommendations which, if accepted, will result in a substantially larger surplus which should be applied to debt retirement.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: One of these recommendations is that the Congress take early action to continue throughout the next fiscal year the war excise tax rates which, under the present law, will expire on June 30, 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Expenditures relating to the war are still high.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Considerable sums are required to alleviate world famine and suffering.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Aid to veterans will continue at peak level.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The world situation is such that large military expenditures are required.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Interest on the public debt and certain other costs are irreducible.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For these reasons I have had to practice stringent economy in preparing the budget;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: and I hope that the Congress will cooperate in this program of economy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: AGRICULTURE: The fifth major policy has to do with the welfare of our farm population.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Production of food reached record heights in 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Much of our tremendous grain crop can readily be sold abroad and thus will become no threat to our domestic markets.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But in the next few years American agriculture can face the same dangers it did after World War I.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the early twenties the Nation failed to maintain outlets for the new productive capacity of our agricultural plant.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It failed to provide means to protect the farmer while he adjusted his acreage to peacetime demands.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The result we all remember too well.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Farm production stayed up while demand and prices fell, in contrast with industry where prices stayed up and output declined.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Farm surpluses piled up, and disaster followed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must make sure of meeting the problems which we failed to meet after the first World War.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Present laws give considerable stability to farm prices for 1947 and 1948, and these 2 years must be utilized to maintain and develop markets for our great productive power.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The purpose of these laws was to permit an orderly transition from war to peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Government plan of support prices was not designed to absorb, at great cost, the unlimited surpluses of a highly productive agriculture.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must not wait until the guarantees expire to set the stage for permanent farm welfare.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The farmer is entitled to a fair income.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Ways can be found to utilize his new skills and better practices, to expand his markets at home and abroad, and to carry out the objectives of a balanced pattern of peacetime production without either undue sacrifice by farm people or undue expense to the Government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: HEALTH AND GENERAL WELFARE: Of all our national resources, none is of more basic value than the health of our people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
