text: Over a year ago I presented to the Congress my views on a national health program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Congress acted on several of the recommendations in this program: mental health, the health of mothers and children, and hospital construction.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I urge this Congress to complete the work begun last year and to enact the most important recommendation of the program-to provide adequate medical care to all who need it, not as charity but on the basis of payments made by the beneficiaries of the program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: One administrative change would help greatly to further our national program in the fields of health, education, and welfare.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I again recommend the establishment of a well-integrated Department of Welfare.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: VETERANS: Fourteen million World War II servicemen have returned to civil life.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The great majority have found their places as citizens of their communities and their Nation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is a tribute to the fiber of our servicemen and to the flexibility of our economy that these adjustments have been made so rapidly and so successfully.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: More than two million of these veterans are attending schools or acquiring job skills through the financial assistance of the Federal Government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Thousands of sick and wounded veterans are daily receiving the best of medical and hospital care.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Half a million have obtained loans, with Government guarantees, to purchase homes or farms or to embark upon new businesses.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Compensation is being paid in almost two million cases for disabilities or death.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: More than three million are continuing to maintain their low-cost National Service Life Insurance policies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Almost seven million veterans have been aided by unemployment and self employment allowances.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Exclusive of mustering-out payments and terminal leave pay, the program for veterans of all wars is costing over seven billion dollars a year - one-fifth of our total Federal budget.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is the most far-reaching and complete veterans program ever conceived by any nation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Except for minor adjustments, I believe that our program of benefits for veterans is now complete.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the long run, the success of the program will not be measured by the number of veterans receiving financial aid or by the number of dollars we spend.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: History will judge us not by the money we spend, but by the further contribution we enable our veterans to make to their country.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In considering any additional legislation, that must be our criterion.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: CIVIL RIGHTS: We have recently witnessed in this country numerous attacks upon the constitutional rights of individual citizens as a result of racial and religious bigotry.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Substantial segments of our people have been prevented from exercising fully their right to participate in the election of public officials, both locally and nationally.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Freedom to engage in lawful callings has been denied.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The will to fight these crimes should be in the hearts of every one of us.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For the Federal Government that fight is now being carried on by the Department of Justice to the full extent of the powers that have been conferred upon it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: While the Constitution withholds from the Federal Government the major task of preserving peace in the several States, I am not convinced that the present legislation reached the limit of Federal power to protect the civil rights of its citizens.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I have, therefore, by Executive order, established the President's Committee on Civil Rights to study and report on the whole problem of federally-secured civil rights, with a view to making recommendations to the Congress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: NATURAL RESOURCES: In our responsibility to promote the general welfare of the people, we have always to consider the natural resources of our country.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They are the foundation of our life.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the development of the great river systems of America there is the major opportunity of our generation to contribute to the increase of the national wealth.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This program is already well along;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: it should be pushed with full vigor.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Nation as to many of our minerals.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The economic progress and the security of our country depend upon an expanding return of mineral discovery and upon improved methods of recovery.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Federal Government must do its part to meet this need.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: FOREIGN AFFAIRS: Progress in reaching our domestic goals is closely related to our conduct of foreign affairs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: All that I have said about maintaining a sound and prosperous economy and improving the welfare of our people has greater meaning because of the world leadership of the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: What we do, or fail to do, at home affects not only ourselves but millions throughout the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we are to fulfill our responsibilities to ourselves and to other peoples, we must make sure that the United States is sound economically, socially, and politically.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Only then will we be able to help bring about the elements of peace in other countries-political stability, economic advancement, and social progress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Peace treaties for Italy, Bulgaria, Rumania, and Hungary have finally been prepared.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Following the signing of these treaties next month in Paris, they will he submitted to the Senate for ratification.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This Government does not regard the treaties as completely satisfactory.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Whatever their defects, however, I am convinced that they are as good as we can hope to obtain by agreement among the principal wartime Allies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Further dispute and delay would gravely jeopardize political stability in the countries concerned for many years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the long months of debate on these treaties, we have made it clear to all nations that the United States will not consent to settlements at the expense of principles we regard as vital to a just and enduring peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have made it equally clear that we will not retreat to isolationism.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our policies will be the same during the forthcoming negotiations in Moscow on the German and Austrian treaties, and during the future conferences on the Japanese treaty.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The delay in arriving at the first peace settlements is due partly to the difficulty of reaching agreement with the Soviet Union on the terms of settlement.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Whatever differences there may have been between us and the Soviet Union, however, should not be allowed to obscure the fact that the basic interests of both nations lie in the early making of a peace under which the peoples of all countries may return, as free men and women, to the essential tasks of production and reconstruction.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The major concern of each of us should be the promotion of collective security, not the advancement of individual security.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our policy toward the Soviet Union is guided by the same principles which determine our policies toward all nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We seek only to uphold the principles of international justice which have been embodied in the Charter of the United Nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must now get on with the peace settlements.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The occupying powers should recognize the independence of Austria and withdraw their troops.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Germans and the Japanese cannot be left in doubt and fear as to their future; they must know their national boundaries, their resources, and what reparations they must pay.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Without trying to manage their internal affairs, we can insure that these countries do not re-arm.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: INTERNATIONAL RELIEF AND DISPLACED PERSONS: The United States can be proud of its part in caring for the peoples reduced to want by the ravages of war, and in aiding nations to restore their national economies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have shipped more supplies to the hungry peoples of the world since the end of the war than all other countries combined!

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: However, insofar as admitting displaced persons is concerned, I do not feel that the United States has done its part.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Only about 5,000 of them have entered this country since May, 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The fact is that the executive agencies are now doing all that is reasonably possible under the limitation of the existing law and established quotas.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Congressional assistance in the form of new legislation is needed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I urge the Congress to turn its attention to this world problem, in an effort to find ways whereby we can fulfill our reponsibilites to these thousands of homeless and suffering refugees of all faiths.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: INTERNATIONAL TRADE: World economic cooperation is essential to world political cooperation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have made a good start on economic cooperation through the International Bank, the International Monetary Fund, and the Export-Import Bank.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must now take other Steps for the reconstruction of world trade and we should continue to Strive for an international trade system as free from obstructions as possible.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: ATOMIC ENERGY: The United States has taken the lead in the endeavor to put atomic energy under effective international control.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We seek no monopoly for ourselves or for any group of nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We ask only that there be safeguards sufficient to insure that no nation will be able to use this power for military purposes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: So long as all governments are not agreed on means of international control of atomic energy, the shadow of fear will obscure the bright prospects for the peaceful use of this enormous power.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In accordance with the Atomic Energy Act of 1946, the Commission established under that law is assuming full jurisdiction over domestic atomic energy enterprise.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The program of the Commission will, of course, be worked out in close collaboration with the military services in conformity with the wish of the Congress, but it is my fervent hope that the military significance of atomic energy will steadily decline.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We look to the Commission to foster the development of atomic energy for industrial use and scientific and medical research.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the vigorous and effective development of peaceful uses of atomic energy rests our hope that this new force may ultimately be turned into a blessing for all nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: MILITARY POLICY: In 1946 the Army and Navy completed the demobilization of their wartime forces.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They are now maintaining the forces which we need for national defense and to fulfill our international obligations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We live in a world in which strength on the part of peace loving nations is still the greatest deterrent to aggression.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: World stability can be destroyed when nations with great responsibilities neglect to maintain the means of discharging those responsibilities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is an age when unforeseen attack could come with unprecedented speed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must be strong enough to defeat, and thus forestall, any such attack.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In our steady progress toward a more rational world order, the need for large armed forces is progressively declining;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: but the stabilizing force of American military strength must not be weakened until our hopes are fully realized.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: When a system of collective security under the United Nations has been established, we shall be willing to lead in collective disarmament, but, until such a system becomes a reality, we must not again allow ourselves to become weak and invite attack.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For those reasons, we need well equipped, well trained armed forces and we must be able to mobilize rapidly our resources in men and material for our own defense, should the need arise.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Army will be reduced to 1,070,000 officers and men by July I, 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Half of the Army will be used for occupation duties abroad and most of the remainder will be employed at home in the support of these overseas forces.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Navy is supporting the occupation troops in Europe and in the Far East.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Its fundamental mission-to support our national interests wherever required-is unchanged.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Navy, including the Marine Corps, will average 571,000 officers and men during the fiscal year 1948.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are encountering serious difficulties in maintaining our forces at even these reduced levels.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Occupation troops are barely sufficient to carry out the duties which our foreign policy requires.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our forces at home are at a point where further reduction is impracticable.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should like an Army and a Navy composed entirely of long-term volunteers, but in spite of liberal inducements the basic needs of the Army are not now being met by voluntary enlistments.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The War Department has advised me that it is unable to make an accurate forecast at the present time as to whether it will be possible to maintain the strength of the Army by relying exclusively on volunteers.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The situation will be much clearer in a few weeks, when the results of the campaign for volunteers are known.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The War Department will make its recommendations as to the need for the extension of Selective Service in sufficient time to enable the Congress to take action prior to the expiration of the present law on March 31st.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The responsibility for maintaining our armed forces at the strength necessary for our national safety rests with the Congress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The development of a trained citizen reserve is also vital to our national security.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This can best be accomplished through universal training.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I have appointed an Advisory Commission on Universal Training to study the various plans for a training program, and I expect that the recommendations of the Commission will be of benefit to the Congress and to me in reaching decisions on this problem.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The cost of the military establishment is substantial.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There is one certain way by which we can cut costs and at the same time enhance our national security.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is by the establishment of a single Department of National Defense.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I shall communicate with the Congress in the near future with reference to the establishment of a single Department of National Defense.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: National security does not consist only of an army, a navy, and an air force.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It rests on a much broader basis.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It depends on a sound economy of prices and wages, on prosperous agriculture, on satisfied and productive workers, on a competitive private enterprise free from monopolistic repression, on continued industrial harmony and production, on civil liberties and human freedoms in all the forces which create in our men and women a strong moral fiber and spiritual stamina.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But we have a higher duty and a greater responsibility than the attainment of our own national security.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our goal is collective security for all mankind.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we can work in a spirit of understanding and mutual respect, we can fulfill this solemn obligation which rests upon us.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The spirit of the American people can set the course of world history.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we maintain and strengthen our cherished ideals, and if we share our great bounty with war-stricken people over the world, then the faith of our citizens in freedom and democracy will be spread over the whole earth and free men everywhere will share our devotion to those ideals.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Let us have the will and the patience to do this job together.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: May the Lord strengthen us in our faith.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: May He give us wisdom to lead the peoples of the world in His ways of peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Mr. President, Mr. Speaker, and Members of the 80th Congress: We are here today to consider the state of the Union.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On this occasion, above all others, the Congress and the President should concentrate their attention, not upon party but upon the country;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: not upon things which divide us but upon those which bind us together the enduring principles of our American system, and our common aspirations for the future welfare and security of the people of the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The United States has become great because we, as a people, have been able to work together for great objectives even while differing about details.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The elements of our strength are many.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They include our democratic government, our economic system, our great natural resources.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But these are only partial explanations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The basic source of our strength is spiritual.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For we are a people with a faith.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We believe in the dignity of man.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We believe that he was created in the image of the Father of us all.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We do not believe that men exist merely to strengthen the state or to be cogs in the economic machine.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We do believe that governments are created to serve the people and that economic systems exist to minister to their wants.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have a profound devotion to the welfare and rights of the individual as a human being.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The faith of our people has particular meaning at this time in history because of the unsettled and changing state of the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The victims of war in many lands are striving to rebuild their lives, and are seeking assurance that the tragedy of war will not occur again.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Throughout the world new ideas are challenging the old.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Men of all nations are re-examining the beliefs by which they live.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Great scientific and industrial changes have released new forces which will affect the future course of civilization.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The state of our Union reflects the changing nature of the modern world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On all sides there is heartening evidence of great energy-of capacity for economic development-and even more important, capacity for spiritual growth.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But accompanying this great activity there are equally great questions, great anxieties, and great aspirations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They represent the concern of an enlightened people that conditions should be so arranged as to make life more worthwhile.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must devote ourselves to finding answers to these anxieties and aspirations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We seek answers which will embody the moral and spiritual elements of tolerance, unselfishness, and brotherhood upon which true freedom and opportunity must rest.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As we examine the state of our Union today, we can benefit from viewing it on a basis of the accomplishments of the last decade and of our goals for the next.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: How far have we come during the last 10 years and how far can we go in the next 10?

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The years that followed brought untold death and destruction.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We shared in the human suffering of the war, but we were fortunate enough to escape most of war's destruction.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We were able through these 10 years to expand the productive strength of our farms and factories.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: More important, however, is the fact that these years brought us new courage, new confidence in the ideals of our free democracy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our deep belief in freedom and justice was reinforced in the crucible of war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On the foundations of our greatly strengthened economy and our renewed confidence in democratic values, we can continue to move forward.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There are some who look with fear and distrust upon planning for the future.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Yet our great national achievements have been attained by those with vision.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our Union was formed, our frontiers were pushed back, and our great industries were built by men who looked ahead.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I propose that we look ahead today toward those goals for the future which have the greatest bearing upon the foundations of our democracy and the happiness of our people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I do so, confident in the thought that with clear objectives and with firm determination, we can, in the next 10 years, build upon the accomplishments of the past decades to achieve a glorious future.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Year by year, beginning now, we must make a substantial part of this progress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our first goal is to secure fully the essential human rights of our citizens.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The United States has always had a deep concern for human rights.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Religious freedom, free speech, and freedom of thought are cherished realities in our land.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Any denial of human rights is a denial of the basic beliefs of democracy and of our regard for the worth of each individual.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Today, however, some of our citizens are still denied equal opportunity for education, for jobs and economic advancement, and for the expression of their views at the polls.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Most serious of all, some are denied equal protection under laws.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Whether discrimination is based on race, or creed, or color, or land of origin, it is utterly contrary to American ideals of democracy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The recent report of the President's Committee on Civil Rights points the way to corrective action by the Federal Government and by State and local governments.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Because of the need for effective Federal action, I shall send a special message to the Congress on this important subject.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should also consider our obligation to assure the fullest possible measure of civil rights to the people of our territories and possessions.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I believe that the time has come for Alaska and Hawaii to be admitted to the Union as States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our second goal is to protect and develop our human resources.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The safeguarding of the rights of our citizens must be accompanied by an equal regard for their opportunities for development and their protection from economic insecurity.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In this Nation the ideals of freedom and equality can be given specific meaning in terms of health, education, social security, and housing.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Over the past 12 years we have erected a sound framework of social security legislation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Many millions of our citizens are now protected against the loss of income which can come with unemployment, old age, or the death of wage earners.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Yet our system has gaps and inconsistencies;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: it is only half finished.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should now extend unemployment compensation, old age benefits, and survivors' benefits to millions who are not now protected.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should also raise the level of benefits.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The greatest gap in our social security structure is the lack of adequate provision for the Nation's health.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are rightly proud of the high standards of medical care we know how to provide in the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The fact is, however, that most of our people cannot afford to pay for the care they need.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I have often and strongly urged that this condition demands a national health program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The heart of the program must be a national system of payment for medical care based on well-tried insurance principles.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This great Nation cannot afford to allow its citizens to suffer needlessly from the lack of proper medical care.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our ultimate aim must be a comprehensive insurance system to protect all our people equally against insecurity and ill health.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Another fundamental aim of our democracy is to provide an adequate education for every person.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our educational systems face a financial crisis.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is deplorable that in a Nation as rich as ours there are millions of children who do not have adequate schoolhouses or enough teachers for a good elementary or secondary education.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If there are educational inadequacies in any State, the whole Nation suffers.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Federal Government has a responsibility for providing financial aid to meet this crisis.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In addition, we must make possible greater equality of opportunity to all our citizens for education.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Only by so doing can we insure that our citizens will be capable of understanding and sharing the responsibilities of democracy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Government's programs for health, education, and security are of such great importance to our democracy that we should now establish an executive department for their administration.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Health and education have their beginning in the home.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: No matter what our hospitals or schools are like, the youth of our Nation are handicapped when millions of them live in city slums and country shacks.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Within the next decade, we must see that every American family has a decent home.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As an immediate step we need the long range housing program which I have recommended on many occasions to this Congress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This should include financial aids designed to yield more housing at lower prices.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It should provide public housing for low-income families, and vigorous development of new techniques to lower the cost of building.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Until we can overcome the present drastic housing shortage, we must extend and strengthen rent control.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have had, and shall continue to have, a special interest in the welfare of our veterans.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Over 14 million men and women who served in the armed forces in World War II have now returned to civilian life.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Over 2 million veterans are being helped through school.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Millions have been aided while finding jobs, and have been helped in buying homes, in obtaining medical care, and in adjusting themselves to physical handicaps.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: All but a very few veterans have successfully made the transition from military life to their home communities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The success of our veterans' program is proved by this fact.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This Nation is proud of the eagerness shown by our veterans to become self-reliant and self-supporting citizens.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our third goal is to conserve and use our natural resources so that they can contribute most effectively to the welfare of our people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The resources given by nature to this country are rich and extensive.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The material foundations of our growth and economic development are the bounty of our fields, the wealth of our mines and forests, and the energy of our waters.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As a Nation, we are coming to appreciate more each day the close relationship between the conservation of these resources and the preservation of our national strength.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are doing far less than we know how to do to make use of our resources without destroying them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Both the public and private use of these resources must have the primary objective of maintaining and increasing these basic supports for an expanding future.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must continue to take specific steps toward this goal.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must vigorously defend our natural wealth against those who would misuse it for selfish gain.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We need accurate and comprehensive knowledge of our mineral resources and must intensify our efforts to develop new supplies and to acquire stockpiles of scarce materials.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We need to protect and restore our land public and private-through combating erosion and rebuilding the fertility of the soil.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must expand our reclamation program to bring millions of acres of arid land into production, and to improve water supplies for additional millions of acres.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This will provide new opportunities for veterans and others, particularly in the West, and aid in providing a rising living standard for a growing population.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must protect and restore our forests by sustained-yield forestry and by planting new trees in areas now slashed and barren.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must continue to erect multiple-purpose dams on our great rivers-not only to reclaim land, but also to prevent floods, to extend our inland waterways and to provide hydroelectric power.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This public power must not be monopolized for private gain.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Only through well established policies of transmitting power directly to its market and thus encouraging widespread use at low rates can the Federal Government assure the people of their full share of its benefits.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Additional power - public and private - is needed to raise the ceilings now imposed by power shortages on industrial and agricultural development.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should achieve the wise use of resources through the integrated development of our great river basins.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We can learn much from our Tennessee Valley experience.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should no longer delay in applying the lessons of that vast undertaking to our other great river basins.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our fourth goal is to lift the standard of living for all our people by strengthening our economic system and sharing more broadly among our people the goods we produce.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The amazing economic progress of the past 10 years points the way for the next 10.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Today 14 million more people have jobs than in 1938.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our yearly output of goods and services has increased by two-thirds.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The average income of our people, measured in dollars of equal purchasing power, has increased-after taxes-by more than 50 percent.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In no other 10 years have farmers, businessmen, and wage earners made such great gains.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We may not be able to expand as rapidly in the next decade as in the last, because we are now starting from full employment and very high production.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But we can increase our annual output by at least one-third above the present level.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We can lift our standard of living to nearly double what it was 10 years ago.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we distribute these gains properly, we can go far toward stamping out poverty in our generation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To do this, agriculture, business, and labor must move forward together.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Permanent farm prosperity and agricultural abundance will be achieved only as our whole economy grows and prospers.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The farmer can sell more food at good prices when the incomes of wage earners are high and when there is full employment.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Adequate diets for every American family, and the needs of our industries at full production, will absorb a farm output well above our present levels.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Although the average farmer is now better off than ever before, farm families as a whole have only begun to catch up with the standards of living enjoyed in the cities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In 1946, the average income of farm people was $779, contrasted with an average income of $1,288 for non-farm people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Within the next decade, we should eliminate elements of inequality in these living standards.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To this end our farm program should enable the farmer to market his varied crops at fair price levels and to improve his standard of living.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We need to continue price supports for major farm commodities on a basis which will afford reasonable protection against fluctuations in the levels of production and demand.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The present price support program must be reexamined and modernized.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Crop insurance should be strengthened and its benefits extended in order to protect the farmer against the special hazards to which he is subject.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We also need to improve the means for getting farm products into markets and into the hands of consumers.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Cooperatives which directly or indirectly serve this purpose must be encouraged - not discouraged.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The school lunch program should be continued and adequately financed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We need to go forward with the rural electrification program to bring the benefits of electricity to all our farm population.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We can, and must, aid and encourage farmers to conserve their soil resources and restore the fertility of the land that has suffered from neglect or unwise use.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: All these are practical measures upon which we should act immediately to enable agriculture to make its full contribution to our prosperity.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must also strengthen our economic system within the next decade by enlarging our industrial capacity within the framework of our free enterprise system.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are today far short of the industrial capacity we need for a growing future.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At least $50 billion should be invested by industry to improve and expand our productive facilities over the next few years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But this is only the beginning.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The industrial application of atomic energy and other scientific advances will constantly open up further opportunities for expansion.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Farm prosperity and high employment will call for an immensely increased output of goods and services.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Growth and vitality in our economy depend on vigorous private enterprise.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Free competition is the key to industrial development, full production and employment, fair prices, and an ever improving standard of living.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Competition is seriously limited today in many industries by the concentration of economic power and other elements of monopoly.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The appropriation of sufficient funds to permit proper enforcement of the present antitrust laws is essential.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Beyond that we should go on to strengthen our legislation to protect competition.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Another basic element of a strong economic system is the well-being of the wage earners.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have learned that the well-being of workers depends on high production and consequent high employment.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have learned equally well that the welfare of industry and agriculture depends on high incomes for our workers.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Government has wisely chosen to set a floor under wages.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But our 40-cent minimum wage is inadequate and obsolete.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I recommend the lifting of the minimum wage to 75 cents an hour.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In general, however, we must continue to rely on our sound system of collective bargaining to set wage scales.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Workers' incomes should increase at a rate consistent with the maintenance of sound price, profit, and wage relationships and with increase of productivity.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Government's part in labor-management relations is now largely controlled by the terms of the Labor-Management Relations Act of 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I made my attitude clear on this act in my veto message to the Congress last June.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Nothing has occurred since to change my opinion of this law.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As long as it remains the law of the land, however, I shall carry out my constitutional duty and administer it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As we look ahead we can understand the crucial importance of restraint and wisdom in arriving at new labor-management contracts.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Work stoppages would result in a loss of production-a loss which could bring higher prices for our citizens and could also deny the necessities of life to the hard pressed peoples of other lands.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is my sincere hope that the representatives of labor and of industry will bear in mind that the Nation as a whole has a vital stake in the success of their bargaining efforts.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we surmount our current economic difficulties, we can move ahead to a great increase in our national income which will enable all our people to enjoy richer and fuller lives.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: All of us must advance together.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: One fifth of our families now have average annual incomes of less than $850.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must see that our gains in national income are made more largely available to those with low incomes, whose need is greatest.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This will benefit us all through providing a stable foundation of buying power to maintain prosperity.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Business, labor, agriculture, and Government, working together, must develop the policies which will make possible the realization of the full benefits of our economic system.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our fifth goal is to achieve world peace based on principles of freedom and justice and the equality of all nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Twice within our generation, world wars have taught us that we cannot isolate ourselves from the rest of the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have learned that the loss of freedom in any area of the world means a loss of freedom to ourselves - that the loss of independence by any nation adds directly to the insecurity of the United States and all free nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have learned that a healthy world economy is essential to world peace-that economic distress is a disease whose evil effects spread far beyond the boundaries of the afflicted nation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For these reasons the United States is vigorously following policies designed to achieve a peaceful and prosperous world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are giving, and will continue to give, our full support to the United Nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: While that organization has encountered unforeseen and unwelcome difficulties, I am confident of its ultimate success.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are also devoting our efforts toward world economic recovery and the revival of world trade.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These actions are closely related and mutually supporting.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We believe that the United States can be an effective force for world peace only if it is strong.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We look forward to the day when nations will decrease their armaments.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Yet so long as there remains serious opposition to the ideals of a peaceful world, we must maintain strong armed forces.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The passage of the National Security Act by the Congress at its last session was a notable step in providing for the security of this country.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A further step which I consider of even greater importance is the early provision for universal training.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There are many elements in a balanced national security program, all interrelated and necessary, but universal training should be the foundation for them all.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A favorable decision by the Congress at an early date is of world importance.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I am convinced that such action is vital to the security of this Nation and to the maintenance of its leadership.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The United States is engaged today in many international activities directed toward the creation of lasting peaceful relationships among nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have been giving substantial aid to Greece and Turkey to assist those nations in preserving their integrity against foreign pressures.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Had it not been for our aid, their situation today might well be radically different.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The continued integrity of those countries will have a powerful effect upon other nations in the Middle East and in Europe struggling to maintain their independence while they repair the damages of war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The United States has special responsibilities with respect to the countries in which we have occupation forces: Germany, Austria, Japan, and Korea.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our efforts to reach agreements on peace settlements for these countries have so far been blocked.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But we shall continue to exert our utmost efforts to obtain satisfactory settlements for each of these nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Many thousands of displaced persons, still living in camps overseas, should be allowed entry into the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I again urge the Congress to pass suitable legislation at once so that this Nation may do its share in caring for the homeless and suffering refugees of all faiths.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I believe that the admission of these persons will add to the strength and energy of this Nation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are moving toward our goal of world peace in many ways.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But the most important efforts which we are now making are those which support world economic reconstruction.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are seeking to restore the world trading system which was shattered by the war and to remedy the economic paralysis which grips many countries.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To restore world trade we have recently taken the lead in bringing about the greatest reduction of world tariffs that the world has ever seen.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The extension of the provisions of the Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act, which made this achievement possible, is of extreme importance.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must also go on to support the International Trade Organization, through which we hope to obtain worldwide agreement on a code of fair conduct in international trade.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our present major effort toward economic reconstruction is to support the program for recovery developed by the countries of Europe.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In my recent message to the Congress, I outlined the reasons why it is wise and necessary for the United States to extend this support.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I want to reaffirm my belief in the soundness and the promise of this proposal.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: When the European economy is strengthened, the product of its industry will be of benefit to many other areas of economic distress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The ability of free men to overcome hunger and despair will be a moral stimulus to the entire world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We intend to work also with other nations in achieving world economic recovery.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We shall continue our cooperation with the nations of the Western Hemisphere.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A special program of assistance to China, to provide urgent relief needs and to speed reconstruction, will be submitted to the Congress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Unfortunately, not all governments share the hope of the people of the United States that economic reconstruction in many areas of the world can be achieved through cooperative effort among nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In spite of these differences we will go forward with our efforts to overcome economic paralysis.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: No nation by itself can carry these programs to success;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: they depend upon the cooperative and honest efforts of all participating countries.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Yet the leadership is inevitably ours.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I consider it of the highest importance that the Congress should authorize support for the European recovery program for the period from April 1, 1948, to June 30, 1952, with an initial amount for the first 15 months of $6.8 billion.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I urge the Congress to act promptly on this vital measure of our foreign policy this decisive contribution to world peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are following a sound, constructive, and practical course in carrying out our determination to achieve peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are fighting poverty, hunger, and suffering.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This leads to peace-not war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are building toward a world where all nations, large and small alike, may live free from the fear of aggression.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This leads to peace-not war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Above all else, we are striving to achieve a concord among the peoples of the world based upon the dignity of the individual and the brotherhood of man.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This leads to peace-not war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We can go forward with confidence that we are following sound policies, both at home and with other nations, which will lead us toward our great goals for economic, social and moral achievement.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As we enter the new year, we must surmount one major problem which affects all our goals.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is the problem of inflation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Already inflation in this country is undermining the living standards of millions of families.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Food costs too much.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Housing has reached fantastic price levels.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Schools and hospitals are in financial distress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Inflation threatens to bring on disagreement and strife between labor and management.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Worst of all, inflation holds the threat of another depression, just as we had a depression after the unstable boom following the First World War.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: When I announced last October that the Congress was being called into session, I described the price increases which had taken place since June 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Wholesale prices had increased 40 percent; retail prices had increased 23 percent.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Since October prices have continued to rise.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Wholesale prices have gone up at an annual rate of 18 percent.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Retail prices have gone up at an annual rate of 10 percent.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The events which have occurred since I presented my 10-point anti-inflation program to the Congress in November have made it even clearer that all in points are essential.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: High prices must not be our means of rationing.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must deal effectively and at once with the high cost of living.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must stop the spiral of inflation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I trust that within the shortest possible time the Congress will make available to the Government the weapons that are so desperately needed in the fight against inflation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: One of the most powerful anti-inflationary factors in our economy today is the excess of Government revenues over expenditures.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Government expenditures have been and must continue to be held at the lowest safe levels.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Since V-J day Federal expenditures have been sharply reduced.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They have been cut from more than $63 billion in the fiscal year 1946 to less than $38 billion in the present fiscal year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The number of civilian employees has been cut nearly in half-from 3/4 million down to 2 million.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On the other hand, Government revenues must not be reduced.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Until inflation has been stopped there should be no cut in taxes that is not offset by additions at another point in our tax structure.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Certain adjustments should be made within our existing tax structure that will not affect total receipts, yet will adjust the tax burden so that those least able to pay will have their burden lessened by the transfer of a portion of it to those best able to pay.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Many of our families today are suffering hardship because of the high cost of living.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At the same time profits of corporations have reached an all-time record in 1947.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Corporate profits total $17 billion after taxes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This compared with $12.5 billion in 1946, the previous high year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Because of this extraordinarily high level of profits, corporations can well afford to carry a larger share of the tax load at this time.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During this period in which the high cost of living is bearing down on so many of our families, tax adjustments should be made to ease their burden.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The low-income group particularly is being pressed very hard.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To this group a tax adjustment would result in a saving that could be used to buy the necessities of life.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I recommend therefore that, effective January I, 1948, a cost of living tax credit be extended to our people consisting of a credit of $40 to each individual taxpayer and an additional credit of $40 for each dependent.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Thus the income tax of a man with a wife and two children would be reduced $160.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The credit would be extended to all taxpayers, but it would be particular helpful to those in the low-income group.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is estimated that such a tax credit would reduce Federal revenue by $3.2 billion.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This reduction should be made up by increasing the tax on corporate profits in an amount that will produce this sum-with appropriate adjustments for small corporations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is the proper method of tax relief at this time.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It gives relief to those who need it most without cutting the total tax revenue of the Government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: When the present danger of inflation has passed we should consider tax reduction based upon a revision of our entire tax structure.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: When we have conquered inflation, we shall be in a position to move forward toward our chosen goals.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As we do so, let us keep ever before us our high purposes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are determined that every citizen of this Nation shall have an equal right and an equal opportunity to grow in wisdom and in stature and to take his place in the control of his Nation's destiny.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are determined that the productive resources of this Nation shall be used wisely and fully for the benefit of all.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are determined that the democratic faith of our people and the strength of our resources shall contribute their full share to the attainment of enduring peace in the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is our faith in human dignity that underlies these purposes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is this faith that keeps us a strong and vital people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is a time to remind ourselves of these fundamentals.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For today the whole world looks to us for leadership.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is the hour to rededicate ourselves to the faith in mankind that makes us strong.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is the hour to rededicate ourselves to the faith in God that gives us confidence as we face the challenge of the years ahead.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Mr. President, Mr. Speaker, Members of the Congress: I am happy to report to this 81st Congress that the state of the Union is good.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our Nation is better able than ever before to meet the needs of the American people, and to give them their fair chance in the pursuit of happiness.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This great Republic is foremost among the nations of the world in the search for peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the last 16 years, our people have been creating a society which offers new opportunities for every man to enjoy his share of the good things of life.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In this society, we are conservative about the values and principles which we cherish; but we are forward-looking in protecting those values and principles and in extending their benefits.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have rejected the discredited theory that the fortunes of the Nation should be in the hands of a privileged few.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: concept of national prosperity.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Instead, we believe that our economic system should rest on a democratic foundation and that wealth should be created for the benefit of all.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The recent election shows that the people of the United States are in favor of this kind of society and want to go on improving it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The American people have decided that poverty is just as wasteful and just as unnecessary as preventable disease.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have pledged our common resources to help one another in the hazards and struggles of individual life.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We believe that no unfair prejudice or artificial distinction should bar any citizen of the United States of America from an education, or from good health, or from a job that he is capable of performing.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The attainment of this kind of society demands the best efforts of every citizen in every walk of life, and it imposes increasing responsibilities on the Government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Government must work with industry, labor, and the farmers in keeping our economy running at full speed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Government must see that every American has a chance to obtain his fair share of our increasing abundance.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These responsibilities go hand in hand.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We cannot maintain prosperity unless we have a fair distribution of opportunity and a widespread consumption of the products of our factories and farms.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our Government has undertaken to meet these responsibilities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have made tremendous public investments in highways, hydroelectric power projects, soil conservation, and reclamation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have established a system of social security.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have enacted laws protecting the rights and the welfare of our working people and the income of our farmers.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These Federal policies have paid for themselves many times over.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They have strengthened the material foundations of our democratic ideals.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Without them, our present prosperity would be impossible.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Reinforced by these policies, our private enterprise system has reached new heights of production.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Since the boom year of 1929, while our population has increased by only 20 percent, our agricultural production has increased by 45 percent, and our industrial production has increased by 75 percent.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are turning out far more goods and more wealth per worker than we have ever done before.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This progress has confounded the gloomy prophets-at home and abroad-who predicted the downfall of American capitalism.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The people of the United States, going their own way, confident in their own powers, have achieved the greatest prosperity the world has even seen.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But, great as our progress has been, we still have a long way to go.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As we look around the country, many of our shortcomings stand out in bold relief.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are suffering from excessively high prices.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our production is still not large enough to satisfy our demands.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our minimum wages are far too low.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Small business is losing ground to growing monopoly.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our farmers still face an uncertain future.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And too many of them lack the benefits of our modern civilization.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Some of our natural resources are still being wasted.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are acutely short of electric power, although the means for developing such power are abundant.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Five million families are still living in slums and firetraps.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Three million families share their homes with others.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our health is far behind the progress of medical science.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Proper medical care is so expensive that it is out of the reach of the great majority of our citizens.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our schools, in many localities, are utterly inadequate.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our democratic ideals are often thwarted by prejudice and intolerance.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Each of these shortcomings is also an opportunity-an opportunity for the Congress and the President to work for the good of the people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: boom and bust.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This objective cannot be attained by government alone.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Indeed, the greater part of the task must be performed by individual efforts under our system of free enterprise.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We can keep our present prosperity, and increase it, only if free enterprise and free government work together to that end.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We cannot afford to float along ceaselessly on a postwar boom until it collapses.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is not enough merely to prepare to weather a recession if it comes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Instead, government and business must work together constancy to achieve more and more jobs and more and more production-which mean more and more prosperity for all the people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The business cycle is man-made;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: and men of good will, working together, can smooth it out.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: So far as business is concerned, it should plan for steady, vigorous expansion-seeking always to increase its output, lower its prices, and avoid the vices of monopoly and restriction.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: So long as business does this, it will be contributing to continued prosperity, and it will have the help and encouragement of the Government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Employment Act of 1946 pledges the Government to use all its resources to promote maximum employment, production, and purchasing power.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This means that the Government is firmly committed to protect business and the people against the dangers of recession and against the evils of inflation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This means that the Government must adapt its plans and policies to meet changing circumstances.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At the present time, our prosperity is threatened by inflationary pressures at a number of critical points in our economy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And the Government must be in a position to take effective action at these danger spots.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To that end, I recommend that the Congress enact legislation for the following purposes: First, to continue the power to control consumer credit and enlarge the power to control bank credit.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Second, to grant authority to regulate speculation on the commodity exchanges.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Third, to continue export control authority and to provide adequate machinery for its enforcement.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Fourth, to continue the priorities and allocation authority in the field of transportation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Fifth, to authorize priorities and allocations for key materials in short supply.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Sixth, to extend and strengthen rent control.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Seventh, to provide standby authority to impose price ceilings for scarce commodities which basically affect essential industrial production or the cost of living, and to limit unjustified wage adjustments which would force a break in an established price ceiling.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Eighth, to authorize an immediate study of the adequacy of production facilities for materials in critically short supply, such as steel;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: and, if found necessary, to authorize Government loans for the expansion of production facilities to relieve such shortages, and to authorize the construction of such facilities directly, if action by private industry fails to meet our needs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Economic Report, which I shall submit to the Congress shortly, will discuss in detail the economic background for these recommendations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: One of the most important factors in maintaining prosperity is the Government's fiscal policy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At this time, it is essential not only that the Federal budget be balanced, but also that there be a substantial surplus to reduce inflationary pressures, and to permit a sizable reduction in the national debt, which now stands at $252 billion.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I recommend, therefore, that the Congress enact new tax legislation to bring in an additional $4 billion of Government revenue.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This should come principally from additional corporate taxes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A portion should come from revised estate and gift taxes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Consideration should be given to raising personal income rates in the middle and upper brackets.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we want to keep our economy running in high gear, we must be sure that every group has the incentive to make its full contribution to the national welfare.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At present, the working men and women of the Nation are unfairly discriminated against by a statute that abridges their rights, curtails their constructive efforts, and hampers our system of free collective bargaining.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That statute is the Labor-Management Relations Act of 1947, sometimes called the Taft-Hartley Act.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That act should be repealed!

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Wagner Act should be reenacted.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: However, certain improvements, which I recommended to the Congress 2 years ago, are needed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Jurisdictional strikes and unjustified secondary boycotts should be prohibited.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The use of economic force to decide issues arising out of the interpretation of existing contracts should be prevented.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Without endangering our democratic freedoms, means should be provided for setting up machinery for preventing strikes in vital industries which affect the public interest.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Department of Labor should be rebuilt and strengthened and those units properly belonging within that department should be placed in it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The health of our economy and its maintenance at high levels further require that the minimum wage fixed by law should be raised to at least 75 cents an hour.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If our free enterprise economy is to be strong and healthy, we must reinvigorate the forces of competition.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must assure small business the freedom and opportunity to grow and prosper.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To this purpose, we should strengthen our antitrust laws by closing those loopholes that permit monopolistic mergers and consolidations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our national farm program should be improved-not only in the interest of the farmers, but for the lasting prosperity of the whole Nation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our goals should he abundant farm production and parity income for agriculture.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Standards of living on the farm should be just as good as anywhere else in the country.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Farm price supports are an essential part of our program to achieve these ends.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Price supports should be used to prevent farm price declines which are out of line with general price levels, to facilitate adjustments in production to consumer demands, and to promote good land use.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our price support legislation must be adapted to these objectives.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The authority of the Commodity Credit Corporation to provide adequate storage space for crops should be restored.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our program for farm prosperity should also seek to expand the domestic market for agricultural products, particularly among low-income groups, and to increase and stabilize foreign markets.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should give special attention to extending modern conveniences and services to our farms.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Rural electrification should be pushed forward.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And in considering legislation relating to housing, education, health, and social security, special attention should be given to rural problems.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our growing population and the expansion of our economy depend upon the wise management of our land, water, forest, and mineral wealth.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In our present dynamic economy, the task of conservation is not to lockup our resources but to develop and improve them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Failure, today, to make the investments which are necessary to support our progress in the future would be false economy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must push forward the development of our rivers for power, irrigation, navigation, and flood control.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should apply the lessons of our Tennessee Valley experience to our other great river basins.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I again recommend action be taken by the Congress to approve the St. Lawrence Seaway and Power project.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is about the fifth time I have recommended it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must adopt a program for the planned use of the petroleum reserves under the sea, which are-and must remain-vested in the Federal Government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must extend our programs of soil conservation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must place our forests on a sustained yield basis, and encourage the development of new sources of vital minerals.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In all this we must make sure that the benefits of these public undertakings are directly available to the people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Public power should be earned to consuming areas by public transmission lines where necessary to provide electricity at the lowest possible rates.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Irrigation waters should serve family farms and not land speculators.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Government has still other opportunities-to help raise the standard of living of our citizens.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These opportunities lie in the fields of social security, health, education, housing, and civil rights.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The present coverage of the social security laws is altogether inadequate; the benefit payments are too low.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: One-third of our workers are not covered.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Those who receive old-age and survivors insurance benefits receive an average payment of only $25 a month.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Many others who cannot work because they are physically disabled are left to the mercy of charity.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should expand our social security program, both as to the size of the benefits and the extent of coverage, against the economic hazards due to unemployment, old age, sickness, and disability.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must spare no effort to raise the general level of health in this country.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In a nation as rich as ours, it is a shocking fact that tens of millions lack adequate medical care.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are short of doctors, hospitals, nurses.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must remedy these shortages.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Moreover, we need-and we must have without further delay-a system of prepaid medical insurance which will enable every American to afford good medical care.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is equally shocking that millions of our children are not receiving a good education.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Millions of them are in overcrowded, obsolete buildings.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are short of teachers, because teachers' salaries are too low to attract new teachers, or to hold the ones we have.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: All these school problems will become much more acute as a result of the tremendous increase in the enrollment in our elementary schools in the next few years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I cannot repeat too strongly my desire for prompt Federal financial aid to the States to help them operate and maintain their school systems.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The governmental agency which now administers the programs of health, education, and social security should be given full departmental status.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The housing shortage continues to be acute.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As an immediate step, the Congress should enact the provisions for low-rent public housing, slum clearance, farm housing, and housing research which I have repeatedly recommended.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The number of low-rent public housing units provided for in the legislation should be increased to 1 million units in the next 7 years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Even this number of units will not begin to meet our need for new housing.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Most of the houses we need will have to be built by private enterprise, without public subsidy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: By producing too few rental units and too large a proportion of high-priced houses, the building industry is rapidly pricing itself out of the market.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Building costs must be lowered.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Government is now engaged in a campaign to induce all segments of the building industry to concentrate on the production of lower priced housing.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Additional legislation to encourage such housing will be submitted.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The authority which I have requested, to allocate materials in short supply and to impose price ceilings on such materials, could be used, if found necessary, to channel more materials into homes large enough for family life at prices which wage earners can afford.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The driving force behind our progress is our faith in our democratic institutions.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That faith is embodied in the promise of equal rights and equal opportunities which the founders of our Republic proclaimed to their countrymen and to the whole world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The fulfillment of this promise is among the highest purposes of government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The civil rights proposals I made to the 80th Congress, I now repeat to the 81st Congress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They should be enacted in order that the Federal Government may assume the leadership and discharge the obligations clearly placed upon it by the Constitution.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I stand squarely behind those proposals.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our domestic programs are the foundation of our foreign policy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The world today looks to us for leadership because we have so largely realized, within our borders, those benefits of democratic government for which most of the peoples of the world are yearning.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are following a foreign policy which is the outward expression of the democratic faith we profess.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are doing what we can to encourage free states and free peoples throughout the world, to aid the suffering and afflicted in foreign lands, and to strengthen democratic nations against aggression.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The heart of our foreign policy is peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are supporting a world organization to keep peace and a world economic policy to create prosperity for mankind.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our guiding star is the principle of international cooperation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To this concept we have made a national commitment as profound as anything in history.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To it we have pledged our resources and our honor.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Until a system of world security is established upon which we can safely rely, we cannot escape the burden of creating and maintaining armed forces sufficient to deter aggression.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
