text: We have made great progress in the last year in the effective organization of our Armed Forces, but further improvements in our national security legislation are necessary.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Universal training is essential to the security of the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the course of this session I shall have occasion to ask the Congress to consider several measures in the field of foreign policy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At this time, I recommend that we restore the Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act to full effectiveness, and extend it for 3 years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should also open our doors to displaced persons without unfair discrimination.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It should be clear by now to all citizens that we are not seeking to freeze the status quo.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have no intention of preserving the injustices of the past.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We welcome the constructive efforts being made by many nations to achieve a better life for their citizens.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the European recovery program, in our good-neighbor policy and in the United Nations, we have begun to batter down those national walls which block the economic growth and the social advancement of the peoples of the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We believe that if we hold resolutely to this course, the principle of international cooperation will eventually command the approval even of those nations which are now seeking to weaken or subvert it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We stand at the opening of an era which can mean either great achievement or terrible catastrophe for ourselves and for all mankind.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The strength of our Nation must continue to be used in the interest of all our people rather than a privileged few.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It must continue to be used unselfishly in the struggle for world peace and the betterment of mankind the world over.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is the task before us.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is not an easy one.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It has many complications, and there will be strong opposition from selfish interests.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I hope for cooperation from farmers, from labor, and from business.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Every segment of our population and every individual has a right to expect from our Government a fair deal.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In 1945, when I came down before the Congress for the first time on April 16, I quoted to you King Solomon's prayer that he wanted wisdom and the ability to govern his people as they should be governed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I explained to you at that time that the task before me was one of the greatest in the history of the world, and that it was necessary to have the complete cooperation of the Congress and the people of the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Well now, we are taking a new start with the same situation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is absolutely essential that your President have the complete cooperation of the Congress to carry out the great work that must be done to keep the peace in this world, and to keep this country prosperous.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The people of this great country have a right to expect that the Congress and the President will work in closest cooperation with one objective-the welfare of the people of this Nation as a whole.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the months ahead I know that I shall be able to cooperate with this Congress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Now, I am confident that the Divine Power which has guided us to this time of fateful responsibility and glorious opportunity will not desert us now.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: With that help from Almighty God which we have humbly acknowledged at every turning point in our national life, we shall be able to perform the great tasks which He now sets before us.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Mr. President, Mr. Speaker, Members of the Congress: A year ago I reported to this Congress that the state of the Union was good.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I am happy to be able to report to you today that the state of the Union Continues to be good.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our Republic continues to increase in the enjoyment of freedom within its borders, and to offer strength and encouragement to all those who love freedom throughout the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the past year we have made notable progress in strengthening the foundations of peace and freedom, abroad and at home.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have taken important steps in securing the North Atlantic community against aggression.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have continued our successful support of European recovery.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have returned to our established policy of expanding international trade through reciprocal agreement.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have strengthened our support of the United Nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: While great problems still confront us, the greatest danger has receded-the possibility which faced us 3 years ago that most of Europe and the Mediterranean area might collapse under totalitarian pressure.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Today, the free peoples of the world have new vigor and new hope for the cause of peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In our domestic affairs, we have made notable advances toward broader opportunity and a better life for all our citizens.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have met and reversed the first significant downturn in economic activity since the war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In accomplishing this, Government programs for maintaining employment and purchasing power have been of tremendous benefit.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As the result of these programs, and t he wisdom and good judgment of our businessmen and workers, major readjustments have been made without widespread suffering.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the past year, we have also made a good start in providing housing for low-income groups;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: we have raised minimum wages;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: we have gone forward with the development of our natural resources;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: we have given a greater assurance of stability to the farmer;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: and we have improved the organization and efficiency of our Government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Today, by the grace of God, we stand a free and prosperous nation with greater possibilities for the future than any people ever had before in the history of the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are now, in this year of 1950, nearing the midpoint of the 20th century.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The first half of this century will be known as the most turbulent and eventful period in recorded history.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The swift pace of events promises to make the next 50 years decisive in the history of man on this planet.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The scientific and industrial revolution which began two centuries ago has, in the last 50 years, caught up the peoples of the globe in a common destiny.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Two world-shattering wars have proved that no corner of the earth can be isolated from the affairs of mankind.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The human race has reached a turning point.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Man has opened the secrets of nature and mastered new powers.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If he uses them wisely, he can reach new heights of civilization.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If he uses them foolishly, they may destroy him.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Man must create the moral and legal framework for the world which will insure that his new powers are used for good and not for evil.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In shaping the outcome, the people of the United States will play a leading role.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Among all the great changes that have occurred in the last 50 years, none is more important than the change in the position of the United States in world affairs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Fifty years ago we were a country devoted largely to our own internal affairs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our industry was growing, and we had new interests in the Far East and in the Caribbean, but we were primarily concerned with the development of vast areas of our own continental territory.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Today, our population has doubled.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our national production has risen from about $50 billion, in terms of today's prices, to the staggering figure of $255 billion a year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have a more productive economic system and a greater industrial potential than any other nation on the globe.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our standard of living is an inspiration for all other peoples.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Even the slightest changes in our economic and social life have their effect on other countries all around the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our tremendous strength has brought with it tremendous responsibilities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have moved from the outer edge to the center of world affairs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Other nations look to us for a wise exercise of our economic and military strength, and for vigorous support of the ideals of representative government and a free society.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We will not fail them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our objective in the world is peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our country has joined with others in the task of achieving peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We know now that this is not an easy task, or a short one.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But we are determined to see it through.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Both of our great political parties are committed to working together-and I am sure they will continue to work together-to achieve this end.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are prepared to devote our energy and our resources to this task, because we know that our own security and the future of mankind are at stake.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Right here, I want to say that no one appreciates more than I the bipartisan cooperation in foreign affairs which has been enjoyed by this administration.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our success in working with other nations to achieve peace depends largely on what we do at home.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must preserve our national strength.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Strength is not simply a matter of arms and force.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is a matter of economic growth, and social health, and vigorous institutions, public and private.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We can achieve peace only if we maintain our productive energy, our democratic institutions, and our firm belief in individual freedom.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our surest guide in the days that lie ahead will be the spirit in which this great Republic was founded.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must make our decisions in the conviction that all men are created equal, that they are equally entitled to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, and that the duty of government is to serve these ends.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This country of ours has experienced many blessings, but none greater than its dedication to these principles.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At every point in our history, these ideals have served to correct our failures and shortcomings, to spur us on to greater efforts, and to keep clearly before us the primary purpose of our existence as a nation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They have enshrined for us, a principle of government, the moral imperative to do justice, and the divine command to men to love one another.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These principles give meaning to all that we do.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In foreign policy, they mean that we can never be tolerant of oppression or tyranny.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They mean that we must throw our weight on the side of greater freedom and a better life for all peoples.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These principles confirm us in carrying out the specific programs for peace which we have already begun.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We shall continue to give our wholehearted support to the United Nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We believe that this organization can ultimately provide the framework of international law and morality without which mankind cannot survive.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It has already set up new standards for the conduct of nations in the Declaration of Human Rights and the Convention on Genocide.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is moving ahead to give meaning to the concept of world brotherhood through a wide variety of cultural, economic, and technical activities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The events of the past year again showed the value of the United Nations in bringing about the peaceful adjustment of tense international controversies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In Indonesia and in Palestine the efforts of the United Nations have put a stop to bloodshed and pave d the way to peaceful settlements.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are working toward the time when the United Nations will control weapons of mass destruction and will have the forces to preserve international law and order.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: While the world remains unsettled, however, and as long as our own security and the security of the free world require, we will maintain a strong and well-balanced defense organization.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Selective Service System is an essential part of our defense plans, and it must be continued.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Under the principles of the United Nations Charter we must continue to share in the common defense of free nations against aggression.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At the last session this Congress laid the basis for this joint effort.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We now must put into effect the common defense plans that are being worked out.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We shall continue our efforts for world economic recovery, because world prosperity is the only sure foundation of a permanent peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As an immediate means to this end we must continue our support of the European recovery program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This program has achieved great success in the first 2 years of its operation, but it has not yet been completed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we were to stop this program now, or cripple it, just because it is succeeding, we should be doing exactly what the enemies of democracy want us to do.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should be just as foolish as a man who, for reasons of false economy, failed to put a roof on his house after building the foundation an d the walls.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: World prosperity also requires that we do all we can to expand world trade.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As a major step in this direction we should promptly join the International Trade Organization.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The purpose of this organization, which the United States has been foremost in creating, is to establish a code of fair practice, and an international authority for adjusting differences in international commercial relations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is an effort to prevent the kind of anarchy and irresponsibility in world trade which did so much to bring about the world depression of the 1930's.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: An expanding world economy requires the improvement of living standards and the development of resources in areas where human poverty and misery now prevail.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Without such improvement the recovery of Europe and the future of our own economy will not be se cure.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I urge that the Congress adopt the legislation now before it to provide for increasing the flow of technical assistance and capital investment in underdeveloped regions.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is more essential now than ever, if the ideals of freedom and representative government are to prevail in these areas, and particularly in the Far East, that their peoples experience, in their own lives, the benefits of scientific and economic advance s.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This program will require the movement of large amounts of capital from the industrial nations, and particularly from the United States, to productive uses in the underdeveloped areas of the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Recent world events make prompt action imperative.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This program is in the interest of all peoples-and has nothing in common with either the old imperialism of the last century or the new imperialism of the Communists.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our aim for a peaceful, democratic world of free peoples will be achieved in the long run, not by force of arms, but by an appeal to the minds and hearts of men.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If the peace policy of the democratic nations is to be successful, they must demonstrate that the benefits of their way of life can be increased and extended to all nations and all races.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the world today we are confronted with the danger that the rising demand of people everywhere for freedom and a better life may be corrupted and betrayed by the false promises of communism.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In its ruthless struggle for power, communism seizes upon our imperfections, and takes advantage of the delays and setbacks which the democratic nations experience in their effort to secure a better life for their citizens.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This challenge to us is more than a military challenge.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is a challenge to the honesty of our profession of the democratic faith; it is a challenge to the efficiency and stability of our economic system;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: it is a challenge to the willingness to work with other peoples for world peace and for world prosperity.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For my part I welcome that challenge.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I believe that our country, at this crucial point in world history, will meet that challenge successfully.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I believe that, in cooperation with the other free nations of the world, we shall extend the full benefits of the democratic way of life to millions who do not now enjoy them, and preserve mankind from dictatorship and tyranny.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I believe that we shall succeed in our struggle for this peace, because I have seen the success we have had in our own country in following the principles of freedom.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Over the last 50 years, the ideals of liberty and equal opportunity to which this Nation is dedicated have been increasingly realized in the lives of our people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The ideal of equal opportunity no longer means simply the opportunity which a man has to advance beyond his fellows.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Some of our citizens do achieve greater success than others as a reward for individual merit and effort, and this is as it should be.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At the same time our country must be more than a land of opportunity for a select few.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It must be a land of opportunity for all of us.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In such a land we can grow and prosper together.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The simple truth that we can all go forward together is often questioned by selfish or shortsighted persons.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is strange that this is so, for this proposition is so clearly demonstrated by our national history.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the last 50 years, for example, our Nation has grown enormously in material well-being.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This growth has come about, not by concentrating the benefits of our progress in the hands of a few, but by increasing the wealth of the great body of our Nation and our citizens.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the last 50 years the income of the average family has increased so greatly that its buying power has doubled.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The average hours of work have declined from 60 to 40 a week, the whole hourly production of the average worker has tripled.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Average wages, allowing for price changes, have increased from about 45 cents an hour to $I.40 an hour.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have accomplished what to earlier ages of mankind would have been a miracle-we work shorter hours, we produce more, and we live better.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Increasing freedom from poverty and drudgery has given a fuller meaning to American life.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our people are better educated; we have more opportunities for travel and recreation and enjoyment of the arts.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We enjoy more personal liberty in the United States today than ever before.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we can continue in the spirit of cooperative adventure which has marked the recent years of our progress, we can expect further scientific advances, further increases in our standard of living, and a still wider enjoyment of democratic freedom.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: No one, of course, can foretell the future exactly.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: However, if we assume that we shall grow as fast in the future as we have grown in the past, we can get a good idea of how much our country should grow in the next 50 years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At present our total national production is $255 billion a year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our working population and our output per worker are increasing.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If our productive power continues to increase at the same rate as it has increased over the past 50 years, our total national production 50 years from now will be nearly four times as much as it is today.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Allowing for the expected growth in population, this would mean that the real income of the average family in the year 2000 A.D. would be about three times what it is today.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These are estimates of what we can do in the future, but we can reach these heights only if we follow the right policies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have learned by bitter experience that progress is not automatic-that wrong policies lead to depression and disaster.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We cannot achieve these gains unless we have a stable economy and avoid the catastrophes of boom and bust that have set us back in the past.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These gains cannot be achieved unless our businessmen maintain their spirit of initiative and enterprise and operate in a competitive economy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They cannot be achieved unless our workingmen and women and their unions help to increase productivity and obtain for labor a fair share of the benefits of our economic system.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They cannot be achieved unless we have a stable and prosperous agriculture.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They cannot be achieved unless we conserve and develop our natural resources in the public interest.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our system will not work unless our people are healthy, well-educated, and confident of the future.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It will not work unless all citizens can participate fully in our national life.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In achieving these gains the Government has a special responsibility to help create and maintain the conditions which will permit the growth we know is possible.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Foremost among these conditions is the need for a fair distribution of our increasing prosperity among all the great groups of our population who help to bring it about - labor, business, agriculture.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Businessmen must continue to have the incentives necessary for investment and for the development of new lines of enterprise.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the future growth of this country, lie possibilities for hundreds of thousands of new and independent businesses.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As our national production increases, as it doubles and redoubles in the next 50 years, the number of independent and competing enterprises should also increase.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If the number does not increase, our constantly growing economy will fall under the control of a few dominant economic groups whose powers will be so great that they will be a challenge to democratic institutions.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To avoid this danger, we must curb monopoly and provide aids to independent business so that it may have the credit and capital to compete in a system of free enterprise.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I recommend that the Congress complete action at this session on the pending bill to close the loopholes in the Clayton Act which now permit monopolistic mergers.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I also hope before this session is over to transmit to the Congress a series of proposals to strengthen the antimonopoly laws, to assist small business, and to encourage the growth of new enterprises.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the case of labor, free collective bargaining must be protected and encouraged.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Collective bargaining is not only a fundamental economic freedom for labor.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is also a strengthening and stabilizing influence for our whole economy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Federal statute now governing labor relations is punitive in purpose and one-sided in operation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This statute is, and always has been, inconsistent with the practice of true and effective collective bargaining.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It should be repealed and replaced by a law that is fair to all and in harmony with our democratic ideals.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A full understanding of the problems of modern labor relations is of such importance that I recommend the establishment of a labor extension service to encourage educational activities in this field.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Another essential for our continued growth is a stable and prosperous agriculture.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For many years we have been building a program to give the farmer a reasonable measure of protection against the special hazards to which he is exposed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That program was improved at the last session of the Congress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: However, our farm legislation is still not adequate.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Although the Congress has properly declared as a matter of national policy that safeguards must be maintained against slumps in farm prices, there are serious shortcomings in the methods now available for carrying out this policy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Mandatory price support s should be provided for the commodities not now covered which are major sources of farm income.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Moreover, we should provide a method of supporting farm income at fair levels which will, at the same time, avoid piling up unmanageable surpluses and allow consumers to obtain the full benefit of our abundant agricultural production.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A system of production payments gives the greatest promise of accomplishing this purpose.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I recommend that the use of such a system be authorized.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: One of the most important factors in our continued growth is the construction of more good, up-to-date housing.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In a country such as ours there is no reason why decent homes should not be within the reach of all.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: With the help of various Government programs we have made great progress in the last few years in increasing the number of homes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Despite this increase, there is still an acute shortage of housing for the lower and middle-income groups, especially in large metropolitan areas.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have laid the groundwork for relieving the plight of lower-income families in the Housing Act of 1949.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To aid the middle-income families, I recommend that the Congress enact new legislation authorizing a vigorous program to help co-operatives and other nonprofit groups build housing which these families can afford.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Rent control has done a great deal to prevent the housing shortage from having had worse effects during this postwar period of adjustment.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Rent control is still necessary to prevent widespread hardship and sharp curtailment of the buying power of million s of consumers in metropolitan areas.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I recommend, therefore, that rent control be continued for another year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we are to achieve a better life for all, the natural resources of the country must be regarded as a public trust.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must use our precious assets of soil, water, and forest, and grassland in such a way that they become constantly more productive and more valuable.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Government investment in the conservation and development of our resources is necessary to the future economic expansion of the country.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We need to enlarge the production and transmission of public power.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is true not only in those regions which have already received great benefits from Federal power projects, but also in regions such as New England where the benefits of large-scale public power development have not yet been experienced.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In our hydroelectric and irrigation undertakings, as well as in our other resource programs, we must continue policies to assure that their benefits will be spread among the many and not restricted to the favored few.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Important resource legislation which should be passed at this session includes the authorization of the St. Lawrence seaway and power project and the establishment of the Columbia Valley Administration - the establishment of the Columbia Valley Administration, I don't want you to miss that.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Lawrence seaway and power project and the establishment of the Columbia Valley Administration - the establishment of the Columbia Valley Administration, I don't want you to miss that.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Through wise Government policies and Government expenditures for the conservation and development of our natural resources, we can be sure of transmitting to our children and our children's children a country far richer and more productive than the one w e know today.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The value of our natural resources is constantly being increased by the progress of science.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Research is finding new ways of using such natural assets as minerals, sea water, and plant life.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the peaceful development of atomic energy, particularly, we stand on the threshold of new wonders.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The first experimental machines for producing useful power from atomic energy are now under construction.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have made only the first beginnings in this field, but in the perspective of history they may loom larger than the first airplane, or even the first tools that started man on the road to civilization.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To take full advantage of the increasing possibilities of nature we must equip ourselves with increasing knowledge.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Government has a responsibility to see that our country maintains its position in the advance of science.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As a step toward this end, the Congress should complete action on the measure to create a National Science Foundation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Another duty of the Government is to promote the economic security, the health, and the education of its citizens.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: By so doing, we strengthen both our economy and the structure of our society.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In a nation as rich as ours, all citizens should be able to live in decency and health.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our Social Security System should be developed into the main reliance of our people for basic protection against the economic hazards of old-age, unemployment, and illness.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I earnestly hope that the Congress will complete action at this session on legislation to increase the benefits and extend the coverage of old-age and survivors insurance.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The widespread movement to provide pensions in private industry dramatizes the need for improvements in the public insurance system.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I also urge that the Congress strengthen our unemployment compensation law to meet present-day needs more adequately.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The economic downturn of the past year was the first real test that our system of unemployment insurance has had to meet.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That test has proved the wisdom of the system, but it has also made strikingly apparent the need for improving its operation and increasing its coverage and its benefits.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the field of health there are immense opportunities to extend to more of our people the benefits of the amazing advances in medical science.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have made a good beginning in expanding our hospitals, but we must also go on to remedy the shortages of doctors, nurses, and public health services, and to establish a system of medical insurance which will enable all Americans to afford good medical care.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must take immediate steps to strengthen our educational system.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In many parts of our country, young people are being handicapped for life because of a poor education.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The rapidly increasing number of children of school age, coupled with the shortage of qualified teachers, makes this problem more critical each year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I believe that the Congress should no longer delay in providing Federal assistance to the States so that they can maintain adequate schools.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As we go forward in achieving greater economic security and greater opportunity for all our people, we should make every effort to extend the benefits of our democratic institutions to every citizen.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The religious ideals which we profess, and the heritage of freedom which we have received from the past, clearly place that duty upon us.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I again urge the Congress to enact the civil rights proposals I made in February 1948.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These proposals are for the enactment of Federal statutes which will protect all our people in the exercise of their democratic rights and their search for economic opportunity, grant statehood to Alaska and Hawaii, provide a greater measure of self-government for our island possessions, and accord home rule to the District of Columbia.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Some of those proposals have been before the Congress for a long time.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Those who oppose them, as well as those who favor them, should recognize that it is the duty of the elected representatives of the people to let these proposals come to a vote.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our democratic ideals, as well as our best interests, require that we do our fair share in providing homes for the unfortunate victims of war and tyranny.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In so doing, we shall add strength to our democracy through the abilities and skills which these men and women will bring here.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I urge the prompt enactment by the Congress of the legislation now before it to extend and broaden the existing displaced persons law and remove its discriminatory features.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The measures I am recommending to the Congress concerning both our foreign and our domestic policies represent a carefully considered program to meet our national needs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is a program which necessarily requires large expenditures of funds.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: More than 70 percent of the Government's expenditures are required to meet the costs of past wars and to work for world peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is the dominant factor in our fiscal policy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At the same time, the Government must make substantial expenditures which are necessary to the growth and expansion of the domestic economy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At present, largely because of the ill-considered tax reduction of the 80th Congress, the Government is not receiving enough revenue to meet its necessary expenditures.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To meet this situation, I am proposing that Federal expenditures be held to the lowest levels consistent with our international requirements and the essential needs of economic growth, and the well-being of our people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I think I had better read that over;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: you interrupted me in the middle.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To meet this situation, I am proposing that Federal expenditures be held to the lowest levels consistent with our international requirements and the essential needs of economic growth, and the well-being of our people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Don't forget that last phrase.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At t he same time, we must guard against the folly of attempting budget slashes which would impair our prospects for peace or cripple the programs essential to our national strength.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The budget recommendations I shall shortly transmit to the Congress show that we can expect a substantial improvement in our fiscal position over the next few years, as the cost of some of our extraordinary postwar programs declines, and as the Government revenue rises as a result of growth in employment and national income.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To further improve our fiscal outlook, we should make some changes in our tax system which will reduce present inequities, stimulate business activity, and yield a moderate amount of additional revenue.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I expect to transmit specific recommendations to the Congress on this subject at a very early date.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The fiscal policy I am recommending is the quickest and safest way of achieving a balanced budget.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As we move forward into the second half of the 20th century, we must always bear in mind the central purpose of our national life.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We do not seek material prosperity for ourselves because we love luxury; we do not aid other nations because we wish to increase our power.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have not devised programs for the security and well-being of our people because we are afraid or unwilling to take risks.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is not the meaning of our past history or our present course.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We work for a better life for all, so that all men may put to good use the great gifts with which they have been endowed by their Creator.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We seek to establish those material conditions of life in which, without exception, men may live in dignity, perform useful work, serve their communities, and worship God as they see fit.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These may seem simple goals, but they are not little ones.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They are worth a great deal more than all the empires and conquests of history.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They are not to be achieved by military aggression or political fanaticism.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They are to be achieved by humbler means---by hard work, by a spirit of self-restraint in our dealings with one another, and by a deep devotion to the principles of justice and equality.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It should make us truly thankful, as we look back to the beginnings of this country, that we have come so far along the road to a better life for all.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It should make us humble to think, as we look ahead, how much farther we have to go to accomplish, at home and abroad, the objectives that were set out for us at the founding of this great Nation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As we approach the halfway mark of the 20th century, we should ask for continued strength and guidance from that Almighty Power who has placed before us such great opportunities for the good of mankind in the years to come.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Mr. President, Mr. Speaker, Members Of the Congress: This 82d Congress faces as grave a task as any Congress in the history of our Republic.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The actions you take will be watched by the whole world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These actions will measure the ability of a free people, acting through their chosen representatives and their free institutions, to meet a deadly challenge to their way of life.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We can meet this challenge foolishly or wisely.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We can meet it timidly or bravely, shamefully or honorably.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I know that the 82d Congress will meet this challenge in a way worthy of our great heritage.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I know that your debates will be earnest, responsible, constructive, and to the point.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I know that from these debates there will come the great decisions needed to carry us forward.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At this critical time, I am glad to say that our country is in a healthy condition.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our democratic institutions are sound and strong.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have more men and women at work than ever before.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are able to produce more than ever before in fact, far more than any country ever produced in the history of the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I am confident that we can succeed in the great task that lies before us.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We will succeed, but we must all do our part.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must all act together as citizens of this great Republic.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As we meet here today, American soldiers are fighting a bitter campaign in Korea.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We pay tribute to their courage, devotion, and gallantry.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our men are fighting, alongside their United Nations allies, because they know, as we do, that the aggression in Korea is part of the attempt of the Russian Communist dictatorship to take over the world, step by step.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our men are fighting a long way from home, but they are fighting for our lives and our liberties.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They are fighting to protect our right to meet here today-our right to govern ourselves as a free nation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The threat of world conquest by Soviet Russia endangers our liberty and endangers the kind of world in which the free spirit of man can survive.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This threat is aimed at all peoples who strive to win or defend their own freedom and national independence.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Indeed, the state of our Nation is in great part the state of our friends and allies throughout the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The gun that points at them points at us, also.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The threat is a total threat and the danger is a common danger.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: All free nations are exposed and all are in peril.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Their only security lies in banding together.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: No one nation can find protection in a selfish search for a safe haven from the storm.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The free nations do not have any aggressive purpose.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We want only peace in the world-peace for all countries.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: No threat to the security of any nation is concealed in our plans and programs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We had hoped that the Soviet Union, with its security assured by the Charter of the United Nations, would be willing to live and let live.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But I am sorry to say that has not been the case.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The imperialism of the czars has been replaced by the even more ambitious, more crafty, and more menacing imperialism of the rulers of the Soviet Union.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This new imperialism has powerful military forces.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is keeping millions of men under arms.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It has a large air force and a strong submarine force.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It has complete control of the men and equipment of its satellites.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It has kept its subject peoples and its economy in a state of perpetual mobilization.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The present rulers of the Soviet Union have shown that they are willing to use this power to destroy the free nations and win domination over the whole world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Soviet imperialists have two ways of going about their destructive work.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They use the method of subversion and internal revolution, and they use the method of external aggression.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In preparation for either of these methods of attack, they stir up class strife and disorder.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They encourage sabotage.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They put out poisonous propaganda.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They deliberately try to prevent economic improvement.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If their efforts are successful, they foment a revolution, as they did in Czechoslovakia and China, and as they tried, unsuccessfully, to do in Greece.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If their methods of subversion are blocked, and if they think they can get away with outright warfare, they resort to external aggression.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is what they did when they loosed the armies of their puppet states against the Republic of Korea, in an evil war by proxy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We of the free world must be ready to meet both of these methods of Soviet action.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must not neglect one or the other.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The free world has power and resources to meet these two forms of aggression resources that are far greater than those of the Soviet dictatorship.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have skilled and vigorous peoples, great industrial strength, and abundant sources of raw materials.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And above all, we cherish liberty.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our common ideals are a great part of our strength.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These ideals are the driving force of human progress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The free nations believe in the dignity and the worth of man.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We believe in independence for all nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We believe that free and independent nations can band together into a world order based on law.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have laid the cornerstone of such a peaceful world in the United Nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We believe that such a world order can and should spread the benefits of modern science and industry, better health and education, more food and rising standards of living-throughout the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These ideals give our cause a power and vitality that Russian communism can never command.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The free nations, however, are bound together by more than ideals.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They are a real community bound together also by the ties of self-interest and self-preservation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If they should fall apart, the results would be fatal to human freedom.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our own national security is deeply involved with that of the other free nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: While they need our support, we equally need theirs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our national safety would be gravely prejudiced if the Soviet Union were to succeed in harnessing to its war machine the resources and the manpower of the free nations on the borders of its empire.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If Western Europe were to fall to Soviet Russia, it would double the Soviet supply of coal and triple the Soviet supply of steel.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If the free countries of Asia and Africa should fall to Soviet Russia, we would lose the sources of many of our most vital raw materials, including uranium, which is the basis of our atomic power.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And Soviet command of the manpower of the free nations of Europe and Asia would confront us with military forces which we could never hope to equal.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In such a situation, the Soviet Union could impose its demands on the world, without resort to conflict, simply through the preponderance of its economic and military power.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Soviet Union does not have to attack the United States to secure domination of the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It can achieve its ends by isolating us and swallowing up all our allies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Therefore, even if we were craven enough-I do not believe we could be-but, I say, even if we were craven enough to abandon our ideals, it would be disastrous for us to withdraw from the community of free nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are the most powerful single member of this community, and we have a special responsibility.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must take the leadership in meeting the challenge to freedom and in helping to protect the rights of independent nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This country has a practical, realistic protect gram of action for meeting this challenge.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: First, we shall have to extend economic assistance, where it can be effective.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The best way to stop subversion by the Kremlin is to strike at the roots of social injustice and economic disorder.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: People who have jobs, homes, and hopes for the future will defend themselves against the underground agents of the Kremlin.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our programs of economic aid have done much to turn back communism.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In Europe the Marshall plan has had an electrifying result.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As European recovery progressed, the strikes led by the Kremlin's agents in Italy and France failed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: All over Western Europe the Communist Party took worse and worse beatings at the polls.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The countries which have received Marshall Plan aid have been able, through hard work, to expand their productive strength in many cases, to levels higher than ever before in their history.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Without this strength they would be completely incapable of def ending themselves today.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They are now ready to use this strength in helping to build a strong combined defense against aggression.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We shall need to continue some economic aid to European countries.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This aid should now be specifically related to the building of their defenses.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In other parts of the world our economic assistance will need to be more broadly directed toward economic development.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the Near East, in Africa, in Asia, we must do what we can to help people who are striving to advance from misery, poverty, and hunger.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must also continue to help the economic growth of our good neighbors in this hemisphere.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These actions will bring greater strength for the free world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They will give many people a real stake in the future and reason to defend their freedom.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They will mean increased production of goods they need and materials we need.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Second, we shall need to continue our military assistance to countries which want to defend themselves.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The heart of our common defense effort is the North Atlantic community.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The defense of Europe is the basis for the defense of the whole free world-ourselves included.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Next to the United States, Europe is the largest workshop in the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is also a homeland of the great religious beliefs shared by many of our citizens-beliefs which are now threatened by the tide of atheistic communism.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Strategically, economically, and morally, the defense of Europe is a part of our own defense.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is why we have joined with the countries of Europe in the North Atlantic Treaty, pledging ourselves to work with them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There has been much discussion recently over whether the European countries are willing to defend themselves.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Their actions are answering this question.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our North Atlantic Treaty partners have strict systems of universal military training.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Several have recently increased the term of service.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: All have taken measures to improve the quality of training.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Forces are being trained and expanded as rapidly as the necessary arms and equipment can be supplied from their factories and ours.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our North Atlantic Treaty partners, together, are building armies bigger than our own.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: None of the North Atlantic Treaty countries, including our own country, has done enough yet.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But real progress is being made.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Together, we have worked out defense plans.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The military leaders of our own country took part in working out these plans, and are agreed that they are sound and within our capabilities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To put these plans into action, we sent to Europe last week one of our greatest military commanders, General Dwight D. Eisenhower.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: General Eisenhower went to Europe to assume command of the united forces of the North Atlantic Treaty countries, including our own forces in Germany.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The people of Europe have confidence in General Eisenhower.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They know his ability to put together a fighting force of allies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: His mission is vital to our security.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should all stand behind him, and give him every bit of help we can.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Part of our job will be to reinforce the military strength of our European partners by sending them weapons and equipment as our military production expands.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our program of military assistance extends to the nations in the Near East and the Far East which are trying to defend their freedom.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Soviet communism is trying to make these nations into colonies, and to use their people as cannon fodder in new wars of conquest.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We want their people to be free men and to enjoy peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our country has always stood for freedom for the peoples of Asia.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Long, long ago it stood for the freedom of the peoples of Asia.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our history shows this.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have demonstrated it in the Philippines.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have demonstrated it in our relations with Indonesia, India, and with China.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We hope to join in restoring the people of Japan to membership in the community of free nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is in the Far East that we have taken up arms, under the United Nations, to preserve the principle of independence for free nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are fighting to keep the forces of Communist aggression from making a slave state out of Korea.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Korea has tremendous significance for the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It means that free nations, acting through the United Nations, are fighting together against aggression.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We will understand the importance of this best if we look back into history.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If the democracies had stood up against the invasion of Manchuria in 1931, or the attack on Ethiopia in 1935, or the seizure of Austria in 1938, if they had stood together against aggression on those occasions as the United Nations has done in Korea, the whole history of our time would have been different.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The principles for which we are fighting in Korea are right and just.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They are the foundations of collective security and of the future of free nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Korea is not only a country undergoing the torment of aggression;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: it is also a symbol.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It stands for right and justice in the world against oppression and slavery.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The free world must always stand for these principles-and we will stand with the free world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As the third part of our program, we will continue to work for peaceful settlements in international disputes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We will support the United Nations and remain loyal to the great principles of international cooperation laid down in its charter.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are willing, as we have always been, to negotiate honorable settlements with the Soviet Union.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But we will not engage in appeasement.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Soviet rulers have made it clear that we must have strength as well as right on our side.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we build our strength-and we are building it-the Soviet rulers may face the facts and lay aside their plans to take over the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is what we hope will happen, and that is what we are trying to bring about.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is the only realistic road to peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These are the main elements of the course our Nation must follow as a member of the community of free nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These are the things we must do to preserve our security and help create a peaceful world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But they will be successful only if we increase the strength of our own country.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Here at home we have some very big jobs to do.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are building much stronger military forces-and we are building them fast.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are preparing for full wartime mobilization, if that should be necessary.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And we are continuing to build a strong and growing economy, able to maintain whatever effort may be required for as long as necessary.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are building our own Army, Navy, and Air Force to an active strength of nearly 3 1/2 million men and women.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are stepping up the training of the reserve forces, and establishing more training facilities, so that we can rapidly increase our active forces far more on short notice.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are going to produce all the weapons and equipment that such an armed force will need.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Furthermore, we will make weapons for our allies, and weapons for our own reserve supplies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On top of this, we will build the capacity to turn out on short notice arms and supplies that may be needed for a full-scale war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Fortunately, we have a good start on this because of our enormous plant capacity and because of the equipment on hand from the last war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: and many others can be put into service on very short notice.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have large reserves of arms and ammunition and thousands of workers skilled in arms production.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In many cases, however, our stocks of weapons are low.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In other cases, those on hand are not the most modern.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have made remarkable technical advances.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have developed new types of jet planes and powerful new tanks.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are concentrating on producing the newest types of weapons and producing them as fast as we can.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This production drive is more selective than the one we had during World War II, but it is just as urgent and intense.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is a big program and it is a costly one.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Let me give you two concrete examples.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our present program calls for expanding the aircraft industry so that it will have the capacity to produce 50,000 modern military planes a year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are preparing the capacity to produce 35,000 tanks a year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are not now ordering that many planes or that many tanks, and we hope that we never have to, but we mean to be able to turn them out if we need them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The planes we are producing now are much bigger, much better, and much more expensive than the planes we had during the last war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We used to think that the B-17 was a huge plane, and the blockbuster it carried a huge load.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But the B-36 can carry five of these blockbusters in its belly, and it can carry them five times as far.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Of course, the B-36 is much more complicated to build than the B-17, and far more expensive.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: One B-17 costs $275,000, while now one B-36 costs 3 million.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I ask you to remember that what we are doing is to provide the best and most modern military equipment in the world for our fighting forces.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This kind of defense production program has two parts.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The first part is to get our defense protect production going as fast as possible.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have to convert plants and channel materials to defense production.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This means heavy cuts in civilian uses of copper, aluminum, rubber, and other essential materials.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It means shortages in various consumer goods.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The second part is to increase our capacity to produce and to keep our economy strong for the long pull.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We do not know how long Communist aggression will threaten the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Only by increasing our output can we carry the burden of preparedness for an indefinite period in the future.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This means that we will have to build more power plants and more steel mills, grow more cotton, mine more copper, and expand our capacity in many other ways.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Congress will need to consider legislation, at this session, affecting all the aspects of our mobilization job.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The main subjects on which legislation will be needed are:   First, appropriations for our military buildup.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Second, extension and revision of the Selective Service Act.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Third, military and economic aid to help build up the strength of the free world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Fourth, revision and extension of the authority to expand production and to stabilize prices, wages, and rents.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Fifth, improvement of our agricultural laws to help obtain the kinds of farm products we need for the defense effort.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Sixth, improvement of our labor laws to help provide stable labor-management relations and to make sure that we have steady production in this emergency.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Seventh, housing and training of defense workers and the full use of all our manpower resources.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Eighth, means for increasing the supply of doctors, nurses, and other trained medical personnel critically needed for the defense effort.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Ninth, aid to the States to meet the most urgent needs of our elementary and secondary schools.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Some of our plans will have to be deferred for the time being.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But we should do all we can to make sure our children are being trained as good and useful citizens in the critical times ahead.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Tenth, a major increase in taxes to meet the cost of the defense effort.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Economic Report and the Budget Message will discuss these subjects further.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In addition, I shall send to the Congress special messages containing detailed recommendations on legislation needed at this session.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the months ahead the Government must give priority to activities that are urgent-like military procurement and atomic energy and power development.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It must practice rigid economy in its non defense activities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Many of the things we would normally do must be curtailed or postponed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But in a long-term defense effort like this one, we cannot neglect the measures needed to maintain a strong economy and a healthy democratic society.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Congress, therefore, should give continued attention to the measures which our country will need for the long pull.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And it should act upon such legislation as promptly as circumstances permit.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To take just one example-we need to continue and complete the work of rounding out our system of social insurance.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We still need to improve our protection against unemployment and old age.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We still need to provide insurance against the loss of earnings through sickness, and against the high costs of modern medical care.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And above all, we must remember that the fundamentals of our strength rest upon the freedoms of our people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must continue our efforts to achieve the full realization of our democratic ideals.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must uphold the freedom of speech and the freedom of conscience in our land.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must assure equal rights and equal opportunities to all our citizens.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As we go forward this year in the defense of freedom, let us keep clearly before us the nature of our present effort.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are building up our strength, in concert with other free nations, to meet the danger of aggression that has been turned loose on the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The strength of the free nations is the world's best hope of peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I ask the Congress for unity in these crucial days.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Make no mistake about my meaning.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I do not ask, or expect, unanimity.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I do not ask for an end to debate.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Only by debate can we arrive at decisions which are wise, and which reflect the desires of the American people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We do not have a dictatorship in this country, and we never will have one in this country.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: When I request unity, what I am really asking for is a sense of responsibility on the part of every Member of this Congress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Let us debate the issues, but let every man among us weigh his words and his deeds.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There is a sharp difference between harmful criticism and constructive criticism.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we are truly responsible as individuals, I am sure that we will be unified as a government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Let us keep our eyes on the issues and work for the things we all believe in.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Let each of us put our country ahead of our party, and ahead of our own personal interests.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I had the honor to be a Member of the Senate during World War II, and I know from experience that unity of purpose and of effort is possible in the Congress without any lessening of the vitality of our two party system.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Let us all stand together as Americans.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Let us stand together with all men every where who believe in human liberty.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Peace is precious to us.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is the way of life we strive for with all the strength and wisdom we possess.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But more precious than peace are freedom and justice.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We will fight, if fight we must, to keep our freedom and to prevent justice from being destroyed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These are the things that give meaning to our lives, and which we acknowledge to be greater than ourselves.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is our cause-peace, freedom, justice.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We will pursue this cause with determination and humility, asking divine guidance that in all we do we may follow the will of God.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I have the honor to report to the Congress on the state of the Union.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At the outset, I should like to speak of the necessity for putting first things first as we work together this year for the good of our country.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The United States and the whole free world are passing through a period of grave danger.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Every action you take here in Congress, and every action that I take as President, must be measured against the test of whether it helps to meet that danger.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This will be a presidential election year--the year in which politics plays a large part in our lives--a larger part than usual.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is perfectly proper.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But we have a greater responsibility to conduct our political fights in a manner that does not harm the national interest.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We can find plenty of things to differ about without destroying our free institutions and without abandoning our bipartisan foreign policy for peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: When everything is said and done, all of us--Republicans and Democrats alike--all of us are Americans; and we are all going to sink or swim together.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are moving through a perilous time.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Faced with a terrible threat of aggression, our Nation has embarked upon a great effort to help establish the kind of world in which peace shall be secure.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Peace is our goal--not peace at any price, but a peace based on freedom and justice.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are now in the midst of our effort to reach that goal.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On the whole, we have been doing very well.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Last year, 1951, was a year in which we threw back aggression, added greatly to our military strength, and improved the chances for peace and freedom in many parts of the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This year, 1952, is a critical year in the defense effort of the whole free world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we falter we can lose all the gains we have made.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we drive ahead, with courage and vigor and determination, we can by the end of 1952 be in a position of much greater security.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: in our effort to build strong defenses.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: When we look at the record of the past year, 1951, we find important things on both the credit and the debit side of the ledger.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have made great advances.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At the same time we have run into new problems which must be overcome.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Now let us look at the credit side first.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Peace depends upon the free nations sticking together, and making a combined effort to check aggression and prevent war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In this respect, 1951 was a year of great achievement.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In Korea the forces of the United Nations turned back the Chinese Communist invasion--and did it without widening the area of conflict.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The action of the United Nations in Korea has been a powerful deterrent to a third world war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: However, the situation in Korea remains very hazardous.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The outcome of the armistice negotiation still remains uncertain.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In Indo-china and Malaya, our aid has helped our allies to hold back the Communist advance, although there are signs of further trouble in that area.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In 1951 we strengthened the chances of peace in the Pacific region by the treaties with Japan and the defense arrangements with Australia, New Zealand, and the Philippines.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In Europe combined defense has become a reality.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The free nations have created a real fighting force.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This force is not yet as strong as it needs to be;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: but it is already a real obstacle to any attempt by hostile forces to sweep across Europe to the Atlantic.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In 1951 we also moved to strengthen the security of Europe by the agreement to bring Greece and Turkey into the North Atlantic Treaty.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The United Nations, the world's greatest hope for peace, has come through a year of trial stronger and more useful than ever.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The free nations have stood together in blocking Communist attempts to tear up the charter.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At the present session of the United Nations in Paris, we, together with the British and the French, offered a plan to reduce and control all armaments under a foolproof inspection system.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is a concrete, practical proposal for disarmament.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But what happened?

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Vishinsky laughed at it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: nan

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The world will be a long time forgetting the spectacle of that fellow laughing at disarmament.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Disarmament is not a joke.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Vishinsky's laughter met with shock and anger from the people all over the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And, as a result, Mr. Stalin's representative received orders to stop laughing and start talking.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If the Soviet leaders were to accept this proposal, it would lighten the burden of armaments, and permit the resources of the earth to be devoted to the good of mankind.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But until the Soviet Union accepts a sound disarmament proposal, and joins in peaceful settlements, we have no choice except to build up our defenses.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During this past year we added more than a million men and women to our Armed Forces.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The total is now nearly 3 1/2 million.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have made rapid progress in the field of atomic weapons.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have turned out $16 billion worth of military supplies and equipment, three times as much as the year before.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Economic conditions in the country are good.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There are 61 million people on the job;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: wages, farm incomes, and business profits are at high levels.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Total production of goods and services in our country has increased 8 percent over last year--about twice the normal rate of growth.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Perhaps the most amazing thing about our economic progress is the way we are increasing our basic capacity to produce.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
