text: For example, we are now in the second year of a 3-year program which will double our output of aluminum, increase our electric power supply by 40 percent, and increase our steel-making capacity by 15 percent.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We can then produce 120 million tons of steel a year, as much as all the rest of the world put together.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This expansion will mean more jobs and higher standards of living for all of us in the years ahead.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At the present time it means greater strength for us and for the rest of the free world in the fight for peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Now, I must turn to the debit side of the ledger for the past year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The outstanding fact to note on the debit side of the ledger is that the Soviet Union, in 1951, continued to expand its military production and increase its already excessive military power.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is true that the Soviets have run into increasing difficulties.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Their hostile policies have awakened stern resistance among free men throughout the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And behind the Iron Curtain the Soviet rule of force has created growing political and economic stresses in the satellite nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Nevertheless, the grim fact remains that the Soviet Union is increasing its armed might.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is still producing more war planes than the free nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It has set off two more atomic explosions.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The world still walks in the shadow of another world war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And here at home, our defense preparations are far from complete.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During 1951 we did not make adequate progress in building up civil defense against atomic attack.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is a major weakness in our plans for peace, since inadequate civilian defense is an open invitation to a surprise attack.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Failure to provide adequate civilian defense has the same effect as adding to the enemy's supply of atomic bombs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the field of defense production we have run into difficulties and delays in designing and producing the latest types of airplanes and tanks.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Some machine tools and metals are still in extremely short supply.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In other free countries the defense buildup has created severe economic problems.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It has increased inflation in Europe and has endangered the continued recovery of our allies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the Middle East political tensions and the oil controversy in Iran are keeping the region in a turmoil.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the Far East the dark threat of Communist imperialism still hangs over many nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This, very briefly, is the good side and the bad side of the picture.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Taking the good and bad together, we have made real progress this last year along the road to peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have increased the power and unity of the free world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And while we were doing this, we have avoided world war on the one hand, and appeasement on the other.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is a hard road to follow, but the events of the last year show that it is the right road to peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We cannot expect to complete the job overnight.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The free nations may have to maintain for years the larger military forces needed to deter aggression.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must build steadily, over a period of years, toward political solidarity and economic progress among the free nations in all parts of the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our task will not be easy; but if we go at it with a will, we can look forward to steady progress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On our side are all the great resources of freedom--the ideals of religion and democracy, the aspiration of people for a better life, and the industrial and technical power of a free civilization.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These advantages outweigh anything the slave world can produce.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The only thing that can defeat us is our own state of mind.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We can lose if we falter.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The middle period of a great national effort like this is a very difficult time.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The way seems long and hard.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The goal seems far distant.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Some people get discouraged.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is only natural.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But if there are any among us who think we ought to ease up in the fight for peace, I want to remind them of three things--just three things.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: First: The threat of world war is still very real.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We had one Pearl Harbor--let's not get caught off guard again.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If you don't think the threat of Communist armies is real, talk to some of our men back from Korea.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Second: If the United States had to try to stand alone against a Soviet-dominated world, it would destroy the life we know and the ideals we hold dear.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our allies are essential to us, just as we are essential to them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The more shoulders there are to bear the burden the lighter that burden will be.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Third: The things we believe in most deeply are under relentless attack.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have the great responsibility of saving the basic moral and spiritual values of our civilization.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have started out well-- with a program for peace that is unparalleled in history.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we believe in ourselves and the faith we profess, we will stick to that job until it is victoriously finished.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is a time for courage, not for grumbling and mumbling.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Now, let us take a look at the things we have to do.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The thing that is uppermost in the minds of all of us is the situation in Korea.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must, and we will, keep up the fight there until we get the kind of armistice that will put an end to the aggression and protect the safety of our forces and the security of the Republic of Korea.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Beyond that we shall continue to work for a settlement in Korea that upholds the principles of the United Nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We went into Korea because we knew that Communist aggression had to be met firmly if freedom was to be preserved in the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We went into the fight to save the Republic of Korea, a free country, established under the United Nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These are our aims.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We will not give up until we attain them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Meanwhile, we must continue to strengthen the forces of freedom throughout the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I hope the Senate will take early and favorable action on the Japanese peace treaty, on our security pacts with the Pacific countries, and on the agreement to bring Greece and Turkey into the North Atlantic Treaty.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are also negotiating an agreement with the German Federal Republic under which it can play an honorable and equal part among nations and take its place in the defense of Western Europe.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But treaties and plans are only the skeleton of our defense structure.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The sinew and muscle of defense are the forces and equipment which must be provided.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In Europe we must go on helping our friends and allies to build up their military forces.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This means we must send weapons in large volume to our European allies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I have directed that weapons for Europe be given a very high priority.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Economic aid is necessary, too, to supply the margin of difference between success and failure in making Europe a strong partner in our joint defense.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the long run we want to see Europe freed from any dependence on our aid.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our European allies want that just as bad as we do.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The steps that are now being taken to build European unity should help bring that about.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Six European countries are pooling their coal and steel production under the Schuman plan.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Work is going forward on the merger of European national forces on the Continent into a single army.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These great projects should become realities in 1952.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should do all we can to help and encourage the move toward a strong and united Europe.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In Asia the new Communist empire is a daily threat to millions of people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The peoples of Asia want to be free to follow their own way of life.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They want to preserve their culture and their traditions against communism, just as much as we want to preserve ours.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They are laboring under terrific handicaps--poverty, ill health, feudal systems of land ownership, and the threat of internal subversion or external attack.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We can and we must increase our help to them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This means military aid, especially to those places like Indo-china which might be hardest hit by some new Communist attack.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It also means economic aid, both technical know-how and capital investment.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This last year we made available millions of bushels of wheat to relieve famine in India.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But far more important, in the long run, is the work Americans are doing in India to help the Indian farmers themselves raise more grain.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: With the help of our technicians, Indian farmers, using simple, inexpensive means, have been able since 1948 to double the crops in one area in India.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: One farmer there raised 63 bushels of wheat to the acre, where 13 bushels had been the average before.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is point 4--our point 4 program at work.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is working--not only in India but in Iran, Paraguay, Liberia--in 33 countries around the globe.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our technical missionaries are out there.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We need more of them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We need more funds to speed their efforts, because there is nothing of greater importance in all our foreign policy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There is nothing that shows more clearly what we stand for, and what we want to achieve.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: My friends of the Congress, less than one-third of the expenditure for the cost of World War II would have created the developments necessary to feed the whole world so we wouldn't have to stomach communism.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is what we have got to fight, and unless we fight that battle and win it, we can't win the cold war or a hot one either.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have recently lost a great public servant who was leading this effort to bring opportunity and hope to the people of half the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Dr. Henry Bennett and his associates died in line of duty on a point 4 mission.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is up to us to carry on the great work for which they gave their lives.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the coming year we must not forget the suffering of the people who live behind the Iron Curtain.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In those areas minorities are being oppressed, human rights violated, religions persecuted.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should continue to expose those wrongs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should continue and expand the activities of the Voice of America, which brings our message of hope and truth to those peoples and other peoples throughout the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I have just had an opportunity to discuss many of these world problems with Prime Minister Churchill.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have had a most satisfactory series of meetings.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We thoroughly reviewed the situation in Europe, the Middle East, and the Far East.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We both look forward to steady progress toward peace through the cooperative action and teamwork of the free nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Turning from our foreign policies, let us consider the jobs we have here at home as a part of our program for peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The first of these jobs is to move ahead full steam on the defense program.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our objective is to have a well-equipped active defense force large enough--in concert with the forces of our allies--to deter aggression and to inflict punishing losses on the enemy immediately if we should be attacked.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This active force must be backed by adequate reserves, and by the plants and tools to turn out the tremendous quantities of new weapons that would be needed if war came.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are not building an active force adequate to carry on full scale war, but we are putting ourselves in a position to mobilize very rapidly if we have to.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This year I shall recommend some increases in the size of the active force we are building, with particular emphasis on air power.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This means we shall have to continue large-scale production of planes and other equipment for a longer period of time than we had originally planned.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: #NAME?

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Deliveries of hard goods now amount to about a billion and a half dollars worth a month.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A year from now, we expect that rate to be doubled.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We shall have to hold to a high rate of military output for about a year after that.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In 1954 we hope to have enough equipment so that we can reduce the production of most military items substantially.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The next 2 years should therefore be the peak period of defense production.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Defense needs will take a lot of steel, aluminum, copper, nickel, and other scarce materials.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This means smaller production of some civilian goods.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The cutbacks will be nothing like those during World War II, when most civilian production was completely stopped.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But there will be considerably less of some goods than we have been used to these past 2 or 3 years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The very critical part of our defense job this year is to keep down inflation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We can control inflation if we make up our minds to do it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On the executive side of the Government, we intend to hold the line on prices just as tightly as the law allows.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We will permit only those wage increases which are clearly justified under sound stabilization policies;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: and we will see to it that industries absorb cost increases out of earnings wherever feasible, before they are authorized to raise prices.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We will do that, at any rate, except where the recent amendments to the law specifically require us to give further price increases.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Congress has a tremendous responsibility in this matter.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our stabilization law was shot full of holes at the last session.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This year, it will be one of the main tasks before the Congress to repair the damage and enact a strong anti-inflation law.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As a part of our program to keep our country strong, we are determined to preserve the financial strength of the Government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This means high taxes over the next few years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must see to it that these taxes are shared among the people as fairly as possible.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I expect to discuss these matters in the Economic Report and the Budget Message which will soon be presented to the Congress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our tax laws must be fair.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And we must make absolutely certain they are administered fairly, without fear or favor of any kind for anybody.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To this end, steps have already been taken to remedy weaknesses which have been disclosed in the administration of the tax laws.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In addition, I hope the Congress will approve my reorganization plan for the Bureau of Internal Revenue.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must do everything necessary in order to make just as certain as is humanly possible that every taxpayer receives equal treatment under the law.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To carry the burden of defense we must have a strong, productive, and expanding economy here at home.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We cannot neglect those things that have made us the great and powerful nation we are today.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our strength depends upon the health, the morale, the freedom of our people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We can take on the burden of leadership in the fight for world peace because, for nearly 20 years, the Government and the people have been working together for the general welfare.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have given more and more of our citizens a fair chance at decent, useful, productive lives.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is the reason we are as strong as we are today.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This Government of ours--the Congress and the executive both-- must keep on working to bring about a fair deal for all the American people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Some people will say that we haven't the time or the money this year for measures for the welfare of the people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But if we want to win the fight for peace, this is a part of the job we cannot ignore.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We will have to give up some things, we will have to go forward on others at a slower pace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But, so far as I am concerned, I do not think we can give up the things that are vital to our national strength.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I believe most people in this country will agree with me on that.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I think most farmers understand that soil conservation and rural electrification and agricultural research are not frills or luxuries, but real necessities in order to boost our farm production.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I think most workers understand that decent housing and good working conditions are not luxuries, but necessities if the working men and women of this country are to continue to out-produce the rest of the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I think our businessmen know that scientific research and transportation services and more steel mills and power projects are not luxuries, but necessities to keep our business and our industry in the forefront of industrial progress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I think everybody knows that social insurance and better schools and health services are not frills, but necessities in helping all Americans to be useful and productive citizens, who can contribute their full share in the national effort to protect and advance our way of life.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We cannot do all we want to in times like these--we have to choose the things that will contribute most to defense--but we must continue to make progress if we are to be a strong nation in the years ahead.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Let me give you some examples.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are going right ahead with the urgently needed work to develop our natural resources, to conserve our soil, and to prevent floods.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are going to produce essential power and build the lines that are necessary and that we have to have to transmit it to our farms and factories.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are going to encourage exploration for new mineral deposits.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are going to keep on building essential highways and taking any other steps that will assure the Nation an adequate transportation system--on land, on the sea, and in the air.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must move right ahead this year to see that defense workers and soldiers' families get decent housing at rents they can afford to pay.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must begin our long deferred program of Federal aid to education--to help the States meet the present crisis in the operation of our schools.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And we must help with the construction of schools in areas where they are critically needed because of the defense effort.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We urgently need to train more doctors and other health personnel, through aid to medical education.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We also urgently need to expand the basic public health services in our home communities--especially in defense areas.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Congress should go ahead with these two measures immediately.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I have set up an impartial commission to make a thorough study of the Nation's health needs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: One of the things this commission is looking into is how to bring the cost of modern medical care within the reach of all the people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I have repeatedly recommended national health insurance as the best way to do this.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: So far as I know, it is still the best way.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If there are any better answers, I hope this commission will find them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But of one thing I am sure: something must be done, and done soon.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This year we ought to make a number of urgently needed improvements in our social security law.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For one thing, benefits under old-age and survivors insurance should be raised $5 a month above the present average of $42.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For another thing, the States should be given special aid to help them increase public assistance payments.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: By doing these things now, we can ease the pressure of living costs for people who depend on those fixed payments.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should also make some cost-of-living adjustments for those receiving veterans' compensation for death or disability incurred in the service of our country.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In addition, now is the time to start a sensible program of readjustment benefits for our veterans who have seen service since the fighting broke out in Korea.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Another thing the Congress should do at this session is to strengthen our system of farm price supports to meet the defense emergency.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: in the price support law should not be allowed to penalize farmers for increasing production to meet defense needs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We should also find a new and less costly method for supporting perishable commodities than the law now provides.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We need to act promptly to improve our labor law.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Taft-Hartley Act has many serious and far-reaching defects.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Experience has demonstrated this so clearly that even the sponsors of the act now admit that it needs to be changed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: A fair law, fair to both management and labor, is indispensable to sound labor relations and to full, uninterrupted production.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I intend to keep on working for a fair law until we get one.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As we build our strength to defend the freedom in the world, we ourselves must extend the benefits of freedom more widely among all our own people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We need to take action toward the wider enjoyment of civil rights.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Freedom is the birthright of every American.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The executive branch has been making real progress toward full equality of treatment and opportunity--in the Armed Forces, in the civil service, and in private firms working for the Government.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Further advances require action by Congress, and I hope that means will be provided to give the Members of the Senate and the House a chance to vote on them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I am glad to hear that home rule for the District of Columbia will be the first item of business before the Senate.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I hope that it, as well as statehood for Hawaii and Alaska, will be adopted promptly.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: All these measures I have been talking about--measures to advance the well-being of our people--demonstrate to the world the forward movement of our free society.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This demonstration of the way free men govern themselves has a more powerful influence on the people of the world--on both sides of the Iron Curtain--than all the trick slogans and pie-in-the-sky promises of the Communists.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But our shortcomings, as well as our progress, are watched from abroad.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And there is one shortcoming I want to speak about plainly.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our kind of government above all others cannot tolerate dishonesty among public servants.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Some dishonest people worm themselves into almost every human organization.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is all the more shocking, however, when they make their way into a Government such as ours, which is based on the principle of justice for all.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Such unworthy public servants must be weeded out.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I intend to see to it that Federal employees who have been guilty of misconduct are punished for it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I also intend to see to it that the honest and hard-working great majority of our Federal employees are protected against partisan slander and malicious attack.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I have already made some recommendations to the Congress to help accomplish these purposes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I intend to submit further recommendations to this end.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I will welcome the wholehearted cooperation of the Congress in this effort.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I also think that the Congress can do a great deal to strengthen confidence in our institutions by applying rigorous standards of moral integrity to its own operations, and by finding an effective way to control campaign expenditures, and by protecting the rights of individuals in congressional investigations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To meet the crisis which now hangs over the world, we need many different kinds of strength--military, economic, political, and moral.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And of all these, I am convinced that moral strength is the most vital.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: When you come right down to it, it is the courage and the character of our Nation--and of each one of us as individuals--that will really decide how well we meet this challenge.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are engaged in a great undertaking at home and abroad--the greatest, in fact, that any nation has ever been privileged to embark upon.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are working night and day to bring peace to the world and to spread the democratic ideals of justice and self-government to all people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our accomplishments are already remarkable.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We ought to be full of pride in what we are doing, and full of confidence and hope in the outcome.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: No nation ever had greater resources, or greater energy, or nobler traditions to inspire it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And yet, day in and day out, we see a long procession of timid and fearful men who wring their hands and cry out that we have lost the way, that we don't know what we are doing, that we are bound to fail.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Some say we should give up the struggle for peace, and others say we should have a war and get it over with.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That's a terrible statement.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I had heard it made, but they want us to forget the great objective of preventing another world war--the objective for which our soldiers have been fighting in the hills of Korea.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we are to be worthy of all that has been done for us by our soldiers in the field, we must be true to the ideals for which they are fighting.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must reject the counsels of defeat and despair.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must have the determination to complete the great work for which our men have laid down their lives.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In all we do, we should remember who we are and what we stand for.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are Americans.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our forefathers had far greater obstacles than we have, and much poorer chances of success.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They did not lose heart, or turn aside from their goals.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must not, in so great a contest, expect to meet with nothing but sunshine.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: With that spirit they won their fight for freedom.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must have that same faith and vision.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the great contest in which we are engaged today, we cannot expect to have fair weather all the way.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But it is a contest just as important for this country and for all men, as the desperate struggle that George Washington fought through to victory.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Let us prove, again, that we are not merely sunshine patriots and summer soldiers.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Let us go forward, trusting in the God of Peace, to win the goals we seek.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I have the honor to report to the Congress on the state of the Union.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is the eighth such report that, as President, I have been privileged to present to you and to the country.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On previous occasions, it has been my custom to set forth proposals for legislative action in the coming year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But that is not my purpose today.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The presentation of a legislative program falls properly to my successor, not to me, and I would not infringe upon his responsibility to chart the forward course.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Instead, I wish to speak of the course we have been following the past eight years and the position at which we have arrived.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In just two weeks, General Eisenhower will be inaugurated as President of the United States and I will resume--most gladly--my place as a private citizen of this Republic.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Presidency last changed hands eight years ago this coming April.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That was a tragic time: a time of grieving for President Roosevelt--the great and gallant human being who had been taken from us; a time of unrelieved anxiety to his successor, thrust so suddenly into the complexities and burdens of the Presidential office.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Not so this time.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This time we see the normal transition under our democratic system.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: One President, at the conclusion of his term, steps back to private life; his successor, chosen by the people, begins his tenure of the office.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And the Presidency of the United States continues to function without a moment's break.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Since the election, I have done my best to assure that the transfer from one Administration to another shall be smooth and orderly.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: From General Eisenhower and his associates, I have had friendly and understanding collaboration in this endeavor.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I have not sought to thrust upon him--nor has he sought to take--the responsibility which must be mine until twelve o'clock noon on January twentieth.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But together, I hope and believe we have found means whereby the incoming President can obtain the full and detailed information he will need to assume the responsibility the moment he takes the oath of office.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The President-elect is about to take up the greatest burdens, the most compelling responsibilities, given to any man.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And I, with you and all Americans, wish for him all possible success in undertaking the tasks that will so soon be his.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: What are these tasks?

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The President is Chief of State, elected representative of all the people, national spokesman for them and to them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: He is Commander-in-Chief of our armed forces.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: He is charged with the conduct of our foreign relations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: He is Chief Executive of the Nation's largest civilian organization.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: He must select and nominate all top officials of the Executive Branch and all Federal judges.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And on the legislative side, he has the obligation and the opportunity to recommend, and to approve or veto legislation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Besides all this, it is to him that a great political party turns naturally for leadership, and that, too, he must provide as President.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This bundle of burdens is unique;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: there is nothing else like it on the face of the earth.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Each task could be a full-time job.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Together, they would be a tremendous undertaking in the easiest of times.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But our times are not easy;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: they are hard--as hard and complex, perhaps as any in our history.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Now, the President not only has to carry on these tasks in such a way that our democracy may grow and flourish and our people prosper, but he also has to lead the whole free world in overcoming the communist menace--and all this under the shadow of the atomic bomb.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is a huge challenge to the human being who occupies the Presidential office.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But it is not a challenge to him alone, for in reality he cannot meet it alone.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The challenge runs not just to him but to his whole Administration, to the Congress, to the country.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Ultimately, no President can master his responsibilities, save as his fellow citizens--indeed, the whole people--comprehend the challenge of our times and move, with him, to meet it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It has been my privilege to hold the Presidential office for nearly eight years now, and much has been done in which I take great pride.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But this is not personal pride.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is pride in the people, in the Nation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is pride in our political system and our form of government--balky sometimes, mechanically deficient perhaps, in many ways--but enormously alive and vigorous; able through these years to keep the Republic on the right course, rising to the great occasions, accomplishing the essentials, meeting the basic challenge of our times.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There have been misunderstandings and controversies these past eight years, but through it all the President of the United States has had that measure of support and understanding without which no man could sustain the burdens of the Presidential office, or hope to discharge its responsibilities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For this I am profoundly grateful--grateful to my associates in the Executive Branch--most of them non-partisan civil servants;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: grateful-- despite our disagreements--to the Members of the Congress on both sides of the aisle;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: grateful especially to the American people, the citizens of this Republic, governors of us all.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are still so close to recent controversies that some of us may find it hard to understand the accomplishments of these past eight years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But the accomplishments are real and very great, not as the President's, not as the Congress', but as the achievements of our country and all the people in it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Let me remind you of some of the things we have done since I first assumed my duties as President of the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I took the oath of office on April 12, 1945.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In May of that same year, the Nazis surrendered.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Then, in July, that great white flash of light, man-made at Alamogordo, heralded swift and final victory in World War II--and opened the doorway to the atomic age.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Consider some of the great questions that were posed for us by sudden, total victory in World War II.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Consider also, how well we as a Nation have responded.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Would the American economy collapse, after the war?

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That was one question.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Would there be another depression here--a repetition of 1921 or 1929?

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The free world feared and dreaded it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The communists hoped for it and built their policies upon that hope.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our economy has grown tremendously.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Free enterprise has flourished as never before.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Sixty-two million people are now gainfully employed, compared with 51 million seven years ago.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Private businessmen and farmers have invested more than 200 billion dollars in new plant and equipment since the end of World War II.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Prices have risen further than they should have done--but incomes, by and large, have risen even more, so that real living standards are now considerably higher than seven years ago.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Aided by sound government policies, our expanding economy has shown the strength and flexibility for swift and almost painless re-conversion from war to peace, in 1945 and 1946;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: for quick reaction and recovery--well before Korea--from the beginnings of recession in 1949.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Above all, this live and vital economy of ours has now shown the remarkable capacity to sustain a great mobilization program for defense, a vast outpouring of aid to friends and allies all around the world--and still to produce more goods and services for peaceful use at home than we have ever known before.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This has been our answer, up to now, to those who feared or hoped for a depression in this country.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: How have we handled our national finances?

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That was another question arising at war's end.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the administration of the Government, no problem takes more of the President's time, year in and year out, than fashioning the Budget, and the related problem of managing the public debt.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Financing World War II left us with a tremendous public debt, which reached 279 billion dollars at its peak in February, 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Beginning in July, 1946, when war and re-conversion financing had ended, we have held quite closely to the sound standard that in times of high employment and high national income, the Federal Budget should be balanced and the debt reduced.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For the four fiscal years from July 1, 1946, to June 30, 1950, we had a net surplus of 4.3 billion dollars.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Using this surplus, and the Treasury's excess cash reserves, the debt was reduced substantially, reaching a low point of 251 billion dollars in June, 1949, and ending up at 257 billion dollars on June 30, 1950.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In July of 1950, we began our rapid rearmament, and for two years held very close to a pay-as-we-go policy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But in the current fiscal year and the next, rising expenditures for defense will substantially outrun receipts.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This will pose an immediate and serious problem for the new Congress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Now let me turn to another question we faced at the war's end.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Would we take up again, and carry forward, the great projects of social welfare--so badly needed, so long overdue--that the New Deal had introduced into our national life?

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Would our Government continue to have a heart for the people, or was the progress of the New Deal to be halted in the aftermath of war as decisively as the progress of Woodrow Wilson's New Freedom had been halted after the first world war?

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This question, too, we have answered.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have answered it by doubling old age insurance benefits and extending coverage to ten million more people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have answered it by increasing our minimum wage.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have answered by the three million privately constructed homes that the Federal Government has helped finance since the war--and the 155 thousand units of low rent public housing placed under construction since 1949.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have answered with the 42 thousand new hospital beds provided since 1946 through the joint efforts of the Federal Government and local communities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have answered by helping eight million veterans of World War II to obtain advanced education, 196 thousand to start in business, and 64 thousand to buy farms.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have answered by continuing to help farmers obtain electric power, until today nearly 90 per cent of our farms have power line electric service.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In these and other ways, we have demonstrated, up to now, that our democracy has not forgotten how to use the powers of the Government to promote the people's welfare and security.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Another of the big post-war questions was this: What we would do with the Nation's natural resources--its soils and water, forests and grasslands.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Would we continue the strong conservation movement of the 1930's, or would we, as we did after the First World War, slip back into the practices of monopoly, exploitation, and waste?

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The answer is plain.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: All across our country, the soil conservation movement has spread, aided by Government programs, enriching private and public lands, preserving them from destruction, improving them for future use.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In our river basins, we have invested nearly 5 billion dollars of public funds in the last eight years--invested them in projects to control floods, irrigate farmlands, produce low-cost power and get it to the housewives and farmers and businessmen who need it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have been vigilant in protecting the people's property--lands and forests and oil and minerals.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have had to fight hard against those who would use our resources for private greed;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: we have met setbacks;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: we have had to delay work because of defense priorities, but on the whole we can be proud of our record in protecting our natural heritage, and in using our resources for the public good.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Here is another question we had to face at the war's close: Would we continue, in peace as well as war, to promote equality of opportunity for all our citizens, seeking ways and means to guarantee for all of them the full enjoyment of their civil rights?

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: During the war we achieved great economic and social gains for millions of our fellow citizens who had been held back by prejudice.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Were we prepared, in peacetime, to keep on moving toward full realization of the democratic promise?

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Or would we let it be submerged, wiped out, in post-war riots and reaction, as after World War I?

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We answered these questions in a series of forward steps at every level of government and in many spheres of private life.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In our armed forces, our civil service, our universities, our railway trains, the residential districts of our cities--in stores and factories all across the Nation--in the polling booths as well--the barriers are coming down.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is happening, in part, at the mandate of the courts;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: in part, at the insistence of Federal, State and local governments;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: in part, through the enlightened action of private groups and persons in every region and every walk of life.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There has been a great awakening of the American conscience on the issues of civil rights.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And all this progress--still far from complete but still continuing--has been our answer, up to now, to those who questioned our intention to live up to the promises of equal freedom for us all.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There was another question posed for us at the war's end, which equally concerned the future course of our democracy: Could the machinery of government and politics in this Republic be changed, improved, adapted rapidly enough to carry through, responsibly and well, the vast, new complicated undertakings called for in our time?

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have answered this question, too, answered it by tackling the most urgent, most specific, problems which the war experience itself had brought into sharp focus.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The reorganization of the Congress in 1946;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: the unification of our armed services, beginning in 1947;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: the closer integration of foreign and military policy through the National Security Council created that same year;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: and the Executive reorganizations, before and after the Hoover-Acheson Commission Report in 1949--these are landmarks in our continuing endeavor to make government an effective instrument of service to the people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I come now to the most vital question of all, the greatest of our concerns: Could there be built in the world a durable structure of security, a lasting peace for all the nations, or would we drift, as after World War I, toward another terrible disaster--a disaster which this time might be the holocaust of atomic war?

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is still the overriding question of our time.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We cannot know the answer yet;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: perhaps we will not know it finally for a long time to come.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But day and night, these past eight years, we have been building for peace, searching out the way that leads most surely to security and freedom and justice in the world for us and all mankind.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This, above all else, has been the task of our Republic since the end of World War II, and our accomplishment so far should give real pride to all Americans.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At the very least, a total war has been averted, each day up to this hour.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And at the most, we may already have succeeded in establishing conditions which can keep that kind of war from happening, for as far ahead as man can see.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Second World War radically changed the power relationships of the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Nations once great were left shattered and weak, channels of communication, routes of trade, political and economic ties of many kinds were ripped apart.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And in this changed, disrupted, chaotic situation, the United States and the Soviet Union emerged as the two strongest powers of the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Each had tremendous human and natural resources, actual or potential, on a scale unmatched by any other nation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Nothing could make plainer why the world is in its present state-- and how that came to pass--than an understanding of the diametrically opposite principles and policies of these two great powers in a war-ruined world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: nan

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That to secure these rights, governments are instituted among men, deriving their just powers from the consent of the governed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our post-war objective has been in keeping with this great idea.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The United States has sought to use its pre-eminent position of power to help other nations recover from the damage and dislocation of the war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We held out a helping hand to enable them to restore their national lives and to regain their positions as independent, self-supporting members of the great family of nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This help was given without any attempt on our part to dominate or control any nation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We did not want satellites but partners.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Soviet Union, however, took exactly the opposite course.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Its rulers saw in the weakened condition of the world not an obligation to assist in the great work of reconstruction, but an opportunity to exploit misery and suffering for the extension of their power.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Instead of help, they brought subjugation.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They extinguished, blotted out, the national independence of the countries that the military operations of World War II had left within their grasp.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The difference stares at us from the map of Europe today.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To the west of the line that tragically divides Europe we see nations continuing to act and live in the light of their own traditions and principles.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: On the other side, we see the dead uniformity of a tyrannical system imposed by the rulers of the Soviet Union.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Nothing could point up more clearly what the global struggle between the free world and the communists is all about.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is a struggle as old as recorded history;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: it is freedom versus tyranny.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For the dominant idea of the Soviet regime is the terrible conception that men do not have rights but live at the mercy of the state.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Inevitably this idea of theirs--and all the consequences flowing from it--collided with the efforts of free nations to build a just and peaceful world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: between the communists and the free world is nothing more or less than the Soviet attempt to checkmate and defeat our peaceful purposes, in furtherance of their own dread objective.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We did not seek this struggle, God forbid.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We did our utmost to avoid it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In World War II, we and the Russians had fought side by side, each in our turn attacked and forced to combat by the aggressors.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: After the war, we hoped that our wartime collaboration could be maintained, that the frightful experience of Nazi invasion, of devastation in the heart of Russia, had turned the Soviet rulers away from their old proclaimed allegiance to world revolution and communist dominion.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But instead, they violated, one by one, the solemn agreements they had made with us in wartime.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They sought to use the rights and privileges they had obtained in the United Nations, to frustrate its purposes and cut down its powers as an effective agent of world progress and the keeper of the world's peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Despite this outcome, the efforts we made toward peaceful collaboration are a source of our present strength.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They demonstrated that we believed what we proclaimed, that we actually sought honest agreements as the way to peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our whole moral position, our leadership in the free world today, is fortified by that fact.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The world is divided, not through our fault or failure, but by Soviet design.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They, not we, began the cold war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And because the free world saw this happen--because men know we made the effort and the Soviet rulers spurned it--the free nations have accepted leadership from our Republic, in meeting and mastering the Soviet offensive.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It seems to me especially important that all of us be clear, in our own thinking, about the nature of the threat we have faced--and will face for a long time to come.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The measures we have devised to meet it take shape and pattern only as we understand what we were--and are--up against.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Soviet Union occupies a territory of 8 million square miles.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Beyond its borders, East and West, are the nearly five million square miles of the satellite states--virtually incorporated into the Soviet Union--and of China, now its close partner.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This vast land mass contains an enormous store of natural resources sufficient to support an economic development comparable to our own.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is the Stalinist world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is a world of great natural diversity in geography and climate, in distribution of resources, in population, language, and living standards, in economic and cultural development.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is a world whose people are not all convinced communists by any means.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is a world where history and national traditions, particularly in its borderlands, tend more toward separation than unification, and run counter to the enforced combination that has been made of these areas today.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But it is also a world of great man-made uniformities, a world that bleeds its population white to build huge military forces;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: a world in which the police are everywhere and their authority unlimited;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: a world where terror and slavery are deliberately administered both as instruments of government and as means of production;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: a world where all effective social power is the state's monopoly--yet the state itself is the creature of the communist tyrants.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Soviet Union, with its satellites, and China are held in the tight grip of communist party chieftains.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The party dominates all social and political institutions.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The party regulates and centrally directs the whole economy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In Moscow's sphere, and in Peiping's, all history, philosophy, morality and law are centrally established by rigid dogmas, incessantly drummed into the whole population and subject to interpretation--or to change--by none except the party's own inner circle.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And lest their people learn too much of other ways of life, the communists have walled off their world, deliberately and uniformly, from the rest of human society.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is the communist base of operation in their cold war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In addition, they have at their command hundreds and thousands of dedicated foreign communists, people in nearly every free country who will serve Moscow's ends.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Thus the masters of the Kremlin are provided with deluded followers all through the free world whom they can manipulate, cynically and quite ruthlessly, to serve the purposes of the Soviet state.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Given their vast internal base of operations, and their agents in foreign lands, what are the communist rulers trying to do?

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Inside their homeland, the communists are trying to maintain and modernize huge military forces.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And simultaneously, they are endeavoring to weld their whole vast area and population into a completely self-contained, advanced industrial society.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They aim, some day, to equal or better the production levels of Western Europe and North America combined--thus shifting the balance of world economic power, and war potential, to their side.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They have a long way to go and they know it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But they are prepared to levy upon living generations any sacrifice that helps strengthen their armed power, or speed industrial development.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Externally, the communist rulers are trying to expand the boundaries of their world, whenever and wherever they can.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This expansion they have pursued steadfastly since the close of World War II, using any means available to them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Where the Soviet army was present, as in the countries of Eastern Europe, they have gradually squeezed free institutions to death.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Where post-war chaos existed in industrialized nations, as in Western Europe, the local Stalinists tried to gain power through political processes, politically-inspired strikes, and every available means for subverting free institutions to their evil ends.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Where conditions permitted, the Soviet rulers have stimulated and aided armed insurrection by communist-led revolutionary forces, as in Greece, Indo-China, the Philippines, and China, or outright aggression by one of their satellites, as in Korea.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Where the forces of nationalism, independence, and economic change were at work throughout the great sweep of Asia and Africa, the communists tried to identify themselves with the cause of progress, tried to picture themselves as the friends of freedom and advancement-- surely one of the most cynical efforts of which history offers record.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Thus, everywhere in the free world, the communists seek to fish in troubled waters, to seize more countries, to enslave more millions of human souls.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They were, and are, ready to ally themselves with any group, from the extreme left to the extreme right, that offers them an opportunity to advance their ends.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Geography gives them a central position.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They are both a European and an Asian power, with borders touching many of the most sensitive and vital areas in the free world around them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: So situated, they can use their armies and their economic power to set up simultaneously a whole series of threats--or inducements--to such widely dispersed places as Western Germany, Iran, and Japan.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These pressures and attractions can be sustained at will, or quickly shifted from place to place.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Thus the communist rulers are moving, with implacable will, to create greater strength in their vast empire, and to create weakness and division in the free world, preparing for the time their false creed teaches them must come: the time when the whole world outside their sway will be so torn by strife and contradictions that it will be ripe for the communist plucking.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is the heart of the distorted Marxist interpretation of history.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is the glass through which Moscow and Peiping look out upon the world, the glass through which they see the rest of us.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They seem really to believe that history is on their side.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: along, at every opportunity, in every way they can.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I have set forth here the nature of the communist menace confronting our Republic and the whole free world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is the measure of the challenge we have faced since World War II--a challenge partly military and partly economic, partly moral and partly intellectual, confronting us at every level of human endeavor and all around the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It has been and must be the free world's purpose not only to organize defenses against aggression and subversion, not only to build a structure of resistance and salvation for the community of nations outside the iron curtain, but in addition to give expression and opportunity to the forces of growth and progress in the free world, to so organize and unify the cooperative community of free men that we will not crumble but grow stronger over the years, and the Soviet empire, not the free world, will eventually have to change its ways or fall.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our whole program of action to carry out this purpose has been directed to meet two requirements.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The first of these had to do with security.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Like the pioneers who settled this great continent of ours, we have had to carry a musket while we went about our peaceful business.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We realized that if we and our allies did not have military strength to meet the growing Soviet military threat, we would never have the opportunity to carry forward our efforts to build a peaceful world of law and order--the only environment in which our free institutions could survive and flourish.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Did this mean we had to drop everything else and concentrate on armies and weapons?

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Of course it did not: side-by-side with this urgent military requirement, we had to continue to help create conditions of economic and social progress in the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This work had to be carried forward alongside the first, not only in order to meet the non-military aspects of the communist drive for power, but also because this creative effort toward human progress is essential to bring about the kind of world we as free men want to live in.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These two requirements--military security and human progress-- are more closely related in action than we sometimes recognize.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Military security depends upon a strong economic underpinning and a stable and hopeful political order;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: conversely, the confidence that makes for economic and political progress does not thrive in areas that are vulnerable to military conquest.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These requirements are related in another way.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Both of them depend upon unity of action among the free nations of the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This, indeed, has been the foundation of our whole effort, for the drawing together of the free people of the world has become a condition essential not only to their progress, but to their survival as free people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is the conviction that underlies all the steps we have been taking to strengthen and unify the free nations during the past seven years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: What have these steps been?

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: First of all, how have we gone about meeting the requirement of providing for our security against this world-wide challenge?

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our starting point, as I have said on many occasions, has been and remains the United Nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We were prepared, and so were the other nations of the free world, to place our reliance on the machinery of the United Nations to safeguard peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But before the United Nations could give full expression to the concept of international security embodied in the Charter, it was essential that the five permanent members of the Security Council honor their solemn pledge to cooperate to that end.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This the Soviet Union has not done.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I do not need to outline here the dreary record of Soviet obstruction and veto and the unceasing efforts of the Soviet representatives to sabotage the United Nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is important, however, to distinguish clearly between the principle of collective security embodied in the Charter and the mechanisms of the United Nations to give that principle effect.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must frankly recognize that the Soviet Union has been able, in certain instances, to stall the machinery of collective security.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Yet it has not been able to impair the principle of collective security.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The free nations of the world have retained their allegiance to that idea.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They have found the means to act despite the Soviet veto, both through the United Nations itself and through the application of this principle in regional and other security arrangements that are fully in harmony with the Charter and give expression to its purposes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The free world refused to resign itself to collective suicide merely because of the technicality of a Soviet veto.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The principle of collective measures to forestall aggression has found expression in the Treaty of Rio de Janeiro, the North Atlantic Treaty, now extended to include Greece and Turkey, and the several treaties we have concluded to reinforce security in the Pacific area.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But the free nations have not this time fallen prey to the dangerous illusion that treaties alone will stop an aggressor.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: By a series of vigorous actions, as varied as the nature of the threat, the free nations have successfully thwarted aggression or the threat of aggression in many different parts of the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our country has led or supported these collective measures.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The aid we have given to people determined to act in defense of their freedom has often spelled the difference between success and failure.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We all know what we have done, and I shall not review in detail the steps we have taken.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Each major step was a milepost in the developing unity, strength and resolute will of the free nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The first was the determined and successful effort made through the United Nations to safeguard the integrity and independence of Iran in 1945 and 1946.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Next was our aid and support to embattled Greece, which enabled her to defeat the forces threatening her national independence.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In Turkey, cooperative action resulted in building up a bulwark of military strength for an area vital to the defenses of the entire free world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In 1949, we began furnishing military aid to our partners in the North Atlantic Community and to a number of other free countries.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Soviet Union's threats against Germany and Japan, its neighbors to the West and to the East, have been successfully withstood.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Free Germany is on its way to becoming a member of the peaceful community of nations, and a partner in the common defense.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Soviet effort to capture Berlin by blockade was thwarted by the courageous Allied airlift.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: An independent and democratic Japan has been brought back into the community of free nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the Far East, the tactics of communist imperialism have reached heights of violence unmatched elsewhere--and the problem of concerted action by the free nations has been at once more acute and more difficult.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Here, in spite of outside aid and support, the free government of China succumbed to the communist assault.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our aid has enabled the free Chinese to rebuild and strengthen their forces on the island of Formosa.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In other areas of the Far East--in Indo-China, Malaya, and the Philippines--our assistance has helped sustain a staunch resistance against communist insurrectionary attacks.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The supreme test, up to this point, of the will and determination of the free nations came in Korea, when communist forces invaded the Republic of Korea, a state that was in a special sense under the protection of the United Nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The response was immediate and resolute.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Under our military leadership, the free nations for the first time took up arms, collectively, to repel aggression.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Aggression was repelled, driven back, punished.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Since that time, communist strategy has seen fit to prolong the conflict, in spite of honest efforts by the United Nations to reach an honorable truce.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The months of deadlock have demonstrated that the communists cannot achieve by persistence, or by diplomatic trickery, what they failed to achieve by sneak attack.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Korea has demonstrated that the free world has the will and the endurance to match the communist effort to overthrow international order through local aggression.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It has been a bitter struggle and it has cost us much in brave lives and human suffering, but it has made it plain that the free nations will fight side by side, that they will not succumb to aggression or intimidation, one by one.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This, in the final analysis, is the only way to halt the communist drive to world power.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At the heart of the free world's defense is the military strength of the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: From 1945 to 1949, the United States was sole possessor of the atomic bomb.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That was a great deterrent and protection in itself.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But when the Soviets produced an atomic explosion--as they were bound to do in time--we had to broaden the whole basis of our strength.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We had to endeavor to keep our lead in atomic weapons.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We had to strengthen our armed forces generally and to enlarge our productive capacity--our mobilization base.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Historically, it was the Soviet atomic explosion in the fall of 1949, nine months before the aggression in Korea, which stimulated the planning for our program of defense mobilization.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: What we needed was not just a central force that could strike back against aggression.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We also needed strength along the outer edges of the free world, defenses for our allies as well as for ourselves, strength to hold the line against attack as well as to retaliate.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have made great progress on this task of building strong defenses.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In the last two and one half years, we have more than doubled our own defenses, and we have helped to increase the protection of nearly all the other free nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: All the measures of collective security, resistance to aggression, and the building of defenses, constitute the first requirement for the survival and progress of the free world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But, as I have pointed out, they are interwoven with the necessity of taking steps to create and maintain economic and social progress in the free nations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There can be no military strength except where there is economic capacity to back it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There can be no freedom where there is economic chaos or social collapse.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For these reasons, our national policy has included a wide range of economic measures.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In Europe, the grand design of the Marshall Plan permitted the people of Britain and France and Italy and a half dozen other countries, with help from the United States, to lift themselves from stagnation and find again the path of rising production, rising incomes, rising standards of living.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The situation was changed almost overnight by the Marshall Plan;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: the people of Europe have a renewed hope and vitality, and they are able to carry a share of the military defense of the free world that would have been impossible a few years ago.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Now the countries of Europe are moving rapidly towards political and economic unity, changing the map of Europe in more hopeful ways than it has been changed for 500 years.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Customs unions, European economic institutions like the Schuman Plan, the movement toward European political integration, the European Defense Community-- all are signs of practical and effective growth toward greater common strength and unity.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The countries of Western Europe, including the free Republic of Germany are working together, and the whole free world is the gainer.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It sometimes happens, in the course of history, that steps taken to meet an immediate necessity serve an ultimate purpose greater than may be apparent at the time.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This, I believe, is the meaning of what has been going on in Europe under the threat of aggression.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The free nations there, with our help, rawing together in defense of their A doing, they have laid the foundations of a unity that will endure as a major creative force beyond the exigencies of this period of history.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We may, at this close range, be but dimly aware of the creative surge this movement represents, but I believe it to be of historic importance.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I believe its benefits will survive long after communist tyranny is nothing but an unhappy memory.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: In Asia and Africa, the economic and social problems are different but no less urgent.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There hundreds of millions of people are in ferment, exploding into the twentieth century, thrusting toward equality and independence and improvement in the hard conditions of their lives.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Politically, economically, socially, things cannot and will not stay in their pre-war mold in Africa and Asia.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Change must come--is coming--fast.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Just in the years I have been President, 12 free nations, with more than 600 million people, have become independent: Burma, Indonesia, the Philippines, Korea, Israel, Libya, India, Pakistan and Ceylon, and the three Associated States of Indo-China, now members of the French Union.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These names alone are testimony to the sweep of the great force which is changing the face of half the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Working out new relationships among the peoples of the free world would not be easy in the best of times.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Even if there were no Communist drive for expansion, there would be hard and complex problems of transition from old social forms, old political arrangements, old economic institutions to the new ones our century demands--problems of guiding change into constructive channels, of helping new nations grow strong and stable.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But now, with the Soviet rulers striving to exploit this ferment for their own purposes, the task has become harder and more urgent--terribly urgent.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
