text: In this situation, we see the meaning and the importance of the Point IV program, through which we can share our store of know-how and of capital to help these people develop their economies and reshape their societies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As we help Iranians to raise more grain, Indians to reduce the incidence of malaria, Liberians to educate their children better, we are at once helping to answer the desires of the people for advancement, and demonstrating the superiority of freedom over communism.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There will be no quick solution for any of the difficulties of the new nations of Asia and Africa--but there may be no solution at all if we do not press forward with full energy to help these countries grow and flourish in freedom and in cooperation with the rest of the free world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our measures of economic policy have already had a tremendous effect on the course of events.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Eight years ago, the Kremlin thought post-war collapse in Western Europe and Japan--with economic dislocation in America--might give them the signal to advance.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We demonstrated they were wrong.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Now they wait with hope that the economic recovery of the free world has set the stage for violent and disastrous rivalry among the economically developed nations, struggling for each other's markets and a greater share of trade.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Here is another test that we shall have to meet and master in the years immediately ahead.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And it will take great ingenuity and effort--and much time--before we prove the Kremlin wrong again.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But we can do it.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is true that economic recovery presents its problems, as does economic decline, but they are problems of another order.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They are the problems of distributing abundance fairly, and they can be solved by the process of international cooperation that has already brought us so far.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These are the measures we must continue.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This is the path we must follow.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must go on, working with our free associates, building an international structure for military defense, and for economic, social, and political progress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must be prepared for war, because war may be thrust upon us.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But the stakes in our search for peace are immensely higher than they have ever been before.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: For now we have entered the atomic age, and war has undergone a technological change which makes it a very different thing from what it used to be.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: War today between the Soviet empire and the free nations might dig the grave not only of our Stalinist opponents, but of our own society, our world as well as theirs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: This transformation has been brought to pass in the seven years from Alamogordo to Eniwetok.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is only seven years, but the new force of atomic energy has turned the world into a very different kind of place.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Science and technology have worked so fast that war's new meaning may not yet be grasped by all the peoples who would be its victims;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: nor, perhaps, by the rulers in the Kremlin.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But I have been President of the United States, these seven years, responsible for the decisions which have brought our science and our engineering to their present place.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I know what this development means now.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I know something of what it will come to mean in the future.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We in this Government realized, even before the first successful atomic explosion, that this new force spelled terrible danger for all mankind unless it were brought under international control.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We promptly advanced proposals in the United Nations to take this new source of energy out of the arena of national rivalries, to make it impossible to use it as a weapon of war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These proposals, so pregnant with benefit for all humanity, were rebuffed by the rulers of the Soviet Union.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The language of science is universal, the movement of science is always forward into the unknown.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We could not assume that the Soviet Union would not develop the same weapon, regardless of all our precautions, nor that there were not other and even more terrible means of destruction lying in the unexplored field of atomic energy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We had no alternative, then, but to press on, to probe the secrets of atomic power to the uttermost of our capacity, to maintain, if we could, our initial superiority in the atomic field.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: At the same time, we sought persistently for some avenue, some formula, for reaching an agreement with the Soviet rulers that would place this new form of power under effective restraints--that would guarantee no nation would use it in war.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I do not have to recount here the proposals we made, the steps taken in the United Nations, striving at least to open a way to ultimate agreement.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I hope and believe that we will continue to make these efforts so long as there is the slightest possibility of progress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: All civilized nations are agreed on the urgency of the problem, and have shown their willingness to agree on effective measures of control--all save the Soviet Union and its satellites.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But they have rejected every reasonable proposal.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Meanwhile, the progress of scientific experiment has outrun our expectations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Atomic science is in the full tide of development;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: the unfolding of the innermost secrets of matter is uninterrupted and irresistible.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Since Alamogordo we have developed atomic weapons with many times the explosive force of the early models, and we have produced them in substantial quantities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And recently, in the thermonuclear tests at Eniwetok, we have entered another stage in the world-shaking development of atomic energy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: From now on, man moves into a new era of destructive power, capable of creating explosions of a new order of magnitude, dwarfing the mushroom clouds of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have no reason to think that the stage we have now reached in the release of atomic energy will be the last.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Indeed, the speed of our scientific and technical progress over the last seven years shows no signs of abating.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are being hurried forward, in our mastery of the atom, from one discovery to another, toward yet unforeseeable peaks of destructive power.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Inevitably, until we can reach international agreement, this is the path we must follow.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And we must realize that no advance we make is unattainable by others, that no advantage in this race can be more than temporary.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The war of the future would be one in which man could extinguish millions of lives at one blow, demolish the great cities of the world, wipe out the cultural achievements of the past--and destroy the very structure of a civilization that has been slowly and painfully built up through hundreds of generations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Such a war is not a possible policy for rational men.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We know this, but we dare not assume that others would not yield to the temptation science is now placing in their hands.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: With that in mind, there is something I would say, to Stalin: You claim belief in Lenin's prophecy that one stage in the development of communist society would be war between your world and ours.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But Lenin was a pre-atomic man, who viewed society and history with pre-atomic eyes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Something profound has happened since he wrote.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: War has changed its shape and its dimension.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: in the development of anything save ruin for your regime and your homeland.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I do not know how much time may elapse before the communist rulers bring themselves to recognize this truth.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But when they do, they will find us eager to reach understandings that will protect the world from the danger it faces today.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: It is no wonder that some people wish that we had never succeeded in splitting the atom.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But atomic power, like any other force of nature, is not evil in itself.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Properly used, it is an instrumentality for human betterment.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As a source of power, as a tool of scientific inquiry, it has untold possibilities.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are already making good progress in the constructive use of atomic power.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We could do much more if we were free to concentrate on its peaceful uses exclusively.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Atomic power will be with us all the days of our lives.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We cannot legislate it out of existence.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We cannot ignore the dangers or the benefits it offers.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I believe that man can harness the forces of the atom to work for the improvement of the lot of human beings everywhere.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is our goal.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: As a nation, as a people, we must understand this problem, we must handle this new force wisely through our democratic processes.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Above all, we must strive, in all earnestness and good faith, to bring it under effective international control.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To do this will require much wisdom and patience and firmness.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The awe-inspiring responsibility in this field now falls on a new Administration and a new Congress.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I will give them my support, as I am sure all our citizens will, in whatever constructive steps they may take to make this newest of man's discoveries a source of good and not of ultimate destruction.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We cannot tell when or whether the attitude of the Soviet rulers may change.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We do not know how long it may be before they show a willingness to negotiate effective control of atomic energy and honorable settlements of other world problems.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We cannot measure how deep-rooted are the Kremlin's illusions about us.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We can be sure, however, that the rulers of the communist world will not change their basic objectives lightly or soon.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The communist rulers have a sense of time about these things wholly unlike our own.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We tend to divide our future into short spans, like the two-year life of this Congress, or the four years of the next Presidential term.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: They seem to think and plan in terms of generations.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And there is, therefore, no easy, short-run way to make them see that their plans cannot prevail.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Above all, this is a test of the will and the steadiness of the people of the United States.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There has been no challenge like this in the history of our Republic.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We are called upon to rise to the occasion, as no people before us.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: What is required of us is not easy.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The way we must learn to live, the world we have to live in, cannot be so pleasant, safe, or simple as most of us have known before, or confidently hoped to know.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Already we have had to sacrifice a number of accustomed ways of working and of living, much nervous energy, material resources, even human life.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Yet if one thing is certain in our future, it is that more sacrifice still lies ahead.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Were we to grow discouraged now, were we to weaken and slack off, the whole structure we have built, these past eight years, would come apart and fall away.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Never then, no matter by what stringent means, could our free world regain the ground, the time, the sheer momentum, lost by such a move.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: There can and should be changes and improvements in our programs, to meet new situations, serve new needs.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But to desert the spirit of our basic policies, to step back from them now, would surely start the free world's slide toward the darkness that the communists have prophesied--toward the moment for which they watch and wait.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: If we value our freedom and our way of life and want to see them safe, we must meet the challenge and accept its implications, stick to our guns and carry out our policies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I have set out the basic conditions, as I see them, under which we have been working in the world, and the nature of our basic policies.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: What, then, of the future?

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The answer, I believe, is this: As we continue to confound Soviet expectations, as our world grows stronger, more united, more attractive to men on both sides of the iron curtain, then inevitably there will come a time of change within the communist world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We do not know how that change will come about, whether by deliberate decision in the Kremlin, by coup d'etat, by revolution, by defection of satellites, or perhaps by some unforeseen combination of factors such as these.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But if the communist rulers understand they cannot win by war, and if we frustrate their attempts to win by subversion, it is not too much to expect their world to change its character, moderate its aims, become more realistic and less implacable, and recede from the cold war they began.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Do not be deceived by the strong face, the look of monolithic power that the communist dictators wear before the outside world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Remember their power has no basis in consent.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Remember they are so afraid of the free world's ideas and ways of life, they do not dare to let their people know about them.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Think of the massive effort they put forth to try to stop our Campaign of Truth from reaching their people with its message of freedom.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The masters of the Kremlin live in fear their power and position would collapse were their own people to acquire knowledge, information, comprehension about our free society.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Their world has many elements of strength, but this one fatal flaw: the weakness represented by their iron curtain and their police state.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Surely, a social order at once so insecure and so fearful, must ultimately lose its competition with our free society.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Provided just one thing--and this I urge you to consider carefully-- provided that the free world retains the confidence and the determination to outmatch the best our adversary can accomplish and to demonstrate for uncertain millions on both sides of the iron curtain the superiority of the free way of life.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is the test upon all the free nations; upon none more than our own Republic.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our resources are equal to the task.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have the industry, the skills, the basic economic strength.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Above all, we have the vigor of free men in a free society.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We have our liberties.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And while we keep them, while we retain our democratic faith, the ultimate advantage in this hard competition lies with us, not with the communists.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But there are some things that could shift the advantage to their side.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: One of the things that could defeat us is fear--fear of the task we face, fear of adjusting to it, fear that breeds more fear, sapping our faith, corroding our liberties, turning citizen against citizen, ally against ally.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Fear could snatch away the very values we are striving to defend.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Already the danger signals have gone up.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Already the corrosive process has begun.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And every diminution of our tolerance, each new act of enforced conformity, each idle accusation, each demonstration of hysteria--each new restrictive law--is one more sign that we can lose the battle against fear.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The communists cannot deprive us of our liberties--fear can.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The communists cannot stamp out our faith in human dignity-- fear can.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Fear is an enemy within ourselves, and if we do not root it out, it may destroy the very way of life we are so anxious to protect.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To beat back fear, we must hold fast to our heritage as free men.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must renew our confidence in one another, our tolerance, our sense of being neighbors, fellow citizens.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We must take our stand on the Bill of Rights.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The inquisition, the star chamber, have no place in a free society.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our ultimate strength lies, not alone in arms, but in the sense of moral values and moral truths that give meaning and vitality to the purposes of free people.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: These values are our faith, our inspiration, the source of our strength and our indomitable determination.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: We face hard tasks, great dangers.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But we are Americans and we have faced hardships and uncertainty before, we have adjusted before to changing circumstances.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Our whole history has been a steady training for the work it is now ours to do.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: No one can lose heart for the task, none can lose faith in our free ways, who stops to remember where we began, what we have sought, and what accomplished, all together as Americans.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I have lived a long time and seen much happen in our country.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And I know out of my own experience, that we can do what must be done.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: When I think back to the country I grew up in--and then look at what our country has become--I am quite certain that having done so much, we can do more.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The very concept of collective security, the foundation-stone of all our actions now, was then strange doctrine, shunned and set aside.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Talk about adapting;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: talk about adjusting;

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: talk about responding as a people to the challenge of changed times and circumstances-- there has never been a more spectacular example than this great change in America's outlook on the world.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Let all of us pause now, think back, consider carefully the meaning of our national experience.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Let us draw comfort from it and faith, and confidence in our future as Americans.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The Nation's business is never finished.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: The basic questions we have been dealing with, these eight years past, present themselves anew.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: That is the way of our society.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Circumstances change and current questions take on different forms, new complications, year by year.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: But underneath, the great issues remain the same--prosperity, welfare, human rights, effective democracy, and above all, peace.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: Now we turn to the inaugural of our new President.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: And in the great work he is called upon to do he will have need for the support of a united people, a confident people, with firm faith in one another and in our common cause.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: I pledge him my support as a citizen of our Republic, and I ask you to give him yours.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: To him, to you, to all my fellow citizens, I say, Godspeed.

speaker: Harry S. Truman
text: May God bless our country and our cause.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Mr. President, Mr. Speaker, Members of the Eighty-third Congress: I welcome the honor of appearing before you to deliver my first message to the Congress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is manifestly the joint purpose of the congressional leadership and of this administration to justify the summons to governmental responsibility issued last November by the American people.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The grand labors of this leadership will involve: Application of America's influence in world affairs with such fortitude and such foresight that it will deter aggression and eventually secure peace;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Establishment of a national administration of such integrity and such efficiency that its honor at home will ensure respect abroad;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Encouragement of those incentives that inspire creative initiative in our economy, so that its productivity may fortify freedom everywhere;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: And Dedication to the well-being of all our citizens and to the attainment of equality of opportunity for all, so that our Nation will ever act with the strength of unity in every task to which it is called.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The purpose of this message is to suggest certain lines along which our joint efforts may immediately be directed toward realization of these four ruling purposes.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The time that this administration has been in office has been too brief to permit preparation of a detailed and comprehensive program of recommended action to cover all phases of the responsibilities that devolve upon our country's new leaders.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Such a program will be filled out in the weeks ahead as, after appropriate study, I shall submit additional recommendations for your consideration.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Today can provide only a sure and substantial beginning.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our country has come through a painful period of trial and disillusionment since the victory of 1945.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We anticipated a world of peace and cooperation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The calculated pressures of aggressive communism have forced us, instead, to live in a world of turmoil.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: From this costly experience we have learned one clear lesson.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We have learned that the free world cannot indefinitely remain in a posture of paralyzed tension, leaving forever to the aggressor the choice of time and place and means to cause greatest hurt to us at least cost to himself.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This administration has, therefore, begun the definition of a new, positive foreign policy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This policy will be governed by certain fixed ideas.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They are these: (1) Our foreign policy must be clear, consistent, and confident.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This means that it must be the product of genuine, continuous cooperation between the executive and the legislative branches of this Government.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It must be developed and directed in the spirit of true bipartisanship.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: (2) The policy we embrace must be a coherent global policy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The freedom we cherish and defend in Europe and in the Americas is no different from the freedom that is imperiled in Asia.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: (3) Our policy, dedicated to making the free world secure, will envision all peaceful methods and devices--except breaking faith with our friends.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We shall never acquiesce in the enslavement of any people in order to purchase fancied gain for ourselves.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I shall ask the Congress at a later date to join in an appropriate resolution making clear that this Government recognizes no kind of commitment contained in secret understandings of the past with foreign governments which permit this kind of enslavement.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: (4) The policy we pursue will recognize the truth that no single country, even one so powerful as ours, can alone defend the liberty of all nations threatened by Communist aggression from without or subversion within.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Mutual security means effective mutual cooperation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: For the United States, this means that, as a matter of common sense and national interest, we shall give help to other nations in the measure that they strive earnestly to do their full share of the common task.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: No wealth of aid could compensate for poverty of spirit.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The heart of every free nation must be honestly dedicated to the preserving of its own independence and security.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: (5) Our policy will be designed to foster the advent of practical unity in Western Europe.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The nations of that region have contributed notably to the effort of sustaining the security of the free world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: From the jungles of Indochina and Malaya to the northern shores of Europe, they have vastly improved their defensive strength.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Where called upon to do so, they have made costly and bitter sacrifices to hold the line of freedom.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But the problem of security demands closer cooperation among the nations of Europe than has been known to date.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Only a more closely integrated economic and political system can provide the greatly increased economic strength needed to maintain both necessary military readiness and respectable living standards.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Europe's enlightened leaders have long been aware of these facts.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: All the devoted work that has gone into the Schuman plan, the European Army, and the Strasbourg Conference has testified to their vision and determination.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These achievements are the more remarkable when we realize that each of them has marked a victory--for France and for Germany alike over the divisions that in the past have brought such tragedy to these two great nations and to the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The needed unity of Western Europe manifestly cannot be manufactured from without;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: it can only be created from within.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But it is right and necessary that we encourage Europe's leaders by informing them of the high value we place upon the earnestness of their efforts toward this goal.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Real progress will be conclusive evidence to the American people that our material sacrifices in the cause of collective security are matched by essential political, economic, and military accomplishments in Western Europe.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: (6) Our foreign policy will recognize the importance of profitable and equitable world trade.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A substantial beginning can and should be made by our friends themselves.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Europe, for example, is now marked by checkered areas of labor surplus and labor shortage, of agricultural areas needing machines and industrial areas needing food.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Here and elsewhere we can hope that our friends will take the initiative in creating broader markets and more dependable currencies, to allow greater exchange of goods and services among themselves.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Action along these lines can create an economic environment that will invite vital help from us.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This help includes: First: Revising our customs regulations to remove procedural obstacles to profitable trade.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I further recommend that the Congress take the Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act under immediate study and extend it by appropriate legislation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This objective must not ignore legitimate safeguarding of domestic industries, agriculture, and labor standards.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In all executive study and recommendations on this problem labor and management and farmers alike will be earnestly consulted.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Second: Doing whatever Government properly can to encourage the flow of private American investment abroad.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This involves, as a serious and explicit purpose of our foreign policy, the encouragement of a hospitable climate for such investment in foreign nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Third: Availing ourselves of facilities overseas for the economical production of manufactured articles which are needed for mutual defense and which are not seriously competitive with our own normal peacetime production.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Fourth: Receiving from the rest of the world, in equitable exchange for what we supply, greater amounts of important raw materials which we do not ourselves possess in adequate quantities.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This war is, for Americans, the most painful phase of Communist aggression throughout the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is clearly a part of the same calculated assault that the aggressor is simultaneously pressing in Indochina and in Malaya, and of the strategic situation that manifestly embraces the island of Formosa and the Chinese Nationalist forces there.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The working out of any military solution to the Korean war will inevitably affect all these areas.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The administration is giving immediate increased attention to the development of additional Republic of Korea forces.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The citizens of that country have proved their capacity as fighting men and their eagerness to take a greater share in the defense of their homeland.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Organization, equipment, and training will allow them to do so.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Increased assistance to Korea for this purpose conforms fully to our global policies.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In June 1950, following the aggressive attack on the Republic of Korea, the United States Seventh Fleet was instructed both to prevent attack upon Formosa and also to insure that Formosa should not be used as a base of operations against the Chinese Communist mainland.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This has meant, in effect, that the United States Navy was required to serve as a defensive arm of Communist China.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Regardless of the situation in 1950, since the date of that order the Chinese Communists have invaded Korea to attack the United Nations forces there.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They have consistently rejected the proposals of the United Nations Command for an armistice.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They recently joined with Soviet Russia in rejecting the armistice proposal sponsored in the United Nations by the Government of India.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This proposal had been accepted by the United States and 53 other nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Consequently there is no longer any logic or sense in a condition that required the United States Navy to assume defensive responsibilities on behalf of the Chinese Communists, thus permitting those Communists, with greater impunity, to kill our soldiers and those of our United Nations allies in Korea.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am, therefore, issuing instructions that the Seventh Fleet no longer be employed to shield Communist China.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This order implies no aggressive intent on our part.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But we certainly have no obligation to protect a nation fighting us in Korea.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our labor for peace in Korea and in the world imperatively demands the maintenance by the United States of a strong fighting service ready for any contingency.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our problem is to achieve adequate military strength within the limits of endurable strain upon our economy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To amass military power without regard to our economic capacity would be to defend ourselves against one kind of disaster by inviting another.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Both military and economic objectives demand a single national military policy, proper coordination of our armed services, and effective consolidation of certain logistics activities.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must eliminate waste and duplication of effort in the armed services.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must realize clearly that size alone is not sufficient.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The biggest force is not necessarily the best--and we want the best.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must not let traditions or habits of the past stand in the way of developing an efficient military force.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: All members of our forces must be ever mindful that they serve under a single flag and for a single cause.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must effectively integrate our armament programs and plan them in such careful relation to our industrial facilities that we assure the best use of our manpower and our materials.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Because of the complex technical nature of our military organization and because of the security reasons involved, the Secretary of Defense must take the initiative and assume the responsibility for developing plans to give our Nation maximum safety at minimum cost.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Accordingly, the new Secretary of Defense and his civilian and military associates will, in the future, recommend such changes in present laws affecting our defense activities as may be necessary to clarify responsibilities and improve the total effectiveness of our defense effort.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This effort must always conform to policies laid down in the National Security Council.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The statutory function of the National Security Council is to assist the President in the formulation and coordination of significant domestic, foreign, and military policies required for the security of the Nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In these days of tension it is essential that this central body have the vitality to perform effectively its statutory role.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I propose to see that it does so.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Careful formulation of policies must be followed by clear understanding of them by all peoples.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A related need, therefore, is to make more effective all activities of the Government related to international information.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I have recently appointed a committee of representative and informed citizens to survey this subject and to make recommendations in the near future for legislative, administrative, or other action.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A unified and dynamic effort in this whole field is essential to the security of the United States and of the other peoples in the community of free nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There is but one sure way to avoid total war--and that is to win the cold war.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: While retaliatory power is one strong deterrent to a would-be aggressor, another powerful deterrent is defensive power.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: No enemy is likely to attempt an attack foredoomed to failure.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Because the building of a completely impenetrable defense against attack is still not possible, total defensive strength must include civil defense preparedness.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Because we have incontrovertible evidence that Soviet Russia possesses atomic weapons, this kind of protection becomes sheer necessity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Civil defense responsibilities primarily belong to the State and local governments--recruiting, training, and organizing volunteers to meet any emergency.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The immediate job of the Federal Government is to provide leadership, to supply technical guidance, and to continue to strengthen its civil defense stockpile of medical, engineering, and related supplies and equipment.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This work must go forward without lag.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I have referred to the inescapable need for economic health and strength if we are to maintain adequate military power and exert influential leadership for peace in the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our immediate task is to chart a fiscal and economic policy that can: (1) Reduce the planned deficits and then balance the budget, which means, among other things, reducing Federal expenditures to the safe minimum;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: (2) Meet the huge costs of our defense;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: (3) Properly handle the burden of our inheritance of debt and obligations;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: (4) Check the menace of inflation;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: (5) Work toward the earliest possible reduction of the tax burden;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: (6) Make constructive plans to encourage the initiative of our citizens.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is important that all of us understand that this administration does not and cannot begin its task with a clean slate.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Much already has been written on the record, beyond our power quickly to erase or to amend.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This record includes our inherited burden of indebtedness and obligations and deficits.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The current year's budget, as you know, carries a 5.9 billion dollar deficit;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: and the budget, which was presented to you before this administration took office, indicates a budgetary deficit of 9.9 billion for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1954.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The national debt is now more than 265 billion dollars.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In addition, the accumulated obligational authority of the Federal Government for future payment totals over 80 billion dollars.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Even this amount is exclusive of large contingent liabilities, so numerous and extensive as to be almost beyond description.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The bills for the payment of nearly all of the 80 billion dollars of obligations will be presented during the next 4 years.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These bills, added to the current costs of government we must meet, make a formidable burden.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The present authorized Government-debt limit is 275 billion dollars.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The forecast presented by the outgoing administration with the fiscal year 1954 budget indicates that--before the end of the fiscal year and at the peak of demand for payments during the year--the total Government debt may approach and even exceed that limit.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Unless budgeted deficits are checked, the momentum of past programs will force an increase of the statutory debt limit.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Permit me this one understatement: to meet and to correct this situation will not be easy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Permit me this one assurance: every department head and I are determined to do everything we can to resolve it.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The first order of business is the elimination of the annual deficit.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This cannot be achieved merely by exhortation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It demands the concerted action of all those in responsible positions in the Government and the earnest cooperation of the Congress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Already, we have begun an examination of the appropriations and expenditures of all departments in an effort to find significant items that may be decreased or canceled without damage to our essential requirements.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Getting control of the budget requires also that State and local governments and interested groups of citizens restrain themselves in their demands upon the Congress that the Federal Treasury spend more and more money for all types of projects.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A balanced budget is an essential first measure in checking further depreciation in the buying power of the dollar.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This is one of the critical steps to be taken to bring an end to planned inflation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our purpose is to manage the Government's finances so as to help and not hinder each family in balancing its own budget.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Reduction of taxes will be justified only as we show we can succeed in bringing the budget under control.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As the budget is balanced and inflation checked, the tax burden that today stifles initiative can and must be eased.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Until we can determine the extent to which expenditures can be reduced, it would not be wise to reduce our revenues.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Meanwhile, the tax structure as a whole demands review.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Secretary of the Treasury is undertaking this study immediately.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must develop a system of taxation which will impose the least possible obstacle to the dynamic growth of the country.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This includes particularly real opportunity for the growth of small businesses.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Many readjustments in existing taxes will be necessary to serve these objectives and also to remove existing inequities.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Clarification and simplification in the tax laws as well as the regulations will be undertaken.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the entire area of fiscal policy--which must, in its various aspects, be treated in recommendations to the Congress in coming weeks--there can now be stated certain basic facts and principles.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: First: It is axiomatic that our economy is a highly complex and sensitive mechanism.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Hasty and ill-considered action of any kind could seriously upset the subtle equation that encompasses debts, obligations, expenditures, defense demands, deficits, taxes, and the general economic health of the Nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our goals can be clear, our start toward them can be immediate--but action must be gradual.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Second: It is clear that too great a part of the national debt comes due in too short a time.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Department of the Treasury will undertake at suitable times a program of extending part of the debt over longer periods and gradually placing greater amounts in the hands of longer-term investors.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Third: Past differences in policy between the Treasury and the Federal Reserve Board have helped to encourage inflation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Henceforth, I expect that their single purpose shall be to serve the whole Nation by policies designed to stabilize the economy and encourage the free play of our people's genius for individual initiative.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In encouraging this initiative, no single item in our current problems has received more thoughtful consideration by my associates, and by the many individuals called into our counsels, than the matter of price and wage control by law.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The great economic strength of our democracy has developed in an atmosphere of freedom.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The character of our people resists artificial and arbitrary controls of any kind.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Direct controls, except those on credit, deal not with the real causes of inflation but only with its symptoms.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In times of national emergency, this kind of control has a role to play.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our whole system, however, is based upon the assumption that, normally, we should combat wide fluctuations in our price structure by relying largely on the effective use of sound fiscal and monetary policy, and upon the natural workings of economic law.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Moreover, American labor and American business can best resolve their wage problems across the bargaining table.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Government should refrain from sitting in with them unless, in extreme cases, the public welfare requires protection.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We are, of course, living in an international situation that is neither an emergency demanding full mobilization, nor is it peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: No one can know how long this condition will persist.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Consequently, we are forced to learn many new things as we go along-clinging to what works, discarding what does not.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In all our current discussions on these and related facts, the weight of evidence is clearly against the use of controls in their present forms.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They have proved largely unsatisfactory or unworkable.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They have not prevented inflation;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: they have not kept down the cost of living.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Dissatisfaction with them is wholly justified.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am convinced that now--as well as in the long run--free and competitive prices will best serve the interests of all the people, and best meet the changing, growing needs of our economy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Accordingly, I do not intend to ask for a renewal of the present wage and price controls on April 30, 1953, when present legislation expires.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the meantime, steps will be taken to eliminate controls in an orderly manner, and to terminate special agencies no longer needed for this purpose.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is obviously to be expected that the removal of these controls will result in individual price changes--some up, some down.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But a maximum of freedom in market prices as well as in collective bargaining is characteristic of a truly free people.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I believe also that material and product controls should be ended, except with respect to defense priorities and scarce and critical items essential for our defense.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I shall recommend to the Congress that legislation be enacted to continue authority for such remaining controls of this type as will be necessary after the expiration of the existing statute on June 30, 1953.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I recommend the continuance of the authority for Federal control over rents in those communities in which serious housing shortages exist.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These are chiefly the so-called defense areas.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In these and all areas the Federal Government should withdraw from the control of rents as soon as practicable.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But before they are removed entirely, each legislature should have full opportunity to take over, within its own State, responsibility for this function.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It would be idle to pretend that all our problems in this whole field of prices will solve themselves by mere Federal withdrawal from direct controls.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We shall have to watch trends closely.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If the freer functioning of our economic system, as well as the indirect controls which can be appropriately employed, prove insufficient during this period of strain and tension, I shall promptly ask the Congress to enact such legislation as may be required.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In facing all these problems--wages, prices, production, tax rates, fiscal policy, deficits--everywhere we remain constantly mindful that the time for sacrifice has not ended.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But we are concerned with the encouragement of competitive enterprise and individual initiative precisely because we know them to be our Nation's abiding sources of strength.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our vast world responsibility accents with urgency our people's elemental right to a government whose clear qualities are loyalty, security, efficiency, economy, and integrity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The safety of America and the trust of the people alike demand that the personnel of the Federal Government be loyal in their motives and reliable in the discharge of their duties.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Only a combination of both loyalty and reliability promises genuine security.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To state this principle is easy;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: to apply it can be difficult.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But this security we must and shall have.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: By way of example, all principal new appointees to departments and agencies have been investigated at their own request by the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Confident of your understanding and cooperation, I know that the primary responsibility for keeping out the disloyal and the dangerous rests squarely upon the executive branch.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: When this branch so conducts itself as to require policing by another branch of the Government, it invites its own disorder and confusion.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am determined to meet this responsibility of the Executive.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The heads of all executive departments and agencies have been instructed to initiate at once effective programs of security with respect to their personnel.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Attorney General will advise and guide the departments and agencies in the shaping of these programs, designed at once to govern the employment of new personnel and to review speedily any derogatory information concerning incumbent personnel.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To carry out these programs, I believe that the powers of the executive branch under existing law are sufficient.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If they should prove inadequate, the necessary legislation will be requested.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These programs will be both fair to the rights of the individual and effective for the safety of the Nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They will, with care and justice, apply the basic principle that public employment is not a right but a privilege.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: All these measures have two clear purposes: Their first purpose is to make certain that this Nation's security is not jeopardized by false servants.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Their second purpose is to clear the atmosphere of that unreasoned suspicion that accepts rumor and gossip as substitutes for evidence.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our people, of course, deserve and demand of their Federal Government more than security of personnel.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They demand, also, efficient and logical organization, true to constitutional principles.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I have already established a Committee on Government Organization.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Committee is using as its point of departure the reports of the Hoover Commission and subsequent studies by several independent agencies.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To achieve the greater efficiency and economy which the Committee analyses show to be possible, I ask the Congress to extend the present Government Reorganization Act for a period of 18 months or 2 years beyond its expiration date of April 1, 1953.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There is more involved here than realigning the wheels and smoothing the gears of administrative machinery.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Congress rightfully-expects the Executive to take the initiative in discovering and removing outmoded functions and eliminating duplication.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: One agency, for example, whose head has promised early and vigorous action to provide greater efficiency is the Post Office.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: One of the oldest institutions of our Federal Government, its service should be of the best.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Its employees should merit and receive the high regard and esteem of the citizens of the Nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There are today in some areas of the postal service, both waste and incompetence to be corrected.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: With the cooperation of the Congress, and taking advantage of its accumulated experience in postal affairs, the Postmaster General will institute a program directed at improving service while at the same time reducing costs and decreasing deficits.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In all departments, dedication to these basic precepts of security and efficiency, integrity, and economy can and will produce an administration deserving of the trust the people have placed in it.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our people have demanded nothing less than good, efficient government.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They shall get nothing less.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Vitally important are the water and minerals, public lands and standing timber, forage and Mid-life of this country.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A fast-growing population will have vast future needs in these resources.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must more than match the substantial achievements in the half-century since President Theodore Roosevelt awakened the Nation to the problem of conservation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This calls for a strong Federal program in the field of resource development.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Its major projects should be timed, where possible to assist in leveling off peaks and valleys in our economic life.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Soundly planned projects already initiated should be carried out.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: New ones will be planned for the future.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The best natural resources program for America will not result from exclusive dependence on Federal bureaucracy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It will involve a partnership of the States and local communities, private citizens, and the Federal Government, all working together.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This combined effort will advance the development of the great river valleys of our Nation and the power that they can generate.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Likewise, such a partnership can be effective in the expansion throughout the Nation of upstream storage;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: the sound use of public lands;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: the wise conservation of minerals;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: and the sustained yield of our forests.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There has been much criticism, some of it apparently justified, of the confusion resulting from overlapping Federal activities in the entire field of resource-conservation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This matter is being exhaustively studied and appropriate reorganization plans will be developed.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Most of these particular resource problems pertain to the Department of the Interior.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Another of its major concerns is our country's island possessions.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Here, one matter deserves attention.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The platforms of both political parties promised immediate statehood to Hawaii.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The people of that Territory have earned that status.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Statehood should be granted promptly with the first election scheduled for 1954.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: One of the difficult problems which face the new administration is that of the slow, irregular decline of farm prices.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This decline, which has been going on for almost 2 years, has occurred at a time when most nonfarm prices and farm costs of production are extraordinarily high.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Present agricultural legislation provides for the mandatory support of the prices of basic farm commodities at 90 percent of parity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Secretary of Agriculture and his associates will, of course, execute the present act faithfully and thereby seek to mitigate the consequences of the downturn in farm income.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This price-support legislation will expire at the end of 1954.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: So we should begin now to consider what farm legislation we should develop for 1955 and beyond.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our aim should be economic stability and full parity of income for American farmers.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But we must seek this goal in ways that minimize governmental interference in the farmers' affairs, that permit desirable shifts in production, and that encourage farmers themselves to use initiative in meeting changing economic conditions.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A continuing study reveals nothing more emphatically than the complicated nature of this subject.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Among other things, it shows that the prosperity of our agriculture depends directly upon the prosperity of the whole country--upon the purchasing power of American consumers.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It depends also upon the opportunity to ship abroad large surpluses of particular commodities, and therefore upon sound economic relationships between the United States and many foreign countries.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It involves research and scientific investigation, conducted on an extensive scale.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It involves special credit mechanisms and marketing, rural electrification, soil conservation, and other programs.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The whole complex of agricultural programs and policies will be studied by a Special Agricultural Advisory Commission, as I know it will by appropriate committees of the Congress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A nonpartisan group of respected authorities in the field of agriculture has already been appointed as an interim advisory group.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The immediate changes needed in agricultural programs are largely budgetary and administrative in nature.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: New policies and new programs must await the completion of the far-reaching studies which have already been launched.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The determination of labor policy must be governed not by the vagaries of political expediency but by the firmest principles and convictions.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Slanted partisan appeals to American workers, spoken as if they were a group apart, necessitating a special language and treatment, are an affront to the fullness of their dignity as American citizens.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The truth in matters of labor policy has become obscured in controversy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The very meaning of economic freedom as it affects labor has become confused.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This misunderstanding has provided a climate of opinion favoring the growth of governmental paternalism in labor relations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This tendency, if left uncorrected, could end only by producing a bureaucratic despotism.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Economic freedom is, in fact, the requisite of greater prosperity for every American who earns his own living.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the field of labor legislation, only a law that merits the respect and support of both labor and management can help reduce the loss of wages and of production through strikes and stoppages, and thus add to the total economic strength of our Nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We have now had 5 years' experience with the Labor Management Act of 1947, commonly known as the Taft-Hartley Act.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: That experience has shown the need for some corrective action, and we should promptly proceed to amend that act.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I know that the Congress is already proceeding with renewed studies of this subject.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Meanwhile, the Department of Labor is at once beginning work to devise further specific recommendations for your consideration.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the careful working out of legislation, I know you will give thoughtful consideration--as will we in the executive branch--to the views of labor, and of management, and of the general public.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In this process, it is only human that each of us should bring forward the arguments of self-interest.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But if all conduct their arguments in the overpowering light of national interest--which is enlightened self-interest--we shall get the right answers.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I profoundly hope that every citizen of our country will follow with understanding your progress in this work.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The welfare of all of us is involved.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Especially must we remember that the institutions of trade unionism and collective bargaining are monuments to the freedom that must prevail in our industrial life.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They have a century of honorable achievement behind them.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our faith in them is proven, firm, and final.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Government can do a great deal to aid the settlement of labor disputes without allowing itself to be employed as an ally of either side.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Its proper role in industrial strife is to encourage the processes of mediation and conciliation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These processes can successfully be directed only by a government free from the taint of any suspicion that it is partial or punitive.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The administration intends to strengthen and to improve the services which the Department of Labor can render to the worker and to the whole national community.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This Department was created--just 40 years ago--to serve the entire Nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It must aid, for example, employers and employees alike in improving training programs that will develop skilled and competent workers.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It must enjoy the confidence and respect of labor and industry in order to play a significant role in the planning of America's economic future.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To that end, I am authorizing the Department of Labor to establish promptly a tripartite advisory committee consisting of representatives of employers, labor, and the public.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our civil and social rights form a central part of the heritage we are striving to defend on all fronts and with all our strength.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I believe with all my heart that our vigilant guarding of these rights is a sacred obligation binding upon every citizen.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To be true to one's own freedom is, in essence, to honor and respect the freedom of all others.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A cardinal ideal in this heritage we cherish is the equality of rights of all citizens of every race and color and creed.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We know that discrimination against minorities persists despite our allegiance to this ideal.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Such discrimination--confined to no one section of the Nation--is but the outward testimony to the persistence of distrust and of fear in the hearts of men.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This fact makes all the more vital the fighting of these wrongs by each individual, in every station of life, in his every deed.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Much of the answer lies in the power of fact, fully publicized;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: of persuasion, honestly pressed;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: and of conscience, justly aroused.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These are methods familiar to our way of life, tested and proven wise.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I propose to use whatever authority exists in the office of the President to end segregation in the District of Columbia, including the Federal Government, and any segregation in the Armed Forces.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Here in the District of Columbia, serious attention should be given to the proposal to develop and authorize, through legislation, a system to provide an effective voice in local self-government.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: While consideration of this proceeds, I recommend an immediate increase of two in the number of District Commissioners to broaden representation of all elements of our local population.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This will be a first step toward insuring that this Capital provide an honored example to all communities of our Nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In this manner, and by the leadership of the office of the President exercised through friendly conferences with those in authority in our States and cities, we expect to make true and rapid progress in civil rights and equality of employment opportunity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There is one sphere in which civil rights are inevitably involved in Federal legislation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This is the sphere of immigration.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is a manifest right of our Government to limit the number of immigrants our Nation can absorb.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is also a manifest right of our Government to set reasonable requirements on the character and the numbers of the people who come to share our land and our freedom.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is well for us, however, to remind ourselves occasionally of an equally manifest fact: we are--one and all--immigrants or sons and daughters of immigrants.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Existing legislation contains injustices.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It does, in fact, discriminate.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am informed by Members of the Congress that it was realized, at the time of its enactment, that future study of the basis of determining quotas would be necessary.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am therefore requesting the Congress to review this legislation and to enact a statute that will at one and the same time guard our legitimate national interests and be faithful to our basic ideas of freedom and fairness to all.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In another but related area--that of social rights--we see most clearly the new application of old ideas of freedom.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This administration is profoundly aware of two great needs born of our living in a complex industrial economy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: First, the individual citizen must have safeguards against personal disaster inflicted by forces beyond his control;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: second, the welfare of the people demands effective and economical performance by the Government of certain indispensable social services.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the light of this responsibility, certain general purposes and certain concrete measures are plainly indicated now.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There is urgent need for greater effectiveness in our programs, both public and private, offering safeguards against the privations that too often come with unemployment, old age, illness, and accident.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The provisions of the old-age and survivors insurance law should promptly be extended to cover millions of citizens who have been left out of the social-security system.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: No less important is the encouragement of privately sponsored pension plans.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Most important of all, of course, is renewed effort to check the inflation which destroys so much of the value of all social-security payments.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our school system demands some prompt, effective help.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: During each of the last 9 years, more than 1 2 million children have swelled the elementary and secondary school population of the country.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Generally, the school population is proportionately higher in States with low per capita income.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This whole situation calls for careful congressional study and action.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am sure that you share my conviction that the firm conditions of Federal aid must be proved need and proved lack of local income.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: One phase of the school problem demands special action.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The school population of many districts has been greatly in- creased by the swift growth of defense activities.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These activities have added little or nothing to the tax resources of the communities affected.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Legislation aiding construction of schools in the districts expires on June 30.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This law should be renewed;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: and likewise, the partial payments for current operating expenses for these particular school districts should be made, including the deficiency requirement of the current fiscal year.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Public interest similarly demands one prompt specific action in protection of the general consumer.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Food and Drug Administration should be authorized to continue its established and necessary program of factory inspections.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The invalidation of these inspections by the Supreme Court of December 8, 1952, was based solely on the fact that the present law contained inconsistent and unclear provisions.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These must be promptly corrected.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am well aware that beyond these few immediate measures there remains much to be done.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The health and housing needs of our people call for intelligently planned programs.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Involved are the solvency of the whole security system;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: and its guarding against exploitation by the irresponsible.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To bring clear purpose and orderly procedure into this field, I anticipate a thorough study of the proper relationship among Federal, State, and local programs.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I shall shortly send you specific recommendations for establishing such an appropriate commission, together with a reorganization plan defining new administrative status for all Federal activities in health, education, and social security.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I repeat that there are many important subjects of which I make no mention today.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Among these is our great and growing body of veterans.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: America has traditionally been generous in caring for the disabled--and the widow and the orphan of the fallen.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These millions remain close to all our hearts.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Proper care of our uniformed citizens and appreciation of the past service of our veterans are part of our accepted governmental responsibilities.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We have surveyed briefly some problems of our people and a portion of the tasks before us.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The hope of freedom itself depends, in real measure, upon our strength, our heart, and our wisdom.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must be strong in arms.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must be strong in the source of all our armament, our productivity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We all--workers and farmers, foremen and financiers, technicians and builders--all must produce, produce more, and produce yet more.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must be strong, above all, in the spiritual resources upon which all else depends.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must be devoted with all our heart to the values we defend.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must know that each of these values and virtues applies with equal force at the ends of the earth and in our relations with our neighbor next door.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must know that freedom expresses itself with equal eloquence in the right of workers to strike in the nearby factory, and in the yearnings and sufferings of the peoples of Eastern Europe.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As our heart summons our strength, our wisdom must direct it.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There is, in world affairs, a steady course to be followed between an assertion of strength that is truculent and a confession of helplessness that is cowardly.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There is, in our affairs at home, a middle way between untrammeled freedom of the individual and the demands for the welfare of the whole Nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This way must avoid government by bureaucracy as carefully as it avoids neglect of the helpless.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In every area of political action, free men must think before they can expect to win.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In this spirit must we live and labor: confident of our strength, compassionate in our heart, clear in our mind.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In this spirit, let us together turn to the great tasks before us.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is a high honor again to present to the Congress my views on the state of the Union and to recommend measures to advance the security, prosperity, and well-being of the American people.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: All branches of this Government--and I venture to say both of our great parties--can support the general objective of the recommendations I make today, for that objective is the building of a stronger America.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A nation whose every citizen has good reason for bold hope; where effort is rewarded and prosperity is shared; where freedom expands and peace is secure--that is what I mean by a stronger America.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Toward this objective a real momentum has been developed during this Administration's first year in office.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We mean to continue that momentum and to increase it.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We mean to build a better future for this nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Much for which we may be thankful has happened during the past year.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: First of all we are deeply grateful that our sons no longer die on the distant mountains of Korea.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Although they are still called from our homes to military service, they are no longer called to the field of battle.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The nation has just completed the most prosperous year in its history.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The damaging effect of inflation on the wages, pensions, salaries and savings of us all has been brought under control.
