speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Taxes have begun to go down.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The cost of our government has been reduced and its work proceeds with some 183,000 fewer employees; thus the discouraging trend of modern governments toward their own limitless expansion has in our case been reversed.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The cost of armaments becomes less oppressive as we near our defense goals; yet we are militarily stronger every day.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: During the year, creation of the new Cabinet Department of Health, Education, and Welfare symbolized the government's permanent concern with the human problems of our citizens.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Segregation in the armed forces and other Federal activities is on the way out.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We have also made progress toward its elimination in the District of Columbia.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These are steps in the continuing effort to eliminate inter-racial difficulty.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Some developments beyond our shores have been equally encouraging.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Communist aggression, halted in Korea, continues to meet in Indo-china the vigorous resistance of France and the Associated States, assisted by timely aid from our country.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In West Germany, in Iran, and in other areas of the world, heartening political victories have been won by the forces of stability and freedom.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Slowly but surely, the free world gathers strength.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Meanwhile, from behind the iron curtain, there are signs that tyranny is in trouble and reminders that its structure is as brittle as its surface is hard.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There has been in fact a great strategic change in the world during the past year.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: That precious intangible, the initiative, is becoming ours.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our policy, not limited to mere reaction against crises provoked by others, is free to develop along lines of our choice not only abroad, but also at home.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As a major theme for American policy during the coming year, let our joint determination be to hold this new initiative and to use it.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We shall use this initiative to promote three broad purposes: First, to protect the freedom of our people; second, to maintain a strong, growing economy; third, to concern ourselves with the human problems of the individual citizen.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Only by active concern for each of these purposes can we be sure that we are on the forward road to a better and a stronger America.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: All my recommendations today are in furtherance of these three purposes.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Foreign Affairs: American freedom is threatened so long as the world Communist conspiracy exists in its present scope, power and hostility.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: More closely than ever before, American freedom is interlocked with the freedom of other people.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the unity of the free world lies our best chance to reduce the Communist threat without war.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the task of maintaining this unity and strengthening all its parts, the greatest responsibility falls naturally on those who, like ourselves, retain the most freedom and strength.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We shall, therefore, continue to advance the cause of freedom on foreign fronts.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the Far East, we retain our vital interest in Korea.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We have negotiated with the Republic of Korea a mutual security pact, which develops our security system for the Pacific and which I shall promptly submit to the Senate for its consent to ratification.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We are prepared to meet any renewal of armed aggression in Korea.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We shall maintain indefinitely our bases in Okinawa.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I shall ask the Congress to authorize continued material assistance to hasten the successful conclusion of the struggle in Indo-china.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This assistance will also bring closer the day when the Associated States may enjoy the independence already assured by France.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We shall also continue military and economic aid to the Nationalist Government of China.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In South Asia, profound changes are taking place in free nations which are demonstrating their ability to progress through democratic methods.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They provide an inspiring contrast to the dictatorial methods and backward course of events in Communist China.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In these continuing efforts, the free peoples of South Asia can be assured of the support of the United States.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the Middle East, where tensions and serious problems exist, we will show sympathetic and impartial friendship.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In Western Europe our policy rests firmly on the North Atlantic Treaty.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It will remain so based as far ahead as we can see.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Within its organization, the building of a united European community, including France and Germany, is vital to a free and self-reliant Europe.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This will be promoted by the European Defense Community which offers assurance of European security.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: With the coming of unity to Western Europe, the assistance this Nation can render for the security of Europe and the free world will be multiplied in effectiveness.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the Western Hemisphere we shall continue to develop harmonious and mutually beneficial cooperation with our neighbors.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Indeed, solid friendship with all our American neighbors is a cornerstone of our entire policy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the world as a whole, the United Nations, admittedly still in a state of evolution, means much to the United States.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It has given uniquely valuable services in many places where violence threatened.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is the only real world forum where we have the opportunity for international presentation and rebuttal.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is a place where the nations of the world can, if they have the will, take collective action for peace and justice.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is a place where the guilt can be squarely assigned to those who fail to take all necessary steps to keep the peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The United Nations deserves our continued firm support.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Foreign Assistance and Trade: In the practical application of our foreign policy, we enter the field of foreign assistance and trade.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Military assistance must be continued.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Technical assistance must be maintained.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Economic assistance can be reduced.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: However, our economic programs in Korea and in a few other critical places of the world are especially important, and I shall ask Congress to continue them in the next fiscal year.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The forthcoming Budget Message will propose maintenance of the Presidential power of transferability of all assistance funds and will ask authority to merge these funds with the regular defense funds.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It will also propose that the Secretary of Defense have primary responsibility for the administration of foreign military assistance in accordance with the policy guidance of the Secretary of State.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The fact that we can now reduce our foreign economic assistance in many areas is gratifying evidence that its objectives are being achieved.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: By continuing to surpass her prewar levels of economic activity, Western Europe gains self-reliance.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Thus our relationship enters a new phase which can bring results beneficial to our taxpayers and our allies alike, if still another step is taken.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This step is the creation of a healthier and freer system of trade and payments within the free world--a system in which our allies can earn their own way and our own economy can continue to flourish.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The free world can no longer afford the kinds of arbitrary restraints on trade that have continued ever since the war.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: On this problem I shall submit to the Congress detailed recommendations, after our Joint Commission on Foreign Economic Policy has made its report.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Atomic Energy Proposal: As we maintain our military strength during the coming year and draw closer the bonds with our allies, we shall be in an improved position to discuss outstanding issues with the Soviet Union.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Indeed we shall be glad to do so whenever there is a reasonable prospect of constructive results.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In this spirit the atomic energy proposals of the United States were recently presented to the United Nations General Assembly.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A truly constructive Soviet reaction will make possible a new start toward an era of peace, and away from the fatal road toward atomic war.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Defense: Since our hope is peace, we owe ourselves and the world a candid explanation of the military measures we are taking to make that peace secure.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As we enter this new year, our military power continues to grow.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This power is for our own defense and to deter aggression.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We shall not be aggressors, but we and our allies have and will maintain a massive capability to strike back.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Here are some of the considerations in our defense planning: First, while determined to use atomic power to serve the usages of peace, we take into full account our great and growing number of nuclear weapons and the most effective means of using them against an aggressor if they are needed to preserve our freedom.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our defense will be stronger if, under appropriate security safeguards, we share with our allies certain knowledge of the tactical use of our nuclear weapons.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I urge the Congress to provide the needed authority.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Second, the usefulness of these new weapons creates new relationships between men and materials.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These new relationships permit economies in the use of men as we build forces suited to our situation in the world today.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As will be seen from the Budget Message on January 21, the airpower of our Navy and Air Force is receiving heavy emphasis.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Third, our armed forces must regain maximum mobility of action.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our strategic reserves must be centrally placed and readily deployable to meet sudden aggression against ourselves and our allies.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Fourth, our defense must rest on trained manpower and its most economical and mobile use.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A professional corps is the heart of any security organization.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is necessarily the teacher and leader of those who serve temporarily in the discharge of the obligation to help defend the Republic.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Pay alone will not retain in the career service of our armed forces the necessary numbers of long-term personnel.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I strongly urge, therefore, a more generous use of other benefits important to service morale.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Among these are more adequate living quarters and family housing units and medical care for dependents.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Studies of military manpower have just been completed by the National Security Training Commission and a Committee appointed by the Director of the Office of Defense Mobilization.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Evident weaknesses exist in the state of readiness and organization of our reserve forces.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Measures to correct these weaknesses will be later submitted to the Congress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Fifth, the ability to convert swiftly from partial to all-out mobilization is imperative to our security.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: For the first time, mobilization officials know what the requirements are for 1,000 major items needed for military uses.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These data, now being related to civilian requirements and our supply potential, will show us the gaps in our mobilization base.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Thus we shall have more realistic plant-expansion and stockpiling goals.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We shall speed their attainment.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This Nation is at last to have an up-to-date mobilization base--the foundation of a sound defense program.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Another part of this foundation is, of course, our continental transport system.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Some of our vital heavy materials come increasingly from Canada.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Indeed our relations with Canada, happily always close, involve more and more the unbreakable ties of strategic interdependence.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Both nations now need the St. Lawrence Seaway for security as well as for economic reasons.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Lawrence Seaway for security as well as for economic reasons.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I urge the Congress promptly to approve our participation in its construction.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Sixth, military and non-military measures for continental defense must be and are being strengthened.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the current fiscal year we are allocating to these purposes an increasing portion of our effort, and in the next fiscal year we shall spend nearly a billion dollars more for them than in 1953.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: An indispensable part of our continental security is our civil defense effort.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This will succeed only as we have the complete cooperation of State Governors, Mayors, and voluntary citizen groups.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: With their help we can advance a cooperative program which, if an attack should come, would save many lives and lessen destruction.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The defense program recommended in the 1955 Budget is consistent with all of the considerations which I have just discussed.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is based on a new military program unanimously recommended by the Joint Chiefs of Staff and approved by me following consideration by the National Security Council.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This new program will make and keep America strong in an age of peril.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Nothing should bar its attainment.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The international and defense policies which I have outlined will enable us to negotiate from a position of strength as we hold our resolute course toward a peaceful world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We now turn to matters which are normally characterized as domestic, well realizing that what we do abroad affects every problem at home--from the amount of taxes to our very state of mind.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Internal Security: Under the standards established for the new employee security program, more than 2,200 employees have been separated from the Federal government.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our national security demands that the investigation of new employees and the evaluation of derogatory information respecting present employees be expedited and concluded at the earliest possible date.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I shall recommend that the Congress provide additional funds where necessary to speed these important procedures.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: From the special employment standards of the Federal government I turn now to a matter relating to American citizenship.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The subversive character of the Communist Party in the United States has been clearly demonstrated in many ways, including court proceedings.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We should recognize by law a fact that is plain to all thoughtful citizens--that we are dealing here with actions akin to treason--that when a citizen knowingly participates in the Communist conspiracy he no longer holds allegiance to the United States.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I recommend that Congress enact legislation to provide that a citizen of the United States who is convicted in the courts of hereafter conspiring to advocate the overthrow of this government by force or violence be treated as having, by such act, renounced his allegiance to the United States and forfeited his United States citizenship.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In addition, the Attorney General will soon appear before your Committees to present his recommendations for needed additional legal weapons with which to combat subversion in our country and to deal with the question of claimed immunity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Strong Economy: I turn now to the second great purpose of our government: Along with the protection of freedom, the maintenance of a strong and growing economy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The American economy is one of the wonders of the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It under girds our international position, our military security, and the standard of living of every citizen.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This Administration is determined to keep our economy strong and to keep it growing.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: At this moment we are in transition from a wartime to a peacetime economy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am confident that we can complete this transition without serious interruption in our economic growth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But we shall not leave this vital matter to chance.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Economic preparedness is fully as important to the nation as military preparedness.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Subsequent special messages and the economic report on January 28 will set forth plans of the Administration and its recommendations for Congressional action.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These will include flexible credit and debt management policies; tax measures to stimulate consumer and business spending; suitable lending, guaranteeing, insuring, and grant-in-aid activities; strengthened old-age and unemployment insurance measures; improved agricultural programs; public-works plans laid well in advance; enlarged opportunities for international trade and investment.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This mere enumeration of these subjects implies the vast amount of study, coordination, and planning, to say nothing of authorizing legislation, that altogether make our economic preparedness complete.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If new conditions arise that require additional administrative or legislative action, the Administration will still be ready.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A government always ready, as this is, to take well-timed and vigorous action, and a business community willing, as ours is, to plan boldly and with confidence, can between them develop a climate assuring steady economic growth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Budget: I shall submit to the Congress on January 21 the first budget prepared by this Administration, for the period July 1, 1954, through June 1955.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This budget is adequate to the current needs of the government.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It recognizes that a Federal budget should be a stabilizing factor in the economy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Its tax and expenditure programs will foster individual initiative and economic growth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Pending the transmittal of my Budget Message, I shall mention here only a few points about our budgetary situation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: First, one of our initial acts was to revise, with the cooperation of the Congress, the Budget prepared before this Administration took office.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Requests for new appropriations were greatly reduced.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In addition, the spending level provided in that Budget for the current fiscal year has been reduced by about $7,000,000,000.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the next fiscal year we estimate a further reduction in expenditures of more than $5,000,000,000.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This will reduce the spending level over the two fiscal years by more than $12,000,000,000.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We are also reducing further our requests for new appropriations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Second, despite the substantial loss of revenue in the coming fiscal year, resulting from tax reductions now in effect and tax adjustments which I shall propose, our reduced spending will move the new budget closer to a balance.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Third, by keeping new appropriation requests below estimated revenues, we continue to reduce the tremendous accumulation of un-financed obligations incurred by the Government under past appropriations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Fourth, until those claims on our Government's revenues are further reduced, the growth in the public debt cannot be entirely stopped.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Because of this--because the government's bills have to be paid every month, while the tax money to pay them comes in with great unevenness within the fiscal year--and because of the need for flexibility to manage this enormous debt, I find it necessary to renew my request for an increase in the statutory debt limit.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Taxes: The new budget provides for a lower level of taxation than has prevailed in preceding years.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Six days ago individual income taxes were reduced and the excess profits tax expired.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These tax reductions are justified only because of the substantial reductions we already have made and are making in governmental expenditures.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As additional reductions in expenditures are brought gradually but surely into sight, further reductions in taxes can and will be made.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: When budget savings and sound governmental financing are assured, tax burdens should be reduced so that taxpayers may spend their own money in their own way.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: While we are moving toward lower levels of taxation we must thoroughly revise our whole tax system.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The groundwork for this revision has already been laid by the Committee on Ways and Means of the House of Representatives, in close consultation with the Department of the Treasury.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We should now remove the more glaring tax inequities, particularly on small taxpayers; reduce restraints on the growth of small business; and make other changes that will encourage initiative, enterprise and production.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Twenty-five recommendations toward these ends will be contained in my budget message.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Without attempting to summarize these manifold reforms, I can here illustrate their tendency.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: For example, we propose more liberal tax treatment for dependent children who work, for widows or widowers with dependent children, and for medical expenses.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: For the business that wants to expand or modernize its plant, we propose liberalized tax treatment of depreciation, research and development expenses, and retained earnings.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Because of the present need for revenue the corporation income tax should be kept at the current rate of 52% for another year, and the excise taxes scheduled to be reduced on April first, including those on liquor, tobacco, gasoline and automobiles, should be continued at present rates.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Immediate extension of the Renegotiation Act of 1951 is also needed to eliminate excessive profits and to prevent waste of public funds in the purchase of defense materials.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Agriculture: The well being of our 160 million people demands a stable and prosperous agriculture.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Conversely, every farmer knows he cannot prosper unless all America prospers.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As we seek to promote increases in our standard of living, we must be sure that the farmer fairly shares in that increase.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Therefore, a farm program promoting stability and prosperity in all elements of our agriculture is urgently needed.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Agricultural laws now in effect successfully accomplished their wartime purpose of encouraging maximum production of many crops.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Today, production of these crops at such levels far exceeds present demand.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Yet the laws encouraging such production are still in effect.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The storage facilities of the Commodity Credit Corporation bulge with surplus stocks of dairy products, wheat, cotton, corn, and certain vegetable oils; and the Corporation's presently authorized borrowing authority--$6,750,000,000--is nearly exhausted.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Some products, priced out of domestic markets, and others, priced out of world markets, have piled up in government hands.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In a world in which millions of people are hungry, destruction of food would, of course, be unconscionable.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Yet surplus stocks continue to threaten the market and in spite of the acreage controls authorized by present law, surpluses will continue to accumulate.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We confront two alternatives.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The first is to impose still greater acreage reductions for some crops and apply rigid Federal controls over the use of the diverted acres.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This will regiment the production of every basic agricultural crop.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It will place every producer of those crops under the domination and control of the Federal government in Washington.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This alternative is contrary to the fundamental interests, not only of the farmer, but of the Nation as a whole.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Nor is it a real solution to the problem facing us.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The second alternative is to permit the market price for these agricultural products gradually to have a greater influence on the planning of production by farmers, while continuing the assistance of the government.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This is the sound approach.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To make it effective, surpluses existing when the new program begins must be insulated from the normal channels of trade for special uses.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These uses would include school lunch programs, disaster relief, emergency assistance to foreign friends, and of particular importance the stockpiling of reserves for a national emergency.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Building on the agricultural laws of 1948 and 1949, we should establish a price support program with enough flexibility to attract the production of needed supplies of essential commodities and to stimulate the consumption of those commodities that are flooding American markets.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Transition to modernized parity must be accomplished gradually.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In no case should there be an abrupt downward change in the dollar level or in the percentage level of price supports.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Next Monday I shall transmit to the Congress my detailed recommendations embodying this approach.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They have been developed through the cooperation of innumerable individuals vitally interested in agriculture.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: My special message on Monday will briefly describe the consultative and advisory processes to which this whole program has been subjected during the past ten months.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I have chosen this farm program because it will build markets, protect the consumers' food supply, and move food into consumption instead of into storage.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is a program that will remove the threat to the farmer of these overhanging surpluses, a program, also, that will stimulate production when a commodity is scarce and encourage consumption when nature is bountiful.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Moreover, it will promote the individual freedom, responsibility, and initiative which distinguish American agriculture.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: And, by helping our agriculture achieve full parity in the market, it promises our farmers a higher and steadier financial return over the years than any alternative plan.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Conservation: Part of our Nation's precious heritage is its natural resources.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is the common responsibility of Federal, state, and local governments to improve and develop them, always working in the closest harmony and partnership.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: All Federal conservation and resource development projects are being reappraised.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Sound projects now under way will be continued.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: New projects in which the Federal Government has a part must be economically sound, with local sharing of cost wherever appropriate and feasible.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the next fiscal year work will be started on twenty-three projects that meet these standards.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Federal Government will continue to construct and operate economically sound flood control, power, irrigation and water supply projects wherever these projects are beyond the capacity of local initiative, public or private, and consistent with the needs of the whole Nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our conservation program will also take into account the important role played by farmers in protecting our soil resources.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I recommend enactment of legislation to strengthen agricultural conservation and upstream flood prevention work, and to achieve a better balance with major flood control structures in the down-stream areas.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Recommendations will be made from time to time for the adoption of: A uniform and consistent water resources policy;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A revised public lands policy;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: and a sound program for safeguarding the domestic production of critical and strategic metals and minerals.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In addition we shall continue to protect and improve our national forests, parks, monuments and other natural and historic sites, as well as our fishery and wildlife resources.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I hope that pending legislation to improve the conservation and management of publicly-owned grazing lands in national forests will soon be approved by the Congress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: National Highways: To protect the vital interest of every citizen in a safe and adequate highway system, the Federal Government is continuing its central role in the Federal Aid Highway Program.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: So that maximum progress can be made to overcome present inadequacies in the Interstate Highway System, we must continue the Federal gasoline tax at two cents per gallon.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This will require cancellation of the 1/2 cent decrease which otherwise will become effective April 1st, and will maintain revenues so that an expanded highway program can be undertaken.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: When the Commission on Intergovernmental Relations completes its study of the present system of financing highway construction, I shall promptly submit it for consideration by the Congress and the governors of the states.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Post Office: It is apparent that the substantial savings already made, and to be made, by the Post Office Department cannot eliminate the postal deficit.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I recommend, therefore, that the Congress approve the bill now pending in the House of Representatives providing for the adjustment of certain postal rates.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To handle the long term aspects of this, I also recommend that the Congress create a permanent commission to establish fair and reasonable postal rates from time to time in the future.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Human Problems: Along with the protection of freedom and maintenance of a strong and growing economy, this Administration recognizes a third great purpose of government: concern for the human problems of our citizens.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In a modern industrial society, banishment of destitution and cushioning the shock of personal disaster on the individual are proper concerns of all levels of government, including the federal government.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This is especially true where remedy and prevention alike are beyond the individual's capacity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Labor and Welfare: Of the many problems in this area, those I shall first discuss are of particular concern to the members of our great labor force, who with their heads, hearts and hands produce so much of the wealth of our country.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Protection against the hazards of temporary unemployment should be extended to some 6 1/2 millions of workers, including civilian Federal workers, who now lack this safeguard.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Moreover, the Secretary of Labor is making available to the states studies and recommendations in the fields of weekly benefits, periods of protection and extension of coverage.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Economic Report will consider the related matter of minimum wages and their coverage.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Labor Management Relations Act of 1947 is basically a sound law.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: However, six years of experience have revealed that in some respects it can be improved.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: On January 11, I shall forward to the Congress suggestions for changes designed to reinforce the basic objectives of the Act.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our basic social security program, the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance system, to which individuals contribute during their productive years and receive benefits based on previous earnings, is designed to shield them from destitution.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Last year I recommended extension of the social insurance system to include more than 10,000,000 additional persons.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I ask that this extension soon be accomplished.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This and other major improvements in the insurance system will bring substantial benefit increases and broaden the membership of the insurance system, thus diminishing the need for Federal grants-in-aid for such purposes.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A new formula will therefore be proposed, permitting progressive reduction in such grants as the need for them declines.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Federal grant-in-aid welfare programs, now based on widely varying formulas, should be simplified.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Concrete proposals on fourteen of them will be suggested to the appropriate Committees.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The program for rehabilitation of the disabled especially needs strengthening.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Through special vocational training, this program presently returns each year some 60,000 handicapped individuals to productive work.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Far more disabled people can be saved each year from idleness and dependence if this program is gradually increased.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: My more detailed recommendations on this and the other social insurance problems I have mentioned will be sent to the Congress on January 14th.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Health: I am flatly opposed to the socialization of medicine.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The great need for hospital and medical services can best be met by the initiative of private plans.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But it is unfortunately a fact that medical costs are rising and already impose severe hardships on many families.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Federal Government can do many helpful things and still carefully avoid the socialization of medicine.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Federal Government should encourage medical research in its battle with such mortal diseases as cancer and heart ailments, and should continue to help the states in their health and rehabilitation programs.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The present Hospital Survey and Construction Act should be broadened in order to assist in the development of adequate facilities for the chronically ill, and to encourage the construction of diagnostic centers, rehabilitation facilities, and nursing homes.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The war on disease also needs a better working relationship between Government and private initiative.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Private and non-profit hospital and medical insurance plans are already in the field, soundly based on the experience and initiative of the people in their various communities.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A limited Government reinsurance service would permit the private and non-profit insurance companies to offer broader protection to more of the many families which want and should have it.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: On January 18 I shall forward to the Congress a special message presenting this Administration's health program in its detail.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Education: Youth--our greatest resource--is being seriously neglected in a vital respect.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The nation as a whole is not preparing teachers or building schools fast enough to keep up with the increase in our population.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The preparation of teachers as, indeed, the control and direction of public education policy, is a state and local responsibility.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: However, the Federal Government should stand ready to assist states which demonstrably cannot provide sufficient school buildings.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In order to appraise the needs, I hope that this year a conference on education will be held in each state, culminating in a national conference.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: From these conferences on education, every level of government--from the Federal Government to each local school board--should gain the information with which to attack this serious problem.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Housing: The details of a program to enlarge and improve the opportunities for our people to acquire good homes will be presented to the Congress by special message on January 25.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This program will include: Modernization of the home mortgage insurance program of the Federal Government;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Insurance of long-term, mortgage loans, with small down payment for low-income families;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Continuation of the public housing program adopted in the Housing Act of 1949.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Redirection of the present system of loans and grants-in-aid to cities for slum clearance and redevelopment;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Extension of the advantages of insured lending to private credit engaged in this task of rehabilitating obsolete neighborhoods;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If the individual, the community, the State and federal governments will alike apply themselves, every American family can have a decent home.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Veterans' Administration: The internal reorganization of the Veterans Administration is proceeding with my full approval.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: When completed, it will afford a single agency whose services, including medical facilities, will be better adapted to the needs of those 20,000,000 veterans to whom this Nation owes so much.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Suffrage: My few remaining recommendations all relate to a basic right of our citizens--that of being represented in the decisions of the government.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I hope that the States will cooperate with the Congress in adopting uniform standards in their voting laws that will make it possible for our citizens in the armed forces overseas to vote.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the District of Columbia the time is long overdue for granting national suffrage to its citizens and also applying the principle of local self-government to the Nation's Capital.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I urge the Congress to move promptly in this direction and also to revise District revenue measures to provide needed public works improvements.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The people of Hawaii are ready for statehood.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I renew my request for this legislation in order that Hawaii may elect its State officials and its representatives in Washington along with the rest of the country this fall.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: For years our citizens between the ages of 18 and 21 have, in time of peril, been summoned to fight for America.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They should participate in the political process that produces this fateful summons.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I urge Congress to propose to the States a constitutional amendment permitting citizens to vote when they reach the age of 18.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I want to add one final word about the general purport of these many recommendations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our government's powers are wisely limited by the Constitution; but quite apart from those limitations, there are things which no government can do or should try to do.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A government can strive, as ours is striving, to maintain an economic system whose doors are open to enterprise and ambition--those personal qualities on which economic growth largely depends.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But enterprise and ambition are qualities which no government can supply.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Fortunately no American government need concern itself on this score; our people have these qualities in good measure.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A government can sincerely strive for peace, as ours is striving, and ask its people to make sacrifices for the sake of peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But no government can place peace in the hearts of foreign rulers.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is our duty then to ourselves and to freedom itself to remain strong in all those ways--spiritual, economic, military--that will give us maximum safety against the possibility of aggressive action by others.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: No government can inoculate its people against the fatal materialism that plagues our age.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Happily, our people, though blessed with more material goods than any people in history, have always reserved their first allegiance to the kingdom of the spirit, which is the true source of that freedom we value above all material things.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But a government can try, as ours tries, to sense the deepest aspirations of the people, and to express them in political action at home and abroad.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: So long as action and aspiration humbly and earnestly seek favor in the sight of the Almighty, there is no end to America's forward road;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: First, I extend cordial greetings to the 84th Congress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We shall have much to do together; I am sure that we shall get it done--and, that we shall do it in harmony and good will.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: At the outset, I believe it would be well to remind ourselves of this great fundamental in our national life: our common belief that every human being is divinely endowed with dignity and worth and inalienable rights.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This faith, with its corollary--that to grow and flourish people must be free--shapes the interests and aspirations of every American.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: From this deep faith have evolved three main purposes of our Federal Government: First, to maintain justice and freedom among ourselves and to champion them for others so that we may work effectively for enduring peace; .

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Foremost among these broad purposes of government is our support of freedom, justice and peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is of the utmost importance, that each of us understand the true nature of the struggle now taking place in the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is not a struggle merely of economic theories, or of forms of government, or of military power.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: At issue is the true nature of man.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: of his Creator; or man is a soulless, animated machine to be enslaved, used and consumed by the state for its own glorification.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is, therefore, a struggle which goes to the roots of the human spirit, and its shadow falls across the long sweep of man's destiny.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This prize, so precious, so fraught with ultimate meaning, is the true object of the contending forces in the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the past year, there has been progress justifying hope, both for continuing peace and for the ultimate rule of freedom and justice in the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Free nations are collectively stronger than at any time in recent years.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Just as nations of this Hemisphere, in the historic Caracas and Rio conferences, have closed ranks against imperialistic Communism and strengthened their economic ties, so free nations elsewhere have forged new bonds of unity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Recent agreements between Turkey and Pakistan have laid a foundation for increased strength in the Middle East.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: With our understanding support, Egypt and Britain, Yugoslavia and Italy, Britain and Iran have resolved dangerous differences.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The security of the Mediterranean has been enhanced by an alliance among Greece, Turkey, and Yugoslavia.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Agreements in Western Europe have paved the way for unity to replace past divisions which have undermined Europe's economic and military vitality.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The defense of the West appears likely at last to include a free, democratic Germany participating as an equal in the councils of NATO.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In Asia and the Pacific, the pending Manila Pact supplements our treaties with Australia, New Zealand, the Philippines, Korea and Japan and our prospective treaty with the Republic of China.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These pacts stand as solemn warning that future military aggression and subversion against the free nations of Asia will meet united response.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Pacific Charter, also adopted at Manila, is a milestone in the development of human freedom and self-government in the Pacific area.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Under the auspices of the United Nations, there is promise of progress in our country's plan for the peaceful use of atomic energy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Finally, today the world is at peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is, to be sure, an insecure peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Yet all humanity finds hope in the simple fact that for an appreciable time there has been no active major battlefield on earth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This same fact inspires us to work all the more effectively with other nations for the well-being, the freedom, the dignity, of every human on earth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These developments are heartening indeed, and we are hopeful of continuing progress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But sobering problems remain.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The massive military machines and ambitions of the Soviet-Communist bloc still create uneasiness in the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: All of us are aware of the continuing reliance of the Soviet Communists on military force, of the power of their weapons, of their present resistance to realistic armament limitation, and of their continuing effort to dominate or intimidate free nations on their periphery.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Their steadily growing power includes an increasing strength in nuclear weapons.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This power, combined with the proclaimed intentions of the Communist leaders to communize the world, is the threat confronting us today.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To protect our nations and our peoples from the catastrophe of a nuclear holocaust, free nations must maintain countervailing military power to persuade the Communists of the futility of seeking their ends through aggression.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If Communist rulers understand that America's response to aggression will be swift and decisive--that never shall we buy peace at the expense of honor or faith--they will be powerfully deterred from launching a military venture engulfing their own peoples and many others in disaster.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This, of course, is merely world stalemate.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But in this stalemate each of us may and must exercise his high duty to strive in every honorable way for enduring peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The military threat is but one menace to our freedom and security.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must not only deter aggression; we must also frustrate the effort of Communists to gain their goals by subversion.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To this end, free nations must maintain and reinforce their cohesion, their internal security, their political and economic vitality, and their faith in freedom.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In such a world, America's course is clear: We must tirelessly labor to make the peace more just and durable.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must strengthen the collective defense under the United Nations Charter and gird ourselves with sufficient military strength and productive capacity to discourage resort to war and protect our nation's vital interests.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must continue to support and strengthen the United Nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: At this very moment, by vote of the United Nations General Assembly, its Secretary-General is in Communist China on a mission of deepest concern to all Americans: seeking the release of our never-to-be-forgotten American aviators and all other United Nations prisoners wrongfully detained by the Communist regime.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must also encourage the efforts being made in the United Nations to limit armaments and to harness the atom to peaceful use.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must expand international trade and investment and assist friendly nations whose own best efforts are still insufficient to provide the strength essential to the security of the free world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must be willing to use the processes of negotiation whenever they will advance the cause of just and secure peace to which the United States and other free nations are dedicated.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In respect to all these matters, we must, through a vigorous information program, keep the peoples of the world truthfully advised of our actions and purposes.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This problem has been attacked with new vigor during the past months.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I urge that the Congress give its earnest consideration to the great advantages that can accrue to our country through the successful operations of this program.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must also carry forward our educational exchange program.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This sharing of knowledge and experience between our citizens and those of free countries is a powerful factor in the development and maintenance of true partnership among free peoples.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To advance these many efforts, the Congress must act in this session on appropriations, legislation, and treaties.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Today I shall mention especially our foreign economic and military programs.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The recent economic progress in many free nations has been most heartening.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The productivity of labor and the production of goods and services are increasing in ever-widening areas.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There is a growing will to improve the living standards of all men.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This progress is important to all our people.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It promises us allies who are strong and self-reliant; it promises a growing world market for the products of our mines, our factories, and our farms.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But only through steady effort can we hope to continue this progress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Barriers still impede trade and the flow of capital needed to develop each nation's human and material resources.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Wise reduction of these barriers is a long-term objective of our foreign economic policy--a policy of an evolutionary and selective nature, assuring broad benefits to our own and other peoples.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must gradually reduce certain tariff obstacles to trade.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These actions should, of course, be accompanied by a similar lowering of trade barriers by other nations, so that we may move steadily toward greater economic advantage for all.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must further simplify customs administration and procedures.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must facilitate the flow of capital and continue technical assistance, both directly and through the United Nations, to less developed countries to strengthen their independence and raise their living standards.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Many another step must be taken in and among the nations of the free world to release forces of private initiative.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In our own nation, these forces have brought strength and prosperity; once released, they will generate rising incomes in these other countries with which to buy the products of American industry, labor and agriculture.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: On January 10, by special message, I shall submit specific recommendations for carrying forward the legislative phases of our foreign economic policy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our many efforts to build a better world include the maintenance of our military strength.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This is a vast undertaking.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Major national security programs consume two-thirds of the entire Federal budget.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Over four million Americans--servicemen and civilians--are on the rolls of the defense establishment.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: During the past two years, by eliminating duplication and overstaffing, by improved procurement and inventory controls, and by concentrating on the essentials, many billions of dollars have been saved in our defense activities.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I should like to mention certain fundamentals underlying this vast program.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: First, a realistic limitation of armaments and an enduring, just peace remain our national goals; we maintain powerful military forces because there is no present alternative--forces designed for deterrent and defensive purposes alone but able instantly to strike back with destructive power in response to an attack.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Second, we must stay alert to the fact that undue reliance on one weapon or preparation for only one kind of warfare simply invites an enemy to resort to another.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must, therefore, keep in our armed forces balance and flexibility adequate for our purposes and objectives.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Third, to keep our armed forces abreast of the advances of science, our military planning must be flexible enough to utilize the new weapons and techniques which flow ever more speedily from our research and development programs.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The forthcoming military budget therefore emphasizes modern airpower in the Air Force, Navy and Marine Corps and increases the emphasis on new weapons, especially those of rapid and destructive striking power.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It assures the maintenance of effective, retaliatory force as the principal deterrent to overt aggression.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It accelerates the continental defense program and the build-up of ready military reserve forces.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It continues a vigorous program of stockpiling strategic and critical materials and strengthening our mobilization base.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The budget also contemplates the strategic concentration of our strength through redeployment of certain forces.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It provides for reduction of forces in certain categories and their expansion in others, to fit them to the military realities of our time.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These emphases in our defense planning have been made at my personal direction after long and thoughtful study.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In my judgment, they will give our nation a defense accurately adjusted to the national need.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Fourth, pending a world agreement on armament limitation, we must continue to improve and expand our supplies of nuclear weapons for our land, naval and air forces, while, at the same time, continuing our encouraging progress in the peaceful use of atomic power.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: And fifth, in the administration of these costly programs, we must demand the utmost in efficiency and ingenuity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must assure our people not only of adequate protection but also of a defense that can be carried forward from year to year until the threat of aggression has disappeared.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To help maintain this kind of armed strength and improve its efficiency, I must urge the enactment of several important measures in this session.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The first concerns the selective service act which expires next June 30th.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: For the foreseeable future, our standing forces must remain much larger than voluntary methods can sustain.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must, therefore, extend the statutory authority to induct men for two years of military service.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The second kind of measure concerns the rapid turnover of our most experienced servicemen.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This process seriously weakens the combat readiness of our armed forces and is exorbitantly expensive.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To encourage more trained servicemen to remain in uniform, I shall, on the thirteenth of this month, propose a number of measures to increase the attractions of a military career.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These measures will include more adequate medical care for dependents, survivors' benefits, more and better housing, and selective adjustments in military pay and other allowances.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: And third--also on January 13--I shall present a program to rebuild and strengthen the civilian components of our armed forces.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This is a comprehensive program, designed to make better use of our manpower of military age.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Because it will go far in assuring fair and equitable participation in military training and service, it is of particular importance to our combat veterans.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In keeping with the historic military policy of our Republic, this program is designed to build and maintain powerful civilian reserves immediately capable of effective military service in an emergency in lieu of maintaining active duty forces in excess of the nation's immediate need.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Maintenance of an effective defense requires continuance of our aggressive attack on subversion at home.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In this effort we have, in the past two years, made excellent progress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: FBI investigations have been powerfully reinforced by a new Internal Security Division in the Department of Justice;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We shall continue to ferret out and to destroy Communist subversion.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We shall, in the process, carefully preserve our traditions and the basic rights of our citizens.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our civil defense program is also a key element in the protection of our country.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We are developing cooperative methods with State Governors, Mayors, and voluntary citizen groups, as well as among Federal agencies, in building the civil defense organization.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Its significance in time of war is obvious; its swift assistance in disaster areas last year proved its importance in time of peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: An industry capable of rapid expansion and essential materials and facilities swiftly available in time of emergency are indispensable to our defense.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I urge, therefore, a two-year extension of the Defense Production Act and Title II of the First War Powers Act of 1941.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These are cornerstones of our program for the development and maintenance of an adequate mobilization base.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: At this point, I should like to make this additional observation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our quest for peace and freedom necessarily presumes that we who hold positions of public trust must rise above self and section--that we must subordinate to the general good our partisan, our personal pride and prejudice.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Tirelessly, with united purpose, we must fortify the material and spiritual foundations of this land of freedom and of free nations throughout the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As never before, there is need for unhesitating cooperation among the branches of our government.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: At this time the executive and legislative branches are under the management of different political parties.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This fact places both parties on trial before the American people.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In less perilous days of the past, division of governmental responsibility among our great parties has produced a paralyzing indecision.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must not let this happen in our time.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must avoid a paralysis of the will for peace and international security.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the traditionally bipartisan areas--military security and foreign relations--I can report to you that I have already, with the leaders of this Congress, expressed assurances of unreserved cooperation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Yet, the strength of our country requires more than mere maintenance of military strength and success in foreign affairs;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I say, therefore, to the 84th Congress: In all areas basic to the strength of America, there will be--to the extent I can insure them--cooperative, constructive relations between the Executive and Legislative Branches of this government.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Let the general good be our yardstick on every great issue of our time.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our efforts to defend our freedom and to secure a just peace are, of course, inseparable from the second great purpose of our government: to help maintain a strong, growing economy--an economy vigorous and free, in which there are ever-increasing opportunities, just rewards for effort, and a stable prosperity that is widely shared.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the past two years, many important governmental actions helped our economy adjust to conditions of peace;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: these and other actions created a climate for renewed economic growth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Controls were removed from wages, prices and materials.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Tax revisions encouraged increased private spending and employment.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Federal expenditures were sharply reduced, making possible a record tax cut.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These actions, together with flexible monetary and debt management policies, helped to halt inflation and stabilize the value of the dollar.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A program of cooperation and partnership in resource development was begun.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Social security and unemployment insurance laws were broadened and strengthened.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: New laws started the long process of balancing farm production with farm markets.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Expanded shipbuilding and stockpiling programs strengthened key sectors of the economy, while improving our mobilization base.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A comprehensive new housing law brought impressive progress in an area fundamental to our economic strength and closed loopholes in the old laws permitting dishonest manipulation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Many of these programs are just beginning to exert their main stimulating effect upon the economy generally and upon specific communities and industries throughout the country.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The past year--1954--was one of the most prosperous years in our history.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Business activity now surges with new strength.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Production is rising.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Employment is high.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Toward the end of last year average weekly wages in manufacturing were higher than ever before.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Personal income after taxes is at a record level.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: So is consumer spending.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Construction activity is reaching new peaks.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Export demand for our goods is strong.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: State and local government expenditures on public works are rising.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Savings are high, and credit is readily available.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: So, today, the transition to a peacetime economy is largely behind us.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The economic outlook is good.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The many promising factors I have mentioned do not guarantee sustained economic expansion; however, they do give us a strong position from which to carry forward our economic growth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If we as a people act wisely, within ten years our annual national output can rise from its present level of about $360 billion to $500 billion, measured in dollars of stable buying power.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: My Budget Message on January 17, the Economic Report on the 20th of this month, and several special messages will set forth in detail major programs to foster the growth of our economy and to protect the integrity of the people's money.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Today I shall discuss these programs only in general terms.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Government efficiency and economy remain essential to steady progress toward a balanced budget.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: More than ten billion dollars were cut from the spending program proposed in the budget of January 9, 1953.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Expenditures of that year were six and a half billion below those of the previous year.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the current fiscal year, government spending will be nearly four and a half billion dollars less than in the fiscal year which ended last June 30.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: New spending authority has been held below expenditures, reducing government obligations accumulated over the years.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Last year we had a large tax cut and, for the first time in seventy-five years a basic revision of Federal tax laws.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is now clear that defense and other essential government costs must remain at a level precluding further tax reductions this year.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Although excise and corporation income taxes must, therefore, be continued at their present rates, further tax cuts will be possible when justified by lower expenditures and by revenue increases arising from the nation's economic growth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am hopeful that such reductions can be made next year.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: At the foundation of our economic growth are the raw materials and energy produced from our minerals and fuels, lands and forests, and water resources.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: With respect to them, I believe that the nation must adhere to three fundamental policies: first, to develop, wisely use and conserve basic resources from generation to generation; second, to follow the historic pattern of developing these resources primarily by private citizens under fair provisions of law, including restraints for proper conservation; and third, to treat resource development as a partnership undertaking--a partnership in which the participation of private citizens and State and local governments is as necessary as Federal participation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This policy of partnership and cooperation is producing good results, most immediately noticeable in respect to water resources.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: First, it has encouraged local public bodies and private citizens to plan their own power sources.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Increasing numbers of applications to the Federal Power Commission to conduct surveys and prepare plans for power development, notably in the Columbia River Basin, are evidence of local response.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Second, the Federal Government and local and private organizations have been encouraged to coordinate their developments.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This is important because Federal hydroelectric developments supply but a small fraction of the nation's power needs.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Such partnership projects as Priest Rapids in Washington, the Coosa River development in Alabama, and Markham Ferry in Oklahoma already have the approval of the Congress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This year justifiable projects of a similar nature will again have Administration support.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Third, the Federal Government must shoulder its own partnership obligations by undertaking projects of such complexity and size that their success requires Federal development.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In keeping with this principle, I again urge the Congress to approve the development of the Upper Colorado River Basin to conserve and assure better use of precious water essential to the future of the West.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In addition, the 1956 budget will recommend appropriations to start six new reclamation and more than thirty new Corps of Engineers projects of varying size.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Going projects and investigations of potential new resource developments will be continued.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Although this partnership approach is producing encouraging results, its full success requires a nation-wide comprehensive water resources policy firmly based in law.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Such a policy is under preparation and when completed will be submitted to the Congress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the interest of their proper conservation, development and use, continued vigilance will be maintained over our fisheries, wildlife resources, the national parks and forests, and the public lands; and we shall continue to encourage an orderly development of the nation's mineral resources.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A modern, efficient highway system is essential to meet the needs of our growing population, our expanding economy, and our national security.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We are accelerating our highway improvement program as rapidly as possible under existing State and Federal laws and authorizations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: However, this effort will not in itself assure our people of an adequate highway system.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: On my recommendation, this problem has been carefully considered by the Conference of State Governors and by a special Advisory Committee on a National Highway Program, composed of leading private citizens.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I have received the recommendations of the Governors' Conference and will shortly receive the views of the special Advisory Committee.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Aided by their findings, I shall submit on January 27th detailed recommendations which will meet our most pressing national highway needs.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In further recognition of the importance of transportation to our economic strength and security, the Administration, through a Cabinet committee, is thoroughly examining existing Federal transportation policies to determine their effect on the adequacy of transportation services.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This is the first such comprehensive review directly undertaken by the Executive Branch of the government in modern times.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We are not only examining major problems facing the various modes of transport; we are also studying closely the inter-relationships of civilian and government requirements for transportation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Legislation will be recommended to correct policy deficiencies which we may find.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The nation's public works activities are tremendous in scope.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is expected that more than $12 billion will be expended in 1955 for the development of land, water and other resources; control of floods, and navigation and harbor improvements; construction of roads, schools, and municipal water supplies, and disposal of domestic and industrial wastes.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Many of the Federal, State and local agencies responsible for this work are, in their separate capacities, highly efficient.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But public works activities are closely inter-related and have a substantial influence on the growth of the country.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Moreover, in times of threatening economic contraction, they may become a valuable sustaining force.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To these ends, efficient planning and execution of the nation's public works require both the coordination of Federal activities and effective cooperation with State and local governments.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Council of Economic Advisers, through its public works planning section, has made important advances during the past year in effecting this coordination and cooperation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
