text: The legislation I have recommended for workers in private industry should be accompanied by a parallel effort for the welfare of Government employees.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We have accomplished much in this field, including a contributory life insurance program; equitable pay increases and a fringe benefits program, covering many needed personnel policy changes, from improved premium pay to a meaningful incentive award program.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Additional personnel management legislation is needed in this Session.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As I stated last year, an executive pay increase is essential to efficient governmental management.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Such an increase, together with needed adjustments in the pay for the top career positions, is also necessary to the equitable completion of the Federal pay program initiated last year.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Other legislation will be proposed, including legislation for prepaid group health insurance for employees and their dependents and to effect major improvements in the Civil Service retirement system.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: All of us share a continuing concern for those who have served this nation in the Armed Forces.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Commission on Veterans Pensions is at this time conducting a study of the entire field of veterans' benefits and will soon submit proposed improvements.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We are proud of the progress our people have made in the field of civil rights.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In Executive Branch operations throughout the nation, elimination of discrimination and segregation is all but completed.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Progress is also being made among contractors engaged in furnishing Government services and requirements.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Every citizen now has the opportunity to fit himself for and to hold a position of responsibility in the service of his country.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the District of Columbia, through the voluntary cooperation of the people, discrimination and segregation are disappearing from hotels, theaters, restaurants and other facilities.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is disturbing that in some localities allegations persist that Negro citizens are being deprived of their right to vote and are likewise being subjected to unwarranted economic pressures.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I recommend that the substance of these charges be thoroughly examined by a Bipartisan Commission created by the Congress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is hoped that such a commission will be established promptly so that it may arrive at findings which can receive early consideration.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The stature of our leadership in the free world has increased through the past three years because we have made more progress than ever before in a similar period to assure our citizens equality in justice, in opportunity and in civil rights.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must expand this effort on every front.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must strive to have every person judged and measured by what he is, rather than by his color, race or religion.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There will soon be recommended to the Congress a program further to advance the efforts of the Government, within the area of Federal responsibility, to accomplish these objectives.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: One particular challenge confronts us.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the Hawaiian Islands, East meets West.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To the Islands, Asia and Europe and the Western Hemisphere, all the continents, have contributed their peoples and their cultures to display a unique example of a community that is a successful laboratory in human brotherhood.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Statehood, supported by the repeatedly expressed desire of the Islands' people and by our traditions, would be a shining example of the American way to the entire earth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Consequently, I urgently request this Congress to grant statehood for Hawaii.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Also, in harmony with the provisions I last year communicated to the Senate and House Committees on Interior and Insular Affairs, I trust that progress toward statehood for Alaska can be made in this Session.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Progress is constant toward full integration of our Indian citizens into normal community life.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: During the past two years the Administration has provided school facilities for thousands of Indian children previously denied this opportunity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must continue to meet the needs of increased numbers of Indian children.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Provision should also be made for the education of adult Indians whose schooling in earlier years was neglected.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In keeping with our responsibility of world leadership and in our own self interest, I again point out to the Congress the urgent need for revision of the immigration and nationality laws.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our nation has always welcomed immigrants to our shores.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The wisdom of such a policy is clearly shown by the fact that America has been built by immigrants and the descendants of immigrants.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: That policy must be continued realistically with present day conditions in mind.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I recommend that the number of persons admitted to this country annually be based not on the 1920 census but on the latest, the 1950 census.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Provision should be made to allow for greater flexibility in the use of quotas so if one country does not use its share, the vacancies may be made available for the use of qualified individuals from other countries.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The law should be amended to permit the Secretary of State and the Attorney General to waive the requirements of fingerprinting on a reciprocal basis for persons coming to this country for temporary visits.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This and other changes in the law are long overdue and should be taken care of promptly.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Detailed recommendations for revision of the immigration laws will be submitted to the Congress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am happy to report substantial progress in the flow of immigrants under the Refugee Relief Act of 1953;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Because of the high prosperity in Germany and Austria, the number of immigrants from those countries will be reduced.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This will make available thousands of unfilled openings which I recommend be distributed to Greece and Italy and to escapees from behind the Iron Curtain.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Once again I ask the Congress to join with me in demonstrating our belief in the right of suffrage.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I renew my request that the principle of self-government be extended and the right of suffrage granted to the citizens of the District of Columbia.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To conclude: the vista before us is bright.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The march of science, the expanding economy, the advance in collective security toward a just peace--in this threefold movement our people are creating new standards by which the future of the Republic may be judged.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Progress, however, will be realized only as it is more than matched by a continuing growth in the spiritual strength of the nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our dedication to moral values must be complete in our dealings abroad and in our relationships among ourselves.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We have single-minded devotion to the common good of America.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Never must we forget that this means the well-being, the prosperity, the security of all Americans in every walk of life.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To the attainment of these objectives, I pledge full energies of the Administration, as in the Session ahead, it works on a program for submission to you, the Congress of the United States.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I appear before the Congress today to report on the State of the Union and the relationships of the Union to the other nations of the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I come here, firmly convinced that at no time in the history of the Republic have circumstances more emphatically underscored the need, in all echelons of government, for vision and wisdom and resolution.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: You meet in a season of stress that is testing the fitness of political systems and the validity of political philosophies.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Each stress stems in part from causes peculiar to itself.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But every stress is a reflection of a universal phenomenon.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the world today, the surging and understandable tide of nationalism is marked by widespread revulsion and revolt against tyranny, injustice, inequality and poverty.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As individuals, joined in a common hunger for freedom, men and women and even children pit their spirit against guns and tanks.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: On a larger scale, in an ever more persistent search for the self-respect of authentic sovereignty and the economic base on which national independence must rest, peoples sever old ties; seek new alliances; experiment--sometimes dangerously--in their struggle to satisfy these human aspirations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Particularly, in the past year, this tide has changed the pattern of attitudes and thinking among millions.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The changes already accomplished foreshadow a world transformed by the spirit of freedom.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This is no faint and pious hope.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The forces now at work in the minds and hearts of men will not be spent through many years.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the main, today's expressions of nationalism are, in spirit, echoes of our forefathers' struggle for independence.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This Republic cannot be aloof to these events heralding a new epoch in the affairs of mankind.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our pledged word, our enlightened self-interest, our character as a Nation commit us to a high role in world affairs: a role of vigorous leadership, ready strength, sympathetic understanding.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The State of the Union, at the opening of the 85th Congress, continues to vindicate the wisdom of the principles on which this Republic is founded.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Proclaimed in the Constitution of the Nation and in many of our historic documents, and founded in devout religious convictions, these principles enunciate: A vigilant regard for human liberty.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A wise concern for human welfare.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A ceaseless effort for human progress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Fidelity to these principles, in our relations with other peoples, has won us new friendships and has increased our opportunity for service within the family of nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The appeal of these principles is universal, lighting fires in the souls of men everywhere.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We shall continue to uphold them, against those who deny them and in counseling with our friends.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: At home, the application of these principles to the complex problems of our national life has brought us to an unprecedented peak in our economic prosperity and has exemplified in our way of life the enduring human values of mind and spirit.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Through the past four years these principles have guided the legislative programs submitted by the Administration to the Congress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As we attempt to apply them to current events, domestic and foreign, we must take into account the complex entity that is the United States of America; what endangers it; what can improve it.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The visible structure is our American economy itself.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: After more than a century and a half of constant expansion, it is still rich in a wide variety of natural resources.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is first among nations in its people's mastery of industrial skills.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is productive beyond our own needs of many foodstuffs and industrial products.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is rewarding to all our citizens in opportunity to earn and to advance in self-realization and in self-expression.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is fortunate in its wealth of educational and cultural and religious centers.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is vigorously dynamic in the limitless initiative and willingness to venture that characterize free enterprise.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is productive of a widely shared prosperity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our economy is strong, expanding, and fundamentally sound.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But in any realistic appraisal, even the optimistic analyst will realize that in a prosperous period the principal threat to efficient functioning of a free enterprise system is inflation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We look back on four years of prosperous activities during which prices, the cost of living, have been relatively stable--that is, inflation has been held in check.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But it is clear that the danger is always present, particularly if the government might become profligate in its expenditures or private groups might ignore all the possible results on our economy of unwise struggles for immediate gain.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This danger requires a firm resolution that the Federal Government shall utilize only a prudent share of the Nation's resources, that it shall live within its means, carefully measuring against need alternative proposals for expenditures.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Through the next four years, I shall continue to insist that the executive departments and agencies of Government search out additional ways to save money and manpower.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I urge that the Congress be equally watchful in this matter.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We pledge the Government's share in guarding the integrity of the dollar.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But the Government's efforts cannot be the entire campaign against inflation, the thief that can rob the individual of the value of the pension and social security he has earned during his productive life.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: For success, Government's efforts must be paralleled by the attitudes and actions of individual citizens.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I have often spoken of the purpose of this Administration to serve the national interest of 170 million people.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The national interest must take precedence over temporary advantages which may be secured by particular groups at the expense of all the people.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In this regard I call on leaders in business and in labor to think well on their responsibility to the American people.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: With all elements of our society, they owe the Nation a vigilant guard against the inflationary tendencies that are always at work in a dynamic economy operating at today's high levels.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They can powerfully help counteract or accentuate such tendencies by their wage and price policies.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Business in its pricing policies should avoid unnecessary price increases especially at a time like the present when demand in so many areas presses hard on short supplies.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A reasonable profit is essential to the new investments that provide more jobs in an expanding economy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But business leaders must, in the national interest, studiously avoid those price rises that are possible only because of vital or unusual needs of the whole nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If our economy is to remain healthy, increases in wages and other labor benefits, negotiated by labor and management, must be reasonably related to improvements in productivity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Such increases are beneficial, for they provide wage earners with greater purchasing power.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Except where necessary to correct obvious injustices, wage increases that outrun productivity, however, are an inflationary factor.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They make for higher prices for the public generally and impose a particular hardship on those whose welfare depends on the purchasing power of retirement income and savings.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Wage negotiations should also take cognizance of the right of the public generally to share in the benefits of improvements in technology.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Freedom has been defined as the opportunity for self-discipline.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This definition has a special application to the areas of wage and price policy in a free economy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Should we persistently fail to discipline ourselves, eventually there will be increasing pressure on government to redress the failure.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: By that process freedom will step by step disappear.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: No subject on the domestic scene should more attract the concern of the friends of American working men and women and of free business enterprise than the forces that threaten a steady depreciation of the value of our money.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Concerning developments in another vital sector of our economy-- agriculture--I am gratified that the long slide in farm income has been halted and that further improvement is in prospect.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This is heartening progress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Three tools that we have developed--improved surplus disposal, improved price support laws, and the soil bank--are working to reduce price-depressing government stocks of farm products.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our concern for the well-being of farm families demands that we constantly search for new ways by which they can share more fully in our unprecedented prosperity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Legislative recommendations in the field of agriculture are contained in the Budget Message.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our soil, water, mineral, forest, fish, and wildlife resources are being conserved and improved more effectively.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Their conservation and development are vital to the present and future strength of the Nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But they must not be the concern of the Federal Government alone.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: State and local entities, and private enterprise should be encouraged to participate in such projects.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I would like to make special mention of programs for making the best uses of water, rapidly becoming our most precious natural resource, just as it can be, when neglected, a destroyer of both life and wealth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There has been prepared and published a comprehensive water report developed by a Cabinet Committee and relating to all phases of this particular problem.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the light of this report, there are two things I believe we should keep constantly in mind.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The first is that each of our great river valleys should be considered as a whole.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Piecemeal operations within each lesser drainage area can be self-defeating or, at the very least, needlessly expensive.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The second is that the domestic and industrial demands for water grow far more rapidly than does our population.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The whole matter of making the best use of each drop of water from the moment it touches our soil until it reaches the oceans, for such purposes as irrigation, flood control, power production, and domestic and industrial uses clearly demands the closest kind of cooperation and partnership between municipalities, States and the Federal Government.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Through partnership of Federal, state and local authorities in these vast projects we can obtain the economy and efficiency of development and operation that springs from a lively sense of local responsibility.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Until such partnership is established on a proper and logical basis of sharing authority, responsibility and costs, our country will never have both the fully productive use of water that it so obviously needs and protection against disastrous flood.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If we fail in this, all the many tasks that need to be done in America could be accomplished only at an excessive cost, by the growth of a stifling bureaucracy, and eventually with a dangerous degree of centralized control over our national life.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In all domestic matters, I believe that the people of the United States will expect of us effective action to remedy past failure in meeting critical needs.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: High priority should be given the school construction bill.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This will benefit children of all races throughout the country--and children of all races need schools now.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A program designed to meet emergency needs for more classrooms should be enacted without delay.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am hopeful that this program can be enacted on its own merits, uncomplicated by provisions dealing with the complex problems of integration.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I urge the people in all sections of the country to approach these problems with calm and reason, with mutual understanding and good will, and in the American tradition of deep respect for the orderly processes of law and justice.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I should say here that we have much reason to be proud of the progress our people are making in mutual understanding--the chief buttress of human and civil rights.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Steadily we are moving closer to the goal of fair and equal treatment of citizens without regard to race or color.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But unhappily much remains to be done.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Last year the Administration recommended to the Congress a four-point program to reinforce civil rights.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: That program included: (1) creation of a bipartisan commission to investigate asserted violations of civil rights and to make recommendations;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I urge that the Congress enact this legislation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Essential to the stable economic growth we seek is a system of well-adapted and efficient financial institutions.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I believe the time has come to conduct a broad national inquiry into the nature, performance and adequacy of our financial system, both in terms of its direct service to the whole economy and in terms of its function as the mechanism through which monetary and credit policy takes effect.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I believe the Congress should authorize the creation of a commission of able and qualified citizens to undertake this vital inquiry.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Out of their findings and recommendations the Administration would develop and present to the Congress any legislative proposals that might be indicated for the purpose of improving our financial machinery.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In this message it seems unnecessary that I should repeat recommendations involving our domestic affairs that have been urged upon the Congress during the past four years, but which, in some instances, did not reach the stage of completely satisfactory legislation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Administration will, through future messages either directly from me or from heads of the departments and agencies, transmit to the Congress specific recommendations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These will involve our financial and fiscal affairs;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There will be special recommendations dealing with such subjects as atomic energy, the furthering of public works, the continued efforts to eliminate government competition with the businesses of tax-paying citizens.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A number of legislative recommendations will be mentioned specifically in my forthcoming Budget Message, which will reach you within the week.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: That message will also recommend such sums as are needed to implement the proposed action.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Turning to the international scene: The existence of a strongly armed imperialistic dictatorship poses a continuing threat to the free world's and thus to our own Nation's security and peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There are certain truths to be remembered here.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: First, America alone and isolated cannot assure even its own security.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must be joined by the capability and resolution of nations that have proved themselves dependable defenders of freedom.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Isolation from them invites war.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our security is also enhanced by the immeasurable interest that joins us with all peoples who believe that peace with justice must be preserved, that wars of aggression are crimes against humanity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Another truth is that our survival in today's world requires modern, adequate, dependable military strength.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our Nation has made great strides in assuring a modern defense, so armed in new weapons, so deployed, so equipped, that today our security force is the most powerful in our peacetime history.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It can punish heavily any enemy who undertakes to attack us.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is a major deterrent to war.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: By our research and development more efficient weapons--some of amazing capabilities--are being constantly created.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These vital efforts we shall continue.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Yet we must not delude ourselves that safety necessarily increases as expenditures for military research or forces in being go up.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Indeed, beyond a wise and reasonable level, which is always changing and is under constant study, money spent on arms may be money wasted on sterile metal or inflated costs, thereby weakening the very security and strength we seek.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: National security requires far more than military power.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Economic and moral factors play indispensable roles.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Any program that endangers our economy could defeat us.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Any weakening of our national will and resolution, any diminution of the vigor and initiative of our individual citizens, would strike a blow at the heart of our defenses.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The finest military establishment we can produce must work closely in cooperation with the forces of our friends.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our system of regional pacts, developed within the Charter of the United Nations, serves to increase both our own security and the security of other nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This system is still a recent introduction on the world scene.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Its problems are many and difficult, because it insists on equality among its members and brings into association some nations traditionally divided.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Repeatedly in recent months, the collapse of these regional alliances has been predicted.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The strains upon them have been at times indeed severe.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Despite these strains our regional alliances have proved durable and strong, and dire predictions of their disintegration have proved completely false.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: With other free nations, we should vigorously prosecute measures that will promote mutual strength, prosperity and welfare within the free world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Strength is essentially a product of economic health and social well-being.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Consequently, even as we continue our programs of military assistance, we must emphasize aid to our friends in building more productive economies and in better satisfying the natural demands of their people for progress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Thereby we shall move a long way toward a peaceful world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A sound and safeguarded agreement for open skies, unarmed aerial sentinels, and reduced armament would provide a valuable contribution toward a durable peace in the years ahead.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: And we have been persistent in our effort to reach such an agreement.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We are willing to enter any reliable agreement which would reverse the trend toward ever more devastating nuclear weapons;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our continuing negotiations in this field are a major part of our quest for a confident peace in this atomic age.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This quest requires as well a constructive attitude among all the nations of the free world toward expansion of trade and investment, that can give all of us opportunity to work out economic betterment.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: An essential step in this field is the provision of an administrative agency to insure the orderly and proper operation of existing arrangements under which multilateral trade is now carried on.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To that end I urge Congressional authorization for United States membership in the proposed Organization for Trade Cooperation, an action which will speed removal of discrimination against our export trade.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We welcome the efforts of a number of our European friends to achieve an integrated community to develop a common market.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We likewise welcome their cooperative effort in the field of atomic energy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To demonstrate once again our unalterable purpose to make of the atom a peaceful servant of humanity, I shortly shall ask the Congress to authorize full United States participation in the International Atomic Energy Agency.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: World events have magnified both the responsibilities and the opportunities of the United States Information Agency.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Just as, in recent months, the voice of communism has become more shaken and confused, the voice of truth must be more clearly heard.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To enable our Information Agency to cope with these new responsibilities and opportunities, I am asking the Congress to increase appreciably the appropriations for this program and for legislation establishing a career service for the Agency's overseas foreign service officers.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The recent historic events in Hungary demand that all free nations share to the extent of their capabilities in the responsibility of granting asylum to victims of Communist persecution.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I request the Congress promptly to enact legislation to regularize the status in the United States of Hungarian refugees brought here as parolees.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I shall shortly recommend to the Congress by special message the changes in our immigration laws that I deem necessary in the light of our world responsibilities.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The cost of peace is something we must face boldly, fearlessly.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Beyond money, it involves changes in attitudes, the renunciation of old prejudices, even the sacrifice of some seeming self-interest.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Only five days ago I expressed to you the grave concern of your Government over the threat of Soviet aggression in the Middle East.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I asked for Congressional authorization to help counter this threat.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I say again that this matter is of vital and immediate importance to the Nation's and the free world's security and peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: By our proposed programs in the Middle East, we hope to assist in establishing a climate in which constructive and long-term solutions to basic problems of the area may be sought.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: From time to time, there will be presented to the Congress requests for other legislation in the broad field of international affairs.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: All requests will reflect the steadfast purpose of this Administration to pursue peace, based on justice.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Although in some cases details will be new, the underlying purpose and objectives will remain the same.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: All proposals made by the Administration in this field are based on the free world's unity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This unity may not be immediately obvious unless we examine link by link the chain of relationships that binds us to every area and to every nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In spirit the free world is one because its people uphold the right of independent existence for all nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I have already alluded to their economic interdependence.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But their interdependence extends also into the field of security.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: First of all, no reasonable man will question the absolute need for our American neighbors to be prosperous and secure.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Their security and prosperity are inextricably bound to our own.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: And we are, of course, already joined with these neighbors by historic pledges.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Again, no reasonable man will deny that the freedom and prosperity and security of Western Europe are vital to our own prosperity and security.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If the institutions, the skills, the manpower of its peoples were to fall under the domination of an aggressive imperialism, the violent change in the balance of world power and in the pattern of world commerce could not be fully compensated for by any American measures, military or economic.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But these people, whose economic strength is largely dependent on free and uninterrupted movement of oil from the Middle East, cannot prosper--indeed, their economies would be severely impaired--should that area be controlled by an enemy and the movement of oil be subject to its decisions.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Next, to the Eastward, are Asiatic and Far Eastern peoples, recently returned to independent control of their own affairs or now emerging into sovereign statehood.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Their potential strength constitutes new assurance for stability and peace in the world--if they can retain their independence.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Should they lose freedom and be dominated by an aggressor, the world-wide effects would imperil the security of the free world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In short, the world has so shrunk that all free nations are our neighbors.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Without cooperative neighbors, the United States cannot maintain its own security and welfare, because: First, America's vital interests are world-wide, embracing both hemispheres and every continent.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Second, we have community of interest with every nation in the free world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Third, interdependence of interests requires a decent respect for the rights and the peace of all peoples.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These principles motivate our actions within the United Nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There, before all the world, by our loyalty to them, by our practice of them, let us strive to set a standard to which all who seek justice and who hunger for peace can rally.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: May we at home, here at the Seat of Government, in all the cities and towns and farmlands of America, support these principles in a personal effort of dedication.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Thereby each of us can help establish a secure world order in which opportunity for freedom and justice will be more widespread, and in which the resources now dissipated on the armaments of war can be released for the life and growth of all humanity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: When our forefathers prepared the immortal document that proclaimed our independence, they asserted that every individual is endowed by his Creator with certain inalienable rights.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As we gaze back through history to that date, it is clear that our nation has striven to live up to this declaration, applying it to nations as well as to individuals.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Today we proudly assert that the government of the United States is still committed to this concept, both in its activities at home and abroad.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The purpose is Divine; the implementation is human.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our country and its government have made mistakes--human mistakes.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They have been of the head--not of the heart.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: And it is still true that the great concept of the dignity of all men, alike created in the image of the Almighty, has been the compass by which we have tried and are trying to steer our course.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: So long as we continue by its guidance, there will be true progress in human affairs, both among ourselves and among those with whom we deal.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To achieve a more perfect fidelity to it, I submit, is a worthy ambition as we meet together in these first days of this, the first session of the 85th Congress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is again my high privilege to extend personal greetings to the members of the 85th Congress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: All of us realize that, as this new session begins, many Americans are troubled about recent world developments which they believe may threaten our nation's safety.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Honest men differ in their appraisal of America's material and intellectual strength, and the dangers that confront us.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But all know these dangers are real.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The purpose of this message is to outline the measures that can give the American people a confidence--just as real--in their own security.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am not here to justify the past, gloss over the problems of the present, or propose easy solutions for the future.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am here to state what I believe to be right and what I believe to be wrong; and to propose action for correcting what I think wrong! I.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There are two tasks confronting us that so far outweigh all others that I shall devote this year's message entirely to them.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The first is to ensure our safety through strength.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As to our strength, I have repeatedly voiced this conviction: We now have a broadly based and efficient defensive strength, including a great deterrent power, which is, for the present, our main guarantee against war;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: but, unless we act wisely and promptly, we could lose that capacity to deter attack or defend ourselves.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: My profoundest conviction is that the American people will say, as one man: No matter what the exertions or sacrifices, we shall maintain that necessary strength!

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But we could make no more tragic mistake than merely to concentrate on military strength.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: For if we did only this, the future would hold nothing for the world but an Age of Terror.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: And so our second task is to do the constructive work of building a genuine peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must never become so preoccupied with our desire for military strength that we neglect those areas of economic development, trade, diplomacy, education, ideas and principles where the foundations of real peace must be laid.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: II. The threat to our safety, and to the hope of a peaceful world, can be simply stated.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is communist imperialism.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This threat is not something imagined by critics of the Soviets.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Soviet spokesmen, from the beginning, have publicly and frequently declared their aim to expand their power, one way or another, throughout the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The threat has become increasingly serious as this expansionist aim has been reinforced by an advancing industrial, military and scientific establishment.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But what makes the Soviet threat unique in history is its all-inclusiveness.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Every human activity is pressed into service as a weapon of expansion.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Trade, economic development, military power, arts, science, education, the whole world of ideas--all are harnessed to this same chariot of expansion.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Soviets are, in short, waging total cold war.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The only answer to a regime that wages total cold war is to wage total peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This means bringing to bear every asset of our personal and national lives upon the task of building the conditions in which security and peace can grow.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: III. Among our assets, let us first briefly glance at our military power.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Military power serves the cause of security by making prohibitive the cost of any aggressive attack.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It serves the cause of peace by holding up a shield behind which the patient constructive work of peace can go on.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But it can serve neither cause if we make either of two mistakes.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The one would be to overestimate our strength, and thus neglect crucially important actions in the period just ahead.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The other would be to underestimate our strength.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Thereby we might be tempted to become irresolute in our foreign relations, to dishearten our friends, and to lose our national poise and perspective in approaching the complex problems ahead.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Any orderly balance-sheet of military strength must be in two parts.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The first is the position as of today.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The second is the position in the period ahead.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As of today: our defensive shield comprehends a vast complex of ground, sea, and air units, superbly equipped and strategically deployed around the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The most powerful deterrent to war in the world today lies in the retaliatory power of our Strategic Air Command and the aircraft of our Navy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They present to any potential attacker who would unleash war upon the world the prospect of virtual annihilation of his own country.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Even if we assume a surprise attack on our bases, with a marked reduction in our striking power, our bombers would immediately be on their way in sufficient strength to accomplish this mission of retaliation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Every informed government knows this.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is no secret.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Since the Korean Armistice, the American people have spent $225 billion in maintaining and strengthening this overall defensive shield.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This is the position as of today.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Now as to the period ahead: Every part of our military establishment must and will be equipped to do its defensive job with the most modern weapons and methods.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But it is particularly important to our planning that we make a candid estimate of the effect of long-range ballistic missiles on the present deterrent power I have described.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: At this moment, the consensus of opinion is that we are probably somewhat behind the Soviets in some areas of long-range ballistic missile development.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But it is my conviction, based on close study of all relevant intelligence, that if we make the necessary effort, we will have the missiles, in the needed quantity and in time, to sustain and strengthen the deterrent power of our increasingly efficient bombers.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: One encouraging fact evidencing this ability is the rate of progress we have achieved since we began to concentrate on these missiles.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The intermediate ballistic missiles, Thor and Jupiter, have already been ordered into production.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The parallel progress in the intercontinental ballistic missile effort will be advanced by our plans for acceleration.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The development of the submarine-based Polaris missile system has progressed so well that its future procurement schedules are being moved forward markedly.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: When it is remembered that our country has concentrated on the development of ballistic missiles for only about a third as long as the Soviets, these achievements show a rate of progress that speaks for itself.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Only a brief time back, we were spending at the rate of only about one million dollars a year on long range ballistic missiles.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In 1957 we spent more than one billion dollars on the Atlas, Titan, Thor, Jupiter, and Polaris programs alone.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But I repeat, gratifying though this rate of progress is, we must still do more! Our real problem, then, is not our strength today; it is rather the vital necessity of action today to ensure our strength tomorrow.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: What I have just said applies to our strength as a single country.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But we are not alone.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I have returned from the recent NATO meeting with renewed conviction that, because we are a part of a world-wide community of free and peaceful nations, our own security is immeasurably increased.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: By contrast, the Soviet Union has surrounded itself with captive and sullen nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Like a crack in the crust of an uneasily sleeping volcano, the Hungarian uprising revealed the depth and intensity of the patriotic longing for liberty that still burns within these countries.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The world thinks of us as a country which is strong, but which will never start a war.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The world also thinks of us as a land which has never enslaved anyone and which is animated by humane ideals.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This friendship, based on common ideals, is one of our greatest sources of strength.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It cements into a cohesive security arrangement the aggregate of the spiritual, military and economic strength of all those nations which, with us, are allied by treaties and agreements.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Up to this point, I have talked solely about our military strength to deter a possible future war.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I now want to talk about the strength we need to win a different kind of war--one that has already been launched against us.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is the massive economic offensive that has been mounted by the communist imperialists against free nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The communist imperialist regimes have for some time been largely frustrated in their attempts at expansion based directly on force.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As a result, they have begun to concentrate heavily on economic penetration, particularly of newly-developing countries, as a preliminary to political domination.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This non-military drive, if underestimated, could defeat the free world regardless of our military strength.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This danger is all the greater precisely because many of us fail or refuse to recognize it.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Thus, some people may be tempted to finance our extra military effort by cutting economic assistance.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But at the very time when the economic threat is assuming menacing proportions, to fail to strengthen our own effort would be nothing less than reckless folly! Admittedly, most of us did not anticipate the psychological impact upon the world of the launching of the first earth satellite.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Let us not make the same kind of mistake in another field, by failing to anticipate the much more serious impact of the Soviet economic offensive.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As with our military potential, our economic assets are more than equal to the task.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our independent farmers produce an abundance of food and fiber.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our free workers are versatile, intelligent, and hardworking.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our businessmen are imaginative and resourceful.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The productivity, the adaptability of the American economy is the solid foundation-stone of our security structure.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We have just concluded another prosperous year.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our output was once more the greatest in the nation's history.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the latter part of the year, some decline in employment and output occurred, following the exceptionally rapid expansion of recent years.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In a free economy, reflecting as it does the independent judgments of millions of people, growth typically moves forward unevenly.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But the basic forces of growth remain unimpaired.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There are solid grounds for confidence that economic growth will be resumed without an extended interruption.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Moreover, the Federal government, constantly alert to signs of weakening in any part of our economy, always stands ready, with its full power, to take any appropriate further action to promote renewed business expansion.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If our history teaches us anything, it is this lesson: so far as the economic potential of our nation is concerned, the believers in the future of America have always been the realists.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I count myself as one of this company.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our long-range problem, then, is not the stamina of our enormous engine of production.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our problem is to make sure that we use these vast economic forces confidently and creatively, not only in direct military defense efforts, but likewise in our foreign policy, through such activities as mutual economic aid and foreign trade.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In much the same way, we have tremendous potential resources on other non-military fronts to help in countering the Soviet threat: education, science, research, and, not least, the ideas and principles by which we live.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: And in all these cases the task ahead is to bring these resources more sharply to bear upon the new tasks of security and peace in a swiftly-changing world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: IV. There are many items in the Administration's program, of a kind frequently included in a State of the Union Message, with which I am not dealing today.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They are important to us and to our prosperity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But I am reserving them for treatment in separate communications because of my purpose today of speaking only about matters bearing directly upon our security and peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I now place before you an outline of action designed to focus our resources upon the two tasks of security and peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In this special category I list eight items requiring action.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They are not merely desirable.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They are imperative.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: DEFENSE REORGANIZATION: The first need is to assure ourselves that military organization facilitates rather than hinders the functioning of the military establishment in maintaining the security of the nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Since World War II, the purpose of achieving maximum organizational efficiency in a modern defense establishment has several times occasioned action by the Congress and by the Executive.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The advent of revolutionary new devices, bringing with them the problem of overall continental defense, creates new difficulties, reminiscent of those attending the advent of the airplane half a century ago.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Some of the important new weapons which technology has produced do not fit into any existing service pattern.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They cut across all services, involve all services, and transcend all services, at every stage from development to operation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In some instances they defy classification according to branch of service.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Unfortunately, the uncertainties resulting from such a situation, and the jurisdictional disputes attending upon it, tend to bewilder and confuse the public and create the impression that service differences are damaging the national interest.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Let us proudly remember that the members of the Armed Forces give their basic allegiance solely to the United States.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Of that fact all of us are certain.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But pride of service and mistaken zeal in promoting particular doctrine has more than once occasioned the kind of difficulty of which I have just spoken.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am not attempting today to pass judgment on the charge of harmful service rivalries.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But one thing is sure.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Whatever they are, America wants them stopped.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Recently I have had under special study the never-ending problem of efficient organization, complicated as it is by new weapons.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Soon my conclusions will be finalized.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I shall promptly take such Executive action as is necessary and, in a separate message, I shall present appropriate recommendations to the Congress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Meanwhile, without anticipating the detailed form that a reorganization should take, I can state its main lines in terms of objectives: A major purpose of military organization is to achieve real unity in the Defense establishment in all the principal features of military activities.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Of all these, one of the most important to our nation's security is strategic planning and control.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This work must be done under unified direction.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The defense structure must be one which, as a whole, can assume, with top efficiency and without friction, the defense of America.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Defense establishment must therefore plan for a better integration of its defensive resources, particularly with respect to the newer weapons now building and under development.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These obviously require full coordination in their development, production and use.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Good organization can help assure this coordination.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In recognition of the need for single control in some of our most advanced development projects, the Secretary of Defense has already decided to concentrate into one organization all the anti-missile and satellite technology undertaken within the Department of Defense.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Another requirement of military organization is a clear subordination of the military services to duly constituted civilian authority.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This control must be real; not merely on the surface.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Next there must be assurance that an excessive number of compartments in organization will not create costly and confusing compartments in our scientific and industrial effort.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Finally, to end inter-service disputes requires clear organization and decisive central direction, supported by the unstinted cooperation of every individual in the defense establishment, civilian and military.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: ACCELERATED DEFENSE EFFORT:The second major action item is the acceleration of the defense effort in particular areas affected by the fast pace of scientific and technological advance.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Some of the points at which improved and increased effort are most essential are these: We must have sure warning in case of attack.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The improvement of warning equipment is becoming increasingly important as we approach the period when long-range missiles will come into use.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must protect and disperse our striking forces and increase their readiness for instant reaction.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This means more base facilities and standby crews.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must maintain deterrent retaliatory power.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This means, among other things, stepped-up long range missile programs;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: accelerated programs for other effective missile systems;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: and, for some years, more advanced aircraft.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must maintain freedom of the seas.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This means nuclear submarines and cruisers; improved anti-submarine weapons; missile ships; and the like.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must maintain all necessary types of mobile forces to deal with local conflicts, should there be need.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This means further improvements in equipment, mobility, tactics and fire power.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Through increases in pay and incentive, we must maintain in the armed forces the skilled manpower modern military forces require.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must be forward-looking in our research and development to anticipate and achieve the unimagined weapons of the future.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: With these and other improvements, we intend to assure that our vigilance, power, and technical excellence keep abreast of any realistic threat we face.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: MUTUAL AID: We must continue to strengthen our mutual security efforts.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Most people now realize that our programs of military aid and defense support are an integral part of our own defense effort.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If the foundation of the Free World structure were progressively allowed to crumble under the pressure of communist imperialism, the entire house of freedom would be in danger of collapse.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As for the mutual economic assistance program, the benefit to us is threefold.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: First, the countries receiving this aid become bulwarks against communist encroachment as their military defenses and economies are strengthened.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Nations that are conscious of a steady improvement in their industry, education, health and standard of living are not apt to fall prey to the blandishments of communist imperialists.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Second, these countries are helped to reach the point where mutually profitable trade can expand between them and us.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Third, the mutual confidence that comes from working together on constructive projects creates an atmosphere in which real understanding and peace can flourish.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To help bring these multiple benefits, our economic aid effort should be made more effective.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In proposals for future economic aid, I am stressing a greater use of repayable loans, through the Development Loan Fund, through funds generated by sale of surplus farm products, and through the Export-Import Bank.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: While some increase in Government funds will be required, it remains our objective to encourage shifting to the use of private capital sources as rapidly as possible.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: give-away program.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The real fact is that no investment we make in our own security and peace can pay us greater dividends than necessary amounts of economic aid to friendly nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: give-away.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Let's stick to facts!

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We cannot afford to have one of our most essential security programs shot down with a slogan!

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: MUTUAL TRADE:Both in our national interest, and in the interest of world peace, we must have a five-year extension of the Trade Agreements Act with broadened authority to negotiate.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: World trade supports a significant segment of American industry and agriculture.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It provides employment for four and one-half million American workers.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It helps supply our ever increasing demand for raw materials.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It provides the opportunity for American free enterprise to develop on a worldwide scale.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It strengthens our friends and increases their desire to be friends.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: World trade helps to lay the groundwork for peace by making all free nations of the world stronger and more self-reliant.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: America is today the world's greatest trading nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If we use this great asset wisely to meet the expanding demands of the world, we shall not only provide future opportunities for our own business, agriculture, and labor, but in the process strengthen our security posture and other prospects for a prosperous, harmonious world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Isolation is no longer possible or desirable.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The period of exclusiveness is past.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: SCIENTIFIC COOPERATION WITH OUR ALLIES: It is of the highest importance that the Congress enact the necessary legislation to enable us to exchange appropriate scientific and technical information with friendly countries as part of our effort to achieve effective scientific cooperation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is wasteful in the extreme for friendly allies to consume talent and money in solving problems that their friends have already solved-- all because of artificial barriers to sharing.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We cannot afford to cut ourselves off from the brilliant talents and minds of scientists in friendly countries.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The task ahead will be hard enough without handcuffs of our own making.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The groundwork for this kind of cooperation has already been laid in discussions among NATO countries.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Promptness in following through with legislation will be the best possible evidence of American unity of purpose in cooperating with our friends.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: EDUCATION AND RESEARCH: In the area of education and research, I recommend a balanced program to improve our resources, involving an investment of about a billion dollars over a four year period.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This involves new activities by the Department of Health, Education and Welfare designed principally to encourage improved teaching quality and student opportunities in the interests of national security.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It also provides a five-fold increase in sums available to the National Science Foundation for its special activities in stimulating and improving science education.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Scrupulous attention has been paid to maintaining local control of educational policy, spurring the maximum amount of local effort, and to avoiding undue stress on the physical sciences at the expense of other branches of learning.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the field of research, I am asking for substantial increases in basic research funds, including a doubling of the funds available to the National Science Foundation for this purpose.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But federal action can do only a part of the job.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In both education and research, redoubled exertions will be necessary on the part of all Americans if we are to rise to the demands of our times.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This means hard work on the part of state and local governments, private industry, schools and colleges, private organizations and foundations, teachers, parents, and--perhaps most important of all--the student himself, with his bag of books and his homework.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: With this kind of all-inclusive campaign, I have no doubt that we can create the intellectual capital we need for the years ahead, invest it in the right places--and do all this, not as regimented pawns, but as free men and women! 7.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: SPENDING AND SAVING Seventh: To provide for this extra effort for security, we must apply stern tests of priority to other expenditures, both military and civilian.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This extra effort involves, most immediately, the need for a supplemental defense appropriation of $1.3 billion for fiscal year 1958.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the 1959 budget, increased expenditures for missiles, nuclear ships, atomic energy, research and development, science and education, a special contingency fund to deal with possible new technological discoveries, and increases in pay and incentives to obtain and retain competent manpower add up to a total increase over the comparable figures in the 1957 budget of about $4 billion.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I believe that, in spite of these necessary increases, we should strive to finance the 1959 security effort out of expected revenues.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: While we now believe that expected revenues and expenditures will roughly balance, our real purpose will be to achieve adequate security, but always with the utmost regard for efficiency and careful management.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This purpose will require the cooperation of Congress in making careful analysis of estimates presented, reducing expenditure on less essential military programs and installations, postponing some new civilian programs, transferring some to the states, and curtailing or eliminating others.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Such related matters as the national debt ceiling and tax revenues will be dealt with in later messages.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: WORKS OF PEACE:My last call for action is not primarily addressed to the Congress and people of the United States.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Rather, it is a message from the people of the United States to all other peoples, especially those of the Soviet Union.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the last analysis, there is only one solution to the grim problems that lie ahead.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The world must stop the present plunge toward more and more destructive weapons of war, and turn the corner that will start our steps firmly on the path toward lasting peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our greatest hope for success lies in a universal fact: the people of the world, as people, have always wanted peace and want peace now.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The problem, then, is to find a way of translating this universal desire into action.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This will require more than words of peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It requires works of peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Now, may I try to give you some concrete examples of the kind of works of peace that might make a beginning in the new direction.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: For a start our people should learn to know each other better.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Recent negotiations in Washington have provided a basis in principle for greater freedom of communication and exchange of people.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I urge the Soviet government to cooperate in turning principle into practice by prompt and tangible actions that will break down the unnatural barriers that have blocked the flow of thought and understanding between our people.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Another kind of work of peace is cooperation on projects of human welfare.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: For example, we now have it within our power to eradicate from the face of the earth that age-old scourge of mankind: malaria.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We are embarking with other nations in an all-out five-year campaign to blot out this curse forever.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We invite the Soviets to join with us in this great work of humanity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Indeed, we would be willing to pool our efforts with the Soviets in other campaigns against the diseases that are the common enemy of all mortals--such as cancer and heart disease.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If people can get together on such projects, is it not possible that we could then go on to a full-scale cooperative program of Science for Peace?

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We have as a guide and inspiration the success of our Atoms-for-Peace proposal, which in only a few years, under United Nations auspices, became a reality in the International Atomic Energy Agency.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A program of Science for Peace might provide a means of funneling into one place the results of research from scientists everywhere and from there making it available to all parts of the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There is almost no limit to the human betterment that could result from such cooperation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Hunger and disease could increasingly be driven from the earth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The age-old dream of a good life for all could, at long last, be translated into reality.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But of all the works of peace, none is more needed now than a real first step toward disarmament.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Last August the United Nations General Assembly, by an overwhelming vote, approved a disarmament plan that we and our allies sincerely believed to be fair and practical.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Soviets have rejected both the plan, and the negotiating procedure set up by the United Nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As a result, negotiation on this supremely important issue is now at a standstill.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But the world cannot afford to stand still on disarmament! We must never give up the search for a basis of agreement.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our allies from time to time develop differing ideas on how to proceed.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must concert these convictions among ourselves.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Thereafter, any reasonable proposal that holds promise for disarmament and reduction of tension must be heard, discussed, and, if possible, negotiated.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But a disarmament proposal, to hold real promise, must at the minimum have one feature: reliable means to ensure compliance by all.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It takes actions and demonstrated integrity on both sides to create and sustain confidence.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: And confidence in a genuine disarmament agreement is vital, not only to the signers of the agreement, but also to the millions of people all over the world who are weary of tensions and armaments.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I say once more, to all peoples, that we will always go the extra mile with anyone on earth if it will bring us nearer a genuine peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: CONCLUSION These, then, are the ways in which we must funnel our energies more efficiently into the task of advancing security and peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These actions demand and expect two things of the American people: sacrifice, and a high degree of understanding.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: For sacrifice to be effective it must be intelligent.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Sacrifice must be made for the right purpose and in the right place--even if that place happens to come close to home!

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: After all, it is no good demanding sacrifice in general terms one day, and the next day, for local reasons, opposing the elimination of some unneeded federal facility.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is pointless to condemn federal spending in general, and the next moment condemn just as strongly an effort to reduce the particular federal grant that touches one's own interest.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: And it makes no sense whatever to spend additional billions on military strength to deter a potential danger, and then, by cutting aid and trade programs, let the world succumb to a present danger in economic guise.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: My friends of the Congress: The world is waiting to see how wisely and decisively a free representative government will now act.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I believe that this Congress possesses and will display the wisdom promptly to do its part in translating into law the actions demanded by our nation's interests.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But, to make law effective, our kind of government needs the full voluntary support of millions of Americans for these actions.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am fully confident that the response of the Congress and of the American people will make this time of test a time of honor.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Mankind then will see more clearly than ever that the future belongs, not to the concept of the regimented atheistic state, but to the people--the God-fearing, peace-loving people of all the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This is the moment when Congress and the Executive annually begin their cooperative work to build a better America.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: One basic purpose unites us: To promote strength and security, side by side with liberty and opportunity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As we meet today, in the 170th year of the Republic, our Nation must continue to provide--as all other free governments have had to do throughout time--a satisfactory answer to a question as old as history.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is: Can Government based upon liberty and the God-given rights of man, permanently endure when ceaselessly challenged by a dictatorship, hostile to our mode of life, and controlling an economic and military power of great and growing strength?

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
