text: For us the answer has always been found, and is still found in the devotion, the vision, the courage and the fortitude of our people.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Moreover, this challenge we face, not as a single powerful nation, but as one that has in recent decades reached a position of recognized leadership in the Free World.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We have arrived at this position of leadership in an era of remarkable productivity and growth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is also a time when man's power of mass destruction has reached fearful proportions.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Possession of such capabilities helps create world suspicion and tension.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We, on our part, know that we seek only a just peace for all, with aggressive designs against no one.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Yet we realize that there is uneasiness in the world because of a belief on the part of peoples that through arrogance, miscalculation or fear of attack, catastrophic war could be launched.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Keeping the peace in today's world more than ever calls for the utmost in the nation's resolution, wisdom, steadiness and unremitting effort.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We cannot build peace through desire alone.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Moreover, we have learned the bitter lesson that international agreements, historically considered by us as sacred, are regarded in Communist doctrine and in practice to be mere scraps of paper.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The most recent proof of their disdain of international obligations, solemnly undertaken, is their announced intention to abandon their responsibilities respecting Berlin.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As a consequence, we can have no confidence in any treaty to which Communists are a party except where such a treaty provides within itself for self-enforcing mechanisms.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Indeed, the demonstrated disregard of the Communists of their own pledges is one of the greatest obstacles to success in substituting the Rule of Law for rule by force.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Yet step by step we must strengthen the institutions of peace--a peace that rests upon justice--a peace that depends upon a deep knowledge and clear understanding by all peoples of the cause and consequences of possible failure in this great purpose.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I. To achieve this peace we seek to prevent war at any place and in any dimension.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If, despite our best efforts, a local dispute should flare into armed hostilities, the next problem would be to keep the conflict from spreading, and so compromising freedom.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In support of these objectives we maintain forces of great power and flexibility.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our formidable air striking forces are a powerful deterrent to general war.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Large and growing portions of these units can depart from their bases in a matter of minutes.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Similar forces are included in our naval fleets.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Ground and other tactical formations can move with swiftness and precision, when requested by friendly and responsible governments, to help curb threatened aggression.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The stabilizing influence of this capacity has been dramatically demonstrated more than once over the past year.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our military and related scientific progress has been highly gratifying.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Great strides have been made in the development of ballistic missiles.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Intermediate range missiles are now being deployed in operational units.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Atlas intercontinental ballistic missile program has been marked by rapid development as evidenced by recent successful tests.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Missile training units have been established and launching sites are far along in construction.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: New aircraft that fly at twice the speed of sound are entering our squadrons.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We have successfully placed five satellites in orbit, which have gathered information of scientific importance never before available.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our latest satellite illustrates our steady advance in rocketry and foreshadows new developments in world-wide communications.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Warning systems constantly improve.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our atomic submarines have shattered endurance records and made historic voyages under the North Polar Sea.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A major segment of our national scientific and engineering community is working intensively to achieve new and greater developments.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Advance in military technology requires adequate financing but, of course, even more, it requires talent and time.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: All this is given only as a matter of history;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: as a record of our progress in space and ballistic missile fields in no more than four years of intensive effort.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: At the same time we clearly recognize that some of the recent Soviet accomplishments in this particular technology are indeed brilliant.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Under the law enacted last year the Department of Defense is being reorganized to give the Secretary of Defense full authority over the military establishment.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Greater efficiency, more cohesive effort and speedier reaction to emergencies are among the many advantages we are already noting from these changes.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These few highlights point up our steady military gains.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We are rightfully gratified by the achievements they represent.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But we must remember that these imposing armaments are purchased at great cost.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: National Security programs account for nearly sixty percent of the entire Federal budget for this coming fiscal year.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Modern weapons are exceedingly expensive.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The overall cost of introducing ATLAS into our armed forces will average $35 million per missile on the firing line.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This year we are investing an aggregate of close to $7 billion in missile programs alone.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Other billions go for research, development, test and evaluation of new weapons systems.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our latest atomic submarines will cost $50 millions each, while some special types will cost three times as much.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We are now ordering fighter aircraft which are priced at fifty times as much as the fighters of World War II.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We are buying certain bombers that cost their weight in gold.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These sums are tremendous, even when compared with the marvelous resiliency and capacity of our economy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Such expenditures demand both balance and perspective in our planning for defense.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: At every turn, we must weigh, judge and select.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Needless duplication of weapons and forces must be avoided.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: maximum peril.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The threat we face is not sporadic or dated: It is continuous.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Hence we must not be swayed in our calculations either by groundless fear or by complacency.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must avoid extremes, for vacillation between extremes is inefficient, costly, and destructive of morale.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In these days of unceasing technological advance, we must plan our defense expenditures systematically and with care, fully recognizing that obsolescence compels the never-ending replacement of older weapons with new ones.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The defense budget for the coming year has been planned on the basis of these principles and considerations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Over these many months I have personally participated in its development.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The aim is a sensible posture of defense.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The secondary aim is increased efficiency and avoidance of waste.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Both are achieved by this budgetary plan.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Working by these guide lines I believe with all my heart that America can be as sure of the strength and efficiency of her armed forces as she is of their loyalty.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am equally sure that the nation will thus avoid useless expenditures which, in the name of security, might tend to undermine the economy and, therefore, the nation's safety.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our own vast strength is only a part of that required for dependable security.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Because of this we have joined with nearly 50 other nations in collective security arrangements.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In these common undertakings each nation is expected to contribute what it can in sharing the heavy load.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Each supplies part of a strategic deployment to protect the forward boundaries of freedom.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Constantly we seek new ways to make more effective our contribution to this system of collective security.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Recently I have asked a Committee of eminent Americans of both parties to re-appraise our military assistance programs and the relative emphasis which should be placed on military and economic aid.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am hopeful that preliminary recommendations of this Committee will be available in time to assist in shaping the Mutual Security program for the coming fiscal year.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Any survey of the free world's defense structure cannot fail to impart a feeling of regret that so much of our effort and resources must be devoted to armaments.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: At Geneva and elsewhere we continue to seek technical and other agreements that may help to open up, with some promise, the issues of international disarmament.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: America will never give up the hope that eventually all nations can, with mutual confidence, drastically reduce these non-productive expenditures.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: II. The material foundation of our national safety is a strong and expanding economy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This we have--and this we must maintain.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Only with such an economy can we be secure and simultaneously provide for the well-being of our people.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A year ago the nation was experiencing a decline in employment and output.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Today that recession is fading into history, and this without gigantic, hastily-improvised public works projects or untimely tax reductions.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A healthy and vigorous recovery has been under way since last May.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: New homes are being built at the highest rate in several years.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Retail sales are at peak levels.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Personal income is at an all-time high.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The marked forward thrust of our economy reaffirms our confidence in competitive enterprise.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But--clearly--wisdom and prudence in both the public and private sectors of the economy are always necessary.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our outlook is this: 1960 commitments for our armed forces, the Atomic Energy Commission and Military Assistance exceed 47 billion dollars.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the foreseeable future they are not likely to be significantly lower.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: With an annual population increase of three million, other governmental costs are bound to mount.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: After we have provided wisely for our military strength, we must judge how to allocate our remaining government resources most effectively to promote our well-being and economic growth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Federal programs that will benefit all citizens are moving forward.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Next year we will be spending increased amounts on health programs; on Federal assistance to science and education; on the development of the nation's water resources; on the renewal of urban areas; and on our vast system of Federal-aid highways.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Each of these additional outlays is being made necessary by the surging growth of America.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Let me illustrate.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Responsive to this growth, Federal grants and long term loans to assist 14 major types of capital improvements in our cities will total over 2 billion dollars in 1960--double the expenditure of two years ago.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The major responsibility for development in these fields rests in the localities, even though the Federal Government will continue to do its proper part in meeting the genuine needs of a burgeoning population.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But the progress of our economy can more than match the growth of our needs.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We need only to act wisely and confidently.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Here, I hope you will permit me to digress long enough to express something that is much on my mind.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The basic question facing us today is more than mere survival--the military defense of national life and territory.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is the preservation of a way of life.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must meet the world challenge and at the same time permit no stagnation in America.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Unless we progress, we regress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We can successfully sustain security and remain true to our heritage of freedom if we clearly visualize the tasks ahead and set out to perform them with resolution and fervor.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must first define these tasks and then understand what we must do to perform them.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If progress is to be steady we must have long term guides extending far ahead, certainly five, possibly even ten years.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They must reflect the knowledge that before the end of five years we will have a population of over 190 million.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They must be goals that stand high, and so inspire every citizen to climb always toward mounting levels of moral, intellectual and material strength.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Every advance toward them must stir pride in individual and national achievements.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To define these goals, I intend to mobilize help from every available source.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We need more than politically ordained national objectives to challenge the best efforts of free men and women.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A group of selfless and devoted individuals, outside of government, could effectively participate in making the necessary appraisal of the potentials of our future.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The result would be establishment of national goals that would not only spur us on to our finest efforts, but would meet the stern test of practicality.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Committee I plan will comprise educators and representatives of labor, management, finance, the professions and every other kind of useful activity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Such a study would update and supplement, in the light of continuous changes in our society and its economy, the monumental work of the Committee on Recent Social Trends which was appointed in 1931 by President Hoover.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Its report has stood the test of time and has had a beneficial influence on national development.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The new Committee would be concerned, among other things, with the acceleration of our economy's growth and the living standards of our people, their health and education, their better assurance of life and liberty and their greater opportunities.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It would also be concerned with methods to meet such goals and what levels of government--Local, State, or Federal--might or should be particularly concerned.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As one example, consider our schools, operated under the authority of local communities and states.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In their capacity and in their quality they conform to no recognizable standards.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In some places facilities are ample, in others meager.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Pay of teachers ranges between wide limits, from the adequate to the shameful.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As would be expected, quality of teaching varies just as widely.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But to our teachers we commit the most valuable possession of the nation and of the family-- our children.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must have teachers of competence.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To obtain and hold them we need standards.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We need a National Goal.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Once established I am certain that public opinion would compel steady progress toward its accomplishment.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Such studies would be helpful, I believe, to government at all levels and to all individuals.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The goals so established could help us see our current needs in perspective.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They will spur progress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We do not forget, of course, that our nation's progress and fiscal integrity are interdependent and inseparable.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We can afford everything we clearly need, but we cannot afford one cent of waste.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must examine every item of governmental expense critically.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To do otherwise would betray our nation's future.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Thrift is one of the characteristics that has made this nation great.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Why should we ignore it now?

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must avoid any contribution to inflationary processes, which could disrupt sound growth in our economy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Prices have displayed a welcome stability in recent months and, if we are wise and resolute, we will not tolerate inflation in the years to come.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But history makes clear the risks inherent in any failure to deal firmly with the basic causes of inflation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Two of the most important of these causes are the wage-price spiral and continued deficit financing.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Inflation would reduce job opportunities, price us out of world markets, shrink the value of savings and penalize the thrift so essential to finance a growing economy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Inflation is not a Robin Hood, taking from the rich to give to the poor.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Rather, it deals most cruelly with those who can least protect themselves.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It strikes hardest those millions of our citizens whose incomes do not quickly rise with the cost of living.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: When prices soar, the pensioner and the widow see their security undermined, the man of thrift sees his savings melt away; the white collar worker, the minister, and the teacher see their standards of living dragged down.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Inflation can be prevented.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But this demands statesmanship on the part of business and labor leaders and of government at all levels.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must encourage the self-discipline, the restraint necessary to curb the wage-price spiral and we must meet current costs from current revenue.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To minimize the danger of future soaring prices and to keep our economy sound and expanding, I shall present to the Congress certain proposals.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: First, I shall submit a balanced budget for the next year, a year expected to be the most prosperous in our history.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is a realistic budget with wholly attainable objectives.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If we cannot live within our means during such a time of rising prosperity, the hope for fiscal integrity will fade.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If we persist in living beyond our means, we make it difficult for every family in our land to balance its own household budget.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But to live within our means would be a tangible demonstration of the self-discipline needed to assure a stable dollar.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Constitution entrusts the Executive with many functions, but the Congress--and the Congress alone--has the power of the purse.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Ultimately upon Congress rests responsibility for determining the scope and amount of Federal spending.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: By working together, the Congress and the Executive can keep a balance between income and outgo.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If this is done there is real hope that we can look forward to a time in the foreseeable future when needed tax reforms can be accomplished.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In this hope, I am requesting the Secretary of the Treasury to prepare appropriate proposals for revising, at the proper time, our tax structure, to remove inequities and to enhance incentives for all Americans to work, to save, and to invest.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Such recommendations will be made as soon as our fiscal condition permits.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These prospects will be brightened if 1960 expenditures do not exceed the levels recommended.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Second, I shall recommend to the Congress that the Chief Executive be given the responsibility either to approve or to veto specific items in appropriations and authorization bills.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: [I assure you gentlemen that I know this recommendation has been made time and again by every President that has appeared in this hall for many years, but I say this, it still is one of the most important corrections that could be made in our annual expenditure program, because this would save tax dollars.]

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Third, to reduce Federal operations in an area where private enterprise can do the job, I shall recommend legislation for greater flexibility in extending Federal credit, and in improving the procedures under which private credits are insured or guaranteed.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Present practices have needlessly added large sums to Federal expenditures.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Fourth, action is required to make more effective use of the large Federal expenditures for agriculture and to achieve greater fiscal control in this area.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Outlays of the Department of Agriculture for the current fiscal year for the support of farm prices on a very few farm products will exceed five billion dollars.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: That is a sum equal to approximately two-fifths of the net income of all farm operators in the entire United States.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: By the end of this fiscal year it is estimated that there will be in Government hands surplus farm products worth about nine billion dollars.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: And by July 1, 1959, Government expenditures for storage, interest, and handling of its agricultural inventory will reach a rate of one billion dollars a year.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This level of expenditure for farm products could be made willingly for a temporary period if it were leading to a sound solution of the problem.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But unfortunately this is not true.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We need new legislation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the past I have sent messages to the Congress requesting greater freedom for our farmers to manage their own farms and greater freedom for markets to reflect the wishes of producers and consumers.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Legislative changes that followed were appropriate in direction but did not go far enough.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The situation calls for prompt and forthright action.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Recommendation for action will be contained in a message to be transmitted to the Congress shortly.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These fiscal and related actions will help create an environment of price stability for economic growth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: However, certain additional measures are needed.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I shall ask Congress to amend the Employment Act of 1946 to make it clear that Government intends to use all appropriate means to protect the buying power of the dollar.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am establishing a continuing Cabinet group on Price Stability for Economic Growth to study governmental and private policies affecting costs, prices, and economic growth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It will strive also to build a better public understanding of the conditions necessary for maintaining growth and price stability.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Studies are being undertaken to improve our information on prices, wages, and productivity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I believe all citizens in all walks of life will support this program of action to accelerate economic growth and promote price stability.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: III. I take up next certain aspects of our international situation and our programs to strengthen it.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: America's security can be assured only within a world community of strong, stable, independent nations, in which the concepts of freedom, justice and human dignity can flourish.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There can be no such thing as Fortress America.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If ever we were reduced to the isolation implied by that term, we would occupy a prison, not a fortress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The question whether we can afford to help other nations that want to defend their freedom but cannot fully do so from their own means, has only one answer: we can and we must, we we have been doing so since 1947.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our foreign policy has long been dedicated to building a permanent and just peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: During the past six years our free world security arrangements have been bolstered and the bonds of freedom have been more closely knit.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our friends in Western Europe are experiencing new internal vitality, and are increasingly more able to resist external threats.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Over the years the world has come to understand clearly that it is our firm policy not to countenance aggression.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In Lebanon, Taiwan, and Berlin--our stand has been clear, right, and expressive of the determined will of a united people.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Acting with other free nations we have undertaken the solemn obligation to defend the people of free Berlin against any effort to destroy their freedom.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the meantime we shall constantly seek meaningful agreements to settle this and other problems, knowing full well that not only the integrity of a single city, but the hope of all free peoples is at stake.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We need, likewise, to continue helping to build the economic base so essential to the Free World's stability and strength.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank have both fully proven their worth as instruments of international financial cooperation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Their Executive Directors have recommended an increase in each member country's subscription.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am requesting the Congress for immediate approval of our share of these increases.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We are now negotiating with representatives of the twenty Latin American Republics for the creation of an inter-American financial institution.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Its purpose would be to join all the American Republics in a common institution which would promote and finance development in Latin America, and make more effective the use of capital from the World Bank, the Export-Import Bank, and private sources.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Private enterprise continues to make major contributions to economic development in all parts of the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But we have not yet marshaled the full potential of American business for this task, particularly in countries which have recently attained their independence.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I shall present to this Congress a program designed to encourage greater participation by private enterprise in economic development abroad.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Further, all of us know that to advance the cause of freedom we must do much more than help build sound economies.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The spiritual, intellectual, and physical strength of people throughout the world will in the last analysis determine their willingness and their ability to resist Communism.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To give a single illustration of our many efforts in these fields: We have been a participant in the effort that has been made over the past few years against one of the great scourges of mankind--disease.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Through the Mutual Security program public health officials are being trained by American universities to serve in less developed countries.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We are engaged in intensive malaria eradication projects in many parts of the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: America's major successes in our own country prove the feasibility of success everywhere.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: By these and other means we shall continue and expand our campaign against the afflictions that now bring needless suffering and death to so many of the world's people.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We wish to be part of a great shared effort toward the triumph of health.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: IV. America is best described by one word, freedom.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If we hope to strengthen freedom in the world we must be ever mindful of how our own conduct reacts elsewhere.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: No nation has ever been so floodlighted by world opinion as the United States is today.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Everything we do is carefully scrutinized by other peoples throughout the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The bad is seen along with the good.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Because we are human we err.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But as free men we are also responsible for correcting the errors and imperfections of our ways.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Last January I made comprehensive recommendations to the Congress for legislation in the labor-management field.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To my disappointment, Congress failed to act.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The McClellan Committee disclosures of corruption, racketeering, and abuse of trust and power in labor-management affairs have aroused America and amazed other peoples.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They emphasize the need for improved local law enforcement and the enactment of effective Federal legislation to protect the public interest and to insure the rights and economic freedoms of millions of American workers.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Halfhearted measures will not do.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I shall recommend prompt enactment of legislation designed: To safeguard workers' funds in union treasuries against misuse of any kind whatsoever.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To protect the rights and freedoms of individual union members, including the basic right to free and secret elections of officers.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To advance true and responsible collective bargaining.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To protect the public and innocent third parties from unfair and coercive practices such as boycotting and blackmail picketing.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The workers and the public must have these vital protections.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In other areas of human rights--freedom from discrimination in voting, in public education, in access to jobs, and in other respects-- the world is likewise watching our conduct.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The image of America abroad is not improved when school children, through closing of some of our schools and through no fault of their own, are deprived of their opportunity for an education.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The government of a free people has no purpose more noble than to work for the maximum realization of equality of opportunity under law.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This is not the sole responsibility of any one branch of our government.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The judicial arm, which has the ultimate authority for interpreting the Constitution, has held that certain state laws and practices discriminate upon racial grounds and are unconstitutional.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Whenever the supremacy of the Constitution of the United States is challenged I shall continue to take every action necessary to uphold it.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: One of the fundamental concepts of our constitutional system is that it guarantees to every individual, regardless of race, religion, or national origin, the equal protection of the laws.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Those of us who are privileged to hold public office have a solemn obligation to make meaningful this inspiring objective.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We can fulfill that obligation by our leadership in teaching, persuading, demonstrating, and in enforcing the law.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We are making noticeable progress in the field of civil rights-- we are moving forward toward achievement of equality of opportunity for all people everywhere in the United States.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the interest of the nation and of each of its citizens, that progress must continue.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Legislative proposals of the Administration in this field will be submitted to the Congress early in the session.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: All of us should help to make clear that the government is united in the common purpose of giving support to the law and the decisions of the Courts.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: By moving steadily toward the goal of greater freedom under law, for our own people, we shall be the better prepared to work for the cause of freedom under law throughout the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: All peoples are sorely tired of the fear, destruction, and the waste of war.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As never before, the world knows the human and material costs of war and seeks to replace force with a genuine rule of law among nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is my purpose to intensify efforts during the coming two years in seeking ways to supplement the procedures of the United Nations and other bodies with similar objectives, to the end that the rule of law may replace the rule of force in the affairs of nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Measures toward this end will be proposed later, including a re-examination of our own relation to the International Court of Justice.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Finally--let us remind ourselves that Marxist scripture is not new; it is not the gospel of the future.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Its basic objective is dictatorship, old as history.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: What is new is the shining prospect that man can build a world where all can live in dignity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We seek victory--not over any nation or people--but over the ancient enemies of us all; victory over ignorance, poverty, disease, and human degradation wherever they may be found.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We march in the noblest of causes--human freedom.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If we make ourselves worthy of America's ideals, if we do not forget that our nation was founded on the premise that all men are creatures of God's making, the world will come to know that it is free men who carry forward the true promise of human progress and dignity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Seven years ago I entered my present office with one long-held resolve overriding all others.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I was then, and remain now, determined that the United States shall become an ever more potent resource for the cause of peace--realizing that peace cannot be for ourselves alone, but for peoples everywhere.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This determination is shared by the entire Congress--indeed, by all Americans.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: My purpose today is to discuss some features of America's position, both at home and in her relations to others.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: First, I point out that for us, annual self-examination is made a definite necessity by the fact that we now live in a divided world of uneasy equilibrium, with our side committed to its own protection and against aggression by the other.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: With both sides of this divided world in possession of unbelievably destructive weapons, mankind approaches a state where mutual annihilation becomes a possibility.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: No other fact of today's world equals this in importance--it colors everything we say, plan, and do.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There is demanded of us, vigilance, determination, and the dedication of whatever portion of our resources that will provide adequate security, especially a real deterrent to aggression.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These things we are doing.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: All these facts emphasize the importance of striving incessantly for a just peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Only through the strengthening of the spiritual, intellectual, economic and defensive resources of the Free World can we, in confidence, make progress toward this goal.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Second, we note that recent Soviet deportment and pronouncements suggest the possible opening of a somewhat less strained period in the relationships between the Soviet Union and the Free World.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If these pronouncements be genuine, there is brighter hope of diminishing the intensity of past rivalry and eventually of substituting persuasion for coercion.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Whether this is to become an era of lasting promise remains to be tested by actions.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Third, we now stand in the vestibule of a vast new technological age--one that, despite its capacity for human destruction, has an equal capacity to make poverty and human misery obsolete.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If our efforts are wisely directed--and if our unremitting efforts for dependable peace begin to attain some success--we can surely become participants in creating an age characterized by justice and rising levels of human well-being.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Over the past year the Soviet Union has expressed an interest in measures to reduce the common peril of war.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: While neither we nor any other Free World nation can permit ourselves to be misled by pleasant promises until they are tested by performance, yet we approach this apparently new opportunity with the utmost seriousness.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must strive to break the calamitous cycle of frustrations and crises which, if unchecked, could spiral into nuclear disaster; the ultimate insanity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Though the need for dependable agreements to assure against resort to force in settling disputes is apparent to both sides yet as in other issues dividing men and nations, we cannot expect sudden and revolutionary results.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But we must find some place to begin.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: One obvious road on which to make a useful start is in the widening of communication between our two peoples.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In this field there are, both sides willing, countless opportunities--most of them well known to us all--for developing mutual understanding, the true foundation of peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Another avenue may be through the reopening, on January twelfth, of negotiations looking to a controlled ban on the testing of nuclear weapons.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Unfortunately, the closing statement from the Soviet scientists who met with our scientists at Geneva in an unsuccessful effort to develop an agreed basis for a test ban, gives the clear impression that their conclusions have been politically guided.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Those of the British and American scientific representatives are their own freely-formed, individual and collective opinions.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am hopeful that as new negotiations begin, truth--not political opportunism--will be the guiding light of the deliberations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Still another avenue may be found in the field of disarmament, in which the Soviets have professed a readiness to negotiate seriously.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They have not, however, made clear the plans they may have, if any, for mutual inspection and verification--the essential condition for any extensive measure of disarmament.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There is one instance where our initiative for peace has recently been successful.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A multi-lateral treaty signed last month provides for the exclusively peaceful use of Antarctica, assured by a system of inspection.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It provides for free and cooperative scientific research in that continent, and prohibits nuclear explosions there pending general international agreement on the subject.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Treaty is a significant contribution toward peace, international cooperation, and the advancement of science.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I shall transmit its text to the Senate for consideration and approval in the near future.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The United States is always ready to participate with the Soviet Union in serious discussion of these or any other subjects that may lead to peace with justice.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Certainly it is not necessary to repeat that the United States has no intention of interfering in the internal affairs of any nation;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: likewise we reject any attempt to impose its system on us or on other peoples by force or subversion.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This concern for the freedom of other peoples is the intellectual and spiritual cement which has allied us with more than forty other nations in a common defense effort.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Not for a moment do we forget that our own fate is firmly fastened to that of these countries;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: we will not act in any way which would jeopardize our solemn commitments to them.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We and our friends are, of course, concerned with self-defense.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Growing out of this concern is the realization that all people of the Free World have a great stake in the progress, in freedom, of the uncommitted and newly emerging nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These peoples, desperately hoping to lift themselves to decent levels of living must not, by our neglect, be forced to seek help from, and finally become virtual satellites of, those who proclaim their hostility to freedom.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Their natural desire for a better life must not be frustrated by withholding from them necessary technical and investment assistance.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This is a problem to be solved not by America alone, but also by every nation cherishing the same ideals and in position to provide help.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In recent years America's partners and friends in Western Europe and Japan have made great economic progress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Their newly found economic strength is eloquent testimony to the striking success of the policies of economic cooperation which we and they have pursued.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The international economy of 1960 is markedly different from that of the early postwar years.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: No longer is the United States the only major industrial country capable of providing substantial amounts of the resources so urgently needed in the newly-developing countries.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To remain secure and prosperous themselves, wealthy nations must extend the kind of cooperation to the less fortunate members that will inspire hope, confidence and progress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A rich nation can for a time, without noticeable damage to itself, pursue a course of self-indulgence, making its single goal the material ease and comfort of its own citizens-- thus repudiating its own spiritual and materials take in a peaceful and prosperous society of nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But the enmities it will incur, the isolation into which it will descend, and the internal moral and physical softness that will be engendered, will, in the long term, bring it to disaster.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: America did not become great through softness and self-indulgence.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Her miraculous progress and achievements flow from other qualities far more worthy and substantial: adherence to principles and methods consonant with our religious philosophy a satisfaction in hard work the readiness to sacrifice for worthwhile causes the courage to meet every challenge to her progress the intellectual honesty and capacity to recognize the true path of her own best interests.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To us and to every nation of the Free World, rich or poor, these qualities are necessary today as never before if we are to march together to greater security, prosperity and peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I believe the industrial countries are ready to participate actively in supplementing the efforts of the developing countries to achieve progress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The immediate need for this kind of cooperation is underscored by the strain in our international balance of payments.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our surplus from foreign business transactions has in recent years fallen substantially short of the expenditures we make abroad to maintain our military establishments overseas, to finance private investment, and to provide assistance to the less developed nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In1959 our deficit in balance of payments approached $4 billion.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Continuing deficits of anything like this magnitude would, over time, impair our own economic growth and check the forward progress of the Free World.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must meet this situation by promoting a rising volume of exports and world trade.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Further, we must induce all industrialized nations of the Free World to work together in a new cooperative endeavor to help lift the scourge of poverty from less fortunate nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This will provide for better sharing of this burden and for still further profitable trade.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: New nations, and others struggling with the problems of development, will progress only if they demonstrate faith in their own destiny and possess the will and use their own resources to fulfill it.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Moreover, progress in a national transformation can be only gradually earned; there is no easy and quick way to follow from the oxcart to the jet plane.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But, just as we drew on Europe for assistance in our earlier years, so now do those new and emerging nations that have this faith and determination deserve help.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Over the last fifteen years, twenty nations have gained political independence.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Others are doing so each year.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Most of them are woefully lacking in technical capacity and in investment capital;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: without Free World support in these matters they cannot effectively progress in freedom.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Respecting their need, one of the major focal points of our concern is the South Asian region.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Here, in two nations alone, are almost five hundred million people, all working, and working hard, to raise their standards, and in doing so, to make of themselves a strong bulwark against the spread of an ideology that would destroy liberty.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I cannot express to you the depth of my conviction that, in our own and Free World interests, we must cooperate with others to help these people achieve their legitimate ambitions, as expressed in their different multi-year plans.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Through the World Bank and other instrumentalities, as well as through individual action by every nation in position to help, we must squarely face this titanic challenge.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: All of us must realize, of course, that development in freedom by the newly emerging nations, is no mere matter of obtaining outside financial assistance.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: An indispensable element in this process is a strong and continuing determination on the part of these nations to exercise the national discipline necessary for any sustained development period.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These qualities of determination are particularly essential because of the fact that the process of improvement will necessarily be gradual and laborious rather than revolutionary.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Moreover, everyone should be aware that the development process is no short term phenomenon.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Many years are required for even the most favorably situated countries.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I shall continue to urge the American people, in the interests of their own security, prosperity and peace, to make sure that their own part of this great project be amply and cheerfully supported.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Free World decisions in this matter may spell the difference between world disaster and world progress in freedom.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Other countries, some of which I visited last month, have similar needs.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A common meeting ground is desirable for those nations which are prepared to assist in the development effort.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: During the past year I have discussed this matter with the leaders of several Western Nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Because of its wealth of experience, the Organization for European Economic Cooperation could help with initial studies.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The goal is to enlist all available economic resources in the industrialized Free World--especially private investment capital.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But I repeat that this help, no matter how great, can be lastingly effective only if it is used as a supplement to the strength of spirit and will of the people of the newly-developing nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: By extending this help we hope to make possible the enthusiastic enrollment of these nations under freedom's banner.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: No more startling contrast to a system of sullen satellites could be imagined.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If we grasp this opportunity to build an age of productive partnership between the less fortunate nations and those that have already achieved a high state of economic advancement, we will make brighter the outlook for a world order based upon security, freedom and peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Otherwise, the outlook could be dark indeed.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We face what may be a turning point in history, and we must act decisively.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As a nation we can successfully pursue these objectives only from a position of broadly based strength.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: No matter how earnest is our quest for guaranteed peace, we must maintain a high degree of military effectiveness at the same time we are engaged in negotiating the issue of arms reduction.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Until tangible and mutually enforceable arms reduction measures are worked out, we will not weaken the means of defending our institutions.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: America possesses an enormous defense power.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is my studied conviction that no nation will ever risk general war against us unless we should be so foolish as to neglect the defense forces we now so powerfully support.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is world-wide knowledge that any nation which might be tempted today to attack the United States, even though our country might sustain great losses, would itself promptly suffer a terrible destruction.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But I once again assure all peoples and all nations that the United States, except in defense, will never turn loose this destructive power.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: During the past year, our long-range striking power, unmatched today in manned bombers, has taken on new strength as the Atlas intercontinental ballistic missile has entered the operational inventory.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In fourteen recent test launchings, at ranges of over 5,000 miles, Atlas has been striking on an average within two miles of the target.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This is less than the length of a jet runway--well within the circle of total destruction.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Such performance is a great tribute to American scientists and engineers, who in the past five years have had to telescope time and technology to develop these long-range ballistic missiles, where America had none before.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This year, moreover, growing numbers of nuclear-powered submarines will enter our active forces, some to be armed with Polaris missiles.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These remarkable ships and weapons, ranging the oceans, will be capable of accurate fire on targets virtually anywhere on earth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Impossible to destroy by surprise attack, they will become one of our most effective sentinels for peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To meet situations of less than general nuclear war, we continue to maintain our carrier forces, our many service units abroad, our always ready Army strategic forces and Marine Corps divisions, and the civilian components.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The continuing modernization of these forces is a costly but necessary process, and is scheduled to go forward at a rate which will steadily add to our strength.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The deployment of a portion of these forces beyond our shores, on land and sea, is persuasive demonstration of our determination to stand shoulder-to-shoulder with our allies for collective security.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Moreover, I have directed that steps betaken to program our military assistance to these allies on a longer range basis.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This is necessary for a sounder collective defense system.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Next I refer to our effort in space exploration, which is often mistakenly supposed to be an integral part of defense research and development.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: First, America has made great contributions in the past two years to the world

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These discoveries are of present interest chiefly to the scientific community;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: but they are important foundation-stones for more extensive exploration of outer space for the ultimate benefit of all mankind.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Second, our military missile program, going forward so successfully, does not suffer from our present lack of very large rocket engines, which are so necessary in distant space exploration.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am assured by experts that the thrust of our present missiles is fully adequate for defense requirements.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Third, the United States is pressing forward in the development of large rocket engines to place much heavier vehicles into space for exploration purposes.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Fourth, in the meantime, it is necessary to remember that we have only begun to probe the environment immediately surrounding the earth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Using launch systems presently available, we are developing satellites to scout the world's weather;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: satellite relay stations to facilitate and extend communications over the globe;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: for navigation aids to give accurate bearings to ships and aircraft;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: and for perfecting instruments to collect and transmit the data we seek.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This is the area holding the most promise for early and useful applications of space technology.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Fifth, we have just completed a year's experience with our new space law.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I believe it deficient in certain particulars and suggested improvements will be submitted shortly.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The accomplishment of the many tasks I have alluded to requires the continuous strengthening of the spiritual, intellectual, and economic sinews of American life.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The steady purpose of our society is to assure justice, before God, for every individual.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must be ever alert that freedom does not wither through the careless amassing of restrictive controls or the lack of courage to deal boldly with the giant issues of the day.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A year ago, when I met with you, the nation was emerging from an economic downturn, even though the signs of resurgent prosperity were not then sufficiently convincing to the doubtful.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Today our surging strength is apparent to everyone.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: 1960 promises to be the most prosperous year in our history.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Yet we continue to be afflicted by nagging disorders.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Among current problems that require solution are: the need to protect the public interest in situations of prolonged labor-management stalemate;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: the persistent refusal to come to grips with a critical problem in one sector of American agriculture;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: the continuing threat of inflation, together with the persisting tendency toward fiscal irresponsibility;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: in certain instances the denial to some of our citizens of equal protection of the law.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Every American was disturbed by the prolonged dispute in the steel industry and the protracted delay in reaching a settlement.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We are all relieved that a settlement has at last been achieved in that industry.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Percentage wise, by this settlement the increase to the steel companies in employment costs is lower than in any prior wage settlement since World War II.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is also gratifying to note that despite the increase in wages and benefits several of the major steel producers have announced that there will be no increase in steel prices at this time.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The national interest demands that in the period of industrial peace which has been assured by the new contract both management and labor make every possible effort to increase efficiency and productivity in the manufacture of steel so that price increases can be avoided.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: One of the lessons of this story is that the potential danger to the entire Nation of longer and greater strikes must be met.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To insure against such possibilities we must of course depend primarily upon the good commonsense of the responsible individuals.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is my intention to encourage regular discussions between management and labor outside the bargaining table, to consider the interest of the public as well as their mutual interest in the maintenance of industrial peace, price stability and economic growth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To me, it seems almost absurd for the United States to recognize the need, and so earnestly to seek, for cooperation among the nations unless we can achieve voluntary, dependable, abiding cooperation among the important segments of our own free society.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Failure to face up to basic issues in areas other than those of labor-management can cause serious strains on the firm freedom supports of our society.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I refer to agriculture as one of these areas.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our basic farm laws were written27 years ago, in an emergency effort to redress hardship caused by a world-wide depression.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They were continued--and their economic distortions intensified--during World War II in order to provide incentives for production of food needed to sustain a war-torn free world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Today our farm problem is totally different.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is that of effectively adjusting to the changes caused by a scientific revolution.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: When the original farm laws were written, an hour's farm labor produced only one-fourth as much wheat as at present.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Farm legislation is woefully out-of-date, ineffective, and expensive.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: For years we have gone on with an outmoded system which not only has failed to protect farm income, but also has produced soaring, threatening surpluses.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our farms have been left producing for war while America has long been at peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Once again I urge Congress to enact legislation that will gear production more closely to markets, make costly surpluses more manageable, provide greater freedom in farm operations, and steadily achieve increased net farm incomes.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Another issue that we must meet squarely is that of living within our means.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This requires restraint in expenditure, constant reassessment of priorities, and the maintenance of stable prices.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must prevent inflation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Here is an opponent of so many guises that it is sometimes difficult to recognize.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But our clear need is to stop continuous and general price rises--a need that all of us can see and feel.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To prevent steadily rising costs and prices calls for stern self-discipline by every citizen.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: No person, city, state, or organized group can afford to evade the obligation to resist inflation, for every American pays its crippling tax.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Inflation's ravages do not end at the water's edge.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Increases in prices of the goods we sell abroad threaten to drive us out of markets that once were securely ours.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Whether domestic prices, so high as to be noncompetitive, result from demands for too-high profit margins or from increased labor costs that outrun growth in productivity, the final result is seriously damaging to the nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must fight inflation as we would a fire that imperils our home.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Only by so doing can we prevent it from destroying our salaries, savings, pensions and insurance, and from gnawing away the very roots of a free, healthy economy and the nation's security.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: One major method by which the Federal government can counter inflation and rising prices is to insure that its expenditures are below its revenues.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The debt with which we are now confronted is about 290 billion dollars.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: With interest charges alone now costing taxpayers about $9 1/2 billions, it is clear that this debt growth must stop.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: You will be glad to know that despite the unsettling influences of the recent steel strike, we estimate that our accounts will show, on June 30, this year, a favorable balance of approximately $200million.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I shall present to the Congress for 1961 a balanced budget.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the area of defense, expenditures continue at the record peace-time levels of the last several years.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: With a single exception, expenditures in every major category of Health, Education and Welfare will be equal or greater than last year.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In Space expenditures the amounts are practically doubled.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But the over-all guiding goal of this budget is national need--not response to specific group, local or political insistence.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Expenditure increases, other than those I have indicated, are largely accounted for by the increased cost of legislation previously enacted.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I repeat, this budget will be a balanced one.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Expenditures will be 79 billion 8hundred million.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The amount of income over outgo, described in the budget as a Surplus, to be applied against our national debt, is 4 billion 2 hundred million.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: as long as the nation is in debt.
