speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Once we have established such payments as normal practice, we can profitably make improvements in our tax structure and thereby truly reduce the heavy burdens of taxation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: [In any event, this one reduction will save taxpayers, each year, approximately 2 hundred million dollars in interest costs.]

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This budget will help ease pressures in our credit and capital markets.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It will enhance the confidence of people all over the world in the strength of our economy and our currency and in our individual and collective ability to be fiscally responsible.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the management of the huge public debt the Treasury is unfortunately not free of artificial barriers.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Its ability to deal with the difficult problems in this field has been weakened greatly by the unwillingness of the Congress to remove archaic restrictions.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The need for a freer hand in debt management is even more urgent today because the costs of the undesirable financing practices which the Treasury has been forced into are mounting.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Removal of this roadblock has high priority in my legislative recommendations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Still another issue relates to civil rights.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In all our hopes and plans for a better world we all recognize that provincial and racial prejudices must be combated.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the long perspective of history, the right to vote has been one of the strongest pillars of a free society.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our first duty is to protect this right against all encroachment.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In spite of constitutional guarantees, and notwithstanding much progress of recent years, bias still deprives some persons in this country of equal protection of the laws.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Early in your last session I recommended legislation which would help eliminate several practices discriminating against the basic rights of Americans.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Civil Rights Commission has developed additional constructive recommendations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I hope that these will be among the matters to be seriously considered in the current session.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I trust that Congress will thus signal to the world that our Government is striving for equality under law for all our people.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Each year and in many ways our nation continues to undergo profound change and growth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the past 18 months we have hailed the entry of two more States of the Union--Alaska and Hawaii.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We salute these two western stars proudly.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our vigorous expansion, which we all welcome as a sign of health and vitality, is many-sided.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We are, for example, witnessing explosive growth in metropolitan areas.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: By 1975 the metropolitan areas of the United States will occupy twice the territory they do today.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The roster of urban problems with which they must cope is staggering.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: They involve water supply, cleaning the air, adjusting local tax systems, providing for essential educational, cultural, and social services, and destroying those conditions which breed delinquency and crime.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In meeting these, we must, if we value our historic freedoms, keep within the traditional framework of our Federal system with powers divided between the national and state governments.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The uniqueness of this system may confound the casual observer, but it has worked effectively for nearly 200 years.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I do not doubt that our urban and other perplexing problems can be solved in the traditional American method.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Federal tax dollar.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our educational system provides a ready example.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: All recognize the vital necessity of having modern school plants, well-qualified and adequately compensated teachers, and of using the best possible teaching techniques and curricula.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We cannot be complacent about educating our youth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But the route to better trained minds is not through the swift administration of a Federal hypodermic or sustained financial transfusion.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The educational process, essentially a local and personal responsibility, cannot be made to leap ahead by crash, centralized governmental action.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Administration has proposed a carefully reasoned program for helping eliminate current deficiencies.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is designed to stimulate classroom construction, not by substitution of Federal dollars for state and local funds, but by incentives to extend and encourage state and local efforts.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This approach rejects the notion of Federal domination or control.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is workable, and should appeal to every American interested in advancement of our educational system in the traditional American way.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I urge the Congress to take action upon it.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There is one other subject concerning which I renew a recommendation I made in my State of the Union Message last January.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I then advised the Congress of my purpose to intensify our efforts to replace force with a rule of law among nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: From many discussions abroad, I am convinced that purpose is widely and deeply shared by other peoples and nations of the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the same Message I stated that our efforts would include a reexamination of our own relation to the International Court of Justice.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Court was established by the United Nations to decide international legal disputes between nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In 1946 we accepted the Court's jurisdiction, but subject to a reservation of the right to determine unilaterally whether a matter lies essentially within domestic jurisdiction.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There is pending before the Senate, a Resolution which would repeal our present self-judging reservation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I support that Resolution and urge its prompt passage.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If this is done, I intend to urge similar acceptance of the Court's jurisdiction by every member of the United Nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Here perhaps it is not amiss for me to say to the Members of the Congress, in this my final year of office, a word about the institutions we respectively represent and the meaning which the relationships between our two branches has for the days ahead.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am not unique as a President in having worked with a Congress controlled by the opposition party--except that no other President ever did it for quite so long!

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Yet in both personal and official relationships we have weathered the storms of the past five years.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: For this I am grateful.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: My deep concern in the next twelve months, before my successor takes office, is with our joint Congressional-Executive duty to our own and to other nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Acting upon the beliefs I have expressed here today, I shall devote my full energies to the tasks at hand, whether these involve travel for promoting greater world understanding, negotiations to reduce international antdiscussions and communications with the Congress and the American people on issues both domestic and foreign.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In pursuit of these objectives, I look forward to, and shall dedicate myself to, a close and constructive association with the Congress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Every minute spent in irrelevant inter-branch wrangling is precious time taken from the intelligent initiation and adoption of coherent policies for our national survival and progress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We seek a common goal--brighter opportunity for our own citizens and a world peace with justice for all.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Before us and our friends is the challenge of an ideology which, for more than four decades, has trumpeted abroad its purpose of gaining ultimate victory overall forms of government at variance with its own.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We realize that however much we repudiate the tenets of imperialistic Communism, it represents a gigantic centerprise grimly pursued by leaders who compel its subjects to subordinate their freedom of action and spirit and personal desires for some hoped-for advantage in the future.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Communists can present an array of material accomplishments over the past fifteen years that lends a false persuasiveness to many of their glittering promises to the uncommitted peoples.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The competition they provide is formidable.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But in our scale of values we place freedom first--our whole national existence and development have been geared to that basic concept and are responsible for the position of free world leadership to which we have succeeded.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is the highest prize that any nation can possess; it is one that Communism can never offer.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: And America's record of material accomplishment in freedom is written not only in the unparalleled prosperity of our own nation, but in the many billions we have devoted to the reconstruction of Free World economies wrecked by World War II and in the effective help of many more billions we have given in saving the independence of many others threatened by outside domination.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Assuredly we have the capacity for handling the problems in the new era of the world's history we are now entering.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But we must use that capacity intelligently and tirelessly, regardless of personal sacrifice.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The fissure that divides our political planet is deep and wide.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We live, moreover, in a sea of semantic disorder in which old labels no longer faithfully describe.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: people's democracies.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Armed conquest of free people is called liberation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Such slippery slogans make more difficult the problem of communicating true faith, facts and beliefs.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must make clear our peaceful intentions, our aspirations for a better world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: So doing, we must use language to enlighten the mind, not as the instrument of the studied innuendo and distorter of truth.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: And we must live by what we say.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: On my recent visit to distant lands I found one statesman after another eager to tell me of the elements of their government that had been borrowed from our American Constitution, and from the indestructible ideals set forth in our Declaration of Independence.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As a nation we take pride that our own constitutional system, and the ideals which sustain it, have been long viewed as a fountainhead of freedom.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: By our every action we must strive to make ourselves worthy of this trust, ever mindful that an accumulation of seemingly minor encroachments upon freedom gradually could break down the entire fabric of a free society.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: So persuaded, we shall get on with the task before us.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: So dedicated, and with faith in the Almighty, humanity shall one day achieve the unity in freedom to which all men have aspired from the dawn of time.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Once again it is my Constitutional duty to assess the state of the Union.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: On each such previous occasion during these past eight years I have outlined a forward course designed to achieve our mutual objective--a better America in a world of peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This time my function is different.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The American people, in free election, have selected new leadership which soon will be entrusted with the management of our government.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A new President shortly will lay before you his proposals to shape the future of our great land.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: To him, every citizen, whatever his political beliefs, prayerfully extends best wishes for good health and for wisdom and success in coping with the problems that confront our Nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: For my part, I should like, first, to express to you of the Congress, my appreciation of your devotion to the common good and your friendship over these difficult years.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I will carry with me pleasant memories of this association in endeavors profoundly significant to all our people.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We have been through a lengthy period in which the control over the executive and legislative branches of government has been divided between our two great political parties.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Differences, of course, we have had, particularly in domestic affairs.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But in a united determination to keep this Nation strong and free and to utilize our vast resources for the advancement of all mankind, we have carried America to unprecedented heights.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: For this cooperative achievement I thank the American people and those in the Congress of both parties who have supported programs in the interest of our country.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I should also like to give special thanks for the devoted service of my associates in the Executive Branch and the hundreds of thousands of career employees who have implemented our diverse government programs.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: My second purpose is to review briefly the record of these past eight years in the hope that, out of the sum of these experiences, lessons will emerge that are useful to our Nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Supporting this review are detailed reports from the several agencies and departments, all of which are now or will shortly be available to the Congress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Throughout the world the years since 1953 have been a period of profound change.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The human problems in the world grow more acute hour by hour; yet new gains in science and technology continually extend the promise of a better life.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: People yearn to be free, to govern themselves; yet a third of the people of the world have no freedom, do not govern themselves.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The world recognizes the catastrophic nature of nuclear war; yet it sees the wondrous potential of nuclear peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: During the period, the United States has forged ahead under a constructive foreign policy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The continuing goal is peace, liberty, and well-being--for others as well as ourselves.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The aspirations of all peoples are one--peace with justice in freedom.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Peace can only be attained collectively as peoples everywhere unite in their determination that liberty and well-being come to all mankind.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Yet while we have worked to advance national aspirations for freedom, a divisive force has been at work to divert that aspiration into dangerous channels.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Communist movement throughout the world exploits the natural striving of all to be free and attempts to subjugate men rather than free them.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These activities have caused and are continuing to cause grave troubles in the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Here at home these have been times for careful adjustment of our economy from the artificial impetus of a hot war to constructive growth in a precarious peace.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: While building a new economic vitality without inflation, we have also increased public expenditures to keep abreast of the needs of a growing population and its attendant new problems, as well as our added international responsibilities.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We have worked toward these ends in a context of shared responsibility--conscious of the need for maximum scope to private effort and for State and local, as well as Federal, governmental action.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Success in designing and executing national purposes, domestically and abroad, can only come from a steadfast resolution that integrity in the operation of government and in our relations with each other be fully maintained.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Only in this way could our spiritual goals be fully advanced.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: FOREIGN POLICY: On January 20, 1953, when I took office, the United States was at war.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Since the signing of the Korean Armistice in 1953, Americans have lived in peace in highly troubled times.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: During the 1956 Suez crisis, the United States government strongly supported United Nations' action--resulting in the ending of the hostilities in Egypt.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Again in 1958, peace was preserved in the Middle East despite new discord.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our government responded to the request of the friendly Lebanese Government for military help, and promptly withdrew American forces as soon as the situation was stabilized.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In 1958 our support of the Republic of China during the all-out bombardment of Quemoy restrained the Communist Chinese from attempting to invade the off-shore islands.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Although, unhappily, Communist penetration of Cuba is real and poses a serious threat, Communist dominated regimes have been deposed in Guatemala and Iran.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The occupation of Austria has ended and the Trieste question has been settled.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Despite constant threats to its integrity, West Berlin has remained free.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Important advances have been made in building mutual security arrangements--which lie at the heart of our hopes for future peace and security in the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Southeast Asia Treaty Organization has been established;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: the NATO alliance has been militarily strengthened;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: the Organization of American States has been further developed as an instrument of inter-American cooperation;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: the Anzus treaty has strengthened ties with Australia and New Zealand, and a mutual security treaty with Japan has been signed.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In addition, the CENTO pact has been concluded, and while we are not officially a member of this alliance we have participated closely in its deliberations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: proposal to the United Nations led to the creation of the International Atomic Energy Agency.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our policy has been to push for enforceable programs of inspection against surprise attack, suspension of nuclear testing, arms reduction, and peaceful use of outer space.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The United Nations has been vigorously supported in all of its actions, including the condemnations of the wholesale murder of the people of Tibet by the Chinese Communists and the brutal Soviet repression of the people of Hungary, as well as the more recent U.N. actions in the Congo.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The United States took the initiative in negotiating the significant treaty to guarantee the peaceful use of vast Antarctica.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The United States Information Agency has been transformed into a greatly improved medium for explaining our policies and actions to audiences overseas, answering the lies of communist propaganda, and projecting a clearer image of American life and culture.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Cultural, technological and educational exchanges with the Soviet Union have been encouraged, and a comprehensive agreement was made which authorized, among other things, the distribution of our Russian language magazine Amerika and the highly successful American Exhibition in Moscow.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This country has continued to withhold recognition of Communist China and to oppose vigorously the admission of this belligerent and unrepentant nation into the United Nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: With communist imperialism held in check, constructive actions were undertaken to strengthen the economies of free world nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The United States government has given sturdy support to the economic and technical assistance activities of the U.N.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This country stimulated a doubling of the capital of the World Bankcent capital increase in t Fund.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Development Loan Fund and the International Development Association were established.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The United States also took the lead in creating the Inter-American Development Bank.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Vice President Nixon, Secretaries of State Dulles and Herter and I traveled extensively through the world for the purpose of strengthening the cause of peace, freedom, and international understanding.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: So rewarding were these visits that their very success became a significant factor in causing the Soviet Union to wreck the planned Summit Conference of 1960.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These vital programs must go on.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: New tactics will have to be developed, of course, to meet new situations, but the underlying principles should be constant.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our great moral and material commitments to collective security, deterrence of force, international law, negotiations that lead to self-enforcing agreements, and the economic interdependence of free nations should remain the cornerstone of a foreign policy that will ultimately bring permanent peace with justice in freedom to all mankind.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The continuing need of all free nations today is for each to recognize clearly the essentiality of an unbreakable bond among themselves based upon a complete dedication to the principles of collective security, effective cooperation and peace with justice.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: NATIONAL DEFENSE:For the first time in our nation's history we have consistently maintained in peacetime, military forces of a magnitude sufficient to deter and if need be to destroy predatory forces in the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Tremendous advances in strategic weapons systems have been made in the past eight years.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Not until 1953 were expenditures on long-range ballistic missile programs even as much as a million dollars a year; today we spend ten times as much each day on these programs as was spent in all of 1952.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: No guided ballistic missiles were operational at the beginning of 1953.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Today many types give our armed forces unprecedented effectiveness.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The explosive power of our weapons systems for all purposes is almost inconceivable.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Today the United States has operational ATLAS missiles which can strike a target 5000 miles away in a half-hour.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The POLARIS weapons system became operational last fall and the TITAN is scheduled to become so this year.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Next year, more than a year ahead of schedule, a vastly improved ICBM, the solid propellant MINUTEMAN, is expected to be ready.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Squadrons of accurate Intermediate Range Ballistic Missiles are now operational.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The THOR and JUPITER IRBMs based in forward areas can hit targets 1500 miles away in 18 minutes.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Aircraft which fly at speeds faster than sound were still in a developmental stage eight years ago.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Today American fighting planes go twice the speed of sound.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: And either our B-58 Medium Range Jet Bomber or our B-52 Long Range Jet Bomber can carry more explosive power than was used by all combatants in World War II--Allies and Axis combined.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Eight years ago we had no nuclear-powered ships.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Today 49 nuclear warships have been authorized.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Of these, 14 have been commissioned, including three of the revolutionary POLARIS submarines.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our nuclear submarines have cruised under the North Pole and circumnavigated the earth while submerged.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Sea warfare has been revolutionized, and the United States is far and away the leader.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our tactical air units overseas and our aircraft carriers are alert;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Army units, guarding the frontiers of freedom in Europe and the Far East, are in the highest state of readiness in peacetime history;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: our Marines, a third of whom are deployed in the Far East, are constantly prepared for action;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: our Reserve establishment has maintained high standards of proficiency, and the Ready Reserve now numbers over 2 1/2 million citizen-soldiers.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Department of Defense, a young and still evolving organization, has twice been improved and the line of command has been shortened in order to meet the demands of modern warfare.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These major reorganizations have provided a more effective structure for unified planning and direction of the vast defense establishment.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Gradual improvements in its structure and procedures are to be expected.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: United States civil defense and nonmilitary defense capacity has been greatly strengthened and these activities have been consolidated in one Federal agency.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The defense forces of our Allies now number five million men, several thousand combatant ships, and over 25,000 aircraft.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Programs to strengthen these allies have been consistently supported by the Administration.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: U.S. military assistance goes almost exclusively to friendly nations on the rim of the communist world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This American contribution to nations who have the will to defend their freedom, but insufficient means, should be vigorously continued.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Combined with our Allies, the free world now has a far stronger shield than we could provide alone.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Since 1953, our defense policy has been based on the assumption that the international situation would require heavy defense expenditures for an indefinite period to come, probably for years.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In this protracted struggle, good management dictates that we resist overspending as resolutely as we oppose under-spending.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Every dollar uselessly spent on military mechanisms decreases our total strength and, therefore, our security.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: psychology of the past when each new feint by the Communists was responded to in panic.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: shows every sign of being the same.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The nation can ill afford to abandon a national policy which provides for a fully adequate and steady level of effort, designed for the long pull;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: a fast adjustment to new scientific and technological advances;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: a balanced force of such strength as to deter general war, to effectively meet local situations and to retaliate to attack and destroy the attacker;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: and a strengthened system of free world collective security.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: THE ECONOMY:The expanding American economy passed the half-trillion dollar mark in gross national product early in 1960.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Nation's output of goods and services is now nearly 25 percent higher than in 1952.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In 1959, the average American family had an income of $6,520, 15 percent higher in dollars of constant buying power than in 1952, and the real wages of American factory workers have risen 20 percent during the past eight years.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These facts reflect the rising standard of individual and family well-being enjoyed by Americans.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our Nation benefits also from a remarkable improvement in general industrial peace through strengthened processes of free collective bargaining.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Time lost since 1952 because of strikes has been half that lost in the eight years prior to that date.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Legislation now requires that union members have the opportunity for full participation in the affairs of their unions.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Administration supported the Landrum-Griffin Act, which I believe is greatly helpful to the vast bulk of American Labor and its leaders, and also is a major step in getting racketeers and gangsters out of labor-management affairs.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The economic security of working men and women has been strengthened by an extension of unemployment insurance coverage to 2.5 million ex-servicemen, 2.4 million Federal employ ees, and 1.2 million employees of small businesses, and by a strengthening of the Railroad Unemployment Insurance Act.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: States have been encouraged to improve their unemployment compensation benefits, so that today average weekly benefits are 40 percent higher than in 1953.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Determined efforts have improved workers' safety standards.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Enforceable safety standards have been established for longshoremen and ship repair workers;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Federal Safety Councils have been increased from 14 to over 100;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: safety awards have been initiated, and a national construction safety program has been developed.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A major factor in strengthening our competitive enterprise system, and promoting economic growth, has been the vigorous enforcement of antitrust laws over the last eight years and a continuing effort to reduce artificial restraints on competition and trade and enhance our economic liberties.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This purpose was also significantly advanced in 1953 when, as one of the first acts of this Administration, restrictive wage and price controls were ended.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: An additional measure to strengthen the American system of competitive enterprise was the creation of the Small Business Administration in 1953 to assist existing small busines ses and encourage new ones.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This agency has approved over $1 billion in loans, initiated a new program to provide long-term capital for small businesses, aided in setting aside $3 1/2 billion in government contracts for award to small business concerns, and brought to the attention of individual businessmen, through programs of information and education, new developments in management and production techniques.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Since 1952, important tax revisions have been made to encourage small businesses.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Many major improvements in the Nation's transportation system have been made:--After long years of debate, the dream of a great St.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Lawrence Seaway, opening the heartland of America to ocean commerce, has been fulfilled.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The new Federal Aviation Agency is fostering greater safety in air travel.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The largest public construction program in history--the 41,000 mile national system of Interstate and Defense highways--has been pushed rapidly forward.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Twenty-five percent of this system is now open to traffic.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Efforts to help every American build a better life have included also a vigorous program for expanding our trade with other nations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A 4-year renewal of the Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act was passed in 1958, and a continuing and rewarding effort has been made to persuade other countries to remove restrictions against our exports.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A new export expansion program was launched in 1960, inaugurating improvement of export credit insurance and broadening research and information programs to awaken Americans to business opportunities overseas.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These actions and generally prosperous conditions abroad have helped push America's export trade to a level of $20 billion in 1960.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Although intermittent declines in economic activity persist as a problem in our enterprise system, recent downturns have been moderate and of short duration.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There is, however, little room for complacency.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Currently our economy is operating at high levels, but unemployment rates are higher than any of us would like, and chronic pockets of high unemployment persist.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Clearly, continued sound and broadly shared economic growth remains a major national objective toward which we must strive through joint private and public efforts.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If government continues to work to assure every American the fullest opportunity to develop and utilize his ability and talent, it will be performing one of its most vital functions, that of advancing the welfare and protecting the dignity, rights, and freedom of all Americans.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: GOVERNMENT FINANCE AND ADMINISTRATION: In January 1953, the consumer's dollar was worth only 52 cents in terms of the food, clothing, shelter and other items it would buy compared to 1939.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Today, the inflationary spiral which had raised the cost of living by 36 percent between 1946 and 1952 has all but ceased and the value of the dollar virtually stabilized.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In 1954 we had the largest tax cut in history, amounting to $7.4 billion annually, of which over 62 percent went to individuals mostly in the small income brackets.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This Administration has directed constant efforts toward fiscal responsibility.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Balanced budgets have been sought when the economy was advancing, and a rigorous evaluation of spending programs has been maintained at all times.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Resort to deficit financing in prosperous times could easily erode international confidence in the dollar and contribute to inflation at home.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In this belief, I shall submit a balanced budget for fiscal 1962 to the Congress next week.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There has been a firm policy of reducing government competition with private enterprise.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This has resulted in the discontinuance of some 2,000 commercial industrial installations and in addition the curtailment of approximately 550 industrial installations operated

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Also an aggressive surplus disposal program has been carried on to identify and dispose of unneeded government-owned real property.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This has resulted in the addition of a substantial number of valuable properties to local tax rolls, and a significant monetary return to the government.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Earnest and persistent attempts have been made to strengthen the position of State and local governments and thereby to stop the dangerous drift toward centralization of governdirectly by government agencies.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Significant strides have been made in increasing the effectiveness of government.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Important new agencies have been established, such as the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare, the Federal Aviation Agency, and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Council of Economic Advisers was reconstituted.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The operation of our postal system has been modernized to get better and more efficient service.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Modernized handling of local mail now brings next-day delivery to 168 million people in our population centers, expanded carrier service now accommodates 9.3 million families in the growing suburbs, and 1.4 million families have been added to the rural delivery service.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Common sense dictates that the Postal Service should be on a self-financing basis.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The concept of a trained and dedicated government career service has been strengthened by the provision of life and health insurance benefits, a vastly improved retirement system, a new merit promotion program, and the first effective incentive awards program.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: With no sacrifice in efficiency, Federal civilian employment since 1953 has been reduced by over a quarter of a million persons.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I am deeply gratified that it was under the urging of this Administration that Alaska and Hawaii became our 49th and 50th States.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: AGRICULTURE: Despite the difficulties of administering Congressional programs which apply outmoded prescriptions and which aggravate rather than solve problems, the past eight years brought notable advances in agriculture.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Total agricultural assets are approximately $200 billion--up $36 billion in eight years.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Farm owner equities are at the near record high of $174 billion.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Farm ownership is at a record high with fewer farmers in a tenant and sharecropper status than at any time in our nation's history.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: program has demonstrated how surplus of American food and fiber can be effectively used to feed and clothe the needy abroad.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Aided by this humanitarian program, total agricultural exports have grown from $2.8 billion in 1953 to an average of about $4 billion annually for the past three years.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: For 1960, exports are estimated at $4.5 billion, the highest volume on record.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Under the Food-for-Peace program, the largest wheat transaction in history was consummated with India in 1960.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The problems of low-income farm families received systematic attention for the first time in the Rural Development Program.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This program has gone forward in 39 States, yielding higher incomes and a better living for rural people most in need.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Rural Electrification Administration has helped meet the growing demand for power and telephones in agricultural areas.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Ninety-seven percent of all farms now have central station electric power.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Dependence upon Federal financing should no longer be necessary.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Farm Credit Administration has been made an independent agency more responsive to the farmer's needs.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The search for new uses for our farm abundance and to develop new crops for current needs has made major progress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Agricultural research appropriations have increased by 171 percent since 1953.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Farmers are being saved approximately $80 million a year by the repeal in 1956 of Federal taxes on gasoline used in tractors and other machinery.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Since 1953, appropriations have been doubled for county agents, home agents and the Extension Service.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Eligibility for Social Security benefits has been extended to farmers and their families.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Yet in certain aspects our agricultural surplus situation is increasingly grave.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: For example, our wheat stocks now total 1.3 billion bushels.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: If we did not harvest one bushel of wheat in this coming year, we would still have all we could eat, all we could sell abroad, all we could give away, and still have a substantial carryover.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Extraordinary costs are involved just in management and disposal of this burdensome surplus.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Obviously important adjustments must still come.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Congress must enact additional legislation to permit wheat and other farm commodities to move into regular marketing channels in an orderly manner and at the same time afford the needed price protection to the farmer.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Only then will agriculture again be free, sound, and profitable.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: NATURAL RESOURCES: New emphasis has been placed on the care of our national parks.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A ten year development program of our National Park System--Mission 66--was initiated and 633,000 acres of park land have been added since 1953.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Appropriations for fish and wildlife operations have more than doubled.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Thirty-five new refuges, containing 11,342,000 acres, have been added to the national wildlife management system.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our Nation's forests have been improved at the most rapid rate in history.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The largest sustained effort in water resources development in our history has taken place.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the field of reclamation alone, over 50 new projects, or project units, have been authorized since 1953--including the billion dollar Colorado River Storage Project.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: When all these projects have been completed they will have a storage capacity of nearly 43 million acre-feet--an increase of 50 percent over the Bureau of Reclamation's storage capacity in mid-1953.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In addition, since 1953 over 450 new navigation flood control and multiple purpose projects of the Corps of Engineers have been started, costing nearly 6 billion dollars.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Soil and water conservation has been advanced as never before.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: One hundred forty-one projects are now being constructed under the Watershed Protection Program.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Hydroelectric power has been impressively developed through a policy which recognizes that the job to be done requires comprehensive development by Federal, State, and local governments and private enterprise.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Teamwork is essential to achieve this objective.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Federal Columbia River power system has grown from two multipurpose dams with a 2.6 million kilowatt capacity to 17 multipurpose projects completed or under construction with an ultimate installed capacity of 8.1 million kilowatts.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: After years of negotiation, a Columbia River Storage Development agreement with Canada now opens the way for early realization of unparalleled power, flood control and resource conservation benefits for the Pacific Northwest.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A treaty implementing this agreement will shortly be submitted to the Senate.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A farsighted and highly successful program for meeting urgent water needs is being carried out by converting salt water to fresh water.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A 75 percent reduction in the cost of this process has already been realized.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Continuous resource development is essential for our expanding economy.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: We must continue vigorous, combined Federal, State and private programs, at the same time preserving to the maximum extent possible our natural and scenic heritage for future generations.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: EDUCATION, SCIENCE, AND TECHNOLOGY: The National Defense Education Act of 1958 is already a milestone in the history of American education.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It provides broad opportunities for the intellectual development of all children by strengthening courses of study in science, mathematics, and foreign languages, by developing new graduate programs to train additional teachers, and by providing loans for young people who need financial help to go to college.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Administration proposed on numerous occasions a broad new five-year program of Federal aid to help overcome the classroom shortage in public elementary and secondary schools.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Recommendations were also made to give assistance to colleges and universities for the construction of academic and residential buildings to meet future enrollment increases.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This Administration greatly expanded Federal loans for building dormitories for students, teachers, and nurses training, a program assisting in the construction of approximately 200,000 living accommodations during the past 8 years.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: There has been a vigorous acceleration of health, resource and education programs designed to advance the role of the American Indian in our society.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Last fall, for example, 91 percent of the Indian children between the ages of 6 and 18 on reservations were enrolled in school.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This is a rise of 12 percent since 1953.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In the field of science and technology, startling strides have been made by the new National Aeronautics and Space Administration.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: In little more than two years, NASA has successfully launched meteorological satellites, such as Tiros I and Tiros II, that promise to revolutionize methods of weather forecasting;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: demonstrated the feasibility of satellites for global communications by the successful launching of Echo I;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: produced an enormous amount of valuable scientific data, such as the discovery of the Van Allen Radiation Belt;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: successfully launched deep-space probes that maintained communication over the greatest range man has ever tracked;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: and made real progress toward the goal of manned space flights.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These achievements unquestionably make us preeminent today in space exploration for the betterment of mankind.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I believe the present organizational arrangements in this area, with the revisions proposed last year, are completely adequate for the tasks ahead.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Americans can look forward to new achievements in space exploration.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The near future will hold such wonders as the orbital flight of an astronaut, the landing of instruments on the moon, the launching of the powerful giant Saturn rocket vehicles, and the reconnaissance of Mars and Venus by unmanned vehicles.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The application of atomic energy to industry, agriculture, and medicine has progressed from hope and experiment to reality.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: American industry and agriculture are making increasing use of radioisotopes to improve manufacturing, testing, and crop-raising.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Atomic energy has improved the ability of the healing professions to combat disease, and holds promise for an eventual increase in man's life span.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Education, science, technology and balanced programs of every kind-- these are the roadways to progress.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: With appropriate Federal support, the States and localities can assure opportunities for achieving excellence at all levels of the educational system;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: and with the Federal government continuing to give wholehearted support to basic scientific research and technology, we can expect to maintain our position of leadership in the world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: CIVIL RIGHTS: The first consequential Federal Civil Rights legislation in 85 years was enacted by Congress on recommendation of the Administration in 1957 and 1960.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A new Civil Rights Division in the Department of Justice has already moved to enforce constitutional rights in such areas as voting and the elimination of Jim Crow laws.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Greater equality of job opportunity in Federal employment and employment with Federal contractors has been effectively provided through the President's Committees on Government Contracts and Government Employment Practices.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Civil Rights Commission has undertaken important surveys in the fields of housing, voting, and education.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Segregation has been abolished in the Armed Forces, in Veterans' Hospitals, in all Federal employment, and throughout the District of Columbia--administratively accomplished progress in this field that is unmatched in America's recent history.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: This pioneering work in civil rights must go on.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Not only because discrimination is morally wrong, but also because its impact is more than national--it is world-wide.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: HEALTH AND WELFARE: Federal medical research expenditures have increased more than fourfold since 1954.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A vast variety of the approaches known to medical science has been explored to find better methods of treatment and prevention of major diseases, particularly heart diseases, cancer, and mental illness.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The control of air and water pollution has been greatly strengthened.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Americans now have greater protection against harmful, unclean, or misrepresented foods, drugs, or cosmetics through a strengthened Food and Drug Administration and by new legislation which requires that food additives be proved safe for human consumption before use.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A newly established Federal Radiation Council, along with the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare, analyzes and coordinates information regarding radiological activities which affect the public health.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Medical manpower has been increased by Federal grants for teaching and research.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Construction of new medical facilities has been stepped up and extended to include nursing homes, diagnostic and treatment centers, and rehabilitation facilities.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The vocational rehabilitation program has been significantly expanded.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: About 90,000 handicapped people are now being rehabilitated annually so they are again able to earn their own living with self-respect and dignity.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: New legislation provides for better medical care for the needy aged, including those older persons, who, while otherwise self-sufficient, need help in meeting their health care costs.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Administration recommended a major expansion of this effort.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The coverage of the Social Security Act has been broadened since 1953 to make 11 million additional people eligible for retirement, disability or survivor benefits for themselves or their dependents, and the Social Security benefits have been substantially improved.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Grants to the States for maternal and child welfare services have been increased.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The States, aided by Federal grants, now assist some 6 million needy people through the programs of Old Age Assistance, Aid to Dependent Children, Aid to the Blind, and Aid to the Totally and Permanently Disabled.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: HOUSING AND URBAN DEVELOPMENT:More houses have been built during the past eight years--over nine million--than during any previous eight years in history.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: An historic new approach--Urban Renewal--now replaces piecemeal thrusts at slum pockets and urban blight.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Communities engaged in urban renewal have doubled and renewal projects have more than tripled since 1953.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: An estimated 68 projects in 50 cities will be completed by the end of the current fiscal year; another 577 projects will be underway, and planning for 310 more will be in process.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A total of $2 billion in Federal grants will ultimately be required to finance these 955 projects.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: New programs have been initiated to provide more and better housing for elderly people.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Approximately 25,000 units especially designed for the elderly have been built, started, or approved in the past three years.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: For the first time, because of Federal help and encouragement, 90 metropolitan areas and urban regions and 1140 smaller towns throughout the country are making comprehensive development plans for their future growth and development.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: American communities have been helped to plan water and sanitation systems and schools through planning advances for 1600 public works projects with a construction cost of nearly $2 billion.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Mortgage insurance on individual homes has been greatly expanded.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: During the past eight years, the Federal Housing Administration alone insured over 2 1/2 million home mortgages valued at $27 billion, and in addition, insured more than ten million property improvement loans.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Federal government must continue to provide leadership in order to make our cities and communities better places in which to live, work, and raise families, but without usurping rightful local authority, replacing individual responsibility, or stifling private initiative.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: IMMIGRATION: Over 32,000 victims of Communist tyranny in Hungary were brought to our shores, and at this time our country is working to assist refugees from tyranny in Cuba.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Since 1953, the waiting period for naturalization applicants has been reduced from 18 months to 45 days.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The Administration also has made legislative recommendations to liberalize existing restrictions upon immigration while still safeguarding the national interest.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: It is imperative that our immigration policy be in the finest American tradition of providing a haven for oppressed peoples and fully in accord with our obligation as a leader of the free world.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: VETERANS: In discharging the nation's obligation to our veterans, during the past eight years there have been: The readjustment of World War II veterans was completed, and the five million Korean conflict veterans were assisted in achieving successful readjustment to civilian life;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Increases in compensation benefits for all eligible veterans with service connected disabilities;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Higher non-service connected pension benefits for needy veterans;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Greatly improved benefits to survivors of veterans dying in or as a result of service;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Authorization, by Presidential directive, of an increase in the number of beds available for sick and disabled veterans;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Development of a 12-year, $900 million construction program to modernize and improve our veterans hospitals;

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: New modern techniques brought into the administration of Veterans Affairs to provide the highest quality service possible to those who have defended us.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: CONCLUSION: In concluding my final message to the Congress, it is fitting to look back to my first--to the aims and ideals I set forth on February 2, 1953: To use America's influence in world affairs to advance the cause of peace and justice, to conduct the affairs of the Executive Branch with integrity and efficiency, to encourage creative initiative in our economy, and to work toward the attainment of the well-being and equality of opportunity of all citizens.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Equally, we have honored our commitment to pursue and attain specific objectives.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Among them, as stated eight years ago: strengthening of the mutual security program; development of world trade and commerce; ending of hostilities in Korea; creation of a powerful deterrent force; practicing fiscal responsibility; checking the menace of inflation; reducing the tax burden; providing an effective internal security program; developing and conserving our natural resources; reducing governmental interference in the affairs of the farmer; strengthening and improving services by the Department of Labor, and the vigilant guarding of civil and social rights.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I do not close this message implying that all is well--that all problems are solved.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: For progress implies both new and continuing problems and, unlike Presidential administrations, problems rarely have terminal dates.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Abroad, there is the continuing Communist threat to the freedom of Berlin, an explosive situation in Laos, the problems caused by Communist penetration of Cuba, as well as the many problems connected with the development of the new nations in Africa.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: These areas, in particular, call for delicate handling and constant review.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: At home, several conspicuous problems remain: promoting higher levels of employment, with special emphasis on areas in which heavy unemployment has persisted; continuing to provide for steady economic growth and preserving a sound currency; bringing our balance of payments into more reasonable equilibrium and continuing a high level of confidence in our national and international systems; eliminating heavily excessive surpluses of a few farm commodities; and overcoming deficiencies in our health and educational programs.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Our goal always has been to add to the spiritual, moral, and material strength of our nation.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I believe we have done this.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: But it is a process that must never end.

speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Let us pray that leaders of both the near and distant future will be able to keep the nation strong and at peace, that they will advance the well-being of all our people, that they will lead us on to still higher moral standards, and that, in achieving these goals, they will maintain a reasonable balance between private and governmental responsibility.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It is a pleasure to return from whence I came.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: You are among my oldest friends in Washington--and this House is my oldest home.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It was here, more than 14 years ago, that I first took the oath of Federal office.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It was here, for 14 years, that I gained both knowledge and inspiration from members of both parties in both Houses-- from your wise and generous leaders--and from the pronouncements which I can vividly recall, sitting where you now sit--including the pro

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: To speak from this same historic rostrum is a sobering experience.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: To be back among so many friends is a happy one.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I am confident that that friendship will continue.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our Constitution wisely assigns both joint and separate roles to each branch of the government;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And a President and a Congress who hold each other in mutual respect will neither permit nor attempt any trespass.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For my part, I shall withhold from neither the Congress nor the people any fact or report, past,present, or future, which is necessary for an informed judgment of our conduct and hazards.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Shall neither shift the burden of executive decisions to the Congress, nor avoid responsibility for the outcome of those decisions.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I speak today in an hour of national peril and national opportunity.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Before my term has ended, we shall have to test anew whether a nation organized and governed such as ours can endure.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The outcome is by no means certain.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The answers are by no means clear.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: All of us together--this Administration, this Congress, this nation-must forge those answers.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But today, were I to offer--after little more than a week in office --detailed legislation to remedy every national ill, the Congress would rightly wonder whether the desire for speed had replaced the duty of responsibility.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: My remarks, therefore, will be limited.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But they will also be candid.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: To state the facts frankly is not to despair the future nor indict the past.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The prudent heir takes careful inventory of his legacies, and gives a faithful accounting to thosewhom he owes an obligation of trust.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And, while the occasion does not call for another recital of our blessings and assets, we do have no greater asset than the willingness of a free and determined people, through its elected officials, to face all problems frankly and meet all dangers free from panic or fear.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The present state of our economy is disturbing.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We take office in the wake of seven months of recession, three and one-half years of slack, seven years of diminished economic growth, and nine years of falling farm income.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Business bankruptcies have reached their highest level since the Great Depression.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Since 1951 farm income has been squeezed down by 25 percent.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Save for a brief period in 1958, insured unemployment is at the highest peak in our history.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Of some five and one-half million Americans who are without jobs, more than one million have been searching for work for more than four months.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And during each month some 150,000 workers are exhausting their already meager jobless benefit rights.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Nearly one-eighth of those who are without jobs live almost without hope in nearly one hundred especially depressed and troubled areas.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The rest include new school graduates unable to use their talents, farmers forced to give up their part time jobs which helped balance their family budgets, skilled and unskilled workers laid off in such important industries as metals, machinery, automobiles and apparel.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our recovery from the 1958 recession, moreover, was anemic and incomplete.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our Gross National Product never regained its full potential.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Unemployment never returned to normal levels.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Maximum use of our national industrial capacity was never restored.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In short, the American economy is in trouble.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The most resourceful industrialized country on earth ranks among the last in the rate of economic growth.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Since last spring our economic growth rate has actually receded.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Business investment is in a decline.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Profits have fallen below predicted levels.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Construction is off.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: A million unsold automobiles are in inventory.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Fewer people are working--and the average work week has shrunk well below 40 hours.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Yet prices have continued to rise--so that now too many Americans have less to spend for items that cost more to buy.

speaker: John F. Kennedy

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We cannot afford to waste idle hours and empty plants while awaiting the end of the recession.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We must show the world what a free economy can do--to reduce unemployment, to put unused capacity to work, to spur new productivity, and to foster higher economic growth within a range of sound fiscal policies and relative price stability.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I will propose to the Congress within the next 14 days measures to improve unemployment compensation through temporary increases in duration on a self supporting basis--to provide more food for the families of the unemployed, and to aid their needy children.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This is not a partisan program concentrating on our weaknesses--it is, I hope, a national program to realize our national strength.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Efficient expansion at home, stimulating the new plant and technology that can make our goods more competitive, is also the key to the international balance of payments problem.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Laying aside all alarmist talk and panicky solutions, let us put that knotty problem in its proper perspective.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It is true that, since 1958, the gap between the dollars we spend or invest abroad and the dollars returned to us has substantially widened.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This overall deficit in our balance of payments increased by nearly $11 billion in the 3 years--and holders of dollars abroad converted them to gold in such a quantity as to cause a total outflow of nearly $5 billion of gold from our reserve.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The 1959 deficit was caused in large part by the failure of our exports to penetrate foreign markets--the result both of restrictions on our goods and our own uncompetitive prices.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The 1960 deficit, on the other hand, was more the result of an increase in private capital outflow seeking new opportunity, higher return or speculative advantage abroad.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Meanwhile this country has continued to bear more than its share of the West's military and foreign aid obligations.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Under existing policies, another deficit of $2 billion is predicted for 1961--and individuals in those countries whose dollar position once depended on these deficits for improvement now wonder aloud whether our gold reserves will remain sufficient to meet our own obligations.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: All this is cause for concern--but it is not cause for panic.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For our monetary and financial position remains exceedingly strong.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Including our drawing rights in the International Monetary Fund and the gold reserve held as backing for our currency and Federal Reserve deposits, we have some $22 billion in total gold stocks and other international monetary reserves available--and I now pledge that their full strength stands behind the value of the dollar for use if needed.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Moreover, we hold large assets abroad--the total owed this nation far exceed the claims upon our reserves--and our exports once again substantially exceed our imports.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In short, we need not--and we shall not--take any action to increase the dollar price of gold from $35 an ounce--to impose exchange controls--to reduce our anti recession efforts--to fall back on restrictive trade policies--or to weaken our commitments around the world.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This Administration will not distort the value of the dollar in any fashion.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And this is a commitment.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Prudence and good sense do require, however, that new steps betaken to ease the payments deficit and prevent any gold crisis.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our success in world affairs has long depended in part upon foreign confidence in our ability to pay.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: A series of executive orders, legislative remedies and cooperative efforts with our allies will get underway immediately--aimed at attracting foreign investment and travel to this country--promoting American exports, at stable prices and with more liberal government guarantees and financing -- curbing tax and customs loopholes that encourage undue spending of private dollars abroad -- and (through OECD, NATO and otherwise) sharing with our allies all efforts to provide for the common defense of the free world and the hopes for growth of the less developed lands.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: While the current deficit lasts, ways will be found to ease our dollar outlays abroad without placing the full burden on the families of men whom we have asked to serve our Flag overseas.
