speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But more than our exchange of international payments is out of balance.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The current Federal budget for fiscal 1961 is almost certain to show a net deficit.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The budget already submitted for fiscal 1962 will remain in balance only if the Congress enacts all the revenue measures requested--and only if an earlier and sharper up-turn in the economy than my economic advisers now think likely produces the tax revenues estimated.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Nevertheless, a new Administration must of necessity build on the spending and revenue estimates already submitted.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Within that framework, barring the development of urgent national defense needs or a worsening of the economy, it is my current intention to advocate a program of expenditures which, including revenues from a stimulation of the economy, will not of and by themselves unbalance the earlier Budget.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: However, we will do what must be done.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For our national household is cluttered with unfinished and neglected tasks.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our cities are being engulfed in squalor.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: we still have 25 million Americans living in substandard homes.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: A new housing program under a new Housing and Urban Affairs Department will be needed this year.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our classrooms contain 2 million more children than they can properly have room for, taught by 90,000 teachers not properly qualified to teach.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: One third of our most promising high school graduates are financially unable to continue the development of their talents.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The war babies of the 1940's, who overcrowded our schools in the 1950's, are now descending in 1960 upon our colleges--with two college students for every one, ten years from now--and our colleges are ill prepared.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We lack the scientists, the engineers and the teachers our world obligations require.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We have neglected oceanography, saline water conversion, and the basic research that lies at the root of all progress.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Federal grants for both higher and public school education can no longer be delayed.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Medical research has achieved new wonders--but these wonders are too often beyond the reach of too many people, owing to a lack of income (particularly among the aged), a lack of hospital beds, a lack of nursing homes and a lack of doctors and dentists.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Measures to provide health care for the aged under Social Security, and to increase the supply of both facilities and personnel, must be undertaken this year.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our supply of clean water is dwindling.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Organized and juvenile crimes cost the taxpayers millions of dollars each year, making it essential that we have improved enforcement and new legislative safeguards.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The denial of constitutional rights to some of our fellow Americans on account of race--at the ballot box and elsewhere -disturbs the national conscience, and subjects us to the charge of world opinion that our democracy is not equal to the high promise of our heritage.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Morality in private business has not been sufficiently spurred by morality in public business.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: A host of problems and projects in all 50 States, though not possible to include in this Message, deserves--and will receive--the attention of both the Congress and the Executive Branch.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: On most of these matters, Messages will be sent to the Congress within the next two weeks.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But all these problems pale when placed beside those which confront us around the world.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: No man entering upon this office, regardless of his party, regardless of his previous service in Washington, could fail to be staggered upon learning--even in this brief 10 day period-- the harsh enormity of the trials through which we must pass in the next four years.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Each day the crises multiply.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Each day their solution grows more difficult.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Each day we draw nearer the hour of maximum danger, as weapons spread and hostile forces grow stronger.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I feel I must inform the Congress that our analyses over the last ten days make it clear that--in each of the principal areas of crisis--the tide of events has been running out and time has not been our friend.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In Asia, the relentless pressures of the Chinese Communists menace the security of the entire area--from the borders of India and South Viet Nam to the jungles of Laos, struggling to protect its newly-won independence.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We seek in Laos what we seek in all Asia, and, indeed, in the entire world--freedom for the people and independence for the government.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And this Nation shall persevere in our pursuit of these objectives.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In Africa, the Congo has been brutally torn by civil strife, political unrest and public disorder.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We shall continue to support the heroic efforts of the United Nations to restore peace and order--efforts which are now endangered by mounting tensions, unsolved problems, and decreasing support from many member states.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In Latin America, Communist agents seeking to exploit that region

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our objection with Cuba is not over the people's drive for a better life.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our objection is to their domination by foreign and domestic tyrannies.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Cuban social and economic reform should be encouraged.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Questions of economic and trade policy can always be negotiated.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But Communist domination in this Hemisphere can never be negotiated.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We are pledged to work with our sister republics to free the Americas of all such foreign domination and all tyranny, working toward the goal of a free hemisphere of free governments, extending from Cape Horn to the Arctic Circle.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In Europe our alliances are unfulfilled and in some disarray.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The unity of NATO has been weakened by economic rivalry and partially eroded by national interest.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It has not yet fully mobilized its resources nor fully achieved a common outlook.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Yet no Atlantic power can meet on its own the mutual problems now facing us in defense, foreign aid, monetary reserves, and a host of other areas;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And our close ties with those whose hopes and interests we share are among this Nation's most powerful assets.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our greatest challenge is still the world that lies beyond the Cold War--but the first great obstacle is still our relations with the Soviet Union and Communist China.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We must never be lulled into believing that either power has yielded its ambitions for world domination-- ambitions which they forcefully restated only a short time ago.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: On the contrary, our task is to convince them that aggression and subversion will not be profitable routes to pursue these ends.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Open and peaceful competition- for prestige, for markets, for scientific achievement, even for men's minds--is something else again.

speaker: John F. Kennedy

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: To meet this array of challenges--to fulfill the role we cannot avoid on the world scene--we must reexamine and revise our whole arsenal of tools: military, economic and political.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: One must not overshadow the other.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: On the Presidential Coat of Arms, the American eagle holds in his right talon the olive branch, while in his left he holds a bundle of arrows.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We intend to give equal attention to both.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: First, we must strengthen our military tools.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We are moving into a period of uncertain risk and great commitment in which both the military and diplomatic possibilities require a Free World force so powerful as to make any aggression clearly futile.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Yet in the past, lack of a consistent, coherent military strategy, and the absence of basic assumptions about our national requirements and the faulty estimates and duplication arising from inter-service rivalries have all made it difficult to assess accurately how adequate -- or inadequate -- our defenses really are.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I have, therefore, instructed the Secretary of Defense to reappraise our entire defense strategy--our ability to fulfill our commitments-- the effectiveness, vulnerability, and dispersal of our strategic bases, forces and warning systems--the efficiency and economy of our operation and organization -- the elimination of obsolete bases and installations -- and the adequacy, modernization and mobility of our present conventional and nuclear forces and weapons systems in light of present and future dangers.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I have asked for preliminary conclusions by the end of February--and I then shall recommend whatever legislative, budgetary or executive action is needed in the light of these conclusions.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In the meantime, I have asked the Defense Secretary to initiate immediately three new steps most clearly needed now: First, I have directed prompt attention to increase our air-lift capacity.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Obtaining additional air transport mobility--and obtaining it now-- will better assure the ability of our conventional forces to respond, with discrimination and speed, to any problem at any spot on the globe at any moment's notice.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In particular it will enable us to meet any deliberate effort to avoid or divert our forces by starting limited wars in widely scattered parts of the globe.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: (b) I have directed prompt action to step up our Polaris submarine program.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Using unobligated ship-building funds now (to let contracts originally scheduled for the next fiscal year) will build and place on station--at least nine months earlier than planned--substantially more units of a crucial deterrent--a fleet that will never attack first, but possess sufficient powers of retaliation, concealed beneath the seas, to discourage any aggressor from launching an attack upon our security.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: (c) I have directed prompt action to accelerate our entire missile program.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Until the Secretary of Defense's reappraisal is completed, the emphasis here will be largely on improved organization and decision-making--on cutting down the wasteful duplications and the time-lag that have handicapped our whole family of missiles.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: If we are to keep the peace, we need an invulnerable missile force powerful enough to deter any aggressor from even threatening an attack that he would know could not destroy enough of our force to prevent his own destruction.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Secondly, we must improve our economic tools.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our role is essential and unavoidable in the construction of a sound and expanding economy for the entire non-communist world, helping other nations build the strength to meet their own problems, to satisfy their own aspirations--to surmount their own dangers.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The problems in achieving this goal are towering and unprecedented--the response must be towering and unprecedented as well, much as Lend-Lease and the Marshall Plan were in earlier years, which brought such fruitful results.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: (a) I intend to ask the Congress for authority to establish a new and more effective program for assisting the economic, educational and social development of other countries and continents.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: That program must stimulate and take more effectively into account the contributions of our allies, and provide central policy direction for all our own programs that now so often overlap, conflict or diffuse our energies and resources.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Such a program, compared to past programs, will require--more flexibility for short run emergencies-more commitment to long term development--new attention to education at all levels--greater emphasis on the recipient nation's role, their effort, their purpose, with greater social justice for their people, broader distribution and participation by their people and more efficient public administration and more efficient tax systems of their own -- and orderly planning for national and regional development instead of a piecemeal approach.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I hope the Senate will take early action approving the Convention establishing the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This will be an important instrument in sharing with our allies this development effort--working toward the time when each nation will contribute in proportion to its ability to pay.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For, while we are prepared to assume our full share of these huge burdens, we cannot and must not be expected to bear them alone.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: To our sister republics to the south, we have pledged a new alliance for progress- alianza para progreso.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our goal is a free and prosperous Latin America, realizing for all its states and all its citizens a degree of economic and social progress that matches their historic contributions of culture, intellect and liberty.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: To start this nation's role at this time in that alliance of neighbors, I am recommending the following: That the Congress appropriate in full the $500 million fund pledged by the Act of Bogot

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: That a new Inter-Departmental Task Force be established under the leadership of the Department of State, to coordinate at the highest level all policies and programs of concern to the Americas.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: That our delegates to the OAS, working with those of other members, strengthen that body as an instrument to preserve the peace and to prevent foreign domination anywhere in the Hemisphere.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: That, in cooperation with other nations, we launch a new hemispheric attack on illiteracy and inadequate educational opportunities to all levels;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: and, finally,--That a Food-for-Peace mission be sent immediately to Latin America to explore ways in which our vast food abundance can be used to help end hunger and malnutrition in certain areas of suffering in our own hemisphere.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This Administration is expanding its Food-for-Peace Program in every possible way.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The product of our abundance must be used more effectively to relieve hunger and help economic growth in all corners of the globe.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And I have asked the Director of this Program to recommend additional ways in which these surpluses can advance the interests of world peace--including the establishment of world food reserves.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: An even more valuable national asset is our reservoir of dedicated men and women--not only on our college campuses but in every age group--who have indicated their desire to contribute their skills, their efforts, and a part of their lives to the fight for world order.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We can mobilize this talent through the formation of a National Peace Corps, enlisting the services of all those with the desire and capacity to help foreign lands meet their urgent needs for trained personnel.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Finally, while our attention is centered on the development of the noncommunist world, we must never forget our hopes for the ultimate freedom and welfare of the Eastern European peoples.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In order to be prepared to help re establish historic ties of friendship, I am asking the Congress for increased discretion to use economic tools in this area whenever this is found to be clearly in the national interest.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This will require amendment of the Mutual Defense Assistance Control Act along the lines I proposed as a member of the Senate, and upon which the Senate voted last summer.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Meanwhile, I hope to explore with the Polish government the possibility of using our frozen Polish funds on projects of peace that will demonstrate our abiding friendship for and interest in the people of Poland.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Third, we must sharpen our political and diplomatic tools--the means of cooperation and agreement on which an enforceable world order must ultimately rest.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I have already taken steps to coordinate and expand our disarmament effort--to increase our programs of research and study--and to make arms control a central goal of our national policy under my direction.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The deadly arms race, and the huge resources it absorbs, have too long overshadowed all else we must do.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We must prevent that arms race from spreading to new nations, to new nuclear powers and to the reaches of outer space.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We must make certain that our negotiators are better informed and better prepared-- to formulate workable proposals of our own and to make sound judgments about the proposals of others.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I have asked the other governments concerned to agree to a reasonable delay in the talks on a nuclear test ban--and it is our intention to resume negotiations prepared to reach a final agreement with any nation that is equally willing to agree to an effective and enforceable treaty.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We must increase our support of the United Nations as an instrument to end the Cold War instead of an arena in which to fight it.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In recognition of its increasing importance and the doubling of its membership--we are enlarging and strengthening our own mission to the U.N.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We shall help insure that it is properly financed.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We shall work to see that the integrity of the office of the Secretary-General is maintained.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And I would address a special plea to the smaller nations of the world--to join with us in strengthening this organization, which is far more essential to their security than it is to ours--the only body in the world where no nation need be powerful to be

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It deserves the support of all.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Finally, this Administration intends to explore promptly all possible areas of cooperation with the Soviet Union and other nations

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Specifically, I now invite all nations--including the Soviet Union--to join with us in developing a weather prediction program, in a new communications satellite program and in preparation for probing the distant planets of Mars and Venus, probes which may someday unlock the deepest secrets of the universe.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Today this country is ahead in the science and technology of space, while the Soviet Union is ahead in the capacity to lift large vehicles into orbit.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Both nations would help themselves as well as other nations by removing these endeavors from the bitter and wasteful competition of the Cold War.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The United States would be willing to join with the Soviet Union and the scientists of all nations in a greater effort to make the fruits of this new knowledge available to all--and, beyond that, in an effort to extend farm technology to hungry nations--to wipe out disease -- to increase the exchanges of scientists and their knowledge -- and to make our own laboratories available to technicians of other lands who lack the facilities to pursue their own work.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Where nature makes natural allies of us all, we can demonstrate that beneficial relations are possible even with those with whom we most deeply disagree--and this must someday be the basis of world peace and world law.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I have commented on the state of the domestic economy, our balance of payments, our Federal and social budget and the state of the world.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I would like to conclude with a few remarks about the state of the Executive branch.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We have found it full of honest and useful public servants--but their capacity to act decisively at the exact time action is needed has too often been muffled in the morass of committees, timidities and fictitious theories which have created a growing gap between decision and execution, between planning and reality.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In a time of rapidly deteriorating situations at home and abroad, this is bad for the public service and particularly bad for the country;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And we mean to make a change.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I have pledged myself and my colleagues in the cabinet to a continuous encouragement of initiative, responsibility and energy in serving the public interest.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Let every public servant know, whether his post is high or low, that a man's rank and reputation in this Administration will be determined by the size of the job he does, and not by the size of his staff, his office or his budget.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Let it be clear that this Administration recognizes the value of dissent and daring-- that we greet healthy controversy as the hallmark of healthy change.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Let the public service be a proud and lively career.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For only with complete dedication by us all to the national interest can we bring our country through the troubled years that lie ahead.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our problems are critical.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The tide is unfavorable.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The news will be worse before it is better.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And while hoping and working for the best, we should prepare ourselves now for the worst.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We cannot escape our dangers--neither must we let them drive us into panic or narrow isolation.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In many areas of the world where the balance of power already rests with our adversaries, the forces of freedom are sharply divided.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It is one of the ironies of our time that the techniques of a harsh and repressive system should be able to instill discipline and ardor in its servants--while the blessings of liberty have too often stood for privilege, materialism and a life of ease.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But I have a different view of liberty.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Life in 1961 will not be easy.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Wishing it, predicting it, even asking for it, will not make it so.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: There will be further setbacks before the tide is turned.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But turn it we must.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The hopes of all mankind rest upon us--not simply upon those of us in this chamber, but upon the peasant in Laos, the fisherman in Nigeria, the exile from Cuba, the spirit that moves every man and Nation who shares our hopes for freedom and the future.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And in the final analysis, they rest most of all upon the pride and perseverance of our fellow citizens of the great Republic.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This week we begin anew our joint and separate efforts to build the American future.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But, sadly, we build without a man who linked a long past with the present and looked strongly to the future.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Mister Sam Rayburn is gone.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Neither this House nor the Nation is the same without him.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Members of the Congress, the Constitution makes us not rivals for power but partners for progress.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We are all trustees for the American people, custodians of the American heritage.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It is my task to report the State of the Union--to improve it is the task of us all.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In the past year, I have traveled not only across our own land but to other lands--to the North and the South, and across the seas.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And I have found--as I am sure you have, in your travels--that people everywhere, in spite of occasional disappointments, look to us--not to our wealth or power, but to the splendor of our ideals.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For our Nation is commissioned by history to be either an observer of freedom's failure or the cause of its success.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our overriding obligation in the months ahead is to fulfill the world's hopes by fulfilling our own faith.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Strengthening the economy:That task must begin at home.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For if we cannot fulfill our own ideals here, we cannot expect others to accept them.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And when the youngest child alive today has grown to the cares of manhood, our position in the world will be determined first of all by what provisions we make today--for his education, his health, and his opportunities for a good home and a good job and a good life.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: At home, we began the year in the valley of recession--we completed it on the high road of recovery and growth.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: With the help of new congressionally approved or administratively increased stimulants to our economy, the number of major surplus labor areas has declined from 101 to 60;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: nonagricultural employment has increased by more than a million jobs;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: and the average factory work-week has risen to well over 40 hours.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: was racing to new records in consumer spending, labor income, and industrial production.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We are gratified--but we are not satisfied.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Too many unemployed are still looking for the blessings of prosperity.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: As those who leave our schools and farms demand new jobs, automation takes old jobs away.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: To expand our growth and job opportunities, I urge on the Congress three measures: First, the Manpower Training and Development Act, to stop the waste of able-bodied men and women who want to work, but whose only skill has been replaced by a machine, or moved with a mill, or shut down with a mine;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Second, the Youth Employment Opportunities Act, to help train and place not only the one million young Americans who are both out of school and out of work, but the twenty-six million young Americans entering the labor market in this decade

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: and Third, the 8 percent tax credit for investment in machinery and equipment, which, combined with planned revisions of depreciation allowances, will spur our modernization, our growth, and our ability to compete abroad.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Moreover--pleasant as it may be to bask in the warmth of recovery--let us not forget that we have suffered three recessions in the last 7 years.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The time to repair the roof is when the sun is shining--by filling three basic gaps in our anti-recession protection.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We need: First, Presidential standby authority, subject to congressional veto, to adjust personal income tax rates downward within a specified range and time, to slow down an economic decline before it has dragged us all down;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Second, Presidential standby authority, upon a given rise in the rate of unemployment, to accelerate Federal and federally-aided capital improvement programs;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: and Third, a permanent strengthening of our unemployment compensation system--to maintain for our fellow citizens searching for a job who cannot find it, their purchasing power and their living standards without constant resort--as we have seen in recent years by the Congress and the administrations--to temporary supplements.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: If we enact this six-part program, we can show the whole world that a free economy need not be an unstable economy--that a free system need not leave men unemployed--and that a free society is not only the most productive but the most stable form of organization yet fashioned by man.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Fighting Inflation: But recession is only one enemy of a free economy--inflation is another.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Last year, 1961, despite rising production and demand, consumer prices held almost steady--and wholesale prices declined.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This is the best record of overall price stability of any comparable period of recovery since the end of World War II.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Inflation too often follows in the shadow of growth--while price stability is made easy by stagnation or controls.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But we mean to maintain both stability and growth in a climate of freedom.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our first line of defense against inflation is the good sense and public spirit of business and labor--keeping their total increases in wages and profits in step with productivity.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: There is no single statistical test to guide each company and each union.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But I strongly urge them--for their country's interest, and for their own--to apply the test of the public interest to these transactions.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Within this same framework of growth and wage-price stability:  This administration has helped keep our economy competitive by widening the access of small business to credit and Government contracts, and by stepping up the drive against monopoly, price-fixing, and racketeering; .

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We will submit a Federal Pay Reform bill aimed at giving our classified, postal, and other employees new pay scales more comparable to those of private industry;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We are holding the fiscal 1962 budget deficit far below the level incurred after the last recession in 1958;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: and, finally, I am submitting for fiscal 1963 a balanced Federal Budget

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This is a joint responsibility, requiring Congressional cooperation on appropriations, and on three sources of income in particular: First, an increase in postal rates, to end the postal deficit;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Secondly, passage of the tax reforms previously urged, to remove unwarranted tax preferences, and to apply to dividends and to interest the same withholding requirements we have long applied to wages;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Third, extension of the present excise and corporation tax rates, except for those changes--which will be recommended in a message--affecting transportation.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Getting America Stronger: But a stronger nation and economy require more than a balanced Budget.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: They require progress in those programs that spur our growth and fortify our strength.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Cities: A strong America depends on its cities--America's glory, and sometimes America's shame.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: To substitute sunlight for congestion and progress for decay, we have stepped up existing urban renewal and housing programs, and launched new ones--redoubled the attack on water pollution--speeded aid to airports, hospitals, highways, and our declining mass transit systems--and secured new weapons to combat organized crime, racketeering, and youth delinquency, assisted by the coordinated and hard-hitting efforts of our investigative services: the FBI, the Internal Revenue, the Bureau of Narcotics, and many others.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We shall need further anti-crime, mass transit, and transportation legislation--and new tools to fight air pollution.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And with all this effort under way, both equity and commonsense require that our nation's urban areas--containing three-fourths of our population--sit as equals at the Cabinet table.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I urge a new Department of Urban Affairs and Housing.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Agriculture and Resourses: A strong America also depends on its farms and natural resources.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: American farmers took heart in 1961--from a billion dollar rise in farm income--and from a hopeful start on reducing the farm surpluses.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But we are still operating under a patchwork accumulation of old laws, which cost us $1 billion a year in CCC carrying charges alone, yet fail to halt rural poverty or boost farm earnings.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our task is to master and turn to fully fruitful ends the magnificent productivity of our farms and farmers.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The revolution on our own countryside stands in the sharpest contrast to the repeated farm failures of the Communist nations and is a source of pride to us all.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Since 1950 our agricultural output per man-hour has actually doubled!

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Without new, realistic measures, it will someday swamp our farmers and our taxpayers in a national scandal or a farm depression.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I will, therefore, submit to the Congress a new comprehensive farm program--tailored to fit the use of our land and the supplies of each crop to the long-range needs of the sixties--and designed to prevent chaos in the sixties with a program of commonsense.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We also need for the sixties--if we are to bequeath our full national estate to our heirs--a new long-range conservation and recreation program--expansion of our superb national parks and forests--preservation of our authentic wilderness areas--new starts on water and power projects as our population steadily increases--and expanded REA generation and transmission loans.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Civil Rights: But America stands for progress in human rights as well as economic affairs, and a strong America requires the assurance of full and equal rights to all its citizens, of any race or of any color.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This administration has shown as never before how much could be done through the full use of Executive powers--through the enforcement of laws already passed by the Congress--through persuasion, negotiation, and litigation, to secure the constitutional rights of all: the right to vote, the right to travel without hindrance across State lines, and the right to free public education.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I issued last March a comprehensive order to guarantee the right to equal employment opportunity in all Federal agencies and contractors.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: which, in all sections of the country, are achieving a quiet but striking success in opening up to all races new professional, supervisory, and other job opportunities.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But there is much more to be done--by the Executive, by the courts, and by the Congress.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Among the bills now pending before you, on which the executive departments will comment in detail, are appropriate methods of strengthening these basic rights which have our full support.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The right to vote, for example, should no longer be denied through such arbitrary devices on a local level, sometimes abused, such as literacy tests and poll taxes.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: righteousness does exalt a nation._

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Health and Welfare: Finally, a strong America cannot neglect the aspirations of its citizens--the welfare of the needy, the health care of the elderly, the education of the young.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For we are not developing the Nation's wealth for its own sake.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Wealth is the means--and people are the ends.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: All our material riches will avail us little if we do not use them to expand the opportunities of our people.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Last year, we improved the diet of needy people--provided more hot lunches and fresh milk to school children--built more college dormitories--and, for the elderly, expanded private housing, nursing homes, health services, and social security.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But we have just begun.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: To help those least fortunate of all, I am recommending a new public welfare program, stressing services instead of support, rehabilitation instead of relief, and training for useful work instead of prolonged dependency.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: To relieve the critical shortage of doctors and dentists--and this is a matter which should concern us all--and expand research, I urge action to aid medical and dental colleges and scholarships and to establish new National Institutes of Health.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: To take advantage of modern vaccination achievements, I am proposing a mass immunization program, aimed at the virtual elimination of such ancient enemies of our children as polio, diphtheria, whooping cough, and tetanus.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: To protect our consumers from the careless and the unscrupulous, I shall recommend improvements in the Food and Drug laws--strengthening inspection and standards, halting unsafe and worthless products, preventing misleading labels, and cracking down on the illicit sale of habit-forming drugs.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But in matters of health, no piece of unfinished business is more important or more urgent than the enactment under the social security system of health insurance for the aged.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For our older citizens have longer and more frequent illnesses, higher hospital and medical bills and too little income to pay them.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Private health insurance helps very few--for its cost is high and its coverage limited.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Public welfare cannot help those too proud to seek relief but hard-pressed to pay their own bills.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Nor can their children or grandchildren always sacrifice their own health budgets to meet this constant drain.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Social security has long helped to meet the hardships of retirement, death, and disability.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I now urge that its coverage be extended without further delay to provide health insurance for the elderly.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Education: Equally important to our strength is the quality of our education.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Eight million adult Americans are classified as functionally illiterate.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This is a disturbing figure--reflected in Selective Service rejection rates--reflected in welfare rolls and crime rates.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And I shall recommend plans for a massive attack to end this adult illiteracy.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I shall also recommend bills to improve educational quality, to stimulate the arts, and, at the college level, to provide Federal loans for the construction of academic facilities and federally financed scholarships.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: If this Nation is to grow in wisdom and strength, then every able high school graduate should have the opportunity to develop his talents.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Yet nearly half lack either the funds or the facilities to attend college.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Enrollments are going to double in our colleges in the short space of 10 years.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The annual cost per student is skyrocketing to astronomical levels--now averaging $1,650 a year, although almost half of our families earn less than $5,000.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: They cannot afford such costs--but this Nation cannot afford to maintain its military power and neglect its brainpower.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But excellence in education must begin at the elementary level.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I sent to the Congress last year a proposal for Federal aid to public school construction and teachers' salaries.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I believe that bill, which passed the Senate and received House Committee approval, offered the minimum amount required by our needs and--in terms of across-the-board aid--the maximum scope permitted by our Constitution.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I therefore see no reason to weaken or withdraw that bill: and I urge its passage at this session.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: is a race between education and catastrophe.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It is up to you in this Congress to determine the winner of that race.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: These are not unrelated measures addressed to specific gaps or grievances in our national life.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: They are the pattern of our intentions and the foundation of our hopes.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: because it releases the energy of every human being.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The dynamic of democracy is the power and the purpose of the individual, and the policy of this administration is to give to the individual the opportunity to realize his own highest possibilities.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our program is to open to all the opportunity for steady and productive employment, to remove from all the handicap of arbitrary or irrational exclusion, to offer to all the facilities for education and health and welfare, to make society the servant of the individual and the individual the source of progress, and thus to realize for all the full promise of American life.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our goals abroad: All of these efforts at home give meaning to our efforts abroad.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Since the close of the Second World War, a global civil war has divided and tormented mankind.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But it is not our military might, or our higher standard of living, that has most distinguished us from our adversaries.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It is our belief that the state is the servant of the citizen and not his master.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This basic clash of ideas and wills is but one of the forces reshaping our globe--swept as it is by the tides of hope and fear, by crises in the headlines today that become mere footnotes tomorrow.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Both the successes and the setbacks of the past year remain on our agenda of unfinished business.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For every apparent blessing contains the seeds of danger--every area of trouble gives out a ray of hope--and the one unchangeable certainty is that nothing is certain or unchangeable.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Yet our basic goal remains the same: a peaceful world community of free and independent states--free to choose their own future and their own system, so long as it does not threaten the freedom of others.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Some may choose forms and ways that we would not choose for ourselves--but it is not for us that they are choosing.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We can welcome diversity--the Communists cannot.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For we offer a world of choice--they offer the world of coercion.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And the way of the past shows clearly that freedom, not coercion, is the wave of the future.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: At times our goal has been obscured by crisis or endangered by conflict--but it draws sustenance from five basic sources of strength:  the moral and physical strength of the United States;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: the united strength of the Atlantic Community;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: the regional strength of our Hemispheric relations;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: the creative strength of our efforts in the new and developing nations; the peace-keeping strength of the United Nations.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our military strength: Our moral and physical strength begins at home as already discussed.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But it includes our military strength as well.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: So long as fanaticism and fear brood over the affairs of men, we must arm to deter others from aggression.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In the past 12 months our military posture has steadily improved.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We increased the previous defense budget by 15 percent--not in the expectation of war but for the preservation of peace.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We more than doubled our acquisition rate of Polaris submarines--we doubled the production capacity for Minuteman missiles--and increased by 50 percent the number of manned bombers standing ready on a 15 minute alert.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This year the combined force levels planned under our new Defense budget--including nearly three hundred additional Polaris and Minuteman missiles--have been precisely calculated to insure the continuing strength of our nuclear deterrent.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But our strength may be tested at many levels.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We intend to have at all times the capacity to resist non-nuclear or limited attacks--as a complement to our nuclear capacity, not as a substitute.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We have rejected any all-or-nothing posture which would leave no choice but inglorious retreat or unlimited retaliation.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Thus we have doubled the number of ready combat divisions in the Army's strategic reserve--increased our troops in Europe--built up the Marines--added new sealift and airlift capacity--modernized our weapons and ammunition--expanded our anti-guerrilla forces--and increased the active fleet by more than 70 vessels and our tactical air forces by nearly a dozen wings.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Because we needed to reach this higher long-term level of readiness more quickly, 155,000 members of the Reserve and National Guard were activated under the Act of this Congress.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Some disruptions and distress were inevitable.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But the overwhelming majority bear their burdens--and their Nation's burdens--with admirable and traditional devotion.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In the coming year, our reserve programs will be revised--two Army Divisions will, I hope, replace those Guard Divisions on duty--and substantial other increases will boost our Air Force fighter units, the procurement of equipment, and our continental defense and warning efforts.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The Nation's first serious civil defense shelter program is under way, identifying, marking, and stocking 50 million spaces; and I urge your approval of Federal incentives for the construction of public fall-out shelters in schools and hospitals and similar centers.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The United Nations: But arms alone are not enough to keep the peace--it must be kept by men.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our instrument and our hope is the United Nations--and I see little merit in the impatience of those who would abandon this imperfect world instrument because they dislike our imperfect world.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For the troubles of a world organization merely reflect the troubles of the world itself.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And if the organization is weakened, these troubles can only increase.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We may not always agree with every detailed action taken by every officer of the United Nations, or with every voting majority.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But as an institution, it should have in the future, as it has had in the past since its inception, no stronger or more faithful member than the United States of America.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In 1961 the peace-keeping strength of the United Nations was reinforced.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And those who preferred or predicted its demise, envisioning a troika in the seat of Hammarskjold--or Red China inside the Assembly--have seen instead a new vigor, under a new Secretary General and a fully independent Secretariat.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In making plans for a new forum and principles on disarmament--for peace-keeping in outer space--for a decade of development effort--the U.N. fulfilled its Charter's lofty aim.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Eighteen months ago the tangled and turbulent Congo presented the U.N. with its gravest challenge.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The prospect was one of chaos--or certain big-power confrontation, with all of its hazards and all of its risks, to us and to others.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Today the hopes have improved for peaceful conciliation within a united Congo.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This is the objective of our policy in this important area.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: No policeman is universally popular--particularly when he uses his stick to restore law and order on his beat.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Those members who are willing to contribute their votes and their views--but very little else--have created a serious deficit by refusing to pay their share of special U.N. assessments.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Yet they do pay their annual assessments to retain their votes--and a new U.N. Bond issue, financing special operations for the next 18 months, is to be repaid with interest from these regular assessments.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This is clearly in our interest.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It will not only keep the U.N. solvent, but require all voting members to pay their fair share of its activities.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our share of special operations has long been much higher than our share of the annual assessment--and the bond issue will in effect reduce our disproportionate obligation, and for these reasons, I am urging Congress to approve our participation.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: With the approval of this Congress, we have undertaken in the past year a great new effort in outer space.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our aim is not simply to be first on the moon, any more than Charles Lindbergh's real aim was to be the first to Paris.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: His aim was to develop the techniques of our own country and other countries in the field of air and the atmosphere, and our objective in making this effort, which we hope will place one of our citizens on the moon, is to develop in a new frontier of science, commerce and cooperation, the position of the United States and the Free World.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This Nation belongs among the first to explore it, and among the first--if not the first--we shall be.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We are offering our know-how and our cooperation to the United Nations.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our satellites will soon be providing other nations with improved weather observations.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And I shall soon send to the Congress a measure to govern the financing and operation of an International Communications Satellite system, in a manner consistent with the public interest and our foreign policy.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But peace in space will help us naught once peace on earth is gone.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: World order will be secured only when the whole world has laid down these weapons which seem to offer us present security but threaten the future survival of the human race.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: That armistice day seems very far away.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The vast resources of this planet are being devoted more and more to the means of destroying, instead of enriching, human life.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But the world was not meant to be a prison in which man awaits his execution.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Nor has mankind survived the tests and trials of thousands of years to surrender everything--including its existence--now.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This Nation has the will and the faith to make a supreme effort to break the log jam on disarmament and nuclear tests--and we will persist until we prevail, until the rule of law has replaced the ever dangerous use of force.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Latin America: I turn now to a prospect of great promise: our Hemispheric relations.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The Alliance for Progress is being rapidly transformed from proposal to program.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Last month in Latin America I saw for myself the quickening of hope, the revival of confidence, the new trust in our country--among workers and farmers as well as diplomats.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We have pledged our help in speeding their economic, educational, and social progress.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The Latin American Republics have in turn pledged a new and strenuous effort of self-help and self-reform.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: To support this historic undertaking, I am proposing--under the authority contained in the bills of the last session of the Congress--a special long-term Alliance for Progress fund of $3 billion.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Combined with our Food for Peace, Export-Import Bank, and other resources, this will provide more than $1 billion a year in new support for the Alliance.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In addition, we have increased twelve fold our Spanish and Portuguese-language broadcasting in Latin America, and improved Hemispheric trade and defense.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And while the blight of communism has been increasingly exposed and isolated in the Americas, liberty has scored a gain.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The people of the Dominican Republic, with our firm encouragement and help, and those of our sister Republics of this Hemisphere are safely passing through the treacherous course from dictatorship through disorder towards democracy.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The New and Developing Nations: Our efforts to help other new or developing nations, and to strengthen their stand for freedom, have also made progress.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: A newly unified Agency for International Development is reorienting our foreign assistance to emphasize long-term development loans instead of grants, more economic aid instead of military, individual plans to meet the individual needs of the nations, and new standards on what they must do to marshal their own resources.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: A newly conceived Peace Corps is winning friends and helping people in fourteen countries--supplying trained and dedicated young men and women, to give these new nations a hand in building a society, and a glimpse of the best that is in our country.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: If there is a problem here, it is that we cannot supply the spontaneous and mounting demand.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: A newly-expanded Food for Peace Program is feeding the hungry of many lands with the abundance of our productive farms--providing lunches for children in school, wages for economic development, relief for the victims of flood and famine, and a better diet for millions whose daily bread is their chief concern.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: These programs help people; and, by helping people, they help freedom.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The views of their governments may sometimes be very different from ours--but events in Africa, the Middle East, and Eastern Europe teach us never to write off any nation as lost to the Communists.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: That is the lesson of our time.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In the past year, for example, we have urged a neutral and independent Laos--regained there a common policy with our major allies--and insisted that a cease-fire precede negotiations.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: While a workable formula for supervising its independence is still to be achieved, both the spread of war--which might have involved this country also--and a Communist occupation have thus far been prevented.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: A satisfactory settlement in Laos would also help to achieve and safeguard the peace in Viet Nam--where the foe is increasing his tactics of terror--where our own efforts have been stepped up--and where the local government has initiated new programs and reforms to broaden the base of resistance.
