speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It is a war of attempted subjugation--and it will be resisted.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The Atlan tic Community: Finally, the united strength of the Atlantic Community has flourished in the last year under severe tests.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: NATO has increased both the number and the readiness of its air, ground, and naval units--both its nuclear and non-nuclear capabilities.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Even greater efforts by all its members are still required.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Nevertheless our unity of purpose and will has been, I believe, immeasurably strengthened.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The threat to the brave city of Berlin remains.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In these last 6 months the Allies have made it unmistakably clear that our presence in Berlin, our free access thereto, and the freedom of two million West Berliners would not be surrendered either to force or through appeasement--and to maintain those rights and obligations, we are prepared to talk, when appropriate, and to fight, if necessary.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Every member of NATO stands with us in a common commitment to preserve this symbol of free man's will to remain free.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I cannot now predict the course of future negotiations over Berlin.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I can only say that we are sparing no honorable effort to find a peaceful and mutually acceptable resolution of this problem.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I believe such a resolution can be found, and with it an improvement in our relations with the Soviet Union, if only the leaders in the Kremlin will recognize the basic rights and interests involved, and the interest of all mankind in peace.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But the Atlantic Community is no longer concerned with purely military aims.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: As its common undertakings grow at an ever-increasing pace, we are, and increasingly will be, partners in aid, trade, defense, diplomacy, and monetary affairs.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The emergence of the new Europe is being matched by the emergence of new ties across the Atlantic.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It is a matter of un-dramatic daily cooperation in hundreds of workaday tasks: of currencies kept in effective relation, of development loans meshed together, of standardized weapons, and concerted diplomatic positions.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The Atlantic Community grows, not like a volcanic mountain, by one mighty explosion, but like a coral reef, from the accumulating activity of all.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Thus, we in the free world are moving steadily toward unity and cooperation, in the teeth of that old Bolshevik prophecy, and at the very time when extraordinary rumbles of discord can be heard across the Iron Curtain.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It is not free societies which bear within them the seeds of inevitable disunity.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our balance of payments: On one special problem, of great concern to our friends, and to us, I am proud to give the Congress an encouraging report.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our efforts to safeguard the dollar are progressing.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In the 11 months preceding last February 1, we suffered a net loss of nearly $2 billion in gold.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In the 11 months that followed, the loss was just over half a billion dollars.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And our deficit in our basic transactions with the rest of the world--trade, defense, foreign aid, and capital, excluding volatile short-term flows--has been reduced from $2 billion for 1960 to about one-third that amount for 1961.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Speculative fever against the dollar is ending--and confidence in the dollar has been restored.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We did not--and could not--achieve these gains through import restrictions, troop withdrawals, exchange controls, dollar devaluation or choking off domestic recovery.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We acted not in panic but in perspective.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But the problem is not yet solved.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Persistently large deficits would endanger our economic growth and our military and defense commitments abroad.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our goal must be a reasonable equilibrium in our balance of payments.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: With the cooperation of the Congress, business, labor, and our major allies, that goal can be reached.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We shall continue to attract foreign tourists and investments to our shores, to seek increased military purchases here by our allies, to maximize foreign aid procurement from American firms, to urge increased aid from other fortunate nations to the less fortunate, to seek tax laws which do not favor investment in other industrialized nations or tax havens, and to urge coordination of allied fiscal and monetary policies so as to discourage large and disturbing capital movements.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Trade: Above all, if we are to pay for our commitments abroad, we must expand our exports.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our businessmen must be export-conscious and export competitive.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our tax policies must spur modernization of our plants--our wage and price gains must be consistent with productivity to hold the line on prices--our export credit and promotion campaigns for American industries must continue to expand.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But the greatest challenge of all is posed by the growth of the European Common Market.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Assuming the accession of the United Kingdom, there will arise across the Atlantic a trading partner behind a single external tariff similar to ours with an economy which nearly equals our own.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Will we in this country adapt our thinking to these new prospects and patterns--or will we wait until events have passed us by?  This is the year to decide.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The Reciprocal Trade Act is expiring.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We need a new law--a wholly new approach--a bold new instrument of American trade policy.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our decision could well affect the unity of the West, the course of the Cold War, and the economic growth of our Nation for a generation to come.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: If we move decisively, our factories and farms can increase their sales to their richest, fastest-growing market.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our exports will increase.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our balance of payments position will improve.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And we will have forged across the Atlantic a trading partnership with vast resources for freedom.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: If, on the other hand, we hang back in deference to local economic pressures, we will find ourselves cut off from our major allies.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Industries--and I believe this is most vital--industries will move their plants and jobs and capital inside the walls of the Common Market, and jobs, therefore, will be lost here in the United States if they cannot otherwise compete for its consumers.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our farm surpluses--our balance of trade, as you all know, to Europe, the Common Market, in farm products, is nearly three or four to one in our favor, amounting to one of the best earners of dollars in our balance of payments structure, and without entrance to this Market, without the ability to enter it, our farm surpluses will pile up in the Middle West, tobacco in the South, and other commodities, which have gone through Western Europe for 15 years.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our balance of payments position will worsen.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our consumers will lack a wider choice of goods at lower prices.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And millions of American workers--whose jobs depend on the sale or the transportation or the distribution of exports or imports, or whose jobs will be endangered by the movement of our capital to Europe, or whose jobs can be maintained only in an expanding economy--these millions of workers in your home States and mine will see their real interests sacrificed.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Members of the Congress: The United States did not rise to greatness by waiting for others to lead.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This Nation is the world's foremost manufacturer, farmer, banker, consumer, and exporter.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The Common Market is moving ahead at an economic growth rate twice ours.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The Communist economic offensive is under way.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The opportunity is ours--the initiative is up to us--and I believe that 1962 is the time.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: To seize that initiative, I shall shortly send to the Congress a new five-year Trade Expansion Action, far-reaching in scope but designed with great care to make certain that its benefits to our people far outweigh any risks.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The bill will permit the gradual elimination of tariffs here in the United States and in the Common Market on those items in which we together supply 80 percent of the world's trade--mostly items in which our own ability to compete is demonstrated by the fact that we sell abroad, in these items, substantially more than we import.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This step will make it possible for our major industries to compete with their counterparts in Western Europe for access to European consumers.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: On other goods the bill will permit a gradual reduction of duties up to 50 percent--permitting bargaining by major categories--and provide for appropriate and tested forms of assistance to firms and employees adjusting to import competition.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We are not neglecting the safeguards provided by peril points, an escape clause, or the National Security Amendment.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: principle.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: On the contrary, the bill will provide new encouragement for their sale of tropical agricultural products, so important to our friends in Latin America, who have long depended upon the European market, who now find themselves faced with new challenges which we must join with them in overcoming.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Concessions, in this bargaining, must of course be reciprocal, not unilateral.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The Common Market will not fulfill its own high promise unless its outside tariff walls are low.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The dangers of restriction or timidity in our own policy have counterparts for our friends in Europe.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For together we face a common challenge: to enlarge the prosperity of free men everywhere--to build in partnership a new trading community in which all free nations may gain from the productive energy of free competitive effort.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: These various elements in our foreign policy lead, as I have said, to a single goal--the goal of a peaceful world of free and independent states.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This is our guide for the present and our vision for the future--a free community of nations, independent but interdependent, uniting north and south, east and west, in one great family of man, outgrowing and transcending the hates and fears that rend our age.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We will not reach that goal today, or tomorrow.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We may not reach it in our own lifetime.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But the quest is the greatest adventure of our century.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We sometimes chafe at the burden of our obligations, the complexity of our decisions, the agony of our choices.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But there is no comfort or security for us in evasion, no solution in abdication, no relief in irresponsibility.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: A year ago, in assuming the tasks of the Presidency, I said that few generations, in all history, had been granted the role of being the great defender of freedom in its hour of maximum danger.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This is our good fortune; and I welcome it now as I did a year ago.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For it is the fate of this generation--of you in the Congress and of me as President--to live with a struggle we did not start, in a world we did not make.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But the pressures of life are not always distributed by choice.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And while no nation has ever faced such a challenge, no nation has ever been so ready to seize the burden and the glory of freedom.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And in this high endeavor, may God watch over the United States of America.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I congratulate you all - not merely on your electoral victory but on your selected role in history.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For you and I are privileged to serve the great Republic in what could be the most decisive decade in its long history.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The choices we make, for good or ill, may well shape the state of the Union for generations yet to come.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Little more than 100 weeks ago I assumed the office of President of the United States.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In seeking the help of the Congress and our countrymen, I pledged no easy answers.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I pledged - and asked - only toil and dedication.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: These the Congress and the people have given in good measure.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And today, having witnessed in recent months a heightened respect for our national purpose and power - having seen the courageous calm of a united people in a perilous hour - and having observed a steady improvement in the opportunities and well-being of our citizens - I can report to you that the state of this old but youthful Union, in the 175th year of its life, is good.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In the world beyond our borders, steady progress has been made in building a world of order.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The people of West Berlin remain both free and secure.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: A settlement, though still precarious, has been reached in Laos.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The spear point of aggression has been blunted in Vietnam.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The end of agony may be in sight in the Congo.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The doctrine of troika is dead.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And, while danger continues, a deadly threat has been removed in Cuba.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: At home, the recession is behind us.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Well over a million more men and women are working today than were working 2 years ago.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The average factory workweek is once again more than 40 hours;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: our industries are turning out more goods than ever before;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: and more than half of the manufacturing capacity that lay silent and wasted 100 weeks ago is humming with activity.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In short, both at home and abroad, there may now be a temptation to relax.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For the road has been long, the burden heavy, and the pace consistently urgent.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But we cannot be satisfied to rest here.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This is the side of the hill, not the top.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The mere absence of war is not peace.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The mere absence of recession is not growth.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We have made a beginning - but we have only begun.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Now the time has come to make the most of our gains - to translate the renewal of our national strength into the achievement of our national purpose.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: America has enjoyed 22 months of uninterrupted economic recovery.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But recovery is not enough.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: If we are to prevail in the long run, we must expand the long-run strength of our economy.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We must move along the path to a higher rate of growth and full employment.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For this would mean tens of billions of dollars more each year in production, profits, wages, and public revenues.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It would mean an end to the persistent slack which has kept our unemployment at or above 5 percent for 61 out of the past 62 months - and an end to the growing pressures for such restrictive measures as the 35-hour week, which alone could increase hourly labor costs by as much as 14 percent, start a new wage-price spiral of inflation, and undercut our efforts to compete with other nations.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: To achieve these greater gains, one step, above all, is essential - the enactment this year of a substantial reduction and revision in Federal income taxes.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For it is increasingly clear - to those in Government, business, and labor who are responsible for our economy's success - that our obsolete tax system exerts too heavy a drag on private purchasing power, profits, and employment.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Designed to check inflation in earlier years, it now checks growth instead.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It discourages extra effort and risk.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It distorts the use of resources.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It invites recurrent recessions, depresses our Federal revenues, and causes chronic budget deficits.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Now, when the inflationary pressures of the war and the post-war years no longer threaten, and the dollar commands new respect - now, when no military crisis strains our resources - now is the time to act.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We cannot afford to be timid or slow.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For this is the most urgent task confronting the Congress in 1963.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In an early message, I shall propose a permanent reduction in tax rates which will lower liabilities by $13.5 billion.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Of this, $11 billion results from reducing individual tax rates, which now range between 20 and 91 percent, to a more sensible range of 14 to 65 percent, with a split in the present first bracket.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Two and one-half billion dollars results from reducing corporate tax rates, from 52 percent - which gives the Government today a majority interest in profits - to the permanent pre-Korean level of 47 percent.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This is in addition to the more than $2 billion cut in corporate tax liabilities resulting from last year's investment credit and depreciation reform.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: To achieve this reduction within the limits of a manageable budgetary deficit, I urge: first, that these cuts be phased over 3 calendar years, beginning in 1963 with a cut of some $6 billion at annual rates;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: second, that these reductions be coupled with selected structural changes, beginning in 1964, which will broaden the tax base, end unfair or unnecessary preferences, remove or lighten certain hardships, and in the net offset some $3.5 billion of the revenue loss;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: and third, that budgetary receipts at the outset be increased by $1.5 billion a year, without any change in tax liabilities, by gradually shifting the tax payments of large corporations to a more current time schedule.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This combined program, by increasing the amount of our national income, will in time result in still higher Federal revenues.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It is a fiscally responsible program - the surest and the soundest way of achieving in time a balanced budget in a balanced full employment economy.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This net reduction in tax liabilities of $10 billion will increase the purchasing power of American families and business enterprises in every tax bracket, with greatest increase going to our low-income consumers.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It will, in addition, encourage the initiative and risk-taking on which our free system depends - induce more investment, production, and capacity use - help provide the 2 million new jobs we need every year - and reinforce the American principle of additional reward for additional effort.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I do not say that a measure for tax reduction and reform is the only way to achieve these goals.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: No doubt a massive increase in Federal spending could also create jobs and growth - but, in today's setting, private consumers, employers, and investors should be given a full opportunity first.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: No doubt a temporary tax cut could provide a spur to our economy - but a long-run problem compels a long-run solution.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: No doubt a reduction in either individual or corporation taxes alone would be of great help - but corporations need customers and job seekers need jobs.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: No doubt tax reduction without reform would sound simpler and more attractive to many - but our growth is also hampered by a host of tax inequities and special preferences which have distorted the flow of investment.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And, finally, there are no doubt some who would prefer to put off a tax cut in the hope that ultimately an end to the cold war would make possible an equivalent cut in expenditures - but that end is not in view and to wait for it would be costly and self-defeating.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In submitting a tax program which will, of course, temporarily increase the deficit but can ultimately end it - and in recognition of the need to control expenditures - I will shortly submit a fiscal 1964 administrative budget which, while allowing for needed rises in defense, space, and fixed interest charges, holds total expenditures for all other purposes below this year's level.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This requires the reduction or postponement of many desirable programs, the absorption of a large part of last year's Federal pay raise through personnel and other economies, the termination of certain installations and projects, and the substitution in several programs of private for public credit.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But I am convinced that the enactment this year of tax reduction and tax reform overshadows all other domestic problems in this Congress.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For we cannot for long lead the cause of peace and freedom, if we ever cease to set the pace here at home.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Tax reduction alone, however, is not enough to strengthen our society, to provide opportunities for the four million Americans who are born every year, to improve the lives of 32 million Americans who live on the outskirts of poverty.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The quality of American life must keep pace with the quantity of American goods.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This country cannot afford to be materially rich and spiritually poor.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Therefore, by holding down the budgetary cost of existing programs to keep within the limitations I have set, it is both possible and imperative to adopt other new measures that we cannot afford to postpone.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: These measures are based on a series of fundamental premises, grouped under four related headings: First, we need to strengthen our Nation by investing in our youth: 6.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The future of any country which is dependent upon the will and wisdom of its citizens is damaged, and irreparably damaged, whenever any of its children is not educated to the full extent of his talent, from grade school through graduate school.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Today, an estimated 4 out of every 10 students in the 5th grade will not even finish high school - and that is a waste we cannot afford.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In addition, there is no reason why one million young Americans, out of school and out of work, should all remain unwanted and often untrained on our city streets when their energies can be put to good use.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Finally, the overseas success of our Peace Corps volunteers, most of them young men and women carrying skills and ideas to needy people, suggests the merit of a similar corps serving our own community needs: in mental hospitals, on Indian reservations, in centers for the aged or for young delinquents, in schools for the illiterate or the handicapped.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: As the idealism of our youth has served world peace, so can it serve the domestic tranquility.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Second, we need to strengthen our Nation by safeguarding its health: 9.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our working men and women, instead of being forced to beg for help from public charity once they are old and ill, should start contributing now to their own retirement health program through the Social Security System.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Moreover, all our miracles of medical research will count for little if we cannot reverse the growing nationwide shortage of doctors, dentists, and nurses, and the widespread shortages of nursing homes and modern urban hospital facilities.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Merely to keep the present ratio of doctors and dentists from declining any further, we must over the next 10 years increase the capacity of our medical schools by 50 percent and our dental schools by 100 percent.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Finally, and of deep concern, I believe that the abandonment of the mentally ill and the mentally retarded to the grim mercy of custodial institutions too often inflicts on them and on their families a needless cruelty which this Nation should not endure.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The incidence of mental retardation in this country is three times as high as that of Sweden, for example - and that figure can and must be reduced.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Third, we need to strengthen our Nation by protecting the basic rights of its citizens: 12.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The right to competent counsel must be assured to every man accused of crime in Federal court, regardless of his means.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And the most precious and powerful right in the world, the right to vote in a free American election, must not be denied to any citizen on grounds of his race or color.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I wish that all qualified Americans permitted to vote were willing to vote, but surely in this centennial year of Emancipation all those who are willing to vote should always be permitted.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Fourth, we need to strengthen our Nation by making the best and the most economical use of its resources and facilities: 14.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our economic health depends on healthy transportation arteries;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: and I believe the way to a more modern, economical choice of national transportation service is through increased competition and decreased regulation.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Local mass transit, faring even worse, is as essential a community service as hospitals and highways.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Nearly three-fourths of our citizens live in urban areas, which occupy only 2 percent of our land - and if local transit is to survive and relieve the congestion of these cities, it needs Federal stimulation and assistance.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Next, this Government is in the storage and stockpile business to the melancholy tune of more than $16 billion.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We must continue to support farm income, but we should not pile more farm surpluses on top of the $7.5 billion we already own.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We must maintain a stockpile of strategic materials, but the $8.5 billion we have acquired - for reasons both good and bad - is much more than we need; and we should be empowered to dispose of the excess in ways which will not cause market disruption.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Finally, our already overcrowded national parks and recreation areas will have twice as many visitors 10 years from now as they do today.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: If we do not plan today for the future growth of these and other great natural assets - not only parks and forests but wildlife and wilderness preserves, and water projects of all kinds - our children and their children will be poorer in every sense of the word.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: These are not domestic concerns alone.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For upon our achievement of greater vitality and strength here at home hang our fate and future in the world: our ability to sustain and supply the security of free men and nations, our ability to command their respect for our leadership, our ability to expand our trade without threat to our balance of payments, and our ability to adjust to the changing demands of cold war competition and challenge.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We shall be judged more by what we do at home than by what we preach abroad.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Nothing we could do to help the developing countries would help them half as much as a booming U.S. economy.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And nothing our opponents could do to encourage their own ambitions would encourage them half as much as a chronic lagging U.S. economy.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: These domestic tasks do not divert energy from our security - they provide the very foundation for freedom's survival and success.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Turning to the world outside, it was only a few years ago - in Southeast Asia, Africa, Eastern Europe, Latin America, even outer space - that communism sought to convey the image of a unified, confident, and expanding empire, closing in on a sluggish America and a free world in disarray.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But few people would hold to that picture today.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In these past months we have reaffirmed the scientific and military superiority of freedom.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We have doubled our efforts in space, to assure us of being first in the future.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We have undertaken the most far-reaching defense improvements in the peacetime history of this country.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And we have maintained the frontiers of freedom from Vietnam to West Berlin.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But complacency or self-congratulation can imperil our security as much as the weapons of tyranny.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: A moment of pause is not a promise of peace.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Dangerous problems remain from Cuba to the South China Sea.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The world's prognosis prescribes, in short, not a year's vacation for us, but a year of obligation and opportunity.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Four special avenues of opportunity stand out: the Atlantic Alliance, the developing nations, the new Sino-Soviet difficulties, and the search for worldwide peace.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: First, how fares the grand alliance?

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Free Europe is entering into a new phase of its long and brilliant history.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The era of colonial expansion has passed; the era of national rivalries is fading; and a new era of interdependence and unity is taking shape.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Defying the old prophecies of Marx, consenting to what no conqueror could ever compel, the free nations of Europe are moving toward a unity of purpose and power and policy in every sphere of activity.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For 17 years this movement has had our consistent support, both political and economic.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Far from resenting the new Europe, we regard her as a welcome partner, not a rival.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For the road to world peace and freedom is still long, and there are burdens which only full partners can share - in supporting the common defense, in expanding world trade, in aligning our balance of payments, in aiding the emergent nations, in concerting political and economic policies, and in welcoming to our common effort other industrialized nations, notably Japan, whose remarkable economic and political development of the 1950's permits it now to play on the world scene a major constructive role.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: No doubt differences of opinion will continue to get more attention than agreements on action, as Europe moves from independence to more formal interdependence.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But these are honest differences among honorable associates - more real and frequent, in fact, among our Western European allies than between them and the United States.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For the unity of freedom has never relied on uniformity of opinion.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But the basic agreement of this alliance on fundamental issues continues.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The first task of the alliance remains the common defense.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Last month Prime Minister Macmillan and I laid plans for a new stage in our long cooperative effort, one which aims to assist in the wider task of framing a common nuclear defense for the whole alliance.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The Nassau agreement recognizes that the security of the West is indivisible, and so must be our defense.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But it also recognizes that this is an alliance of proud and sovereign nations, and works best when we do not forget it.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It recognizes further that the nuclear defense of the West is not a matter for the present nuclear powers alone - that France will be such a power in the future - and that ways must be found without increasing the hazards of nuclear diffusion, to increase the role of our other partners in planning, manning, and directing a truly multilateral nuclear force within an increasingly intimate NATO alliance.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Finally, the Nassau agreement recognizes that nuclear defense is not enough, that the agreed NATO levels of conventional strength must be met, and that the alliance cannot afford to be in a position of having to answer every threat with nuclear weapons or nothing.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We remain too near the Nassau decisions, and too far from their full realization, to know their place in history.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But I believe that, for the first time, the door is open for the nuclear defense of the alliance to become a source of confidence, instead of a cause of contention.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The next most pressing concern of the alliance is our common economic goals of trade and growth.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This Nation continues to be concerned about its balance-of-payments deficit, which, despite its decline, remains a stubborn and troublesome problem.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We believe, moreover, that closer economic ties among all free nations are essential to prosperity and peace.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And neither we nor the members of the European Common Market are so affluent that we can long afford to shelter high cost farms or factories from the winds of foreign competition, or to restrict the channels of trade with other nations of the free world.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: If the Common Market should move toward protectionism and restrictionism, it would undermine its own basic principles.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This Government means to use the authority conferred on it last year by the Congress to encourage trade expansion on both sides of the Atlantic and around the world.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Second, what of the developing and nonaligned nations?

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: They were shocked by the Soviets' sudden and secret attempt to transform Cuba into a nuclear striking base - and by Communist China's arrogant invasion of India.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: They have been reassured by our prompt assistance to India, by our support through the United Nations of the Congo's unification, by our patient search for disarmament, and by the improvement in our treatment of citizens and visitors whose skins do not happen to be white.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And as the older colonialism recedes, and the neo-colonialism of the Communist powers stands out more starkly than ever, they realize more clearly that the issue in the world struggle is not communism versus capitalism, but coercion versus free choice.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: They are beginning to realize that the longing for independence is the same the world over, whether it is the independence of West Berlin or Vietnam.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: They are beginning to realize that such independence runs athwart all Communist ambitions but is in keeping with our own - and that our approach to their diverse needs is resilient and resourceful, while the Communists are still relying on ancient doctrines and dogmas.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Nevertheless it is hard for any nation to focus on an external or subversive threat to its independence when its energies are drained in daily combat with the forces of poverty and despair.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It makes little sense for us to assail, in speeches and resolutions, the horrors of communism, to spend $50 billion a year to prevent its military advance - and then to begrudge spending, largely on American products, less than one-tenth of that amount to help other nations strengthen their independence and cure the social chaos in which communism always has thrived.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I am proud - and I think most Americans are proud - of a mutual defense and assistance program, evolved with bipartisan support in three administrations, which has, with all its recognized problems, contributed to the fact that not a single one of the nearly fifty U.N. members to gain independence since the Second World War has succumbed to Communist control.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I am proud of a program that has helped to arm and feed and clothe millions of people who live on the front lines of freedom.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I am especially proud that this country has put forward for the 60's a vast cooperative effort to achieve economic growth and social progress throughout the Americas - the Alliance for Progress.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I do not underestimate the difficulties that we face in this mutual effort among our close neighbors, but the free states of this hemisphere, working in close collaboration, have begun to make this alliance a living reality.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Today it is feeding one out of every four school age children in Latin America an extra food ration from our farm surplus.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It has distributed 1.5 million school books and is building 17,000 classrooms.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It has helped resettle tens of thousands of farm families on land they can call their own.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It is stimulating our good neighbors to more self-help and self-reform - fiscal, social, institutional, and land reforms.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It is bringing new housing and hope, new health and dignity, to millions who were forgotten.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The men and women of this hemisphere know that the alliance cannot succeed if it is only another name for United States handouts - that it can succeed only as the Latin American nations themselves devote their best effort to fulfilling its goals.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This story is the same in Africa, in the Middle East, and in Asia.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Wherever nations are willing to help themselves, we stand ready to help them build new bulwarks of freedom.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We are not purchasing votes for the cold war; we have gone to the aid of imperiled nations, neutrals and allies alike.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: What we do ask - and all that we ask - is that our help be used to best advantage, and that their own efforts not be diverted by needless quarrels with other independent nations.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Despite all its past achievements, the continued progress of the mutual assistance program requires a persistent discontent with present performance.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We have been reorganizing this program to make it a more effective, efficient instrument - and that process will continue this year.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But free world development will still be an uphill struggle.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Government aid can only supplement the role of private investment, trade expansion, commodity stabilization, and, above all, internal self-improvement.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The processes of growth are gradual - bearing fruit in a decade, not a day.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our successes will be neither quick nor dramatic.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But if these programs were ever to be ended, our failures in a dozen countries would be sudden and certain.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Neither money nor technical assistance, however, can be our only weapon against poverty.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In the end, the crucial effort is one of purpose, requiring the fuel of finance but also a torch of idealism.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And nothing carries the spirit of this American idealism more effectively to the far corners of the earth than the American Peace Corps.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: A year ago, less than 900 Peace Corps volunteers were on the job.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: A year from now they will number more than 9,000 - men and women, aged 18 to 79, willing to give 2 years of their lives to helping people in other lands.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: There are, in fact, nearly a million Americans serving their country and the cause of freedom in overseas posts, a record no other people can match.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Surely those of us who stay at home should be glad to help indirectly;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: by supporting our aid programs;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: by opening our doors to foreign visitors and diplomats and students;

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: and by proving, day by day, by deed as well as word, that we are a just and generous people.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Third, what comfort can we take from the increasing strains and tensions within the Communist bloc?

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Here hope must be tempered with caution.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For the Soviet-Chinese disagreement is over means, not ends.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: A dispute over how best to bury the free world is no grounds for Western rejoicing.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Nevertheless, while a strain is not a fracture, it is clear that the forces of diversity are at work inside the Communist camp, despite all the iron disciplines of regimentation and all the iron dogmatisms of ideology.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Marx is proven wrong once again: for it is the closed Communist societies, not the free and open societies which carry within themselves the seeds of internal disintegration.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The disarray of the Communist empire has been heightened by two other formidable forces.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: One is the historical force of nationalism - and the yearning of all men to be free.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The other is the gross inefficiency of their economies.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For a closed society is not open to ideas of progress - and a police state finds that it cannot command the grain to grow.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: New nations asked to choose between two competing systems need only compare conditions in East and West Germany, Eastern and Western Europe, North and South Vietnam.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: They need only compare the disillusionment of Communist Cuba with the promise of the Alliance for Progress.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: And all the world knows that no successful system builds a wall to keep its people in and freedom out - and the wall of shame dividing Berlin is a symbol of Communist failure.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Finally, what can we do to move from the present pause toward enduring peace? Again I would counsel caution.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I foresee no spectacular reversal in Communist methods or goals.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But if all these trends and developments can persuade the Soviet Union to walk the path of peace, then let her know that all free nations will journey with her.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But until that choice is made, and until the world can develop a reliable system of international security, the free peoples have no choice but to keep their arms nearby.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: This country, therefore, continues to require the best defense in the world - a defense which is suited to the sixties.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: way of achieving it.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: It means the expenditure of more than $15 billion this year on nuclear weapons systems alone, a sum which is about equal to the combined defense budgets of our European Allies.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But it also means improved air and missile defenses, improved civil defense, a strengthened anti-guerrilla capacity and, of prime importance, more powerful and flexible non-nuclear forces.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For threats of massive retaliation may not deter piecemeal aggression - and a line of destroyers in a quarantine, or a division of well-equipped men on a border, may be more useful to our real security than the multiplication of awesome weapons beyond all rational need.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But our commitment to national safety is not a commitment to expand our military establishment indefinitely.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We do not dismiss disarmament as merely an idle dream.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For we believe that, in the end, it is the only way to assure the security of all without impairing the interests of any.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Nor do we mistake honorable negotiation for appeasement.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: While we shall never weary in the defense of freedom, neither shall we ever abandon the pursuit of peace.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In this quest, the United Nations requires our full and continued support.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Its value in serving the cause of peace has been shown anew in its role in the West New Guinea settlement, in its use as a forum for the Cuban crisis, and in its task of unification in the Congo.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Today the United Nations is primarily the protector of the small and the weak, and a safety valve for the strong.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Tomorrow it can form the framework for a world of law - a world in which no nation dictates the destiny of another, and in which the vast resources now devoted to destructive means will serve constructive ends.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: In short, let our adversaries choose.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: If they choose peaceful competition, they shall have it.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: and subversion will ultimately fail - if they recognize that there is more security in accepting inspection than in permitting new nations to master the black arts of nuclear war - and if they are willing to turn their energies, as we are, to the great unfinished tasks of our own peoples - then, surely, the areas of agreement can be very wide indeed: a clear understanding about Berlin, stability in Southeast Asia, an end to nuclear testing, new checks on surprise or accidental attack, and, ultimately, general and complete disarmament.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For we seek not the worldwide victory of one nation or system but a worldwide victory of man.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: The modern globe is too small, its weapons are too destructive, and its disorders are too contagious to permit any other kind of victory.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: To achieve this end, the United States will continue to spend a greater portion of its national production than any other people in the free world.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For 15 years no other free nation has demanded so much of itself.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Through hot wars and cold, through recession and prosperity, through the ages of the atom and outer space, the American people have never faltered and their faith has never flagged.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: If at times our actions seem to make life difficult for others, it is only because history has made life difficult for us all.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But difficult days need not be dark.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: I think these are proud and memorable days in the cause of peace and freedom.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We are proud, for example, of Major Rudolf Anderson who gave his life over the island of Cuba.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We salute Specialist James Allen Johnson who died on the border of South Korea.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We pay honor to Sergeant Gerald Pendell who was killed in Vietnam.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: They are among the many who in this century, far from home, have died for our country.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Our task now, and the task of all Americans is to live up to their commitment.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: My friends: I close on a note of hope.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We are not lulled by the momentary calm of the sea or the somewhat clearer skies above.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: We know the turbulence that lies below, and the storms that are beyond the horizon this year.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: But now the winds of change appear to be blowing more strongly than ever, in the world of communism as well as our own.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: For 175 years we have sailed with those winds at our back, and with the tides of human freedom in our favor.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: leaving Fear astern.

speaker: John F. Kennedy
text: Today we still welcome those winds of change - and we have every reason to believe that our tide is running strong.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Mr. Speaker, Mr. President, Members of the House and Senate, my fellow Americans: I will be brief, for our time is necessarily short and our agenda is already long.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Last year's congressional session was the longest in peacetime history.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: With that foundation, let us work together to make this year's session the best in the Nation's history.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Let this session of Congress be known as the session which did more for civil rights than the last hundred sessions combined;

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: as the session which enacted the most far-reaching tax cut of our time;

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: as the session which declared all-out war on human poverty and unemployment in these United States;

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: as the session which finally recognized the health needs of all of our older citizens;

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: as the session which reformed our tangled transportation and transit policies;

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: as the session which achieved the most effective, efficient foreign aid program ever;

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: and as the session which helped to build more homes, more schools, more libraries, and more hospitals than any single session of Congress in the history of our Republic.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: All this and more can and must be done.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It can be done by this summer, and it can be done without any increase in spending.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In fact, under the budget that I shall shortly submit, it can be done with an actual reduction in Federal expenditures and Federal employment.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We have in 1964 a unique opportunity and obligation--to prove the success of our system;

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: If we fail, if we fritter and fumble away our opportunity in needless, senseless quarrels between Democrats and Republicans, or between the House and the Senate, or between the South and North, or between the Congress and the administration, then history will rightfully judge us harshly.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But if we succeed, if we can achieve these goals by forging in this country a greater sense of union, then, and only then, can we take full satisfaction in the State of the Union.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Here in the Congress you can demonstrate effective legislative leadership by discharging the public business with clarity and dispatch, voting each important proposal up, or voting it down, but at least bringing it to a fair and a final vote.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Let us carry forward the plans and programs of John Fitzgerald Kennedy--not because of our sorrow or sympathy, but because they are right.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In his memory today, I especially ask all members of my own political faith, in this election year, to put your country ahead of your party, and to always debate principles; never debate personalities.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: For my part, I pledge a progressive administration which is efficient, and honest and frugal.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The budget to be submitted to the Congress shortly is in full accord with this pledge.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It will cut our deficit in half--from $10 billion to $4,900 million.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It will be, in proportion to our national output, the smallest budget since 1951.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It will call for a substantial reduction in Federal employment, a feat accomplished only once before in the last 10 years.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: While maintaining the full strength of our combat defenses, it will call for the lowest number of civilian personnel in the Department of Defense since 1950.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It will call for total expenditures of $97,900 million--compared to $98,400 million for the current year, a reduction of more than $500 million.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It will call for new obligational authority of $103,800 million--a reduction of more than $4 billion below last year's request of $107,900 million.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But it is not a standstill budget, for America cannot afford to stand still.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our population is growing.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Unfortunately, many Americans live on the outskirts of hope--some because of their poverty, and some because of their color, and all too many because of both.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our economy is more complex.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our task is to help replace their despair with opportunity.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our people's needs are expanding.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This administration today, here and now, declares unconditional war on poverty in America.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I urge this Congress and all Americans to join with me in that effort.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But by closing down obsolete installations, by curtailing less urgent programs, by cutting back where cutting back seems to be wise, by insisting on a dollar's worth for a dollar spent, I am able to recommend in this reduced budget the most Federal support in history for education, for health, for retraining the unemployed, and for helping the economically and the physically handicapped.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It will not be a short or easy struggle, no single weapon or strategy will suffice, but we shall not rest until that war is won.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This budget, and this year's legislative program, are designed to help each and every American citizen fulfill his basic hopes--his hopes for a fair chance to make good;

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The richest Nation on earth can afford to win it.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We cannot afford to lose it.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: One thousand dollars invested in salvaging an unemployable youth today can return $40,000 or more in his lifetime.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Poverty is a national problem, requiring improved national organization and support.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But this attack, to be effective, must also be organized at the State and the local level and must be supported and directed by State and local efforts.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: For the war against poverty will not be won here in Washington.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It must be won in the field, in every private home, in every public office, from the courthouse to the White House.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The program I shall propose will emphasize this cooperative approach to help that one-fifth of all American families with incomes too small to even meet their basic needs.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our chief weapons in a more pinpointed attack will be better schools, and better health, and better homes, and better training, and better job opportunities to help more Americans, especially young Americans, escape from squalor and misery and unemployment rolls where other citizens help to carry them.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Very often a lack of jobs and money is not the cause of poverty, but the symptom.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The cause may lie deeper--in our failure to give our fellow citizens a fair chance to develop their own capacities, in a lack of education and training, in a lack of medical care and housing, in a lack of decent communities in which to live and bring up their children.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But whatever the cause, our joint Federal-local effort must pursue poverty, pursue it wherever it exists--in city slums and small towns, in sharecropper shacks or in migrant worker camps, on Indian Reservations, among whites as well as Negroes, among the young as well as the aged, in the boom towns and in the depressed areas.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our aim is not only to relieve the symptom of poverty, but to cure it and, above all, to prevent it.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: No single piece of legislation, however, is going to suffice.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We will launch a special effort in the chronically distressed areas of Appalachia.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must expand our small but our successful area redevelopment program.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must enact youth employment legislation to put jobless, aimless, hopeless youngsters to work on useful projects.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must distribute more food to the needy through a broader food stamp program.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must create a National Service Corps to help the economically handicapped of our own country as the Peace Corps now helps those abroad.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must modernize our unemployment insurance and establish a high-level commission on automation.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: If we have the brain power to invent these machines, we have the brain power to make certain that they are a boon and not a bane to humanity.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must extend the coverage of our minimum wage laws to more than 2 million workers now lacking this basic protection of purchasing power.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must, by including special school aid funds as part of our education program, improve the quality of teaching, training, and counseling in our hardest hit areas.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must build more libraries in every area and more hospitals and nursing homes under the Hill-Burton Act, and train more nurses to staff them.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must provide hospital insurance for our older citizens financed by every worker and his employer under Social Security, contributing no more than $1 a month during the employee's working career to protect him in his old age in a dignified manner without cost to the Treasury, against the devastating hardship of prolonged or repeated illness.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must, as a part of a revised housing and urban renewal program, give more help to those displaced by slum clearance, provide more housing for our poor and our elderly, and seek as our ultimate goal in our free enterprise system a decent home for every American family.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must help obtain more modern mass transit within our communities as well as low-cost transportation between them.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Above all, we must release $11 billion of tax reduction into the private spending stream to create new jobs and new markets in every area of this land.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: These programs are obviously not for the poor or the underprivileged alone.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Every American will benefit by the extension of social security to cover the hospital costs of their aged parents.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Every American community will benefit from the construction or modernization of schools, libraries, hospitals, and nursing homes, from the training of more nurses and from the improvement of urban renewal in public transit.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And every individual American taxpayer and every corporate taxpayer will benefit from the earliest possible passage of the pending tax bill from both the new investment it will bring and the new jobs that it will create.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: That tax bill has been thoroughly discussed for a year.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Now we need action.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The new budget clearly allows it.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our taxpayers surely deserve it.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our economy strongly demands it.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And every month of delay dilutes its benefits in 1964 for consumption, for investment, and for employment.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: For until the bill is signed, its investment incentives cannot be deemed certain, and the withholding rate cannot be reduced-- and the most damaging and devastating thing you can do to any businessman in America is to keep him in doubt and to keep him guessing on what our tax policy is.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And I say that we should now reduce to 14 percent instead of 15 percent our withholding rate.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I therefore urge the Congress to take final action on this bill by the first of February, if at all possible.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: For however proud we may be of the unprecedented progress of our free enterprise economy over the last 3 years, we should not and we cannot permit it to pause.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In 1963, for the first time in history, we crossed the 70 million job mark, but we will soon need more than 75 million jobs.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In 1963 our gross national product reached the $600 billion level--$100 billion higher than when we took office.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But it easily could and it should be still $30 billion higher today than it is.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Wages and profits and family income are also at their highest levels in history--but I would remind you that 4 million workers and 13 percent of our industrial capacity are still idle today.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We need a tax cut now to keep this country moving.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: For our goal is not merely to spread the work.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our goal is to create more jobs.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I believe the enactment of a 35-hour week would sharply increase costs, would invite inflation, would impair our ability to compete, and merely share instead of creating employment.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But I am equally opposed to the 45- or 50-hour week in those industries where consistently excessive use of overtime causes increased unemployment.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: So, therefore, I recommend legislation authorizing the creation of a tripartite industry committee to determine on an industry-by-industry basis as to where a higher penalty rate for overtime would increase job openings without unduly increasing costs, and authorizing the establishment of such higher rates.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Let me make one principle of this administration abundantly clear: All of these increased opportunities--in employment, in education, in housing, and in every field--must be open to Americans of every color.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: As far as the writ of Federal law will run, we must abolish not some, but all racial discrimination.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: For this is not merely an economic issue, or a social, political, or international issue.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It is a moral issue, and it must be met by the passage this session of the bill now pending in the House.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: All members of the public should have equal access to facilities open to the public.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: All members of the public should be equally eligible for Federal benefits that are financed by the public.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: All members of the public should have an equal chance to vote for public officials and to send their children to good public schools and to contribute their talents to the public good.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Today, Americans of all races stand side by side in Berlin and in Viet Nam.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: They died side by side in Korea.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Surely they can work and eat and travel side by side in their own country.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must also lift by legislation the bars of discrimination against those who seek entry into our country, particularly those who have much needed skills and those joining their families.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must advance toward this goal in 1964 in at least 10 different ways, not as partisans, but as patriots.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: First, we must maintain--and our reduced defense budget will maintain--that margin of military safety and superiority obtained through 3 years of steadily increasing both the quality and the quantity of our strategic, our conventional, and our anti-guerrilla forces.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In 1964 we will be better prepared than ever before to defend the cause of freedom, whether it is threatened by outright aggression or by the infiltration practiced by those in Hanoi and Havana, who ship arms and men across international borders to foment insurrection.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And we must continue to use that strength as John Kennedy used it in the Cuban crisis and for the test ban treaty--to demonstrate both the futility of nuclear war and the possibilities of lasting peace.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Second, we must take new steps--and we shall make new proposals at Geneva--toward the control and the eventual abolition of arms.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Even in the absence of agreement, we must not stockpile arms beyond our needs or seek an excess of military power that could be provocative as well as wasteful.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It is in this spirit that in this fiscal year we are cutting back our production of enriched uranium by 25 percent.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We are shutting down four plutonium piles.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We are closing many nonessential military installations.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And it is in this spirit that we today call on our adversaries to do the same.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Third, we must make increased use of our food as an instrument of peace--making it available by sale or trade or loan or donation-- to hungry people in all nations which tell us of their needs and accept proper conditions of distribution.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Fourth, we must assure our pre-eminence in the peaceful exploration of outer space, focusing on an expedition to the moon in this decade-- in cooperation with other powers if possible, alone if necessary.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Fifth, we must expand world trade.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Having recognized in the Act of 1962 that we must buy as well as sell, we now expect our trading partners to recognize that we must sell as well as buy.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We are willing to give them competitive access to our market, asking only that they do the same for us.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Sixth, we must continue, through such measures as the interest equalization tax, as well as the cooperation of other nations, our recent progress toward balancing our international accounts.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This administration must and will preserve the present gold value of the dollar.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Seventh, we must become better neighbors with the free states of the Americas, working with the councils of the OAS, with a stronger Alliance for Progress, and with all the men and women of this hemisphere who really believe in liberty and justice for all.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Eighth, we must strengthen the ability of free nations everywhere to develop their independence and raise their standard of living, and thereby frustrate those who prey on poverty and chaos.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: To do this, the rich must help the poor--and we must do our part.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must achieve a more rigorous administration of our development assistance, with larger roles for private investors, for other industrialized nations, and for international agencies and for the recipient nations themselves.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Ninth, we must strengthen our Atlantic and Pacific partnerships, maintain our alliances and make the United Nations a more effective instrument for national independence and international order.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Tenth, and finally, we must develop with our allies new means of bridging the gap between the East and the West, facing danger boldly wherever danger exists, but being equally bold in our search for new agreements which can enlarge the hopes of all, while violating the interests of none.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In short, I would say to the Congress that we must be constantly prepared for the worst, and constantly acting for the best.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must be strong enough to win any war, and we must be wise enough to prevent one.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We shall neither act as aggressors nor tolerate acts of aggression.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We intend to bury no one, and we do not intend to be buried.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We can fight, if we must, as we have fought before, but we pray that we will never have to fight again.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: My good friends and my fellow Americans: In these last 7 sorrowful weeks, we have learned anew that nothing is so enduring as faith, and nothing is so degrading as hate.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: John Kennedy was a victim of hate, but he was also a great builder of faith--faith in our fellow Americans, whatever their creed or their color or their station in life; faith in the future of man, whatever his divisions and differences.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This faith was echoed in all parts of the world.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: On every continent and in every land to which Mrs.Johnson and I traveled, we found faith and hope and love toward this land of America and toward our people.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: So I ask you now in the Congress and in the country to join with me in expressing and fulfilling that faith in working for a nation, a nation that is free from want and a world that is free from hate--a world of peace and justice, and freedom and abundance, for our time and for all time to come.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: On this Hill which was my home, I am stirred by old friendships.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Though total agreement between the Executive and the Congress is impossible, total respect is important.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I am proud to be among my colleagues of the Congress whose legacy to their trust is their loyalty to their Nation.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I am not unaware of the inner emotions of the new Members of this body tonight.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Twenty-eight years ago, I felt as you do now.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: You will soon learn that you are among men whose first love is their country, men who try each day to do as best they can what they believe is right.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We are entering the third century of the pursuit of American union.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Two hundred years ago, in 1765, nine assembled colonies first joined together to demand freedom from arbitrary power.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: For the first century we struggled to hold together the first continental union of democracy in the history of man.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: One hundred years ago, in 1865, following a terrible test of blood and fire, the compact of union was finally sealed.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: For a second century we labored to establish a unity of purpose and interest among the many groups which make up the American community.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: That struggle has often brought pain and violence.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It is not yet over.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But we have achieved a unity of interest among our people that is unmatched in the history of freedom.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And so tonight, now, in 1965, we begin a new quest for union.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We seek the unity of man with the world that he has built--with the knowledge that can save or destroy him--with the cities which can stimulate or stifle him--with the wealth and the machines which can enrich or menace his spirit.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We seek to establish a harmony between man and society which will allow each of us to enlarge the meaning of his life and all of us to elevate the quality of our civilization.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This is the search that we begin tonight.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: State of the World: But the unity we seek cannot realize its full promise in isolation.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: For today the state of the Union depends, in large measure, upon the state of the world.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our concern and interest, compassion and vigilance, extend to every corner of a dwindling planet.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Yet, it is not merely our concern but the concern of all free men.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We will not, and we should not, assume that it is the task of Americans alone to settle all the conflicts of a torn and troubled world.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Let the foes of freedom take no comfort from this.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: For in concert with other nations, we shall help men defend their freedom.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our first aim remains the safety and the well-being of our own country.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We are prepared to live as good neighbors with all, but we cannot be indifferent to acts designed to injure our interests, or our citizens, or our establishments abroad.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The community of nations requires mutual respect.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We shall extend it--and we shall expect it.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I intend to ask for nothing that is not clearly right and to submit to nothing that is wrong.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And he promised, that the honor of my country shall never be stained by an apology from me for the statement of truth or for the performance of duty.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: That was this Nation's policy in the 1830's and that is this Nation's policy in the 1960's.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our own freedom and growth have never been the final goal of the American dream.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We were never meant to be an oasis of liberty and abundance in a worldwide desert of disappointed dreams.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our Nation was created to help strike away the chains of ignorance and misery and tyranny wherever they keep man less than God means him to be.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We are moving toward that destiny, never more rapidly than we have moved in the last 4 years.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In this period we have built a military power strong enough to meet any threat and destroy any adversary.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And that superiority will continue to grow so long as this office is mine--and you sit on Capitol Hill.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In this period no new nation has become Communist, and the unity of the Communist empire has begun to crumble.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In this period we have resolved in friendship our disputes with our neighbors of the hemisphere, and joined in an Alliance for Progress toward economic growth and political democracy.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In this period we have taken more steps toward peace--including the test ban treaty--than at any time since the cold war began.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In this period we have relentlessly pursued our advances toward the conquest of space.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Most important of all, in this period, the United States has reemerged into the fullness of its self-confidence and purpose.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: No longer are we called upon to get America moving.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We are moving.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: No longer do we doubt our strength or resolution.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We are strong and we have proven our resolve.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
