text: So let us resolve, now, to do all that we can, with what we have-knowing that it is far, far more than we have ever done before, and far, far less than our problems will ultimately require.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Let us create new opportunities for our children and our young Americans who need special help.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We should strengthen the Head Start program, begin it for children 3 years old, and maintain its educational momentum by following through in the early years.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We should try new methods of child development and care from the earliest years, before it is too late to correct.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And I will propose these measures to the 90th Congress.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Let us insure that older Americans, and neglected Americans, share in their Nation's progress.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We should raise social security payments by an overall average of 20 percent.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: That will add $4 billion 100 million to social security payments in the first year.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I will recommend that each of the 23 million Americans now receiving payments get an increase of at least 15 percent.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I will ask that you raise the minimum payments by 59 percent-from $44 to $70 a month, and to guarantee a minimum benefit of $100 a month for those with a total of 25 years of coverage.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must raise the limits that retired workers can earn without losing social security income.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must eliminate by law unjust discrimination in employment because of age.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We should embark upon a major effort to provide self-help assistance to the forgotten in our midst-the American Indians and the migratory farm workers.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And we should reach with the hand of understanding to help those who live in rural poverty.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And I will propose these measures to the 90th Congress.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: So let us keep on improving the quality of life and enlarging the meaning of justice for all of our fellow Americans.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We should transform our decaying slums into places of decency through the landmark Model Cities program.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I intend to seek for this effort, this year, the full amount that you in Congress authorized last year.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We should call upon the genius of private industry and the most advanced technology to help rebuild our great cities.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: throughout this great land.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We should continue to carry to every corner of the Nation our campaign for a beautiful America-to clean up our towns, to make them more beautiful, our cities, our countryside, by creating more parks, and more seashores, and more open spaces for our children to play in, and for the generations that come after us to enjoy.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We should continue to seek equality and justice for each citizen-before a jury, in seeking a job, in exercising his civil rights.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We should find a solution to fair housing, so that every American, regardless of color, has a decent home of his choice.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We should modernize our Selective Service System.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The National Commission on Selective Service will shortly submit its report.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I will send you new recommendations to meet our military manpower needs.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But let us resolve that this is to be the Congress that made our draft laws as fair and as effective as possible.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: #NAME?

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We should outlaw all wiretapping-public and private- wherever and whenever it occurs, except when the security of this Nation itself is at stake-and only then with the strictest governmental safeguards.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: snooping.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I hope this Congress will try to help me do more for the consumer.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We should demand that the cost of credit be clearly and honestly expressed where average citizens can understand it.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We should immediately take steps to prevent massive power failures, to safeguard the home against hazardous household products, and to assure safety in the pipelines that carry natural gas across our Nation.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We should extend Medicare benefits that are now denied to 1,300,000 permanently and totally disabled Americans under 65 years of age.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We should improve the process of democracy by passing our election reform and financing proposals, by tightening our laws regulating lobbying, and by restoring a reasonable franchise to Americans who move their residences.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We should develop educational television into a vital public resource to enrich our homes, educate our families, and to provide assistance in our classrooms.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We should insist that the public interest be fully served through the public's airwaves.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And I will propose these measures to the 90th Congress.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson

text: We also know that this Nation was not forged and did not survive and grow and prosper without a great deal of sacrifice from a great many men.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: those who expect to reap the blessings of freedom must, like men, undergo the fatigues of supporting it.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But let us also count not only our burdens but our blessings-for they are many.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And let us give thanks to the One who governs us all.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Let us draw encouragement from the signs of hope-for they, too, are many.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Let us remember that we have been tested before and America has never been found wanting.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: So with your understanding, I would hope your confidence, and your support, we are going to persist-and we are going to succeed.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I was thinking as I was walking down the aisle tonight of what Sam Rayburn told me many years ago: The Congress always extends a very warm welcome to the President -- as he comes in.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Thank all of you very, very much.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Information of the State of the Union.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I report to you that our country is challenged, at home and abroad: -that it is our will that is being tried, not our strength;

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: our sense of purpose, not our ability to achieve a better America;

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: that we have the strength to meet our every challenge;

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: the physical strength to hold the course of decency and compassion at home;

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: and the moral strength to support the cause of peace in the world.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And I report to you that I believe, with abiding conviction, that this people-nurtured by their deep faith, tutored by their hard lessons, moved by their high aspirations- have the will to meet the trials that these times impose.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Since I reported to you last January: -Three elections have been held in Vietnam-in the midst of war and under the constant threat of violence.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: A President, A Vice President, A House and Senate, and village officials have been chosen by popular, contested ballot.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The enemy has been defeated in battle after battle.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The number of South Vietnamese living in areas under Government protection tonight has grown by more than A million since January of last year.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: These are all marks of progress.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Yet: -The enemy continues to pour men and material across frontiers and into battle, despite his continuous heavy losses.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: He continues to hope that America's will to persevere can be broken.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Well-he is wrong.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: America will persevere.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our patience and our perseverance will match our power.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Aggression will never prevail.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But our goal is peace-and peace at the earliest possible moment.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Right now we are exploring the meaning of Hanoi's recent statement.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: There is no mystery about the questions which must be answered before the bombing is stopped.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We believe that any talks should follow the San Antonio formula that I stated last September, which said: -The bombing would stop immediately if talks would take place promptly and with reasonable hopes that they would be productive.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: and The other side must not take advantage of our restraint as they have in The past.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This Nation simply cannot accept anything less without jeopardizing the lives of our men and of our allies.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: If a basis for peace talks can be established on the San Antonio foundations-and it is my hope and my prayer that they can-we would consult with our allies and with the other side to see if a complete cessation of hostilities-a really true cease-fire-could be made the first order of business.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I will report at the earliest possible moment the results of these explorations to the American people.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I have just recently returned from a very fruitful visit and talks with His Holiness the Pope and I share his hope-as he expressed it earlier today-that both sides will extend themselves in an effort to bring an end to the war in Vietnam.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I have today assured him that we and our allies will do our full part to bring this about.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Since I spoke to you last January, other events have occurred that have major consequences for world peace.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The Kennedy Round achieved The greatest reduction in tariff barriers in all The history of trade negotiations.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The nations of Latin America at Punta del Este resolved to move toward economic integration.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In Asia, the nations from Korea and Japan to Indonesia and Singapore worked behind America's shield to strengthen their economies and to broaden their political cooperation.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: in Africa, from which The distinguished Vice President has just returned, He reports to me that there is A spirit of regional cooperation that is beginning to take hold in very practical ways.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: These events we all welcomed.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Yet since I last reported to you, we and the world have been confronted by a number of crises: -During the Arab-Israeli war last June, the hot line between Washington and Moscow was used for the first time in our history.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: A cease-fire was achieved without a major power confrontation.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Now the nations of the Middle East have the opportunity to cooperate with Ambassador Jarring's U.N. mission and they have the responsibility to find the terms of living

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: together in stable peace and dignity, and we shall do all in our power to help them achieve that result.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Not far from this scene of conflict, a crisis flared on Cyprus involving two peoples who are America's friends: Greece and Turkey.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our very able representative, Mr.Cyrus Vance, and others helped to ease this tension.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Turmoil continues on The mainland of China after A year of violent disruption.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The radical extremism of their Government has isolated the Chinese people behind their own borders.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The United States, however, remains willing to permit the travel of journalists to both our countries;

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: to undertake cultural and educational exchanges;

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: and to talk about the exchange of basic food crop materials.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Since I spoke to you last, the United States and the Soviet Union have taken several important steps toward the goal of international cooperation.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: As you will remember, I met with Chairman Kosygin at Glassboro and we achieved, if not accord, at least a clearer understanding of our respective positions after 2 days of meeting.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Because we believe the nuclear danger must be narrowed, we have worked with the Soviet Union and with other nations to reach an agreement that will halt the spread of nuclear weapons.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: On the basis of communications from Ambassador Fisher in Geneva this afternoon, I am encouraged to believe that a draft treaty can be laid before the conference in Geneva in the very near future.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I hope to be able to present that treaty to the Senate this year for the Senate's approval.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We achieved, in 1967, a consular treaty with the Soviets, the first commercial air agreement between the two countries, and a treaty banning weapons in outer space.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We shall sign, and submit to the Senate shortly, a new treaty with the Soviets and with others for the protection of astronauts.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Serious differences still remain between us, yet in these relations, we have made some progress since Vienna, the Berlin Wall, and the Cuban missile crisis.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But despite this progress, we must maintain a military force that is capable of deterring any threat to this Nation's security, whatever the mode of aggression.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our choices must not be confined to total war- or to total acquiescence.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We have such a military force today.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We shall maintain it.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I wish-with all of my heart-that the expenditures that are necessary to build and to protect our power could all be devoted to the programs of peace.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But until world conditions permit, and until peace is assured, America's might-and America's bravest sons who wear our Nation's uniform-must continue to stand guard for all of us-as they gallantly do tonight in Vietnam and other places in the world.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Yet neither great weapons nor individual courage can provide the conditions of peace.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: For two decades America has committed itself against the tyranny of want and ignorance in the world that threatens the peace.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We shall sustain that commitment.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This year I shall propose: -That we launch, with other nations, an exploration of the ocean depths to tap its wealth, and its energy, and its abundance.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: that we contribute our fair share to A major expansion of The International Development Association, and to increase The resources of The Asian Development Bank.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: that we adopt A prudent aid program, rooted in The principle of self-help.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: that we renew and extend The food for freedom program.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our food programs have already helped millions avoid the horrors of famine.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But unless the rapid growth of population in developing countries is slowed, the gap between rich and poor will widen steadily.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Governments in the developing countries must take such facts into consideration.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We in the United States are prepared to help assist them in those efforts.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But we must also improve the lives of children already born in the villages and towns and cities on this earth.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: They can be taught by great teachers through space communications and the miracle of satellite television- and we are going to bring to bear every resource of mind and technology to help make this dream come true.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Let me speak now about some matters here at home.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Tonight our Nation is accomplishing more for its people than has ever been accomplished before.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Americans are prosperous as men have never been in recorded history.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Yet there is in the land a certain restlessness- a questioning.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The total of our Nation's annual production is now above $800 billion.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: For 83 months this Nation has been on a steady upward trend of growth.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: All about them, most American families can see the evidence of growing abundance: higher paychecks, humming factories, new cars moving down new highways.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: More and more families own their own homes, equipped with more than 70 million television sets.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: A new college is founded every week.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Today more than half of the high school graduates go on to college.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: There are hundreds of thousands of fathers and mothers who never completed grammar school-who will see their children graduate from college.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Why, then, this restlessness? Because when a great ship cuts through the sea, the waters are always stirred and troubled.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And our ship is moving.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It is moving through troubled and new waters; it is moving toward new and better shores.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We ask now, not how can we achieve abundance?-but how shall we use our abundance? Not, is there abundance enough for all?-but, how can all share in our abundance? While we have accomplished much, much remains for us to meet and much remains for us to master.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: in some areas, The jobless rate is still three or four times The national average.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Violence has shown its face in some of our cities.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Crime increases on our streets.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Income for farm workers remains far behind that for urban;

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: and parity for our farmers who produce our food is still just a hope-not an achievement.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: new housing construction is far less than we need-to assure decent shelter for every family.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Hospital and medical costs are high, and they are rising.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Many rivers-and The air in Many cities-remain badly polluted.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And our citizens suffer from breathing that air.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We have lived with conditions like these for many, many years.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But much that we once accepted as inevitable, we now find absolutely intolerable.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In our cities last summer, we saw how wide is the gulf for some Americans between the promise and the reality of our society.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We know that we cannot change all of this in a day.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It represents the bitter consequences of more than three centuries.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But the issue is not whether we can change this; the issue is whether we will change this.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Well, I know we can.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And I believe we will.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This then is the work we should do in the months that are ahead of us in this Congress.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The first essential is more jobs, useful jobs for tens of thousands who can become productive and can pay their own way.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our economy has created 7 1/2 million new jobs in the past 4 years.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It is adding more than a million and a half new jobs this year.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Through programs passed by the Congress, job training is being given tonight to more than a million Americans in this country.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This year, the time has come when we must get to those who are last in line-the hard-core unemployed-the hardest to reach.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Employment officials estimate that 500,000 of these persons are now unemployed in the major cities of America.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our objective is to place these 500,000 in private industry jobs within the next 3 years.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: To do this, I propose a $2.1 billion manpower program in the coming fiscal year-a 25 percent increase over the current year.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Most of this increase will be used to start a new partnership between government and private industry to train and to hire the hard-core unemployed persons.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I know of no task before us of more importance to us, to the country, or to our future.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Another essential is to rebuild our cities.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Last year the Congress authorized $662 million for the Model Cities program.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I requested the full amount of that authorization to help meet the crisis in the cities of America.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But the Congress appropriated only $312 million-less than half.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This year I urge the Congress to honor my request for model cities funds to rebuild the centers of American cities by granting us the full amount that you in the Congress authorized-$1 billion.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The next essential is more housing-and more housing now.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Surely a nation that can go to the moon can place a decent home within the reach of its families.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Therefore we must call together the resources of industry and labor, to start building 300,000 housing units for low- and middle-income families next year-that is three times more than this year.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must make it possible for thousands of families to become homeowners, not rent-payers.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I propose, for the consideration of this Congress, a 10-year campaign to build 6 million new housing units for low- and middle-income families.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Six million units in the next 10 years.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We have built 530,000 the last 10 years.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Better health for our children-all of our children-is essential if we are to have a better America.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Last year, Medicare, Medicaid, and other new programs that you passed in the Congress brought better health to more than 25 million Americans.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: American medicine-with the very strong support and cooperation of public resources-has produced a phenomenal decline in the death rate from many of the dread diseases.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But it is a shocking fact that, in saving the lives of babies, America ranks 15th among the nations of the world.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And among children, crippling defects are often discovered too late for any corrective action.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This is a tragedy that Americans can, and Americans should, prevent.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I shall, therefore, propose to the Congress a child health program to provide, over the next 5 years, for families unable to afford it-access to health services from prenatal care of the mother through the child's first year.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: When we do that you will find it is the best investment we ever made because we will get these diseases in their infancy and we will find a cure in a great many instances that we can never find by overcrowding our hospitals when they are grown.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Now when we act to advance the consumer's cause I think we help every American.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Last year, with very little fanfare the Congress and the executive branch moved in that field.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We enacted the Wholesome Meat Act, the Flammable Fabrics Act, the Product Safety Commission, and a law to improve clinical laboratories.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And now, I think, the time has come to complete our unfinished work.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The Senate has already passed the truth-in-lending bill, the fire safety bill, and the pipeline safety laws.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Tonight I plead with the House to immediately act upon these measures and I hope take favorable action upon all of them.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I call upon the Congress to enact, without delay, the remainder of the 12 vital consumer protection laws that I submitted to the Congress last year.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I also urge final action on a measure that is already passed by the House to guard against fraud and manipulation in the Nation's commodity exchange market.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: These measures are a pledge to our people-to keep them safe in their homes and at work, and to give them a fair deal in the marketplace.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And I think we must do more.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I propose: -New powers for the Federal Trade Commission to stop those who defraud and who swindle our public.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: new safeguards to insure The quality of fish and poultry, and The safety of our community water supplies.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: A major study of automobile insurance.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: protection against hazardous radiation from television sets and other electronic equipment.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And to give the consumer a stronger voice, I plan to appoint a consumer counsel in the Justice Department-a lawyer for the American consumer-to work directly under the Attorney General, to serve the President's Special Assistant for Consumer Affairs, and to serve the consumers of this land.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This Congress-Democrats and Republicans-can earn the thanks of history.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We can make this truly a new day for the American consumer, and by giving him this protection we can live in history as the consumer-conscious Congress.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: So let us get on with the work.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Let us act soon.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We, at every level of the government, State, local, Federal, know that the American people have had enough of rising crime and lawlessness in this country.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: They recognize that law enforcement is first the duty of local police and local government.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: They recognize that the frontline headquarters against crime is in the home, the church, the city hall and the county courthouse and the statehouse-not in the far-removed National Capital of Washington.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But the people also recognize that the National Government can and the National Government should help the cities and the States in their war on crime to the full extent of its resources and its constitutional authority.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And this we shall do.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This does not mean a national police force.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It does mean help and financial support: -to develop State and local master plans to combat crime, -to provide better training and better pay for police, and -to bring the most advanced technology to the war on crime in every city and every county in America.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: There is no more urgent business before this Congress than to pass the Safe Streets Act this year that I proposed last year.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: That law will provide these required funds.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: They are so critically needed that I have doubled my request under this act to $100 million in fiscal 1969.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And I urge the Congress to stop the trade in mail-order murder, to stop it this year by adopting a proper gun control law.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This year, I will propose a Drug Control Act to provide stricter penalties for those who traffic in LSD and other dangerous drugs with our people.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I will ask for more vigorous enforcement of all of our drug laws by increasing the number of Federal drug and narcotics control officials by more than 30 percent.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The time has come to stop the sale of slavery to the young.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I also request you to give us funds to add immediately 100 assistant United States attorneys throughout the land to help prosecute our criminal laws.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We have increased our judiciary by 40 percent and we have increased our prosecutors by 16 percent.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The dockets are full of cases because we don't have assistant district attorneys to go before the Federal judge and handle them.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We start these young lawyers at $8,200 a year.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And the docket is clogged because we don't have authority to hire more of them.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I ask the Congress for authority to hire 100 more.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: These young men will give special attention to this drug abuse, too.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Finally, I ask you to add 100 FBI agents to strengthen law enforcement in the Nation and to protect the individual rights of every citizen.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: A moment ago I spoke of despair and frustrated hopes in the cities where the fires of disorder burned last summer.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We can-and in time we will-change that despair into confidence, and change those frustrations into achievements.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But violence will never bring progress.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We can make progress only by attacking the causes of violence and only where there is civil order founded on justice.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Today we are helping local officials improve their capacity to deal promptly with disorders.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Those who preach disorder and those who preach violence must know that local authorities are able to resist them swiftly, to resist them sternly, and to resist them decisively.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I shall recommend other actions: -To raise the farmers' income by establishing a security commodity reserve that will protect the market from price-depressing stocks and protect the consumer from food scarcity.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I shall recommend programs to help farmers bargain more effectively for fair prices.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I shall recommend programs for new air safety measures.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Measures to stem The rising costs of medical care.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Legislation to encourage our returning veterans to devote themselves to careers in community service such as teaching, and being firemen, and joining our police force, and our law enforcement officials.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I shall recommend programs to strengthen and finance our anti-pollution efforts.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Fully funding all of the $2.18 billion poverty program that you in the Congress had just authorized in order to bring opportunity to those who have been left far behind.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I shall recommend an Educational opportunity Act to speed up our drive to break down The financial barriers that are separating our young people from college.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I shall also urge the Congress to act on several other vital pending bills-especially the civil rights measures-fair jury trials, protection of Federal rights, enforcement of equal employment opportunity, and fair housing.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The unfinished work of the first session must be completed-the Higher Education Act, the Juvenile Delinquency Act, conservation measures to save the redwoods of California, and to preserve the wonders of our scenic rivers, the Highway Beautification Act-and all the other measures for a cleaner, and for a better, and for a more beautiful America.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Next month we'll begin our 8th year of uninterrupted prosperity.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The economic outlook for this year is one of steady growth-if we are vigilant.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: True, there are some clouds on the horizon.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Prices are rising.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Interest rates have passed the peak of 1966; and if there is continued inaction on the tax bill, they will climb even higher.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I warn the Congress and the Nation tonight that this failure to act on the tax bill will sweep us into an accelerating spiral of price increases, a slump in homebuilding, and a continuing erosion of the American dollar.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This would be a tragedy for every American family.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And I predict that if this happens, they will all let us know about it.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We-those of us in the executive branch, in the Congress, and the leaders of labor and business-must do everything we can to prevent that kind of misfortune.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Under the new budget, the expenditures for 1969 will increase by $10.4 billion.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Receipts will increase by $22.3 billion including the added tax revenues.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Virtually all of this expenditure increase represents the mandatory cost of our defense efforts, $3 billion; increased interest, almost $1 billion;

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: or mandatory payments under laws passed by Congress-such as those provided in the Social Security Act that you passed in 1967, and to Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries, veterans, and farmers, of about $4 1/2 billion;

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: and the additional $1 billion 600 million next year for the pay increases that you passed in military and civilian pay.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: That makes up the $10 billion that is added to the budget.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: With few exceptions, very few, we are holding the fiscal 1969 budget to last year's level, outside of those mandatory and required increases.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: A Presidential commission composed of distinguished congressional fiscal leaders and other prominent Americans recommended this year that we adopt a new budget approach.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I am carrying out their recommendations in this year's budget.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This budget, therefore, for the first time accurately covers all Federal expenditures and all Federal receipts, including for the first time in one budget $47 billion from the social security, Medicare, highway, and other trust funds.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The fiscal 1969 budget has expenditures of approximately $186 billion, with total estimated revenues, including the tax bill, of about $178 billion.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: If the Congress enacts the tax increase, we will reduce the budget deficit by some $12 billion.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The war in Vietnam is costing us about $25 billion and we are asking for about $12 billion in taxes-and if we get that $12 billion tax bill we will reduce the deficit from about $20 billion in 1968 to about $8 billion in 1969.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Now, this is a tight budget.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It follows the reduction that I made in cooperation with the Congress-a reduction made after you had reviewed every appropriations bill and reduced the appropriations by some $5 or $6 billion and expenditures by $1.5 billion.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We conferred together and I recommended to the Congress and you subsequently approved taking 2 percent from payrolls and 10 percent from controllable expenditures.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We therefore reduced appropriations almost $10 billion last session and expenditures over $4 billion.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Now, that was in the budget last year.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I ask the Congress to recognize that there are certain selected programs that meet the Nation's most urgent needs and they have increased.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We have insisted that decreases in very desirable but less urgent programs be made before we would approve any increases.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: So I ask the Congress tonight: -to hold its appropriations to the budget requests, and -to act responsibly early this year by enacting the tax surcharge which for the average American individual amounts to about a penny out of each dollar's income.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This tax increase would yield about half of the $23 billion per year that we returned to the people in the tax reduction bills of 1964 and 1965.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This must be a temporary measure, which expires in less than 2 years.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Congress can repeal it sooner if the need has passed.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But Congress can never repeal inflation.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The leaders of American business and the leaders of American labor-those who really have power over wages and prices-must act responsibly, and in their Nation's interest by keeping increases in line with productivity.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: If our recognized leaders do not do this, they and those for whom they speak and all of us are going to suffer very serious consequences.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: On January 1st, I outlined a program to reduce our balance of payments deficit sharply this year.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We will ask the Congress to help carry out those parts of the program which require legislation.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must restore equilibrium to our balance of payments.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must also strengthen the international monetary system.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We have assured the world that America's full gold stock stands behind our commitment to maintain the price of gold at $35 an ounce.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must back this commitment by legislating now to free our gold reserves.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Americans, traveling more than any other people in history, took $4 billion out of their country last year in travel costs.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must try to reduce the travel deficit that we have of more than $2 billion.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We are hoping that we can reduce it by $500 million-without unduly penalizing the travel of teachers, students, business people who have essential and necessary travel, or people who have relatives abroad whom they want to see.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Even with this reduction of $500 million, the American people will still be traveling more overseas than they did in 1967, 1966, or 1965 or any other year in their history.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: If we act together as I hope we can, I believe we can continue our economic expansion which has already broken all past records.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And I hope that we can continue that expansion in the days ahead.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Each of these questions I have discussed with you tonight is a question of policy for our people.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Therefore, each of them should be-and doubtless will be-debated by candidates for public office this year.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I hope those debates will be marked by new proposals and by a seriousness that matches the gravity of the questions themselves.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: These are not appropriate subjects for narrow partisan oratory.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: They go to the heart of what we Americans are all about-all of us, Democrats and Republicans.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Tonight I have spoken of some of the goals I should like to see America reach.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Many of them can be achieved this year- others by the time we celebrate our Nation's 200th birthday-the bicentennial of our independence.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Several of these goals are going to be very hard to reach.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But the State of our Union will be much stronger 8 years from now on our 200th birthday if we resolve to reach these goals now.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: They are more important-much more important-than the identity of the party or the President who will then be in office.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: These goals are what the fighting and our alliances are really meant to protect.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Can we achieve these goals?

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Of course we can-if we will.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: If ever there was a people who sought more than mere abundance, it is our people.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: If ever there was a nation that was capable of solving its problems, it is this Nation.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: If ever there were a time to know the pride and the excitement and the hope of being an American-it is this time.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: So this, my friends, is the State of our Union: seeking, building, tested many times in this past year-and always equal to the test.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Thank you and good night.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: For the sixth and the last time, I present to the Congress my assessment of the State of the Union.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I shall speak to you tonight about challenge and opportunity-and about the commitments that all of us have made together that will, if we carry them out, give America our best chance to achieve the kind of great society that we all want.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Every President lives, not only with what is, but with what has been and what could be.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Most of the great events in his Presidency are part of a larger sequence extending back through several years and extending back through several other administrations.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Urban unrest, poverty, pressures on welfare, education of our people, law enforcement and law and order, the continuing crisis in the Middle East, the conflict in Vietnam, the dangers of nuclear war, the great difficulties of dealing with the Communist powers, all have this much in common: They and their causes-the causes that gave rise to them-all of these have existed with us for many years.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Several Presidents have already sought to try to deal with them.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: One or more Presidents will try to resolve them or try to contain them in the years that are ahead of us.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But if the Nation's problems are continuing, so are this great Nation's assets: -our economy, -the democratic system, -our sense of exploration, symbolized most recently by the wonderful flight of the Apollo 8, in which all Americans took great pride, -the good commonsense and sound judgment of the American people, and -their essential love of justice.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must not ignore our problems.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But neither should we ignore our strengths.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Those strengths are available to sustain a President of either party-to support his progressive efforts both at home and overseas.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Unfortunately, the departure of an administration does not mean the end of the problems that this administration has faced.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The effort to meet the problems must go on, year after year, if the momentum that we have all mounted together in these past years is not to be lost.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Although the struggle for progressive change is continuous, there are times when a watershed is reached-when there is-if not really a break with the past-at least the fulfillment of many of its oldest hopes, and a stepping forth into a new environment, to seek new goals.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I think the past 5 years have been such a time.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We have finished a major part of the old agenda.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Some of the laws that we wrote have already, in front of our eyes, taken on the flesh of achievement.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Medicare that we were unable to pass for so many years is now a part of American life.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Voting rights and the voting booth that we debated so long back in the fifties, and the doors to public service, are open at last to all Americans regardless of their color.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Schools and school children all over America tonight are receiving Federal assistance to go to good schools.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Preschool education-Head Start-is already here to stay and, I think, so are the Federal programs that tonight are keeping more than a million and a half of the cream of our young people in the colleges and the universities of this country.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Part of the American earth-not only in description on a map, but in the reality of our shores, our hills, our parks, our forests, and our mountains-has been permanently set aside for the American public and for their benefit.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And there is more that will be set aside before this administration ends.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Five million Americans have been trained for jobs in new Federal programs.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I think it is most important that we all realize tonight that this Nation is close to full employment--with less unemployment than we have had at any time in almost 20 years.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: That is not in theory; that is in fact.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Tonight, the unemployment rate is down to 3.3 percent.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The number of jobs has grown more than 8 1/2 million in the last 5 years.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: That is more than in all the preceding 12 years.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: These achievements completed the full cycle, from idea to enactment and, finally, to a place in the lives of citizens all across this country.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I wish it were possible to say that everything that this Congress and the administration achieved during this period had already completed that cycle.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But a great deal of what we have committed needs additional funding to become a tangible realization.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Yet the very existence of these commitments- these promises to the American people, made by this Congress and by the executive branch of the Government-are achievements in themselves, and failure to carry through on our commitments would be a tragedy for this Nation.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This much is certain: No one man or group of men made these commitments alone.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Congress and the executive branch, with their checks and balances, reasoned together and finally wrote them into the law of the land.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: They now have all the moral force that the American political system can summon when it acts as one.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: They express America's common determination to achieve goals.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: They imply action.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In most cases, you have already begun that action--but it is not fully completed, of course.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Let me speak for a moment about these commitments.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I am going to speak in the language which the Congress itself spoke when it passed these measures.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I am going to quote from your words.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: improving the quality of urban life is the most critical domestic problem facing the United States.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Two years later it affirmed the historic goal of a decent home for every American family.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: That is your language.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Now to meet these commitments, we must increase our support for the model cities program, where blueprints of change are already being prepared in more than 150 American cities.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: To achieve the goals of the Housing Act of 1968 that you have already passed, we should begin this year more than 500,000 homes for needy families in the coming fiscal year.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Funds are provided in the new budget to do just this.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This is almost 10 times-10 times-the average rate of the past 10 years.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our cities and our towns are being pressed for funds to meet the needs of their growing populations.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: So I believe an urban development bank should be created by the Congress.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This bank could obtain resources through the issuance of taxable bonds and it could then lend these resources at reduced rates to the communities throughout the land for schools, hospitals, parks, and other public facilities.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: make more adequate provision for aged persons through maternal and child welfare and public health.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Those are the words of the Congress-more adequate.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The time has come, I think, to make it more adequate.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I believe we should increase social security benefits, and I am so recommending tonight.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I am suggesting that there should be an overall increase in benefits of at least 13 percent.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Those who receive only the minimum of $55 should get $80 a month.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our Nation, too, is rightfully proud of our medical advances.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But we should remember that our country ranks 15th among the nations of the world in its infant mortality rate.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I think we should assure decent medical care for every expectant mother and for their children during the first year of their life in the United States of America.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I think we should protect our children and their families from the costs of catastrophic illness.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: As we pass on from medicine, I think nothing is clearer to the Congress than the commitment that the Congress made to end poverty.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It is the policy of the United States to eliminate the paradox of poverty in the midst of plenty in this nation.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This is the richest nation in the world.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The antipoverty program has had many achievements.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It also has some failures.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But we must not cripple it after only 3 years of trying to solve the human problems that have been with us and have been building up among us for generations.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I believe the Congress this year will want to improve the administration of the poverty program by reorganizing portions of it and transferring them to other agencies.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I believe, though, it will want to continue, until we have broken the back of poverty, the efforts we are now making throughout this land.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I believe, and I hope the next administration- I believe they believe-that the key to success in this effort is jobs.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It is work for people who want to work.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In the budget for fiscal 1970, I shall recommend a total of $3.5 billion for our job training program, and that is five times as much as we spent in 1964 trying to prepare Americans where they can work to earn their own living.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The Nation's commitment in the field of civil rights began with the Declaration of Independence.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: They were extended by the 13th, 14th, and 15th amendments.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: They have been powerfully strengthened by the enactment of three far-reaching civil rights laws within the past 5 years, that this Congress, in its wisdom, passed.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: On January 1 of this year, the Fair Housing Act of 1968 covered over 20 million American homes and apartments.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The prohibition against racial discrimination in that act should be remembered and it should be vigorously enforced throughout this land.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I believe we should also extend the vital provisions of the Voting Rights Act for another 5 years.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: To assist state and local governments in reducing the incidence of crime.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This year I am proposing that the Congress provide the full $300 million that the Congress last year authorized to do just that.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I hope the Congress will put the money where the authorization is.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I believe this is an essential contribution to justice and to public order in the United States.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I hope these grants can be made to the States and they can be used effectively to reduce the crime rate in this country.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But all of this is only a small part of the total effort that must be made-I think chiefly by the local governments throughout the Nation-if we expect to reduce the toll of crime that we all detest.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Frankly, as I leave the Office of the Presidency, one of my greatest disappointments is our failure to secure passage of a licensing and registration act for firearms.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I think if we had passed that act, it would have reduced the incidence of crime.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I believe that the Congress should adopt such a law, and I hope that it will at a not too distant date.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In order to meet our longstanding commitment to make government as efficient as possible, I believe that we should reorganize our postal system along the lines of the Kappel report.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I hope we can all agree that public service should never impose an unreasonable financial sacrifice on able men and women who want to serve their country.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I believe that the recommendations of the Commission on Executive, Legislative and Judicial Salaries are generally sound.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Later this week, I shall submit a special message which I reviewed with the leadership this evening containing a proposal that has been reduced and has modified the Commission's recommendation to some extent on the congressional salaries.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: For Members of Congress, I will recommend the basic compensation not of the $50,000 unanimously recommended by the Kappel Commission and the other distinguished Members, but I shall reduce that $50,000 to $42,500.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I will suggest that Congress appropriate a very small additional allowance for official expenses, so that Members will not be required to use their salary increase for essential official business.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I would have submitted the Commission's recommendations, except the advice that I received from the leadership-and you usually are consulted about matters that affect the Congress-was that the Congress would not accept the $50,000 recommendation, and if I expected my recommendation to be seriously considered, I should make substantial reductions.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: That is the only reason I didn't go along with the Kappel report.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In 1967 I recommended to the Congress a fair and impartial random selection system for the draft.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I submit it again tonight for your most respectful consideration.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I know that all of us recognize that most of the things we do to meet all of these commitments I talk about will cost money.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: If we maintain the strong rate of growth that we have had in this country for the past 8 years, I think we shall generate the resources that we need to meet these commitments.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We have already been able to increase our support for major social programs-although we have heard a lot about not being able to do anything on the home front because of Vietnam;

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: but we have been able in the last 5 years to increase our commitments for such things as health and education from $30 billion in 1964 to $68 billion in the coming fiscal year.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: That is more than double.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: That is more than it has ever been increased in the 188 years of this Republic, notwithstanding Vietnam.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We must continue to budget our resources and budget them responsibly in a way that will preserve our prosperity and will strengthen our dollar.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Greater revenues and the reduced Federal spending required by Congress last year have changed the budgetary picture dramatically since last January when we made our estimates.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: At that time, you will remember that we estimated we would have a deficit of $8 billion.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Well, I am glad to report to you tonight that the fiscal year ending June 30, 1969, this June, we are going to have not a deficit, but we are going to have a $2.4 billion surplus.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: You will receive the budget tomorrow.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The budget for the next fiscal year, that begins July 1-which you will want to examine very carefully in the days ahead-will provide a $3.4 billion surplus.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This budget anticipates the extension of the surtax that Congress enacted last year.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I have communicated with the President-elect, Mr.Nixon, in connection with this policy of continuing the surtax for the time being.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I want to tell you that both of us want to see it removed just as soon as circumstances will permit, but the President-elect has told me that he has concluded that until his administration, and this Congress, can examine the appropriation bills, and each item in the budget, and can ascertain that the facts justify permitting the surtax to expire or to be reduced, he, Mr.Nixon, will support my recommendation that the surtax be continued.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Americans, I believe, are united in the hope that the Paris talks will bring an early peace to Vietnam.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And if our hopes for an early settlement of the war are realized, then our military expenditures can be reduced and very substantial savings can be made to be used for other desirable purposes, as the Congress may determine.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In any event, I think it is imperative that we do all that we responsibly can to resist inflation while maintaining our prosperity.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I think all Americans know that our prosperity is broad and it is deep, and it has brought record profits, the highest in our history, and record wages.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our gross national product has grown more in the last 5 years than any other period in our Nation's history.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our wages have been the highest.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Our profits have been the best.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This prosperity has enabled millions to escape the poverty that they would have otherwise had the last few years.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I think also you will be very glad to hear that the Secretary of the Treasury informs me tonight that in 1968 in our balance of payments we have achieved a surplus.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It appears that we have, in fact, done better this year than we have done in any year in this regard since the year 1957.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The quest for a durable peace, I think, has absorbed every administration since the end of World War II.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It has required us to seek a limitation of arms races not only among the superpowers, but among the smaller nations as well.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We have joined in the Test Ban Treaty of 1963, the outer space treaty of 1967, and the treaty against the spread of nuclear weapons in 1968.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This latter agreement-the nonproliferation treaty-is now pending in the Senate and it has been pending there since last July.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In my opinion, delay in ratifying it is not going to be helpful to the cause of peace.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: America took the lead in negotiating this treaty and America should now take steps to have it approved at the earliest possible date.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Until a way can be found to scale down the level of arms among the superpowers, mankind cannot view the future without fear and great apprehension.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: So, I believe that we should resume the talks with the Soviet Union about limiting offensive and defensive missile systems.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I think they would already have been resumed except for Czechoslovakia and our election this year.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It was more than 20 years ago that we embarked on a program of trying to aid the developing nations.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We knew then that we could not live in good conscience as a rich enclave on an earth that was seething in misery.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: During these years there have been great advances made under our program, particularly against want and hunger, although we are disappointed at the appropriations last year.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We thought they were woefully inadequate.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: This year I am asking for adequate funds for economic assistance in the hope that we can further peace throughout the world.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I think we must continue to support efforts in regional cooperation.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Among those efforts, that of Western Europe has a very special place in America's concern.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The only course that is going to permit Europe to play the great world role that its resources permit is to go forward to unity.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I think America remains ready to work with a united Europe, to work as a partner on the basis of equality.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: For the future, the quest for peace, I believe, requires: -that we maintain the liberal trade policies that have helped us become the leading nation in world trade, -that we strengthen the international monetary system as an instrument of world prosperity, and -that we seek areas of agreement with the Soviet Union where the interests of both nations and the interests of world peace are properly served.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The strained relationship between us and the world's leading Communist power has not ended-especially in the light of the brutal invasion of Czechoslovakia.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But totalitarianism is no less odious to us because we are able to reach some accommodation that reduces the danger of world catastrophe.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: What we do, we do in the interest of peace in the world.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: We earnestly hope that time will bring a Russia that is less afraid of diversity and individual freedom.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The quest for peace tonight continues in Vietnam, and in the Paris talks.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I regret more than any of you know that it has not been possible to restore peace to South Vietnam.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The prospects, I think, for peace are better today than at any time since North Vietnam began its invasion with its regular forces more than 4 years ago.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The free nations of Asia know what they were not sure of at that time: that America cares about their freedom, and it also cares about America's own vital interests in Asia and throughout the Pacific.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The North Vietnamese know that they cannot achieve their aggressive purposes by force.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: There may be hard fighting before a settlement is reached; but, I can assure you, it will yield no victory to the Communist cause.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I cannot speak to you tonight about Vietnam without paying a very personal tribute to the men who have carried the battle out there for all of us.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I have been honored to be their Commander in Chief.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The Nation owes them its unstinting support while the battle continues-and its enduring gratitude when their service is done.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Finally, the quest for stable peace in the Middle East goes on in many capitals tonight.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: America fully supports the unanimous resolution of the U.N. Security Council which points the way.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: There must be a settlement of the armed hostility that exists in that region of the world today.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: It is a threat not only to Israel and to all the Arab States, but it is a threat to every one of us and to the entire world as well.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Now, my friends in Congress, I want to conclude with a few very personal words to you.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I rejected and rejected and then finally accepted the congressional leadership's invitation to come here to speak this farewell to you in person tonight.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I did that for two reasons.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: One was philosophical.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I wanted to give you my judgment, as I saw it, on some of the issues before our Nation, as I view them, before I leave.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: The other was just pure sentimental.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Most all of my life as a public official has been spent here in this building.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: For 38 years- since I worked on that gallery as a doorkeeper in the House of Representatives-I have known these halls, and I have known most of the men pretty well who walked them.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I know the questions that you face.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I know the conflicts that you endure.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I know the ideals that you seek to serve.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I left here first to become Vice President, and then to become, in a moment of tragedy, the President of the United States.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: My term of office has been marked by a series of challenges, both at home and throughout the world.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In meeting some of these challenges, the Nation has found a new confidence.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: In meeting others, it knew turbulence and doubt, and fear and hate.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Throughout this time, I have been sustained by my faith in representative democracy- a faith that I had learned here in this Capitol Building as an employee and as a Congressman and as a Senator.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I believe deeply in the ultimate purposes of this Nation-described by the Constitution, tempered by history, embodied in progressive laws, and given life by men and women that have been elected to serve their fellow citizens.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Now for 5 most demanding years in the White House, I have been strengthened by the counsel and the cooperation of two great former Presidents, Harry S.Truman and Dwight David Eisenhower.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I have been guided by the memory of my pleasant and close association with the beloved John F. Kennedy, and with our greatest modern legislator, Speaker Sam Rayburn.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I have been assisted by my friend every step of the way, Vice President Hubert Humphrey.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I am so grateful that I have been supported daily by the loyalty of Speaker McCormack and Majority Leader Albert.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I have benefited from the wisdom of Senator Mike Mansfield, and I am sure that I have avoided many dangerous pitfalls by the good commonsense counsel of the President Pro Tem of the Senate, Senator Richard Brevard Russell.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I have received the most generous cooperation from the leaders of the Republican Party in the Congress of the United States, Senator Dirksen and Congressman Gerald Ford, the Minority Leader.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: No President should ask for more, although I did upon occasions.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But few Presidents have ever been blessed with so much.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: President-elect Nixon, in the days ahead, is going to need your understanding, just as I did.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: And he is entitled to have it.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I hope every Member will remember that the burdens he will bear as our President, will be borne for all of us.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Each of us should try not to increase these burdens for the sake of narrow personal or partisan advantage.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: Now, it is time to leave.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: I hope it may be said, a hundred years from now, that by working together we helped to make our country more just, more just for all of its people, as well as to insure and guarantee the blessings of liberty for all of our posterity.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: That is what I hope.

speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
text: But I believe that at least it will be said that we tried.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: To address a joint session of Congress in this great Chamber in which I was once privileged to serve is an honor for which I am deeply grateful.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The State of the Union Address is traditionally an occasion for a lengthy and detailed account by the President of what he has accomplished in the past, what he wants the Congress to do in the future, and, in an election year, to lay the basis for the political issues which might be decisive in the fall.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Occasionally there comes a time when profound and far-reaching events command a break with tradition.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This is such a time.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I say this not only because 1970 marks the beginning of a new decade in which America will celebrate its 200th birthday.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I say it because new knowledge and hard experience argue persuasively that both our programs and our institutions in American need to be reformed.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The moment has arrived to harness the vast energies and abundance of this land to the creation of a new American experience, an experience richer and deeper and more truly a reflection of the goodness and grace of the human spirit.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The seventies will be a time of new beginnings, a time of exploring both on the earth and in the heavens, a time of discovery.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But the time has also come for emphasis on developing better ways of managing what we have and completing what man's genius has begun but left unfinished.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Our land, this land that is ours together, is a great and a good land.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It is also an unfinished land, and the challenge of perfecting it is the summons of the seventies.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It is in that spirit that I address myself to those great issues facing our Nation which are above partisanship.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: When we speak of America's priorities the first priority must always be peace for America and the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The major immediate goal of our foreign policy is to bring an end to the war in Vietnam in a way that out generation will be remembered -- not so much as the generation that suffered in war, but more for the fact that we had the courage and character to win the kind of a just peace that the next generation was able to keep.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We are making progress toward that goal.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The prospects for peace are far greater today they were a year ago.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: A major part of the credit for this development goes to the Members of this Congress who, despite their differences on the conduct of the war, have overwhelmingly indicated their support of a just peace.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: By this action, you have completely demolished the enemy's hopes that they can gain in Washington the victory our fighting men have denied them in Vietnam.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: No goal could be greater than to make the next generation the first in this century in which America was at peace with every nation in the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I shall discuss in detail the new concepts and programs designed to achieve this goal in a separate report on foreign policy, which I will submit to the Congress at a later date.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Today, let me describe the direction of our new policies.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We have based our policies on an evaluation of the world as it is, not as it was 25 years ago at the conclusion of World War II.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Many of the policies which were necessary and right then are obsolete today.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Then, because of America's overwhelming military and economic strength, because of the weakness of other major free world powers and the inability of scores of newly independent nations to defend, or even govern, themselves, America had to assume the major burden for the defense of the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In two wars, first in Korea and now in Vietnam, we furnished most of the money, most of the arms, most of the men to help other nations defend their freedom.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Today the great industrial nations of Europe, as well as Japan, have regained their economic strength;

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: and the nations of Latin America -- and many of the nations who acquired their freedom from colonialism after World War II in Asia and Africa -- have a new sense of pride and dignity and a determination to assume the responsibility for their own defense.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: That is the basis of the doctrine I announced at Guam.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Neither the defense nor the development of other nations can be exclusively or primarily an American undertaking.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The nations of each part of the world should assume the primary responsibility for their own well-being; and they themselves should determine the terms of that well-being.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We shall be faithful to our treaty commitments, but we shall reduce our involvement and our presence in other nations' affairs.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: To insist that other nations play a role is not a retreat from responsibility; it is a sharing of responsibility.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The results of this new policy has been not to weaken our alliances, but to give then new life, new strength, a new sense of common purpose.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Relations with our European allies are once again strong and healthy, based on mutual consultation and mutual responsibility.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We have initiated a new approach to Latin America in which we deal with those nations as partners rather than patrons.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The new partnership concept has been welcomed in Asia.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We have developed an historic new basis for Japanese-American friendship and cooperation, which is the linchpin for peace in the Pacific.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: If we are to have peace in the last third of the century, a major factor will be the development of a new relationship between the United States and the Soviet Union.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I would not underestimate our differences, but we are moving with precision and purpose from an era of confrontation to an era of negotiation.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
