text: Our negotiations on strategic arms limitations and in other areas will have far greater chance for success if both sides enter them motivated by mutual self-interest rather than na

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It is with this same spirit that we have resumed discussions with Communist China in our talks at Warsaw.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Our concern in our relations with both these nations is to avoid a catastrophic collision and to build a solid basis for peaceful settlement of our differences.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I would be the last to suggest that the road to peace is not difficult and dangerous, but I believe our new policies have contributed to the prospect that America may have the best chance since World War II to enjoy a generation of uninterrupted peace.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And that chance will be enormously increased if we continue to have a relationship between Congress and the Executive in which, despite differences in detail, where the security of America and the peace of mankind are concerned, we act not as Republicans, not as Democrats, but as Americans.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As we move into the decade of the seventies, we have the greatest opportunity for progress at home of any people in world history.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Our gross nation product will increase by $500 billion in the next 10 years.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This increase alone is greater than the entire growth of the American economy from 1790 to 1950.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The critical question is not whether we will grow, but how we will use that growth.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The decade of the sixties was also a period of great growth economically.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But in that same 10-year period we witnessed the greatest growth of crime, the greatest increase of inflation, the greatest social unrest in America in 100 years.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Never has a nation seemed to have had more and enjoyed it less.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: At hear, the issue is the effectiveness of government.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Ours has become -- as it continues to be, and should remain -- a society of large expectation.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Government helped to generate these expectations.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It undertook to meet them.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Yet, increasingly, it proved unable to do so.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As a people, we had too many visions -- and too little vision.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Now, as we enter the seventies, we should enter also a great age of reform of the institutions of American government.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Our purpose in this period should not be simply better management of the programs of the past.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The time has come for a new quest -- a quest not for a greater quantity of what we have, but for a new quality of life in America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: A major part of the substance for an unprecedented advance in this Nation's approach to its problems and opportunities is contained in more than two score legislative proposals which I sent to the Congress last year and which still await enactment.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I will offer at least a dozen more major programs in the course of this session.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: At this point I do not intend to do through a detailed listing of what I have proposed or will propose, but I would like to mention three areas in which urgent priorities demand that we move and move now: First, we cannot delay longer in accomplishing a total reform of our welfare system.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: When a system penalizes work, breaks up homes, robs recipients of dignity, there is no alternative to abolishing that system and adopting in its place the program of income support, job training, and work incentives which I recommended to the Congress last year.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Second, the time has come to assess and reform all of our institutions of government at the Federal, State, and local level.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It is time for a New Federalism, in which, after 190 years of power flowing from the people and local and State governments to Washington, D.C., it will begin to flow from Washington back to the States and to the people of the United States.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Third, we must adopt reforms which will expand the range of opportunities for all Americans.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We can fulfill the American dream only when each person has a fair chance to fulfill his own dreams.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This means equal voting rights, equal employment opportunity, and new opportunities for expanded ownership.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Because in order to be secure in their human rights, people need access to property rights.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I could give similar examples of the need for reform in our programs for health, education, housing, transportation, as well as other critical areas which directly affect the well-being of millions of Americans.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The people of the United States should wait no longer for these reforms that would so deeply enhance the quality of their life.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: When I speak of actions which would be beneficial to the American people, I can think of none more important than for the Congress to join this administration in the battle to stop the rise in the cost of living.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Now, I realize it is tempting to blame someone else for inflation.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Some blame business for raising prices.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Some blame unions for asking for more wages.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But a review of the stark fiscal facts of the 1960's clearly demonstrates where the primary blame for rising prices must be placed, In the decade of the sixties the Federal Government spent $57 billion more than it took in in taxes.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In that same decade the American people paid the bill for that deficit in price increases which raised the cost of living for the average family of four by $200 per month in America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Now millions of Americans are forced to go into debt today because the Federal Government decided to go into debt yesterday.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We must balance our Federal budget so that American families will have a better chance to balance their family budgets.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Only with the cooperation of the Congress can we meet this highest priority objective of responsible government.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We are on the right track.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We had a balanced budget in 1969.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This administration cut more than $7 billion out of spending plans in order to produce a surplus in 1970, and in spite of the fact that Congress reduced revenues by $3 billion, I shall recommend a balanced budget for 1971.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But I can assure you that not only to present, but to stay within, a balanced budget requires some very hard decisions.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It means rejecting spending programs which would benefit some of the people when their net effect would result in price increases for all the people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It is time to quit putting money into bad programs.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Otherwise, we will end up with bad money and bad programs.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I recognize the political popularity of spending programs, and particularly in an election year.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But unless we stop the rise in prices, the cost of living for millions of American families will become unbearable and government's ability to plan programs for progress for the future will become impossible.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In referring to budget cuts, there is one area where I have ordered an increase rather than a cut -- and that is the requests of those agencies with the responsibilities for law enforcement.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We have a tragic example of this problem in the Nation's Capital, for whose safety the Congress and the Executive have the primary responsibility.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I doubt if many Members of this Congress who life more than a few blocks from here would dare leave their cars in the Capital garage and walk home alone tonight.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Last year this administration sent to the Congress 13 separate pieces of legislation dealing with organized crime, pornography, street crime, narcotics, crime in the District of Columbia.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: None of these bills has reached my desk for signature.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I am confident that the Congress will act now to adopt the legislation I placed before you last year.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We in the Executive have done everything we can under existing law, but new and stronger weapons are needed in that fight.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: While it is true that State and local law enforcement agencies are the cutting edge in the effort to eliminate street crime, burglaries, murder, my proposals to you have embodied my belief that the Federal Government should play a greater role in working in partnership with these agencies.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: That is why 1971 Federal spending for local law enforcement will double that budgeted for 1970.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The primary responsibility for crimes that affect individuals is with local and State rather than with Federal Government.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But in the field of organized crime, narcotics, pornography, the Federal Government has a special responsibility it should fulfill.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And we should make Washington, D.C., where we have the primary responsibility, an example to the Nation and the world of respect for law rather than lawlessness.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I now turn to a subject which, next to our desire for peace, may well become the major concern of the American people in the decade of the seventies.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In the next 10 years we shall increase our wealth by 50 percent.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The profound question is: Does this mean we will be 50 percent richer in a real sense.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: 50 percent better off, 50 percent happier?

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Or does it mean that in the year 1980 the President standing in this place will look back on a decade in which 70 percent of our people lived in metropolitan areas choked by traffic, suffocated by smog, poisoned by water, deafened by noise, and terrorized by crime?

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: These are not the great questions that concern world leaders at summit conferences.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But people do not live at the summit.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: They life in the foothills of everyday experience, and it is time for all of us to concern ourselves with the way real people live in real life.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The great question of the seventies is, shall we surrender to our surroundings, or shall we make our peace with nature and begin to make reparations for the damage we have done to our air, to our land, and to our water?

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Restoring nature to its natural state is a cause beyond party and beyond factions.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It has become a common cause of all the people of this country.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It is a cause of particular concern to young Americans, because they more than we will reap the grim consequences of our failure to act on programs which are needed now if we are to prevent disaster later.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Clean air, clean water, open spaces -- these should once again be the birthright of every American.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: If we act now, they can be.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We still think of air as free.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But clean air is not free, and neither is clean water.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The price tag on pollution control is high.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Through our years of past carelessness we incurred a debt to nature, and now that debt is being called.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The program I shall propose to Congress will be the most comprehensive and costly program in this field in America's history.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It is not a program for just one year.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: A year's plan in this field is not plan at all.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This is a time to look ahead not a year, but 5 years or 10 years -- whatever time is required to do the job.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I shall propose to this Congress a $10 billion nationwide clean waters program to put modern municipal waste treatment plants in every place in America where they are needed to make our waters clean again, and do it now.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We have the industrial capacity, if we begin now, to build all within 5 years.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This program will get them built within 5 years.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As our cities and suburbs relentlessly expand, those priceless open spaces needed for recreation areas accessible to their people are swallowed up -- often forever.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Unless we preserve these spaces while they are still available, we will have none to preserve.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Therefore, I shall propose now financing methods for purchasing open space and parklands now, before they are lost to us.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The automobile is our worst polluter of the air.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Adequate control requires further advances in engine design and fuel composition.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We shall intensify our research, set increasingly strict standards, and strengthen enforcement procedures -- and we shall do it now.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We can no longer afford to consider air and water common property, free to be abused by anyone without regard to the consequences.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Instead, we should begin now to treat them as scarce resources, which we are no more free to contaminate than we are free to throw garbage into our neighbor's yard.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This requires that the argument is often made that there is a fundamental contradiction between economic growth and the quality of life, so that to have one we must forsake the other.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The answer is not to abandon growth, but to redirect it.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: For example, we should turn toward ending congestion and eliminating smog the same reservoir of inventive genius that created them in the first place.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Continued vigorous economic growth provides us with the means to enrich life itself and to enhance our planet as a place hospitable to man.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Each individual must enlist in this fight if it is to be won.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It has been said that no matter how many national parks and historical monuments we buy and develop, the truly significant environment for each of us is that in which we spend 80 percent of our time -- in our homes, in our places of work, the streets over which we travel.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Street litter, rundown parking strips and yards, dilapidated fences, broken windows, smoking automobiles, dingy working places, all should be the object of our fresh view.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We have been too tolerant of our surroundings and too willing to leave it to others to clean up our environment.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It is time for those who make massive demands on society to make some minimal demands on themselves.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Each of us must resolve that each day he will leave his home, his property, the public places of the city or town a little cleaner, a little better, a little more pleasant for himself and those around him.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: With the help of people we can do anything, and without their help, we can do nothing.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In this spirit, together, we can reclaim our land for ours and generations to come.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Between now and the year 2000, over 100 million children will be born in the United States.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Where they grown up -- and how -- will, more than any one thing, measure the quality of American life in these years ahead.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This should be a warning to us.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: For the past 30 years our population has also been growing and shifting.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The result is exemplified in the vast areas of rural America emptying out of people and promise -- a third of our counties lost population in the sixties.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The violent and decayed central cities of our great metropolitan complexes are the most conspicuous area of failure in American life today.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I propose that before these problems become insoluble, the Nation develop a national growth policy.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In the future, government decisions as to where to build highways, locate airports, acquire land, or sell land should be made with a clear objective of aiding a balanced growth for America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In particular, the Federal Government must be in a position to assist in the building of new cities and the rebuilding of old ones.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: At the same time, we will carry our concern with the quality of late in America to the farm as well as the suburb, to the village as well as to the city.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: What rural America needs most is a new kind of assistance.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It needs to be dealt with, not as a separate nation, but as part of an overall growth policy for America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We must create a new rural environment which will not only stem the migration to urban centers, but reverse it.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: If we seize our growth as a challenge, we can make the 1970's an historic period when by conscious choice we transformed our land into what we want it to become.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: America, which has pioneered in the new abundance, and in the new technology, is called upon today to pioneer in meeting the concerns which have followed in their wake -- in turning the wonders of science to the service of man.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In the majesty of this great Chamber we hear the echoes of America's history, of debates that rocked the Union and those that repaired it, of the summons to war and the search for peace, of the uniting of the people, the building of a nation.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Those echoes of history remind us of our roots and our strengths.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: They remind us also of that special genius of American democracy, which at one critical turning point after another has led us to spot the new road to the future and given us the wisdom and the courage to take it.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As I look down the new road which I have tried to map out today, I see a new America as we celebrate our 200th anniversary 6 years from now.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I see an America in which we have abolished hunger, provided the means for every family in the Nation to obtain a minimum income, made enormous progress in providing better housing, faster transportation, improved health, and superior education.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I see an America in which we have made great strides in stopping the pollution of our air, cleaning up our water, opening up our parks, continuing to explore space.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Most important, I see an America at peace with all the nations of the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This is not an impossible dream.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: These goals are all within our reach.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In times past, our forefathers had the vision but not the means to achieve such goals.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let it not be recorded that we were the first American generation that had the means but not the vision to make this dream come true.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But let us, above all, recognize a fundamental truth.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We can be the best clothed, best fed, best housed people in the world, enjoying clean air, clean water, beautiful parks, but we could still be the unhappiest people in the world without an indefinable spirit -- the lift of a driven dream which has made America, from its beginning, the hope of the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Two hundred years ago this was a new nation of 3 million people, weak militarily, poor economically.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But America meant something to the world then which could not be measured in dollars, something far more important than military might.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: for ourselves alone, but for the whole human race.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We had a spiritual quality then which caught the imagination of millions of people in the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Today, when we are the richest and strongest nation in the world, let it not be recorded that we lacked the moral and spiritual idealism which made us the hope of the world at the time of our birth.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The demands of us in 1976 are even greater than in 1776.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It is no longer enough to live and let live.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Now we must live and help live.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We need a fresh climate in America, one in which a person can breathe freely and breathe in freedom.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Our recognition of the truth that wealth and happiness are not the same thing requires us to measure success or failure by new criteria.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Even more than the programs I have described today, what this Nation needs is an example from its elected leaders in providing the spiritual and moral leadership which no programs for material progress can satisfy.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Above all, let us inspire young Americans with a sense of excitement, a sense of destiny, a sense of involvement, in meeting the challenges we face in this great period of our history.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Only then are they going to have any sense of satisfaction in their lives.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The greatest privilege an individual can have is to server in a cause bigger than himself.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We have such a cause.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: How we seize the opportunities I have described today will determine not only our future, but the future of peace and freedom in this world in the last third of the century.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: May God give us the wisdom, the strength and, above all, the idealism to be worthy of that challenge, so that America can fulfill its destiny of being the world's best hope for liberty, for opportunity, for progress and peace for all peoples.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As this 92d Congress begins its session, America has lost a great Senator, and all of us who had the privilege to know him have lost a loyal friend.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I had the privilege of visiting Senator Russell in the hospital just a few days before he died.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: He never spoke about himself.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: He only spoke eloquently about the need for a strong national defense.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In tribute to one of the most magnificent Americans of all time, I respectfully ask that all those here will rise in silent prayer for Senator Russell.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Thank you.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Mr. Speaker, before I begin my formal address, I want to use this opportunity to congratulate all of those who were winners in the rather for leadership positions in the House and winners in the Senate and, also, to express my condolences to the losers.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I know how both of you feel.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And I particularly want to join with all of the Members of the House and the Senate as well in congratulating the new Speaker of the United States Congress.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: To those new Members of this House who may have some doubts about the possibilities for advancement in the years ahead, I would remind you that the Speaker and I met just 24 years ago in this Chamber as freshmen Members of the 80th Congress.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As you see, we both have come up in the world a bit since then.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Mr. Speaker, this 92d Congress has a chance to be recorded as the greatest Congress in America's history.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In these troubled years just past, America has been going through a long nightmare of war and division, of crime and inflation.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Even more deeply, we have gone through a long, dark night of the American spirit.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But now that night is ending.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Now we must let our spirits soar again.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Now we are ready for the lift of a driving dream.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The people of this Nation are eager to get on with the quest for new greatness.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: They see challenges, and they are prepared to meet those challenges.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It is for us here to open the doors that will set free again the real greatness of this Nation-- the genius of the American people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: How shall we meet this challenge?

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: How can we truly open the doors, and set free the full genius of our people?

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The way in which the 92d Congress answers these questions will determine its place in history.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: More importantly, it can determine this Nation's place in history as we enter the third century of our independence.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Tonight I shall present to the Congress six great goals.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I shall ask not simply for more new programs in the old framework.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I shall ask to change the framework of government itself--to reform the entire structure of American government so we can make it again fully responsive to the needs and the wishes of the American people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: If we act boldly--if we seize this moment and achieve these goals--we can close the gap between promise and performance in American government.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We can bring together the resources of this Nation and the spirit of the American people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In discussing these great goals, I shall deal tonight only with matters on the domestic side of the Nation's agenda.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I shall make a separate report to the Congress and the Nation next month on developments in foreign policy.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The first of these great goals is already before the Congress.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I urge that the unfinished business of the 91st Congress be made the first priority business of the 92d Congress.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Over the next 2 weeks, I will call upon Congress to take action on more than 35 pieces of proposed legislation on which action was not completed last year.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The most important is welfare reform.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The present welfare system has become a monstrous, consuming outrage--an outrage against the community, against the taxpayer, and particularly against the children it is supposed to help.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We may honestly disagree, as we do, on what to do about it.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But we can all agree that we must meet the challenge, not by pouring more money into a bad program, but by abolishing the present welfare system and adopting a new one.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: So let us place a floor under the income of every family with children in America-- and without those demeaning, soul-stifling affronts to human dignity that so blight the lives of welfare children today.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But let us also establish an effective work incentive and an effective work requirement.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let us provide the means by which more can help themselves.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This shall be our goal.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let us generously help those who are not able to help themselves.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But let us stop helping those who are able to help themselves but refuse to do so.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The second great goal is to achieve what Americans have not enjoyed since 1957--full prosperity in peacetime.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The tide of inflation has turned.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The rise in the cost of living, which had been gathering dangerous momentum in the late sixties, was reduced last year.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Inflation will be further reduced this year.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But as we have moved from runaway inflation toward reasonable price stability and at the same time as we have been moving from a wartime economy to a peacetime economy, we have paid a price in increased unemployment.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We should take no comfort from the fact that the level of unemployment in this transition from a wartime to a peacetime economy is lower than in any peacetime year of the sixties.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This is not good enough for the man who is unemployed in the seventies.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We must do better for workers in peacetime and we will do better.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: To achieve this, I will submit an expansionary budget this year--one that will help stimulate the economy and thereby open up new job opportunities for millions of Americans.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It will be a full employment budget, a budget designed to be in balance if the economy were operating at its peak potential.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: By spending as if we were at full employment, we will help to bring about full employment.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I ask the Congress to accept these expansionary policies--to accept the concept of a full employment budget.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: At the same time, I ask the Congress to cooperate in resisting expenditures that go beyond the limits of the full employment budget.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: For as we wage a campaign to bring about a widely shared prosperity, we must not reignite the fires of inflation and so undermine that prosperity.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: With the stimulus and the discipline of a full employment budget, with the commitment of the independent Federal Reserve System to provide fully for the monetary needs of a growing economy, and with a much greater effort on the part of labor and management to make their wage and price decisions in the light of the national interest and their own self-interest-- then for the worker, the farmer, the consumer, for Americans everywhere we shall gain the goal of a new prosperity: more jobs, more income, more profits, without inflation and without war.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This is a great goal, and one that we can achieve together.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The third great goal is to continue the effort so dramatically begun last year: to restore and enhance our natural environment.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Building on the foundation laid in the 37-point program that I submitted to Congress last year, I will propose a strong new set of initiatives to clean up our air and water, to combat noise, and to preserve and restore our surroundings.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I will propose programs to make better use of our land, to encourage a balanced national growth--growth that will revitalize our rural heartland and enhance the quality of life in America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And not only to meet today's needs but to anticipate those of tomorrow, I will put forward the most extensive program ever proposed by a President of the United States to expand the Nation's parks, recreation areas, open spaces, in a way that truly brings parks to the people where the people are.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: For only if we leave a legacy of parks will the next generation have parks to enjoy.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As a fourth great goal, I will offer a far-reaching set of proposals for improving America's health care and making it available more fairly to more people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I will propose: A program to insure that no American family will be prevented from obtaining basic medical care by inability to pay.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I will propose a major increase in and redirection of aid to medical schools, to greatly increase the number of doctors and other health personnel.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Incentives to improve the delivery of health services, to get more medical care resources into those areas that have not been adequately served, to make greater use of medical assistants, and to slow the alarming rise in the costs of medical care.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: New programs to encourage better preventive medicine, by attacking the causes of disease and injury, and by providing incentives to doctors to keep people well rather than just to treat them when they are sick.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I will also ask for an appropriation of an extra $100 million to launch an intensive campaign to find a cure for cancer, and I will ask later for whatever additional funds can effectively be used.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The time has come in America when the same kind of concentrated effort that split the atom and took man to the moon should be turned toward conquering this dread disease.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let us make a total national commitment to achieve this goal.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: America has long been the wealthiest nation in the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Now it is time we became the healthiest nation in the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The fifth great goal is to strengthen and to renew our State and local governments.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As we approach our 200th anniversary in 1976, we remember that this Nation launched itself as a loose confederation of separate States, without a workable central government.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: At that time, the mark of its leaders' vision was that they quickly saw the need to balance the separate powers of the States with a government of central powers.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And so they gave us a constitution of balanced powers, of unity with diversity-- and so clear was their vision that it survives today as the oldest written constitution still in force in the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: For almost two centuries since--and dramatically in the 1930's--at those great turning points when the question has been between the States and the Federal Government, that question has been resolved in favor of a stronger central Federal Government.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: During this time the Nation grew and the Nation prospered.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But one thing history tells us is that no great movement goes in the same direction forever.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Nations change, they adapt, or they slowly die.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The time has now come in America to reverse the flow of power and resources from the States and communities to Washington, and start power and resources flowing back from Washington to the States and communities and, more important, to the people all across America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The time has come for a new partnership between the Federal Government and the States and localities--a partnership in which we entrust the States and localities with a larger share of the Nation's responsibilities, and in which we share our Federal revenues with them so that they can meet those responsibilities.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: To achieve this goal, I propose to the Congress tonight that we enact a plan of revenue sharing historic in scope and bold in concept.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: All across America today, States and cities are confronted with a financial crisis.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Some have already been cutting back on essential services--for example, just recently San Diego and Cleveland cut back on trash collections.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Most are caught between the prospects of bankruptcy on the one hand and adding to an already crushing tax burden on the other.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As one indication of the rising costs of local government, I discovered the other day that my home town of Whittier, California-- which has a population of 67,000-- has a larger budget for 1971 than the entire Federal budget was in 1791.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Now the time has come to take a new direction, and once again to introduce a new and more creative balance to our approach to government.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: So let us put the money where the needs are.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And let us put the power to spend it where the people are.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I propose that the Congress make a $16 billion investment in renewing State and local government.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Five billion dollars of this will be in new and unrestricted funds to be used as the States and localities see fit.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The other $11 billion will be provided by allocating $1 billion of new funds and converting one-third of the money going to the present narrow-purpose aid programs into Federal revenue sharing funds for six broad purposes--for urban development, rural development, education, transportation, job training, and law enforcement-- but with the States and localities making their own decisions on how it should be spent within each category.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: For the next fiscal year, this would increase total Federal aid to the States and localities more than 25 percent over the present level.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The revenue sharing proposals I send to the Congress will include the safeguards against discrimination that accompany all other Federal funds allocated to the States.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Neither the President nor the Congress nor the conscience of this Nation can permit money which comes from all the people to be used in a way which discriminates against some of the people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The Federal Government will still have a large and vital role to play in achieving our national progress.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Established functions that are clearly and essentially Federal in nature will still be performed by the Federal Government.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: New functions that need to be sponsored or performed by the Federal Government--such as those I have urged tonight in welfare and health--will be added to the Federal agenda.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Whenever it makes the best sense for us to act as a whole nation, the Federal Government should and will lead the way.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But where States or local governments can better do what needs to be done, let us see that they have the resources to do it there.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Under this plan, the Federal Government will provide the States and localities with more money and less interference-- and by cutting down the interference the same amount of money will go a lot further.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let us share our resources.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let us share them to rescue the States and localities from the brink of financial crisis.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let us share them to give homeowners and wage earners a chance to escape from ever-higher property taxes and sales taxes.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let us share our resources for two other reasons as well.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The first of these reasons has to do with government itself, and the second has to do with each of us, with the individual.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let's face it.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Most Americans today are simply fed up with government at all levels.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: They will not--and they should not--continue to tolerate the gap between promise and performance in government.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The fact is that we have made the Federal Government so strong it grows muscle bound and the States and localities so weak they approach impotence.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: If we put more power in more places, we can make government more creative in more places.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: That way we multiply the number of people with the ability to make things happen--and we can open the way to a new burst of creative energy throughout America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The final reason I urge this historic shift is much more personal, for each and for every one of us.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As everything seems to have grown bigger and more complex in America, as the forces that shape our lives seem to have grown more distant and more impersonal, a great feeling of frustration has crept across this land.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Things are in the saddle, and ride mankind.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Millions of frustrated young Americans today are crying out--asking not what will government do for me, but what can I do, how can I contribute, how can I matter? And so let us answer them.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We hear you.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We will give you a chance.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We are going to give you a new chance e more to say about the decisions that affect your future--a chance to participate in government--because we are going to provide more centers of power where what you do can make a difference that you can see and feel in your own life and the life of your whole community.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The further away government is from people, the stronger government becomes and the weaker people become.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And a nation with a strong government and a weak people is an empty shell.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I reject the patronizing idea that government in Washington, D.C., is inevitably more wise, more honest, and more efficient than government at the local or State level.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The honesty and efficiency of government depends on people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Government at all levels has good people and bad people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And the way to get more good people into government is to give them more opportunity to do good things.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The idea that a bureaucratic elite in Washington knows best what is best for people everywhere and that you cannot trust local governments is really a contention that you cannot trust people to govern themselves.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This notion is completely foreign to the American experience.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Local government is the government closest to the people, it is most responsive to the individual person.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It is people's government in a far more intimate way than the Government in Washington can ever be.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: People came to America because they wanted to determine their own future rather than to live in a country where others determined their future for them.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: What this change means is that once again in America we are placing our trust in people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I have faith in people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I trust the judgment of people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let us give the people of America a chance, a bigger voice in deciding for themselves those questions that so greatly affect their lives.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The sixth great goal is a complete reform of the Federal Government itself.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Based on a long and intensive study with the aid of the best advice obtainable, I have concluded that a sweeping reorganization of the executive branch is needed if the Government is to keep up with the times and with the needs of the people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I propose, therefore, that we reduce the present 12 Cabinet Departments to eight.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I propose that the Departments of State, Treasury, Defense, and Justice remain, but that all the other departments be consolidated into four: Human Resources, Community Development, Natural Resources, and Economic Development.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let us look at what these would be: First, a department dealing with the concerns of people--as individuals, as members of a family--a department focused on human needs.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Second, a department concerned with the community--rural communities and urban communities-- and with all that it takes to make a community function as a community.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Third, a department concerned with our physical environment, with the preservation and balanced use of those great natural resources on which our Nation depends.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And fourth, a department concerned with our prosperity--with our jobs, our businesses, and those many activities that keep our economy running smoothly and well.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Under this plan, rather than dividing up our departments by narrow subjects, we would organize them around the great purposes of government.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Rather than scattering responsibility by adding new levels of bureaucracy, we would focus and concentrate the responsibility for getting problems solved.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: With these four departments, when we have a problem we will know where to go--and the department will have the authority and the resources to do something about it.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Over the years we have added departments and created agencies at the Federal level, each to serve a new constituency, to handle a particular task--and these have grown and multiplied in what has become a hopeless confusion of form and function.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The time has come to match our structure to our purposes--to look with a fresh eye, to organize the Government by conscious, comprehensive design to meet the new needs of a new era.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: government of the people, by the people, for the people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Too often since then, we have become a nation of the Government, by the Government, for the Government.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: By enacting these reforms, we can renew that principle that Lincoln stated so simply and so well.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: By giving everyone's voice a chance to be heard, we will have government that truly is of the people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: By creating more centers of meaningful power, more places where decisions that really count can be made, by giving more people a chance to do something, we can have government that truly is by the people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And by setting up a completely modern, functional system of government at the national level, we in Washington will at last be able to provide government that is truly for the people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I realize that what I am asking is that not only the executive branch in Washington but that even this Congress will have to change by giving up some of its power.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Change is hard.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But without change there can be no progress.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: nan

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Giving up power is hard.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But I would urge all of you, as leaders of this country, to remember that the truly revered leaders in world history are those who gave power to people, and not those who took it away.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As we consider these reforms we will be acting, not for the next 2 years or for the next 10 years, but for the next 100 years.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: So let us approach these six great goals with a sense not only of this moment in history but also of history itself.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let us act with the willingness to work together and the vision and the boldness and the courage of those great Americans who met in Philadelphia almost 190 years ago to write a constitution.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let us leave a heritage as they did--not just for our children but for millions yet unborn--of a nation where every American will have a chance not only to live in peace and to enjoy prosperity and opportunity but to participate in a system of government where he knows not only his votes but his ideas count--a system of government which will provide the means for America to reach heights of achievement undreamed of before.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Those men who met at Philadelphia left a great heritage because they had a vision--not only of what the Nation was but of what it could become.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As I think of that vision, I recall that America was founded as the land of the open door--as a haven for the oppressed, a land of opportunity, a place of refuge, of hope.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: When the first settlers opened the door of America three and a half centuries ago, they came to escape persecution and to find opportunity--and they left wide the door of welcome for others to follow.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: When the Thirteen Colonies declared their independence almost two centuries ago, they opened the door to a new vision of liberty and of human fulfillment--not just for an elite but for all.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: To the generations that followed, America's was the open door that beckoned millions from the old world to the new in search of a better life, a freer life, a fuller life, and in which, by their own decisions, they could shape their own destinies.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: For the black American, the Indian, the Mexican-American, and for those others in our land who have not had an equal chance, the Nation at last has begun to confront the need to press open the door of full and equal opportunity, and of human dignity.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: For all Americans, with these changes I have proposed tonight we can open the door to a new era of opportunity.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We can open the door to full and effective participation in the decisions that affect their lives.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We can open the door to a new partnership among governments at all levels, between those governments and the people themselves.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And by so doing, we can open wide the doors of human fulfillment for millions of people here in America now and in the years to come.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In the next few weeks I will spell out in greater detail the way I propose that we achieve these six great goals.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I ask this Congress to be responsive.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: If it is, then the 92d Congress, your Congress, our Congress, at the end of its term, will be able to look back on a record more splendid than any in our history.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This can be the Congress that helped us end the longest war in the Nation's history, and end it in a way that will give us at last a genuine chance to enjoy what we have not had in this century: a full generation of peace.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This can be the Congress that helped achieve an expanding economy, with full employment and without inflation--and without the deadly stimulus of war.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This can be the Congress that reformed a welfare system that has robbed recipients of their dignity and robbed States and cities of their resources.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This can be the Congress that pressed forward the rescue of our environment, and established for the next generation an enduring legacy of parks for the people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This can be the Congress that launched a new era in American medicine, in which the quality of medical care was enhanced while the costs were made less burdensome.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But above all, what this Congress can be remembered for is opening the way to a new American revolution--a peaceful revolution in which power was turned back to the people--in which government at all levels was refreshed and renewed and made truly responsive.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This can be a revolution as profound, as far-reaching, as exciting as that first revolution almost 200 years ago--and it can mean that just 5 years from now America will enter its third century as a young nation new in spirit, with all the vigor and the freshness with which it began its first century.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: My colleagues in the Congress, these are great goals.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: They can make the sessions of this Congress a great moment for America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: So let us pledge together to go forward together--by achieving these goals to give America the foundation today for a new greatness tomorrow and in all the years to come, and in so doing to make this the greatest Congress in the history of this great and good country.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Twenty-five years ago I sat here as a freshman Congressman--along with Speaker Albert--and listened for the first time to the President address the State of the Union.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I shall never forget that moment.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The Senate, the diplomatic corps, the Supreme Court, the Cabinet entered the Chamber, and then the President of the United States.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As all of you are aware, I had some differences with President Truman.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: He had some with me.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But I remember that on that day--the day he addressed that joint session of the newly elected Republican 80th Congress, he spoke not as a partisan, but as President of all the people--calling upon the Congress to put aside partisan considerations in the national interest.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The Greek-Turkish aid program, the Marshall Plan, the great foreign policy initiatives which have been responsible for avoiding a world war for over 25 years were approved by the 80th Congress, by a bipartisan majority of which I was proud to be a part.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Nineteen hundred seventy-two is now before us.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It holds precious time in which to accomplish good for the Nation.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We must not waste it.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I know the political pressures in this session of the Congress will be great.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: There are more candidates for the Presidency in this Chamber today than there probably have been at any one time in the whole history of the Republic.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And there is an honest difference of opinion, not only between the parties, but within each party, on some foreign policy issues and on some domestic policy issues.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: However, there are great national problems that are so vital that they transcend partisanship.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: So let us have our debates.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let us have our honest differences.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But let us join in keeping the national interest first.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let us join in making sure that legislation the Nation needs does not become hostage to the political interests of any party or any person.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: There is ample precedent, in this election year, for me to present you with a huge list of new proposals, knowing full well that there would not be any possibility of your passing them if you worked night and day.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I shall not do that.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I have presented to the leaders of the Congress today a message of 15,000 words discussing in some detail where the Nation stands and setting forth specific legislative items on which I have asked the Congress to act.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Much of this is legislation which I proposed in 1969, in 1970, and also in the first session of this 92d Congress and on which I feel it is essential that action be completed this year.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I am not presenting proposals which have attractive labels but no hope of passage.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I am presenting only vital programs which are within the capacity of this Congress to enact, within the capacity of the budget to finance, and which I believe should be above partisanship--programs which deal with urgent priorities for the Nation, which should and must be the subject of bipartisan action by this Congress in the interests of the country in 1972.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: When I took the oath of office on the steps of this building just 3 years ago today, the Nation was ending one of the most tortured decades in its history.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The 1960's were a time of great progress in many areas.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But as we all know, they were also times of great agony;

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: the agonies of war, of inflation, of rapidly rising crime, of deteriorating cities, of hopes raised and disappointed, and of anger and frustration that led finally to violence and to the worst civil disorder in a century.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I recall these troubles not to point any fingers of blame.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The Nation was so torn in those final years of the sixties that many in both parties questioned whether America could be governed at all.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The Nation has made significant progress in these first years of the seventies: Our cities are no longer engulfed by civil disorders.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Our colleges and universities have again become places of learning instead of battlegrounds.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: A beginning has been made in preserving and protecting our environment.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The rate of increase in crime has been slowed--and here in the District of Columbia, the one city where the Federal Government has direct jurisdiction, serious crime in 1971 was actually reduced by 13 percent from the year before.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Most important, because of the beginnings that have been made, we can say today that this year 1972 can be the year in which America may make the greatest progress in 25 years toward achieving our goal of being at peace with all the nations of the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As our involvement in the war in Vietnam comes to an end, we must now go on to build a generation of peace.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: To achieve that goal, we must first face realistically the need to maintain our defense.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In the past 3 years, we have reduced the burden of arms.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: For the first time in 20 years, spending on defense has been brought below spending on human resources.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As we look to the future, we find encouraging progress in our negotiations with the Soviet Union on limitation of strategic arms.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And looking further into the future, we hope there can eventually be agreement on the mutual reduction of arms.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But until there is such a mutual agreement, we must maintain the strength necessary to deter war.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And that is why, because of rising research and development costs, because of increases in military and civilian pay, because of the need to proceed with new weapons systems, my budget for the coming fiscal year will provide for an increase in defense spending.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Strong military defenses are not the enemy of peace;

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: they are the guardians of peace.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: There could be no more misguided set of priorities than one which would tempt others by weakening America, and thereby endanger the peace of the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In our foreign policy, we have entered a new era.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: we shall pay any price, bear any burden, meet any hardship, support any friend, oppose any foe to assure the survival and the success of liberty.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Our policy has been carefully and deliberately adjusted to meet the new realities of the new world we live in.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We make today only those commitments we are able and prepared to meet.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Our commitment to freedom remains strong and unshakable.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But others must bear their share of the burden of defending freedom around the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And so this, then, is our policy: We will maintain a nuclear deterrent adequate to meet any threat to the security of the United States or of our allies.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We will help other nations develop the capability of defending themselves.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We will faithfully honor all of our treaty commitments.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We will act to defend our interests, whenever and wherever they are threatened anyplace in the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But where our interests or our treaty commitments are not involved, our role will be limited: We will not intervene militarily.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But we will use our influence to prevent war.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: If war comes, we will use our influence to stop it.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Once it is over, we will do our share in helping to bind up the wounds of those who have participated in it.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As you know, I will soon be visiting the People's Republic of China and the Soviet Union.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I go there with no illusions.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We have great differences with both powers.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We shall continue to have great differences.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But peace depends on the ability of great powers to live together on the same planet despite their differences.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We would not be true to our obligation to generations yet unborn if we failed to seize this moment to do everything in our power to insure that we will be able to talk about those differences, rather than to fight about them, in the future.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As we look back over this century, let us, in the highest spirit of bipartisanship, recognize that we can be proud of our Nation's record in foreign affairs.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: America has given more generously of itself toward maintaining freedom, preserving peace, alleviating human suffering around the globe, than any nation has ever done in the history of man.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We have fought four wars in this century, but our power has never been used to break the peace, only to keep it;

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: never been used to destroy freedom, only to defend it.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We now have within our reach the goal of insuring that the next generation can be the first generation in this century to be spared the scourges of war.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Turning to our problems at home, we are making progress toward our goal of a new prosperity without war.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Industrial production, consumer spending, retail sales, personal income all have been rising.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Total employment, real income are the highest in history.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: New homebuilding starts this past year reached the highest level ever.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Business and consumer confidence have both been rising.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Interest rates are down.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The rate of inflation is down.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We can look with confidence to 1972 as the year when the back of inflation will be broken.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Now, this is a good record, but it is not good enough--not when we still have an unemployment rate of 6 percent.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It is not enough to point out that this was the rate of the early peacetime years of the sixties, or that if the more than 2 million men released from the Armed Forces and defense-related industries were still in their wartime jobs, unemployment would be far lower.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Our goal in this country is full employment in peacetime.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We intend to meet that goal, and we can.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The Congress has helped to meet that goal by passing our job-creating tax program last month.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The historic monetary agreements, agreements that we have reached with the major European nations, Canada, and Japan, will help meet it by providing new markets for American products, new jobs for American workers.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Our budget will help meet it by being expansionary without being inflationary-- a job-producing budget that will help take up the gap as the economy expands to full employment.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Our program to raise farm income will help meet it by helping to revitalize rural America, by giving to America's farmers their fair share of America's increasing productivity.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We also will help meet our goal of full employment in peacetime with a set of major initiatives to stimulate more imaginative use of America's great capacity for technological advance, and to direct it toward improving the quality of life for every American.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In reaching the moon, we demonstrated what miracles American technology is capable of achieving.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Now the time has come to move more deliberately toward making full use of that technology here on earth, of harnessing the wonders of science to the service of man.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I shall soon send to the Congress a special message proposing a new program of Federal partnership in technological research and development--with Federal incentives to increase private research, federally supported research on projects designed to improve our everyday lives in ways that will range from improving mass transit to developing new systems of emergency health care that could save thousands of lives annually.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Historically, our superior technology and high productivity have made it possible for American workers to be the highest paid in the world by far, and yet for our goods still to compete in world markets.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Now we face a new situation.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As other nations move rapidly forward in technology, the answer to the new competition is not to build a wall around America, but rather to remain competitive by improving our own technology still further and by increasing productivity in American industry.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Our new monetary and trade agreements will make it possible for American goods to compete fairly in the world's markets-- but they still must compete.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The new technology program will put to use the skills of many highly trained Americans, skills that might otherwise be wasted.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It will also meet the growing technological challenge from abroad, and it will thus help to create new industries, as well as creating more jobs for America's workers in producing for the world's markets.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This second session of the 92d Congress already has before it more than 90 major Administration proposals which still await action.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I have discussed these in the extensive written message that I have presented to the Congress today.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: They include, among others, our programs to improve life for the aging;

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: to combat crime and drug abuse;

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: to improve health services and to ensure that no one will be denied needed health care because of inability to pay;

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: to protect workers' pension rights;

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: to promote equal opportunity for members of minorities, and others who have been left behind;

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: to expand consumer protection;

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: to improve the environment;

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: to revitalize rural America;

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: to help the cities;

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: to launch new initiatives in education;

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: to improve transportation, and to put an end to costly labor tie-ups in transportation.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The west coast dock strike is a case in point.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This Nation cannot and will not tolerate that kind of irresponsible labor tie-up in the future.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The messages also include basic reforms which are essential if our structure of government is to be adequate in the decades ahead.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: They include reform of our wasteful and outmoded welfare system--substitution of a new system that provides work requirements and work incentives for those who can help themselves, income support for those who cannot help themselves, and fairness to the working poor.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: They include a $17 billion program of Federal revenue sharing with the States and localities as an investment in their renewal, an investment also of faith in the American people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: They also include a sweeping reorganization of the executive branch of the Federal Government so that it will be more efficient, more responsive, and able to meet the challenges of the decades ahead.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: One year ago, standing in this place, I laid before the opening session of this Congress six great goals.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: One of these was welfare reform.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: That proposal has been before the Congress now for nearly 2 1/2 years.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: My proposals on revenue sharing, government reorganization, health care, and the environment have now been before the Congress for nearly a year.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Many of the other major proposals that I have referred to have been here that long or longer.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Now, 1971, we can say, was a year of consideration of these measures.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Now let us join in making 1972 a year of action on them, action by the Congress, for the Nation and for the people of America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Now, in addition, there is one pressing need which I have not previously covered, but which must be placed on the national agenda.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We long have looked in this Nation to the local property tax as the main source of financing for public primary and secondary education.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As a result, soaring school costs, soaring property tax rates now threaten both our communities and our schools.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: They threaten communities because property taxes, which more than doubled in the 10 years from 1960 to '70, have become one of the most oppressive and discriminatory of all taxes, hitting most cruelly at the elderly and the retired;

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: and they threaten schools, as hard-pressed voters understandably reject new bond issues at the polls.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The problem has been given even greater urgency by four recent court decisions, which have held that the conventional method of financing schools through local property taxes is discriminatory and unconstitutional.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Nearly 2 years ago, I named a special Presidential commission to study the problems of school finance, and I also directed the Federal departments to look into the same problems.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We are developing comprehensive proposals to meet these problems.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This issue involves two complex and interrelated sets of problems: support of the schools and the basic relationships of Federal, State, and local governments in any tax reforms.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Under the leadership of the Secretary of the Treasury, we are carefully reviewing all of the tax aspects, and I have this week enlisted the Advisory Commission on Intergovernmental Relations in addressing the intergovernmental relations aspects.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I have asked this bipartisan Commission to review our proposals for Federal action to cope with the gathering crisis of school finance and property taxes.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Later in the year, when both Commissions have completed their studies, I shall make my final recommendations for relieving the burden of property taxes and providing both fair and adequate financing for our children's education.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: These recommendations will be revolutionary.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But all these recommendations, however, will be rooted in one fundamental principle with which there can be no compromise: Local school boards must have control over local schools.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As we look ahead over the coming decades, vast new growth and change are not only certainties, they will be the dominant reality of this world, and particularly of our life in America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Surveying the certainty of rapid change, we can be like a fallen rider caught in the stirrups--or we can sit high in the saddle, the masters of change, directing it on a course we choose.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The secret of mastering change in today's world is to reach back to old and proven principles, and to adapt them with imagination and intelligence to the new realities of a new age.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: That is what we have done in the proposals that I have laid before the Congress.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: They are rooted in basic principles that are as enduring as human nature, as robust as the American experience;

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: and they are responsive to new conditions.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Thus they represent a spirit of change that is truly renewal.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As we look back at those old principles, we find them as timely as they are timeless.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We believe in independence, and self-reliance, and the creative value of the competitive spirit.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We believe in full and equal opportunity for all Americans and in the protection of individual rights and liberties.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We believe in the family as the keystone of the community, and in the community as the keystone of the Nation.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We believe in compassion toward those in need.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We believe in a system of law, justice, and order as the basis of a genuinely free society.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We believe that a person should get what he works for--and that those who can, should work for what they get.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We believe in the capacity of people to make their own decisions in their own lives, in their own communities--and we believe in their right to make those decisions.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In applying these principles, we have done so with the full understanding that what we seek in the seventies, what our quest is, is not merely for more, but for better--for a better quality of life for all Americans.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Thus, for example, we are giving a new measure of attention to cleaning up our air and water, making our surroundings more attractive.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We are providing broader support for the arts, helping stimulate a deeper appreciation of what they can contribute to the Nation's activities and to our individual lives.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But nothing really matters more to the quality of our lives than the way we treat one another, than our capacity to live respectfully together as a unified society, with a full, generous regard for the rights of others and also for the feelings of others.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As we recover from the turmoil and violence of recent years, as we learn once again to speak with one another instead of shouting at one another, we are regaining that capacity.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As is customary here, on this occasion, I have been talking about programs.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Programs are important.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But even more important than programs is what we are as a Nation--what we mean as a Nation, to ourselves and to the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In New York Harbor stands one of the most famous statues in the world--the Statue of Liberty, the gift in 1886 of the people of France to the people of the United States.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
