text: This statue is more than a landmark; it is a symbol--a symbol of what America has meant to the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It reminds us that what America has meant is not its wealth, and not its power, but its spirit and purpose--a land that enshrines liberty and opportunity, and that has held out a hand of welcome to millions in search of a better and a fuller and, above all, a freer life.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The world's hopes poured into America, along with its people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And those hopes, those dreams, that have been brought here from every corner of the world, have become a part of the hope that we now hold out to the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Four years from now, America will celebrate the 200th anniversary of its founding as a Nation.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: There are those who say that the old Spirit of '76 is dead--that we no longer have the strength of character, the idealism, the faith in our founding purposes that that spirit represents.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Those who say this do not know America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We have been undergoing self-doubts and self-criticism.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But these are only the other side of our growing sensitivity to the persistence of want in the midst of plenty, of our impatience with the slowness with which age-old ills are being overcome.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: If we were indifferent to the shortcomings of our society, or complacent about our institutions, or blind to the lingering inequities--then we would have lost our way.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But the fact that we have those concerns is evidence that our ideals, deep down, are still strong.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Indeed, they remind us that what is really best about America is its compassion.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: They remind us that in the final analysis, America is great not because it is strong, not because it is rich, but because this is a good country.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let us reject the narrow visions of those who would tell us that we are evil because we are not yet perfect, that we are corrupt because we are not yet pure, that all the sweat and toil and sacrifice that have gone into the building of America were for naught because the building is not yet done.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let us see that the path we are traveling is wide, with room in it for all of us, and that its direction is toward a better Nation and a more peaceful world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Never has it mattered more that we go forward together.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Look at this Chamber.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The leadership of America is here today--the Supreme Court, the Cabinet, the Senate, the House of Representatives.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Together, we hold the future of the Nation, and the conscience of the Nation in our hands.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Because this year is an election year, it will be a time of great pressure.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: If we yield to that pressure and fail to deal seriously with the historic challenges that we face, we will have failed the trust of millions of Americans and shaken the confidence they have a right to place in us, in their Government.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Never has a Congress had a greater opportunity to leave a legacy of a profound and constructive reform for the Nation than this Congress.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: If we succeed in these tasks, there will be credit enough for all--not only for doing what is right, but doing it in the right way, by rising above partisan interest to serve the national interest.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And if we fail, more than any one of us, America will be the loser.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: That is why my call upon the Congress today is for a high statesmanship, so that in the years to come Americans will look back and say because it withstood the intense pressures of a political year, and achieved such great good for the American people and for the future of this Nation, this was truly a great Congress.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The traditional form of the President's annual report giving to the Congress Information of the State of the Union is a single message or address.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As the affairs and concerns of our Union have multiplied over the years, however, so too have the subjects that require discussion in State of the Union Messages.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This year in particular, with so many changes in Government programs under consideration--and with our very philosophy about the relationship between the individual and the State at an historic crossroads--a single, all-embracing State of the Union Message would not appear to be adequate.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I have therefore decided to present my 1973 State of the Union report in the form of a series of messages during these early weeks of the 93rd Congress.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The purpose of this first message in the series is to give a concise overview of where we stand as a people today, and to outline some of the general goals that I believe we should pursue over the next year and beyond.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In coming weeks, I will send to the Congress further State of the Union reports on specific areas of policy including economic affairs, natural resources, human resources, community development and foreign and defense policy.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The new course these messages will outline represents a fresh approach to Government: an approach that addresses the realities of the 1970s, not those of the 1930s or of the 1960s.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The role of the Federal Government as we approach our third century of independence should not be to dominate any facet of American life, but rather to aid and encourage people, communities and institutions to deal with as many of the difficulties and challenges facing them as possible, and to help see to it that every American has a full and equal opportunity to realize his or her potential.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: If we were to continue to expand the Federal Government at the rate of the past several decades, it soon would consume us entirely.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The time has come when we must make clear choices-- choices between old programs that set worthy goals but failed to reach them and new programs that provide a better way to realize those goals;

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: and choices, too, between competing programs--all of which may be desirable in themselves but only some of which we can afford with the finite resources at our command.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Because our resources are not infinite, we also face a critical choice in 1973 between holding the line in Government spending and adopting expensive programs which will surely force up taxes and refuel inflation.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Finally, it is vital at this time that we restore a greater sense of responsibility at the State and local level, and among individual Americans.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: WHERE WE STAND: The basic state of our Union today is sound, and full of promise.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We enter 1973 economically strong, militarily secure and, most important of all, at peace after a long and trying war.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: America continues to provide a better and more abundant life for more of its people than any other nation in the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We have passed through one of the most difficult periods in our history without surrendering to despair and without dishonoring our ideals as a people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Looking back, there is a lesson in all this for all of us.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The lesson is one that we sometimes had to learn the hard way over the past few years.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But we did learn it.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: That lesson is that even potentially destructive forces can be converted into positive forces when we know how to channel them, and when we use common sense and common decency to create a climate of mutual respect and goodwill.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: By working together and harnessing the forces of nature, Americans have unlocked some of the great mysteries of the universe.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Men have walked the surface of the moon and soared to new heights of discovery.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This same spirit of discovery is helping us to conquer disease and suffering that have plagued our own planet since the dawn of time.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: By working together with the leaders of other nations, we have been able to build a new hope for lasting peace--for a structure of world order in which common interest outweighs old animosities, and in which a new generation of the human family can grow up at peace in a changing world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: At home, we have learned that by working together we can create prosperity without fanning inflation; we can restore order without weakening freedom.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: THE CHALLENGES WE FACE: These first years of the 1970s have been good years for America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Our job--all of us together--is to make 1973 and the years to come even better ones.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I believe that we can.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I believe that we can make the years leading to our Bicentennial the best four years in American history.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But we must never forget that nothing worthwhile can be achieved without the will to succeed and the strength to sacrifice.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Hard decisions must be made, and we must stick by them.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In the field of foreign policy, we must remember that a strong America--an America whose word is believed and whose strength is respected--is essential to continued peace and understanding in the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The peace with honor we have achieved in Vietnam has strengthened this basic American credibility.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We must act in such a way in coming years that this credibility will remain intact, and with it, the world stability of which it is so indispensable a part.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: At home, we must reject the mistaken notion--a notion that has dominated too much of the public dialogue for too long--that ever bigger Government is the answer to every problem.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We have learned only too well that heavy taxation and excessive Government spending are not a cure-all.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In too many cases, instead of solving the problems they were aimed at, they have merely placed an ever heavier burden on the shoulders of the American taxpayer, in the form of higher taxes and a higher cost of living.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: At the same time they have deceived our people because many of the intended beneficiaries received far less than was promised, thus undermining public faith in the effectiveness of Government as a whole.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The time has come for us to draw the line.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The time has come for the responsible leaders of both political parties to take a stand against overgrown Government and for the American taxpayer.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We are not spending the Federal Government's money, we are spending the taxpayer's money, and it must be spent in a way which guarantees his money's worth and yields the fullest possible benefit to the people being helped.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The answer to many of the domestic problems we face is not higher taxes and more spending.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It is less waste, more results and greater freedom for the individual American to earn a rightful place in his own community--and for States and localities to address their own needs in their own ways, in the light of their own priorities.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: to excessive Federal spending and higher taxes, we can help achieve this goal.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: COMING MESSAGES: The policies which I will outline to the Congress in the weeks ahead represent a reaffirmation, not an abdication, of Federal responsibility.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: They represent a pragmatic rededication to social compassion and national excellence, in place of the combination of good intentions and fuzzy follow-through which too often in the past was thought sufficient.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In the field of economic affairs, our objectives will be to hold down taxes, to continue controlling inflation, to promote economic growth, to increase productivity, to encourage foreign trade, to keep farm income high, to bolster small business, and to promote better labor-management relations.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In the area of natural resources, my recommendations will include programs to preserve and enhance the environment, to advance science and technology, and to assure balanced use of our irreplaceable natural resources.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In developing human resources, I will have recommendations to advance the Nation's health and education, to improve conditions of people in need, to carry forward our increasingly successful attacks on crime, drug abuse and injustice, and to deal with such important areas of special concern as consumer affairs.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We will continue and improve our Nation's efforts to assist those who have served in the Armed Services in Vietnam through better job and training opportunities.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We must do a better job in community development--in creating more livable communities, in which all of our children can grow up with fuller access to opportunity and greater immunity to the social evils and blights which now plague so many of our towns and cities.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I shall have proposals to help us achieve this.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I shall also deal with our defense and foreign policies, and with our new approaches to the role and structure of Government itself.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Considered as a whole, this series of messages will be a blueprint for modernizing the concept and the functions of American Government to meet the needs of our people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Converting it into reality will require a spirit of cooperation and shared commitment on the part of all branches of the Government, for the goals we seek are not those of any single party or faction, they are goals for the betterment of all Americans.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As President, I recognize that I cannot do this job alone.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The Congress must help, and I pledge to do my part to achieve a constructive working relationship with the Congress.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: My sincere hope is that the executive and legislative branches can work together in this great undertaking in a positive spirit of mutual respect and cooperation.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Working together--the Congress, the President and the people-- I am confident that we can translate these proposals into an action program that can reform and revitalize American Government and, even more important, build a better life for all Americans.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We meet here tonight at a time of great challenge and great opportunities for America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We meet at a time when we face great problems at home and abroad that will test the strength of our fiber as a nation.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But we also meet at a time when that fiber has been tested, and it has proved strong.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: America is a great and good land, and we are a great and good land because we are a strong, free, creative people and because America is the single greatest force for peace anywhere in the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Today, as always in our history, we can base our confidence in what the American people will achieve in the future on the record of what the American people have achieved in the past.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Tonight, for the first time in 12 years, a President of the United States can report to the Congress on the state of a Union at peace with every nation of the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Because of this, in the 22,000-word message on the state of the Union that I have just handed to the Speaker of the House and the President of the Senate, I have been able to deal primarily with the problems of peace--with what we can do here at home in America for the American people--rather than with the problems of war.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The measures I have outlined in this message set an agenda for truly significant progress for this Nation and the world in 1974.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Before we chart where we are going, let us see how far we have come.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It was 5 years ago on the steps of this Capitol that I took the oath of office as your President.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In those 5 years, because of the initiatives undertaken by this Administration, the world has changed.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: America has changed.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As a result of those changes, America is safer today, more prosperous today, with greater opportunity for more of its people than ever before in our history.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Five years ago, America was at war in Southeast Asia.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We were locked in confrontation with the Soviet Union.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We were in hostile isolation from a quarter of the world's people who lived in Mainland China.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Five years ago, our cities were burning and besieged.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Five years ago, our college campuses were a battleground.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Five years ago, crime was increasing at a rate that struck fear across the Nation.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Five years ago, the spiraling rise in drug addiction was threatening human and social tragedy of massive proportion, and there was no program to deal with it.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Five years ago--as young Americans had done for a generation before that--America's youth still lived under the shadow of the military draft.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Five years ago, there was no national program to preserve our environment.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Day by day, our air was getting dirtier, our water was getting more foul.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And 5 years ago, American agriculture was practically a depressed industry with 100,000 farm families abandoning the farm every year.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As we look at America today, we find ourselves challenged by new problems.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But we also find a record of progress to confound the professional criers of doom and prophets of despair.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We met the challenges we faced 5 years ago, and we will be equally confident of meeting those that we face today.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let us see for a moment how we have met them.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: After more than 10 years of military involvement, all of our troops have returned from Southeast Asia, and they have returned with honor.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And we can be proud of the fact that our courageous prisoners of war, for whom a dinner was held in Washington tonight, that they came home with their heads high, on their feet and not on their knees.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In our relations with the Soviet Union, we have turned away from a policy of confrontation to one of negotiation.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: For the first time since World War II, the world's two strongest powers are working together toward peace in the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: With the People's Republic of China after a generation of hostile isolation, we have begun a period of peaceful exchange and expanding trade.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Peace has returned to our cities, to our campuses.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The 17-year rise in crime has been stopped.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We can confidently say today that we are finally beginning to win the war against crime.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Right here in this Nation's Capital--which a few years ago was threatening to become the crime capital of the world--the rate in crime has been cut in half.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: A massive campaign against drug abuse has been organized.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And the rate of new heroin addiction, the most vicious threat of all, is decreasing rather than increasing.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: For the first time in a generation, no young Americans are being drafted into the armed services of the United States.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And for the first time ever, we have organized a massive national effort to protect the environment.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Our air is getting cleaner, our water is getting purer, and our agriculture, which was depressed, is prospering.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Farm income is up 70 percent, farm production is setting all time records, and the billions of dollars the taxpayers were paying in subsidies has been cut to nearly zero.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Overall, Americans are living more abundantly than ever before, today.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: More than 2 1/2 million new jobs were created in the past year alone.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: That is the biggest percentage increase in nearly 20 years.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: People are earning more.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: What they earn buys more, more than ever before in history.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In the past 5 years, the average American's real spendable income--that is, what you really can buy with your income, even after allowing for taxes and inflation--has increased by 16 percent.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Despite this record of achievement, as we turn to the year ahead we hear once again the familiar voice of the perennial prophets of gloom telling us now that because of the need to fight inflation, because of the energy shortage, America may be headed for a recession.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let me speak to that issue head on.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: There will be no recession in the United States of America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Primarily due to our energy crisis, our economy is passing through a difficult period.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But I pledge to you tonight that the full powers of this Government will be used to keep America's economy producing and to protect the jobs of America's workers.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We are engaged in a long and hard fight against inflation.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: There have been, and there will be in the future, ups and downs in that fight.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But if this Congress cooperates in our efforts to hold down the cost of Government, we shall win our fight to hold down the cost of living for the American people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As we look back over our history, the years that stand out as the ones of signal achievement are those in which the Administration and the Congress, whether one party or the other, working together, had the wisdom and the foresight to select those particular initiatives for which the Nation was ready and the moment was right--and in which they seized the moment and acted.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Looking at the year 1974 which lies before us, there are 10 key areas in which landmark accomplishments are possible this year in America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: If we make these our national agenda, this is what we will achieve in 1974: We will break the back of the energy crisis;

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: we will lay the foundation for our future capacity to meet America's energy needs from America's own resources.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And we will take another giant stride toward lasting   peace in the world--not only by continuing our policy of negotiation rather than confrontation where the great powers are concerned but also by helping toward the achievement of a just and lasting settlement in the Middle East.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We will check the rise in prices without administering the harsh medicine of recession, and we will move the economy into a steady period of growth at a sustainable level.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We will establish a new system that makes high-quality health care available to every American in a dignified manner and at a price he can afford.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We will make our States and localities more responsive to the needs of their own citizens.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We will make a crucial breakthrough toward better transportation in our towns and in our cities across America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We will reform our system of Federal aid to education, to provide it when it is needed, where it is needed, so that it will do the most for those who need it the most.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We will make an historic beginning on the task of defining and protecting the right of personal privacy   for every American.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And we will start on a new road toward reform of a welfare system that bleeds the taxpayer, corrodes the community, and demeans those it is intended to assist.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And together with the other nations of the world, we will establish the economic framework within which Americans will share more fully in an expanding   worldwide trade and prosperity in the years ahead, with more open access to both markets and supplies.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In all of the 186 State of the Union messages delivered from this place, in our history this is the first in which the one priority, the first priority, is energy.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let me begin by reporting a new development which I know will be welcome news to every American.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As you know, we have committed ourselves to an active role in helping to achieve a just and durable peace in the Middle East, on the basis of full implementation of Security Council Resolutions 242 and 338.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The first step in the process is the disengagement of Egyptian and Israeli forces which is now taking place.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Because of this hopeful development, I can announce tonight that I have been assured, through my personal contacts with friendly leaders in the Middle Eastern area, that an urgent meeting will be called in the immediate future to discuss the lifting of the oil embargo.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This is an encouraging sign.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: However, it should be clearly understood by our friends in the Middle East that the United States will not be coerced on this issue.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Regardless of the outcome of this meeting, the cooperation of the American people in our energy conservation program has already gone a long way towards achieving a goal to which I am deeply dedicated.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let us do everything we can to avoid gasoline rationing in the United States of America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Last week, I sent to the Congress a comprehensive special message setting forth our energy situation, recommending the legislative measures which are necessary to a program for meeting our needs.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: If the embargo is lifted, this will ease the crisis, but it will not mean an end to the energy shortage in America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Voluntary conservation will continue to be necessary.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And let me take this occasion to pay tribute once again to the splendid spirit of cooperation the American people have shown which has made possible our success in meeting this emergency up to this time.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The new legislation I have requested will also remain necessary.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Therefore, I urge again that the energy measures that I have proposed be made the first priority of this session of the Congress.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: These measures will require the oil companies and other energy producers to provide the public with the necessary information on their supplies.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: They will prevent the injustice of windfall profits for a few as a result of the sacrifices of the millions of Americans.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And they will give us the organization, the incentives, the authorities needed to deal with the short-term emergency and to move toward meeting our long-term needs.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Just as 1970 was the year in which we began a full-scale effort to protect the environment, 1974 must be the year in which we organize a full-scale effort to provide for our energy needs, not only in this decade but through the 21st century.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As we move toward the celebration 2 years from now of the 200th anniversary of this Nation's independence, let us press vigorously on toward the goal I announced last November for Project Independence.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Let this be our national goal: At the end of this decade, in the year 1980, the United States will not be dependent on any other country for the energy we need to provide our jobs, to heat our homes, and to keep our transportation moving.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: To indicate the size of the Government commitment, to spur energy research and development, we plan to spend $10 billion in Federal funds over the next 5 years.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: That is an enormous amount.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But during the same 5 years, private enterprise will be investing as much as $200 billion-- and in 10 years, $500 billion--to develop the new resources, the new technology, the new capacity America will require for its energy needs in the 1980's.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: That is just a measure of the magnitude of the project we are undertaking.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But America performs best when called to its biggest tasks.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It can truly be said that only in America could a task so tremendous be achieved so quickly, and achieved not by regimentation, but through the effort and ingenuity of a free people, working in a free system.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Turning now to the rest of the agenda for 1974, the time is at hand this year to bring comprehensive, high quality health care within the reach of every American.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I shall propose a sweeping new program that will assure comprehensive health insurance protection to millions of Americans who cannot now obtain it or afford it, with vastly improved protection against catastrophic illnesses.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This will be a plan that maintains the high standards of quality in America's health care.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And it will not require additional taxes.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Now, I recognize that other plans have been put forward that would cost $80 billion or even $100 billion and that would put our whole health care system under the heavy hand of the Federal Government.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This is the wrong approach.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This has been tried abroad, and it has failed.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It is not the way we do things here in America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This kind of plan would threaten the quality of care provided by our whole health care system.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The right way is one that builds on the strengths of the present system and one that does not destroy those strengths, one based on partnership, not paternalism.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Most important of all, let us keep this as the guiding principle of our health programs.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Government has a great role to play, but we must always make sure that our doctors will be working for their patients and not for the Federal Government.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: and I recommended a sweeping set of proposals to revitalize State and local governments, to make them more responsive to the people they serve.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I can report to you today that as a result of revenue sharing passed by the Congress, and other measures, we have made progress toward that goal.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: After 40 years of moving power from the States and the communities to Washington, D.C., we have begun moving power back from Washington to the States and communities and, most important, to the people of America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In this session of the Congress, I believe we are near the breakthrough point on efforts which I have suggested, proposals to let people themselves make their own decisions for their own communities and, in particular, on those to provide broad new flexibility in Federal aid for community development, for economic development, for education.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And I look forward to working with the Congress, with members of both parties in resolving whatever remaining differences we have in this legislation so that we can make available nearly $5 1/2 billion to our States and localities to use not for what a Federal bureaucrat may want, but for what their own people in those communities want.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The decision should be theirs.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I think all of us recognize that the energy crisis has given new urgency to the need to improve public transportation, not only in our cities but in rural areas as well.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The program I have proposed this year will give communities not only more money but also more freedom to balance their own transportation needs.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It will mark the strongest Federal commitment ever to the improvement of mass transit as an essential element of the improvement of life in our towns and cities.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: One goal on which all Americans agree is that our children should have the very best education this great Nation can provide.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In a special message last week, I recommended a number of important new measures that can make 1974 a year of truly significant advances for our schools and for the children they serve.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: If the Congress will act on these proposals, more flexible funding will enable each Federal dollar to meet better the particular need of each particular school district.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Advance funding will give school authorities a chance to make each year's plans, knowing ahead of time what Federal funds they are going to receive.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Special targeting will give special help to the truly disadvantaged among our people.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: College students faced with rising costs for their education will be able to draw on an expanded program of loans and grants.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: These advances are a needed investment in America's most precious resource, our next generation.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And I urge the Congress to act on this legislation in 1974.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: One measure of a truly free society is the vigor with which it protects the liberties of its individual citizens.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As technology has advanced in America, it has increasingly encroached on one of those liberties--what I term the right of personal privacy.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Modern information systems, data banks, credit records, mailing list abuses, electronic snooping, the collection of personal data for one purpose that may be used for another--all these have left millions of Americans deeply concerned by the privacy they cherish.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And the time has come, therefore, for a major initiative to define the nature and extent of the basic rights of privacy and to erect new safeguards to ensure that those rights are respected.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I shall launch such an effort this year at the highest levels of the Administration, and I look forward again to working with this Congress in establishing a new set of standards that respect the legitimate needs of society, but that also recognize personal privacy as a cardinal principle of American liberty.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: a monstrous, consuming outrage--an outrage against the community, against the taxpayer, and particularly against the children that it is supposed to help.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: That system is still an outrage.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: By improving its administration, we have been able to reduce some of the abuses.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As a result, last year, for the first time in 18 years, there has been a halt in the growth of the welfare caseload.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But as a system, our welfare program still needs reform as urgently today as it did when I first proposed in 1969 that we completely replace it with a different system.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In these final 3 years of my Administration, I urge the Congress to join me in mounting a major new effort to replace the discredited present welfare system with one that works, one that is fair to those who need help or cannot help themselves, fair to the community, and fair to the taxpayer.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And let us have as our goal that there will be no Government program which makes it more profitable to go on welfare than to go to work.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I recognize that from the debates that have taken place within the Congress over the past 3 years on this program that we cannot expect enactment overnight of a new reform.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But I do propose that the Congress and the Administration together make this the year in which we discuss, debate, and shape such a reform so that it can be enacted as quickly as possible.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: America's own prosperity in the years ahead depends on our sharing fully and equitably in an expanding world prosperity.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Historic negotiations will take place this year that will enable us to ensure fair treatment in international markets for American workers, American farmers, American investors, and American consumers.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It is vital that the authorities contained in the trade bill I submitted to the Congress be enacted so that the United States can negotiate flexibly and vigorously on behalf of American interests.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: These negotiations can usher in a new era of international trade that not only increases the prosperity of all nations but also strengthens the peace among all nations.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In the past 5 years, we have made more progress toward a lasting structure of peace in the world than in any comparable time in the Nation's history.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We could not have made that progress if we had not maintained the military strength of America.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Thomas Jefferson once observed that the price of liberty is eternal vigilance.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: By the same token, and for the same reason, in today's world the price of peace is a strong defense as far as the United States is concerned.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In the past 5 years, we have steadily reduced the burden of national defense as a share of the budget, bringing it down from 44 percent in 1969 to 29 percent in the current year.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We have cut our military manpower over the past 5 years by more than a third, from 3.5 million to 2.2 million.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In the coming year, however, increased expenditures will be needed.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: They will be needed to assure the continued readiness of our military forces, to preserve present force levels in the face of rising costs, and to give us the military strength we must have if our security is to be maintained and if our initiatives for peace are to succeed.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The question is not whether we can afford to maintain the necessary strength of our defense, the question is whether we can afford not to maintain it, and the answer to that question is no.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We must never allow America to become the second strongest nation in the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I do not say this with any sense of belligerence, because I recognize the fact that is recognized around the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: America's military strength has always been maintained to keep the peace, never to break it.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It has always been used to defend freedom, never to destroy it.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: The world's peace, as well as our own, depends on our remaining as strong as we need to be as long as we need to be.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In this year 1974, we will be negotiating with the Soviet Union to place further limits on strategic nuclear arms.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Together with our allies, we will be negotiating with the nations of the Warsaw Pact on mutual and balanced reduction of forces in Europe.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And we will continue our efforts to promote peaceful economic development in Latin America, in Africa, in Asia.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We will press for full compliance with the peace accords that brought an end to American fighting in Indo-china, including particularly a provision that promised the fullest possible accounting for those Americans who are missing in action.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And having in mind the energy crisis to which I have referred to earlier, we will be working with the other nations of the world toward agreement on means by which oil supplies can be assured at reasonable prices on a stable basis in a fair way to the consuming and producing nations alike.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: All of these are steps toward a future in which the world's peace and prosperity, and ours as well as a result, are made more secure.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Throughout the 5 years that I have served as your President, I have had one overriding aim, and that was to establish a new structure of peace in the world that can free future generations of the scourge of war.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I can understand that others may have different priorities.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This has been and this will remain my first priority and the chief legacy I hope to leave from the 8 years of my Presidency.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This does not mean that we shall not have other priorities, because as we strengthen the peace, we must also continue each year a steady strengthening of our society here at home.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Our conscience requires it, our interests require it, and we must insist upon it.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As we create more jobs, as we build a better health care system, as we improve our education, as we develop new sources of energy, as we provide more abundantly for the elderly and the poor, as we strengthen the system of private enterprise that produces our prosperity--as we do all of this and even more, we solidify those essential bonds that hold us together as a nation.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Even more importantly, we advance what in the final analysis government in America is all about.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: What it is all about is more freedom, more security, a better life for each one of the 211 million people that live in this land.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: We cannot afford to neglect progress at home while pursuing peace abroad.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But neither can we afford to neglect peace abroad while pursuing progress at home.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: With a stable peace, all is possible, but without peace, nothing is possible.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: In the written message that I have just delivered to the Speaker and to the President of the Senate, I commented that one of the continuing challenges facing us in the legislative process is that of the timing and pacing of our initiatives, selecting each year among many worthy projects those that are ripe for action at that time.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: What is true in terms of our domestic initiatives is true also in the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: This period we now are in, in the world--and I say this as one who has seen so much of the world, not only in these past 5 years but going back over many years--we are in a period which presents a juncture of historic forces unique in this century.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: They provide an opportunity we may never have again to create a structure of peace solid enough to last a lifetime and more, not just peace in our time but peace in our children's time as well.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It is on the way we respond to this opportunity, more than anything else, that history will judge whether we in America have met our responsibility.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And I am confident we will meet that great historic responsibility which is ours today.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It was 27 years ago that John F. Kennedy and I sat in this Chamber, as freshmen Congressmen, hearing our first State of the Union address delivered by Harry Truman.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I know from my talks with him, as members of the Labor Committee on which we both served, that neither of us then even dreamed that either one or both might eventually be standing in this place that I now stand in now and that he once stood in, before me.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: It may well be that one of the freshmen Members of the 93rd Congress, one of you out there, will deliver his own State of the Union message 27 years from now, in the year 2001.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Well, whichever one it is, I want you to be able to look back with pride and to say that your first years here were great years and recall that you were here in this 93rd Congress when America ended its longest war and began its longest peace.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I would like to add a personal word with regard to an issue that has been of great concern to all Americans over the past year.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I refer, of course, to the investigations of the so-called Watergate affair.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: As you know, I have provided to the Special Prosecutor voluntarily a great deal of material.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I believe that I have provided all the material that he needs to conclude his investigations and to proceed to prosecute the guilty and to clear the innocent.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I believe the time has come to bring that investigation and the other investigations of this matter to an end.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: One year of Watergate is enough.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And the time has come, my colleagues, for not only the Executive, the President, but the Members of Congress, for all of us to join together in devoting our full energies to these great issues that I have discussed tonight which involve the welfare of all of the American people in so many different ways, as well as the peace of the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I recognize that the House Judiciary Committee has a special responsibility in this area, and I want to indicate on this occasion that I will cooperate with the Judiciary Committee in its investigation.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I will cooperate so that it can conclude its investigation, make its decision, and I will cooperate in any way that I consider consistent with my responsibilities to the Office of the Presidency of the United States.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: There is only one limitation.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: I will follow the precedent that has been followed by and defended by every President from George Washington to Lyndon B. Johnson of never doing anything that weakens the Office of the President of the United States or impairs the ability of the Presidents of the future to make the great decisions that are so essential to this Nation and the world.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Another point I should like to make very briefly: Like every Member of the House and Senate assembled here tonight, I was elected to the office that I hold.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And like every Member of the House and Senate, when I was elected to that office, I knew that I was elected for the purpose of doing a job and doing it as well as I possibly can.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And I want you to know that I have no intention whatever of ever walking away from the job that the people elected me to do for the people of the United States.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: Now, needless to say, it would be understatement if I were not to admit that the year 1973 was not a very easy year for me personally or for my family.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: And as I have already indicated, the year 1974 presents very great and serious problems, as very great and serious opportunities are also presented.

speaker: Richard M. Nixon
text: But my colleagues, this I believe: With the help of God, who has blessed this land so richly, with the cooperation of the Congress, and with the support of the American people, we can and we will make the year 1974 a year of unprecedented progress toward our goal of building a structure of lasting peace in the world and a new prosperity without war in the United States of America.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Mr. Speaker, Mr. Vice President, Members of the 94th Congress, and distinguished guests: Twenty-six years ago, a freshman Congressman, a young fellow with lots of idealism who was out to change the world, stood before Sam Rayburn in the well of the House and solemnly swore to the same oath that all of you took yesterday--an unforgettable experience, and I congratulate you all.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Two days later, that same freshman stood at the back of this great Chamber--over there someplace--as President Truman, all charged up by his single-handed election victory, reported as the Constitution requires on the state of the Union.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I am happy to report to this 81st Congress that the state of the Union is good.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Our Nation is better able than ever before to meet the needs of the American people, and to give them their fair chance in the pursuit of happiness.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: [It] is foremost among the nations of the world in the search for peace.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Today, that freshman Member from Michigan stands where Mr.Truman stood, and I must say to you that the state of the Union is not good: Millions of Americans are out of work.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Recession and inflation are eroding the money of millions more.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Prices are too high, and sales are too slow.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: This year's Federal deficit will be about $30 billion; next year's probably $45 billion.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: The national debt will rise to over $500 billion.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Our plant capacity and productivity are not increasing fast enough.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: We depend on others for essential energy.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Some people question their Government's ability to make hard decisions and stick with them; they expect Washington politics as usual.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Yet, what President Truman said on January 5, 1949, is even more true in 1975.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: We are better able to meet our people's needs.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: All Americans do have a fairer chance to pursue happiness.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Not only are we still the foremost nation in the pursuit of peace but today's prospects of attaining it are infinitely brighter.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: There were 59 million Americans employed at the start of 1949; now there are more than 85 million Americans who have jobs.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: In comparable dollars, the average income of the American family has doubled during the past 26 years.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Now, I want to speak very bluntly.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I've got bad news, and I don't expect much, if any, applause.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: The American people want action, and it will take both the Congress and the President to give them what they want.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Progress and solutions can be achieved, and they will be achieved.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: My message today is not intended to address all of the complex needs of America.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I will send separate messages making specific recommendations for domestic legislation, such as the extension of general revenue sharing and the Voting Rights Act.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: The moment has come to move in a new direction.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: We can do this by fashioning a new partnership between the Congress on the one hand, the White House on the other, and the people we both represent.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Let us mobilize the most powerful and most creative industrial nation that ever existed on this Earth to put all our people to work.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: The emphasis on our economic efforts must now shift from inflation to jobs.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: To bolster business and industry and to create new jobs, I propose a 1-year tax reduction of $16 billion.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Three-quarters would go to individuals and one-quarter to promote business investment.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: This cash rebate to individuals amounts to 12 percent of 1974 tax payments--a total cut of $12 billion, with a maximum of $1,000 per return.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I call on the Congress to act by April 1.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: If you do--and I hope you will--the Treasury can send the first check for half of the rebate in May and the second by September.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: The other one-fourth of the cut, about $4 billion, will go to business, including farms, to promote expansion and to create more jobs.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: The 1-year reduction for businesses would be in the form of a liberalized investment tax credit increasing the rate to 12 percent for all businesses.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: This tax cut does not include the more fundamental reforms needed in our tax system.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: But it points us in the right direction--allowing taxpayers rather than the Government to spend their pay.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Cutting taxes now is essential if we are to turn the economy around.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: A tax cut offers the best hope of creating more jobs.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Unfortunately, it will increase the size of the budget deficit.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Therefore, it is more important than ever that we take steps to control the growth of Federal expenditures.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Part of our trouble is that we have been self-indulgent.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: For decades, we have been voting ever-increasing levels of Government benefits, and now the bill has come due.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: We have been adding so many new programs that the size and the growth of the Federal budget has taken on a life of its own.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: One characteristic of these programs is that their cost increases automatically every year because the number of people eligible for most of the benefits increases every year.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: When these programs are enacted, there is no dollar amount set.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: No one knows what they will cost.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: All we know is that whatever they cost last year, they will cost more next year.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: It is a question of simple arithmetic.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Unless we check the excessive growth of Federal expenditures or impose on ourselves matching increases in taxes, we will continue to run huge inflationary deficits in the Federal budget.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: If we project the current built-in momentum of Federal spending through the next 15 years, State, Federal, and local government expenditures could easily comprise half of our gross national product.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: This compares with less than a third in 1975.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I have just concluded the process of preparing the budget submissions for fiscal year 1976.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: In that budget, I will propose legislation to restrain the growth of a number of existing programs.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I have also concluded that no new spending programs can be initiated this year, except for energy.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Further, I will not hesitate to veto any new spending programs adopted by the Congress.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: As an additional step toward putting the Federal Government's house in order, I recommend a 5-percent limit on Federal pay increases in 1975.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: In all Government programs tied to the Consumer Price Index--including social security, civil service and military retirement pay, and food stamps--I also propose a 1-year maximum increase of 5 percent.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: None of these recommended ceiling limitations, over which Congress has final authority, are easy to propose, because in most cases they involve anticipated payments to many, many deserving people.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Nonetheless, it must be done.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I must emphasize that I am not asking to eliminate, to reduce, to freeze these payments.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I am merely recommending that we slow down the rate at which these payments increase and these programs grow.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Only a reduction in the growth of spending can keep Federal borrowing down and reduce the damage to the private sector from high interest rates.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Only a reduction in spending can make it possible for the Federal Reserve System to avoid an inflationary growth in the money supply and thus restore balance to our economy.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: A major reduction in the growth of Federal spending can help dispel the uncertainty that so many feel about our economy and put us on the way to curing our economic ills.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: If we don't act to slow down the rate of increase in Federal spending, the United States Treasury will be legally obligated to spend more than $360 billion in fiscal year 1976, even if no new programs are enacted.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: These are not matters of conjecture or prediction, but again, a matter of simple arithmetic.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: The size of these numbers and their implications for our everyday life and the health of our economic system are shocking.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I submitted to the last Congress a list of budget deferrals and rescissions.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: There will be more cuts recommended in the budget that I will submit.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Even so, the level of outlays for fiscal year 1976 is still much, much too high.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Not only is it too high for this year but the decisions we make now will inevitably have a major and growing impact on expenditure levels in future years.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I think this is a very fundamental issue that we, the Congress and I, must jointly solve.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Economic disruptions we and others are experiencing stem in part from the fact that the world price of petroleum has quadrupled in the last year.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: But in all honesty, we cannot put all of the blame on the oil-exporting nations.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: We, the United States, are not blameless.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Our growing dependence upon foreign sources has been adding to our vulnerability for years and years, and we did nothing to prepare ourselves for such an event as the embargo of 1973.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: During the 1960's, this country had a surplus capacity of crude oil which we were able to make available to our trading partners whenever there was a disruption of supply.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: This surplus capacity enabled us to influence both supplies and prices of crude oil throughout the world.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Our excess capacity neutralized any effort at establishing an effective cartel, and thus the rest of the world was assured of adequate supplies of oil at reasonable prices.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: By 1970, our surplus capacity had vanished, and as a consequence, the latent power of the oil cartel could emerge in full force.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Europe and Japan, both heavily dependent on imported oil, now struggle to keep their economies in balance.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Even the United States, our country, which is far more self-sufficient than most other industrial countries, has been put under serious pressure.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I am proposing a program which will begin to restore our country's surplus capacity in total energy.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: In this way, we will be able to assure ourselves reliable and adequate energy and help foster a new world energy stability for other major consuming nations.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: But this Nation and, in fact, the world must face the prospect of energy difficulties between now and 1985.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: This program will impose burdens on all of us with the aim of reducing our consumption of energy and increasing our production.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Great attention has been paid to the considerations of fairness, and I can assure you that the burdens will not fall more harshly on those less able to bear them.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I am recommending a plan to make us invulnerable to cutoffs of foreign oil.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: It will require sacrifices, but it--and this is most important--it will work.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I have set the following national energy goals to assure that our future is as secure and as productive as our past: First, we must reduce oil imports by 1 million barrels per day by the end of this year and by 2 million barrels per day by the end of 1977.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Second, we must end vulnerability to economic disruption by foreign suppliers by 1985.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Third, we must develop our energy technology and resources so that the United States has the ability to supply a significant share of the energy needs of the free world by the end of this century.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: To attain these objectives, we need immediate action to cut imports.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Unfortunately, in the short term there are only a limited number of actions which can increase domestic supply.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I will press for all of them.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I urge quick action on the necessary legislation to allow commercial production at the Elk Hills, California, Naval Petroleum Reserve.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: In order that we make greater use of domestic coal resources, I am submitting amendments to the Energy Supply and Environmental Coordination Act which will greatly increase the number of power plants that can be promptly converted to coal.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Obviously, voluntary conservation continues to be essential, but tougher programs are needed--and needed now.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Therefore, I am using Presidential powers to raise the fee on all imported crude oil and petroleum products.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: The crude oil fee level will be increased $1 per barrel on February 1, by $2 per barrel on March 1, and by $3 per barrel on April 1.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I will take actions to reduce undue hardships on any geographical region.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: The foregoing are interim administrative actions.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: They will be rescinded when broader but necessary legislation is enacted.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: To that end, I am requesting the Congress to act within 90 days on a more comprehensive energy tax program.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: It includes: excise taxes and import fees totaling $2 per barrel on product imports and on all crude oil;

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: deregulation of new natural gas and enactment of a natural gas excise tax.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I plan to take Presidential initiative to decontrol the price of domestic crude oil on April 1.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I urge the Congress to enact a windfall profits tax by that date to ensure that oil producers do not profit unduly.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: The sooner Congress acts, the more effective the oil conservation program will be and the quicker the Federal revenues can be returned to our people.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I am prepared to use Presidential authority to limit imports, as necessary, to guarantee success.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I want you to know that before deciding on my energy conservation program, I considered rationing and higher gasoline taxes as alternatives.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: In my judgment, neither would achieve the desired results and both would produce unacceptable inequities.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: A massive program must be initiated to increase energy supply to cut demand, and provide new standby emergency programs to achieve the independence we want by 1985.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: The largest part of increased oil production must come from new frontier areas on the Outer Continental Shelf and from the Naval Petroleum Reserve No. 4 in Alaska.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: It is the intent of this Administration to move ahead with exploration, leasing, and production on those frontier areas of the Outer Continental Shelf where the environmental risks are acceptable.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Use of our most abundant domestic resource--coal--is severely limited.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: We must strike a reasonable compromise on environmental concerns with coal.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I am submitting Clean Air [Act] amendments which will allow greater coal use without sacrificing clean air goals.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I vetoed the strip mining legislation passed by the last Congress.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: With appropriate changes, I will sign a revised version when it comes to the White House.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I am proposing a number of actions to energize our nuclear power program.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I will submit legislation to expedite nuclear leasing [licensing] and the rapid selection of sites.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: In recent months, utilities have cancelled or postponed over 60 percent of planned nuclear expansion and 30 percent of planned additions to non-nuclear capacity.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Financing problems for that industry are worsening.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I am therefore recommending that the 1-year investment tax credit of 12 percent be extended an additional 2 years to specifically speed the construction of power plants that do not use natural gas or oil.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I am also submitting proposals for selective reform of State utility commission regulations.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: To provide the critical stability for our domestic energy production in the face of world price uncertainty, I will request legislation to authorize and require tariffs, import quotas, or price floors to protect our energy prices at levels which will achieve energy independence.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Increasing energy supplies is not enough.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: We must take additional steps to cut long-term consumption.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I therefore propose to the Congress: legislation to make thermal efficiency standards mandatory for all new buildings in the United States;

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: a new tax credit of up to $150 for those homeowners who install insulation equipment;

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: the establishment of an energy conservation program to help low-income families purchase insulation supplies;

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: legislation to modify and defer automotive pollution standards for 5 years, which will enable us to improve automobile gas mileage by 40 percent by 1980.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: These proposals and actions, cumulatively, can reduce our dependence on foreign energy supplies from 3 to 5 million barrels per day by 1985.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: To make the United States invulnerable to foreign disruption, I propose standby emergency legislation and a strategic storage program of 1 billion barrels of oil for domestic needs and 300 million barrels for national defense purposes.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I will ask for the funds needed for energy research and development activities.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I have established a goal of 1 million barrels of synthetic fuels and shale oil production per day by 1985 together with an incentive program to achieve it.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I have a very deep belief in America's capabilities.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Within the next 10 years, my program envisions: 200 major nuclear power plants;

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: 250 major new coal mines;

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: 150 major coal-fired power plants;

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: 30 major new [oil] refineries;

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: 20 major new synthetic fuel plants;

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: the drilling of many thousands of new oil wells;

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: the insulation of 18 million homes;

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: and the manufacturing and the sale of millions of new automobiles, trucks, and buses that use much less fuel.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I happen to believe that we can do it.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: In another crisis--the one in 1942--President Franklin D.Roosevelt said this country would build 60,000 [50,000] military aircraft.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: By 1943, production in that program had reached 125,000 aircraft annually.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: They did it then.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: We can do it now.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: If the Congress and the American people will work with me to attain these targets, they will be achieved and will be surpassed.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: From adversity, let us seize opportunity.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Revenues of some $30 billion from higher energy taxes designed to encourage conservation must be refunded to the American people in a manner which corrects distortions in our tax system wrought by inflation.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: People have been pushed into higher tax brackets by inflation, with consequent reduction in their actual spending power.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Business taxes are similarly distorted because inflation exaggerates reported profits, resulting in excessive taxes.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Accordingly, I propose that future individual income taxes be reduced by $16.5 billion.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: This will be done by raising the low-income allowance and reducing tax rates.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: This continuing tax cut will primarily benefit lower- and middle-income taxpayers.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: For example, a typical family of four with a gross income of $5,600 now pays $185 in Federal income taxes.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Under this tax cut plan, they would pay nothing.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: A family of four with a gross income of $12,500 now pays $1,260 in Federal taxes.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: My proposal reduces that total by $300.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Families grossing $20,000 would receive a reduction of $210.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Those with the very lowest incomes, who can least afford higher costs, must also be compensated.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: I propose a payment of $80 to every person 18 years of age and older in that very limited category.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: State and local governments will receive $2 billion in additional revenue sharing to offset their increased energy costs.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: To offset inflationary distortions and to generate more economic activity, the corporate tax rate will be reduced from 48 percent to 42 percent.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Now let me turn, if I might, to the international dimension of the present crisis.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: At no time in our peacetime history has the state of the Nation depended more heavily on the state of the world.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: And seldom, if ever, has the state of the world depended more heavily on the state of our Nation.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: The economic distress is global.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: We will not solve it at home unless we help to remedy the profound economic dislocation abroad.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: World trade and monetary structure provides markets, energy, food, and vital raw materials--for all nations.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: This international system is now in jeopardy.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: This Nation can be proud of significant achievements in recent years in solving problems and crises.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: The Berlin agreement, the SALT agreements, our new relationship with China, the unprecedented efforts in the Middle East are immensely encouraging.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: But the world is not free from crisis.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: In a world of 150 nations, where nuclear technology is proliferating and regional conflicts continue, international security cannot be taken for granted.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: So, let there be no mistake about it: International cooperation is a vital factor of our lives today.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: This is not a moment for the American people to turn inward.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: More than ever before, our own well-being depends on America's determination and America's leadership in the whole wide world.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: We are a great Nation--spiritually, politically, militarily, diplomatically, and economically.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: America's commitment to international security has sustained the safety of allies and friends in many areas-- in the Middle East, in Europe, and in Asia.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Our turning away would unleash new instabilities, new dangers around the globe, which, in turn, would threaten our own security.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: At the end of World War II, we turned a similar challenge into an historic opportunity and, I might add, an historic achievement.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: An old order was in disarray; political and economic institutions were shattered.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: In that period, this Nation and its partners built new institutions, new mechanisms of mutual support and cooperation.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Today, as then, we face an historic opportunity.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: If we act imaginatively and boldly, as we acted then, this period will in retrospect be seen as one of the great creative moments of our Nation's history.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: The whole world is watching to see how we respond.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: A resurgent American economy would do more to restore the confidence of the world in its own future than anything else we can do.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: The program that this Congress passes can demonstrate to the world that we have started to put our own house in order.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: If we can show that this Nation is able and willing to help other nations meet the common challenge, it can demonstrate that the United States will fulfill its responsibilities as a leader among nations.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Quite frankly, at stake is the future of industrialized democracies, which have perceived their destiny in common and sustained it in common for 30 years.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: The developing nations are also at a turning point.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: The poorest nations see their hopes of feeding their hungry and developing their societies shattered by the economic crisis.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: The long-term economic future for the producers of raw materials also depends on cooperative solutions.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Our relations with the Communist countries are a basic factor of the world environment.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: We must seek to build a long-term basis for coexistence.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: We will stand by our principles.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: We will stand by our interests.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: We will act firmly when challenged.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: The kind of a world we want depends on a broad policy of creating mutual incentives for restraint and for cooperation.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: As we move forward to meet our global challenges and opportunities, we must have the tools to do the job.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Our military forces are strong and ready.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: This military strength deters aggression against our allies, stabilizes our relations with former adversaries, and protects our homeland.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Fully adequate conventional and strategic forces cost many, many billions, but these dollars are sound insurance for our safety and for a more peaceful world.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
text: Military strength alone is not sufficient.

speaker: Gerald R. Ford
