text: The single biggest factor in the inflation rate last year, the increase in the inflation rate last year, was from one cause: the skyrocketing prices of OPEC oil.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: We must take whatever actions are necessary to reduce our dependence on foreign oil--and at the same time reduce inflation.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: As individuals and as families, few of us can produce energy by ourselves.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: But all of us can conserve energy--every one of us, every day of our lives.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: Tonight I call on you--in fact, all the people of America--to help our Nation.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: Conserve energy.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: Eliminate waste.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: Make 1980 indeed a year of energy conservation.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: Of course, we must take other actions to strengthen our Nation's economy.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: First, we will continue to reduce the deficit and then to balance the Federal budget.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: Second, as we continue to work with business to hold down prices, we'll build also on the historic national accord with organized labor to restrain pay increases in a fair fight against inflation.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: Third, we will continue our successful efforts to cut paperwork and to dismantle unnecessary Government regulation.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: Fourth, we will continue our progress in providing jobs for America, concentrating on a major new program to provide training and work for our young people, especially minority youth.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: a mind is a terrible thing to waste.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: We will give our young people new hope for jobs and a better life in the 1980's.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: And fifth, we must use the decade of the 1980's to attack the basic structural weaknesses and problems in our economy through measures to increase productivity, savings, and investment.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: With these energy and economic policies, we will make America even stronger at home in this decade--just as our foreign and defense policies will make us stronger and safer throughout the world.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: We will never abandon our struggle for a just and a decent society here at home.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: That's the heart of America--and it's the source of our ability to inspire other people to defend their own rights abroad.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: Our material resources, great as they are, are limited.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: Our problems are too complex for simple slogans or for quick solutions.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: We cannot solve them without effort and sacrifice.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: You took the good things for granted.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: Now you must earn them again.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: For every right that you cherish, you have a duty which you must fulfill.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: For every good which you wish to preserve, you will have to sacrifice your comfort and your ease.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: There is nothing for nothing any longer.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: Our challenges are formidable.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: But there's a new spirit of unity and resolve in our country.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: We move into the 1980's with confidence and hope and a bright vision of the America we want: an America strong and free, an America at peace, an America with equal rights for all citizens-- and for women, guaranteed in the United States Constitution--an America with jobs and good health and good education for every citizen, an America with a clean and bountiful life in our cities and on our farms, an America that helps to feed the world, an America secure in filling its own energy needs, an America of justice, tolerance, and compassion.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: For this vision to come true, we must sacrifice, but this national commitment will be an exciting enterprise that will unify our people.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: Together as one people, let us work to build our strength at home, and together as one indivisible union, let us seek peace and security throughout the world.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: Together let us make of this time of challenge and danger a decade of national resolve and of brave achievement.

speaker: Jimmy (James E.) Carter
text: Thank you very much.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Mr. Speaker, Mr. President, distinguished Members of Congress, honored guests, and fellow citizens:Only a month ago I was your guest in this historic building, and I pledged to you my cooperation in doing what is right for this Nation that we all love so much.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I'm here tonight to reaffirm that pledge and to ask that we share in restoring the promise that is offered to every citizen by this, the last, best hope of man on Earth.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: All of us are aware of the punishing inflation which has for the first time in 60 years held to double-digit figures for 2 years in a row.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Interest rates have reached absurd levels of more that 20 percent and over 15 percent for those who would borrow to buy a home.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: All across this land one can see newly built homes standing vacant, unsold because of mortgage interest rates.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Almost 8 million Americans are out of work.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: These are people who want to be productive.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: But as the months go by, despair dominates their lives.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The threats of layoff and unemployment hang over other millions, and all who work are frustrated by their inability to keep up with inflation.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: One worker in a Midwest city put it to me this way: He said, ""I'm bringing home more dollars than I ever believed I could possibly earn, but I seem to be getting worse off.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And he is.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Not only have hourly earnings of the American worker, after adjusting for inflation, declined 5 percent over the past 5 years, but in these 5 years, Federal personal taxes for the average family have increased 67 percent.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We can no longer procrastinate and hope that things will get better.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: They will not.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Unless we act forcefully-and now-the economy will get worse.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Can we, who man the ship of state, deny it is somewhat out of control?

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Our national debt is approaching $1 trillion.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: A few weeks ago I called such a figure, a trillion dollars, incomprehensible, and I've been trying ever since to think of a way to illustrate how big a trillion really is.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And the best I could come up with is that if you had a stack of thousand-dollar bills in your hand only 4 inches high, you'd be a millionaire.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: A trillion dollars would be a stack of thousand-dollar bills 67 miles high.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The interest on the public debt this year we know will be over $90 billion, and unless we change the proposed spending for the fiscal year beginning October 1st, we'll add another almost $80 billion to the debt.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Adding to our troubles is a mass of regulations imposed on the shopkeeper, the farmer, the craftsman, professionals, and major industry that is estimated to add $100 billion to the price of the things we buy, and it reduces our ability to produce.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The rate of increase in American productivity, once one of the highest in the world, is among the lowest of all major industrial nations.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Indeed, it has actually declined in the last 3 years.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Now, I've painted a pretty grim picture, but I think I've painted it accurately.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: It is within our power to change this picture, and we can act with hope.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: There's nothing wrong with our internal strengths.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: There has been no breakdown of the human, technological, and natural resources upon which the economy is built.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Based on this confidence in a system which has never failed us, but which we have failed through a lack of confidence and sometimes through a belief that we could fine-tune the economy and get it tuned to our liking, I am proposing a comprehensive four-point program.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Now, let me outline in detail some of the principal parts of this program.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: You'll each be provided with a completely detailed copy of the entire program.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: This plan is aimed at reducing the growth in government spending and taxing, reforming and eliminating regulations which are unnecessary and unproductive or counterproductive, and encouraging a consistent monetary policy aimed at maintaining the value of the currency.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: If enacted in full, this program can help America create 13 million new jobs, nearly 3 million more than we would have without these measures.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: It will also help us to gain control of inflation.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: It's important to note that we're only reducing the rate of increase in taxing and spending.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We're not attempting to cut either spending or taxing levels below that which we presently have.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: This plan will get our economy moving again, [create] productivity growth, and thus create the jobs that our people must have.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And I'm asking that you join me in reducing direct Federal spending by $41.4 billion in fiscal year 1982, and this goes along with another $7.7 billion in user fees and off-budget savings for a total of $49.1 billion.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And this will still allow an increase of $40.8 billion over 1981 spending.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Now, I know that exaggerated and inaccurate stories about these cuts have disturbed many people, particularly those dependent on grant and benefit programs for their basic needs.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Some of you have heard from constituents, I know, afraid that social security checks, for example, were going to be taken away from them.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Well, I regret the fear that these unfounded stories have caused, and I welcome this opportunity to set things straight.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We will continue to fulfill the obligations that spring from our national conscience.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Those who, through no fault of their own, must depend on the rest of us-the poverty stricken, the disabled, the elderly, all those with true need-can rest assured that the social safety net of programs they depend on are exempt from any cuts.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The full retirement benefits of the more than 31 million social security recipients will be continued, along with an annual cost-of-living increase.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Medicare will not be cut, nor will supplemental income for the blind, the aged, and the disabled.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And funding will continue for veterans pensions.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: School breakfasts and lunches for the children of low-income families will continue, as will nutrition and other special services for the aging.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: There will be no cut in Project Head Start or summer youth jobs.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: All in all, nearly $216 billion worth of programs providing help for tens of millions of Americans will be fully funded.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: But government will not continue to subsidize individuals or particular business interests where real need cannot be demonstrated.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And while we will reduce some subsidies to regional and local governments, we will at the same time convert a number of categorical grant programs into block grants to reduce wasteful administrative overhead and to give local governments and States more flexibility and control.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We call for an end in duplication to Federal programs and reform of those which are not cost-effective.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Now, already some have protested that there must be no reduction in aid to schools.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Well, let me point out that Federal aid to education amounts to only 8 percent of the total educational funding, and for this 8 percent, the Federal Government has insisted on tremendously disproportionate share of control over our schools.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Whatever reductions we've proposed in that 8 percent will amount to very little in the total cost of education.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: They will, however, restore more authority to States and local school districts.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Historically, the American people have supported by voluntary contributions more artistic and cultural activities than all the other countries in the world put together.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I wholeheartedly support this approach and believe that Americans will continue their generosity.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Therefore, I'm proposing a savings of $85 million in the Federal subsidies now going to the arts and humanities.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: There are a number of subsidies to business and industry that I believe are unnecessary, not because the activities being subsidized aren't of value, but because the marketplace contains incentives enough to warrant continuing these activities without a government subsidy.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: One such subsidy is the Department of Energy's synthetic fuels program.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We will continue support of research leading to development of new technologies and more independence from foreign oil, but we can save at least $3.2 billion by leaving to private industry the building of plants to make liquid or gas fuels from coal.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We're asking that another major industry-business subsidy I should say, the Export-Import Bank loan authority, be reduced by one-third in 1982.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We're doing this because the primary beneficiaries of taxpayer funds in this case are the exporting companies themselves-most of them profitable corporations.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: This brings me to a number of other lending programs in which government makes low-interest loans, some of them at an interest rate as low as 2 percent.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: What has not been very well understood is that the Treasury Department has no money of its own to lend;

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: it has to go into the private capital market and borrow the money.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: So, in this time of excessive interest rates, the government finds itself borrowing at an interest rate several times as high as the interest it gets back from those it lends the money to.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And this difference, of course, is paid by your constituents-the taxpayers.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: They get hit again if they try to borrow, because government borrowing contributes to raising all interest rates.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: By terminating the Economic Development Administration, we can save hundreds of millions of dollars in 1982 and billions more over the next few years.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: There's a lack of consistent and convincing evidence that EDA and its Regional Commissions have been effective in creating new jobs.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: They have been effective in creating an array of planners, grantsmen, and professional middlemen.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We believe we can do better just by the expansion of the economy and the job creation which will come from our economic program.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The Food Stamp program will be restored to its original purpose, to assist those without resources to purchase sufficient nutritional food.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We will, however, save $1.8 billion in fiscal year 1982 by removing from eligibility those who are not in real need or who are abusing the program.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: But even with this reduction, the program will be budgeted for more than $10 billion.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We will tighten welfare and give more attention to outside sources of income when determining the amount of welfare that an individual is allowed.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: This, plus strong and effective work requirements, will save $520 million in the next year.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I stated a moment ago our intention to keep the school breakfast and lunch programs for those in true need.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: But by cutting back on meals for children of families who can afford to pay, the savings will be $1.6 billion in the fiscal year 1982.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Now, let me just touch on a few other areas which are typical of the kind of reductions we've included in this economic package.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The Trade Adjustment Assistance program provides benefits for workers who are unemployed when foreign imports reduce the market for various American products, causing shutdown of plants and layoff of workers.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The purpose is to help these workers find jobs in growing sectors of our economy.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: There's nothing wrong with that, but because these benefits are paid out on top of normal unemployment benefits, we wind up paying greater benefits to those who lose their jobs because of foreign competition than we do to their friends and neighbors who are laid off due to domestic competition.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Anyone must agree that this is unfair.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Putting these two programs on the same footing will save $1.15 billion in just 1 year.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Earlier I made mention of changing categorical grants to States and local governments into block grants.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Now, we know of course that the categorical grant programs burden local and State governments with a mass of Federal regulations and Federal paperwork.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Ineffective targeting, wasteful administrative overhead-all can be eliminated by shifting the resources and decision-making authority to local and State government.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: This will also consolidate programs which are scattered throughout the Federal bureaucracy, bringing government closer to the people and saving $23.9 billion over the next 5 years.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Our program for economic renewal deals with a number of programs which at present are not cost-effective.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: An example is Medicaid.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Right now Washington provides the States with unlimited matching payments for their expenditures;

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: at the same time, we here in Washington pretty much âÃÂ¬â _âÃÂ¬â _âÃÂ¬â âÃÂ¬ÃâÃÂ¬Ã¥âÃÂ¬ÃâÃÂ¬â âÃÂ¬ÃâÃÂ¬Ã¥âÃÂ¬Ã¨âÃÂ¬â _ dictate how the States are going to manage those programs.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We want to put a cap on how much the Federal Government will contribute, but at the same time allow the States much more flexibility in managing and structuring the programs.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I know from our experience in California that such flexibility could have led to far more cost-effective reforms.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Now, this will bring a savings of $1 billion next year.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The space program has been and is important to America, and we plan to continue it.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We believe, however, that a reordering of priorities to focus on the most important and cost-effective NASA programs can result in a savings of a quarter of a million dollars.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Now, coming down from space to the mailbox, the Postal Service has been consistently unable to live within its operating budget.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: It is still dependent on large Federal subsidies.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We propose reducing those subsidies by $632 million in 1982 to press the Postal Service into becoming more effective, and in subsequent years the savings will continue to add up.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The Economic Regulatory Administration in the Department of Energy has programs to force companies to convert to specific fuels.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: It has the authority to administer a gas rationing plan, and prior to decontrol it ran the oil price control program.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: With these and other regulations gone we can save several hundreds of millions of dollars over the next few years.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I'm sure there's one department you've been waiting for me to mention, the Department of Defense.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: It's the only department in our entire program that will actually be increased over the present budgeted figure.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: But even here there was no exemption.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The Department of Defense came up with a number of cuts which reduce the budget increase needed to restore our military balance.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: These measures will save $2.9 billion in 1982 outlays, and by 1986 a total of $28.2 billion will have been saved-or perhaps I should say, will have been made available for the necessary things that we must do.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The aim will be to provide the most effective defense for the lowest possible cost.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I believe that my duty as President requires that I recommend increases in defense spending over the coming years.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I know that you're all aware-but I think it bears saying again-that since 1970 the Soviet Union has invested $300 billion more in its military forces than we have.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: As a result of its massive military buildup, the Soviets have made a significant numerical advantage in strategic nuclear delivery systems, tactical aircraft, submarines, artillery, and anti-aircraft defense.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: To allow this imbalance to continue is a threat to our national security.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Notwithstanding our economic straits, making the financial changes beginning now is far less costly than waiting and having to attempt a crash program several years from now.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We remain committed to the goal of arms limitation through negotiation.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I hope we can persuade our adversaries to come to realistic balanced and verifiable agreements.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: But, as we negotiate, our security must be fully protected by a balanced and realistic defense program.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Now, let me say a word here about the general problem of waste and fraud in the Federal Government.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: One government estimate indicated that fraud alone may account for anywhere from 1 to 10 percent-as much as $25 billion of Federal expenditures for social programs.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: If the tax dollars that are wasted or mismanaged are added to this fraud total, the staggering dimensions of this problem begin to emerge.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The Office of Management and Budget is now putting together an interagency task force to attack waste and fraud.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We're also planning to appoint as Inspectors General highly trained professionals who will spare no effort to do this job.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: No administration can promise to immediately stop a trend that has grown in recent years as quickly as government expenditures themselves, but let me say this: Waste and fraud in the Federal Government is exactly what I've called it before-an unrelenting national scandal, a scandal we're bound and determined to do something about.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Marching in lockstep with the whole program of reductions in spending is the equally important program of reduced tax rates.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Both are essential if we're to have economic recovery.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: It's time to create new jobs, to build and rebuild industry, and to give the American people room to do what they do best.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And that can only be done with a tax program which provides incentive to increase productivity for both workers and industry.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Our proposal is for a 10-percent across the-board cut every year for 3 years in the tax rates for all individual income taxpayers, making a total cut in the tax-cut rates of 30 percent.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: This 3-year reduction will also apply to the tax on unearned income, leading toward an eventual elimination of the present differential between the tax on earned and unearned income.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Now, I would have hoped that we could be retroactive with this.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: But as it stands, the effective starting date for these 10-percent personal income tax rate reductions will call for as of July 1st of this year.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Again, let me remind you that while this 30-percent reduction will leave the taxpayers with $500 billion more in their pockets over the next 5 years, it's actually only a reduction in the tax increase already built into the system.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Unlike some past ""tax reforms,"" this is not merely a shift of wealth between different sets of taxpayers.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: This proposal for an equal reduction in everyone's tax rates will expand our national prosperity, enlarge national incomes, and increase opportunities for all Americans.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Some will argue, I know, that reducing tax rates now will be inflationary.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: A solid body of economic experts does not agree.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And tax cuts adopted over the past three-fourths of a century indicate these economic experts are right.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: They will not be inflationary.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I've had advice that in 1985 our real production in goods and services will grow by 20 percent and be $300 billion higher than it is today.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The average worker's wage will rise in real purchasing power 8 percent, and this is in after-tax dollars.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And this, of course, is predicated on a complete program of tax cuts and spending reductions being implemented.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The other part of the tax package is aimed directly at providing business and industry with the capital needed to modernize and engage in more research and development.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: This will involve an increase in depreciation allowances, and this part of our tax proposal will be retroactive to January 1st.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The present depreciation system is obsolete, needlessly complex, and economically counterproductive.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Very simply, it bases the depreciation of plant machinery and vehicles and tools on their original cost, with no recognition of how inflation has increased their replacement cost.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We're proposing a much shorter write-off time than is presently allowed-a 5-year-write-off for machinery, 3 years for vehicles and trucks, and a 10-year write-off for plant.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: In fiscal year 1982 under this plan, business would acquire nearly $10 billion for investment;

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: by 1985, the figure would be nearly 45 billion.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: These changes are essential to provide the new investment which is needed to create millions of new jobs between now and 1985 [1986], and to make America competitive once again in the world market.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: These won't be make-work jobs.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: They are productive jobs, jobs with a future.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I'm well aware that there are many other desirable and needed tax changes, such as indexing the income tax brackets to protect taxpayers against inflation;

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: the unjust discrimination against married couples if both are working and earning;

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: tuition tax credits;

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: the unfairness of the inheritance tax, especially to the family-owned farm and the family-owned business;

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: and a number of others.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: But our program for economic recovery is so urgently needed to begin to bring down inflation that I'm asking you to act on this plan first and with great urgency.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And then, I pledge I will join with you in seeking these additional tax changes at the earliest date possible.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: American society experienced a virtual explosion in government regulation during the past decade.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Between 1970 and 1979, expenditures for the major regulatory agencies quadrupled.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The number of pages published annually in the Federal Register nearly tripled, and the number of pages in the Code of Federal Regulations increased by nearly two-thirds.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The result has been higher prices, higher unemployment, and lower productivity growth.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Overregulation causes small and independent business men and women, as well as large businesses to defer or terminate plans for expansion.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And since they're responsible for most of the new jobs, those new jobs just aren't created.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Now, we have no intention of dismantling the regulatory agencies, especially those necessary to protect environment and assure the public health and safety.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: However, we must come to grips with inefficient and burdensome regulations, eliminate those we can and reform the others.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I have asked Vice President Bush to head a Cabinet-level Task Force on Regulatory Relief.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Second, I asked each member of my Cabinet to postpone the effective dates of the hundreds of new regulations which have not yet been implemented.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Third, in coordination with the Task Force, many of the agency heads have already taken prompt action to review and rescind existing burdensome regulations.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And finally, just yesterday I signed an Executive order that for the first time provides for effective and coordinated management of the regulatory process.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Much has been accomplished, but it's only a beginning.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We will eliminate those regulations that are unproductive and unnecessary by Executive order where possible and cooperate fully with you on those that require legislation.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The final aspect of our plan requires a national monetary policy which does not allow money growth to increase consistently faster than the growth of goods and services.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: In order to curb inflation we need to slow the growth in our money supply.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Now, we fully recognize the independence of the Federal Reserve System and will do nothing to interfere with or undermine that independence.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We will consult regularly with the Federal Reserve Board on all aspects of our economic program and will vigorously pursue budget policies that'll make their job easier in reducing monetary growth.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: A successful program to achieve stable and and moderate growth patterns in the money supply will keep both inflation and interest rates down and restore vigor to our financial institutions and markets.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: This, then, is our proposal-America's new beginning: a program for economic recovery.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I don't want it to be simply the plan of my administration.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I'm here tonight to ask you to join me in making it our plan.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Together we can embark on this road [applause].

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Thank you very much.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I should have arranged to quit right here [Laughter].

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Well, together we can embark on this road, not to make things easy, but to make things better.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Our social, political, and cultural, as well as our economic institutions, can no longer absorb the repeated shocks that have been dealt them over the past decades.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Can we do the job?

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The answer is yes.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: But we must begin now.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We're in control here.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: There's nothing wrong with America that together we can't fix.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I'm sure there'll be some who raise the old familiar cry, ""Don't touch my program;

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: cut somewhere else.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I hope I've made it plain that our approach has been evenhanded, that only the programs for the truly deserving needy remain untouched.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The question is, are we simply going to go down the same path we've gone down before, carving out one special program here, another special program there?

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I don't think that's what the American people expect of us.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: More important, I don't think that's what they want.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: They're ready to return to the source of our strength.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The substance and prosperity of our nation is built by wages brought home from the factories and the mills, the farms, and the shops.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: They are the services provided in 10,000 corners of America;

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: the interest on the thrift of our people and the returns for their risk-taking.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The production of America is the possession of those who build, serve, create, and produce.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: For too long now, we've removed from our people the decisions on how to dispose of what they created.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We've strayed from first principles.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We must alter our course.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The taxing power of government must be used to provide revenues for legitimate government purposes.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: It must not be used to regulate the the economy or bring about social change.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We've tried that, and surely we must be able to see it doesn't work.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Spending by government must be limited to those functions which are the proper province of government.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We can no longer afford things simply because we think of them.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Next year we can reduce the budget by $41.4 billion, without harm to government's legitimate purposes or to our responsibility to all who need our benevolence.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: This, plus the reduction in tax rates, will help bring an end to inflation.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: In the health and social services area alone, the plan we're proposing will substantially reduce the need for 465 pages of law, 1,400 pages of regulations, 5,000 Federal employees who presently administer 7,600 separate grants in about 25,000 separate locations.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Over 7 million man and woman hours of work by State and local officials are required to fill out government forms.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I would direct a question to those who have indicated already an unwillingness to accept such a plan: Have they an alternative which offers a greater chance of balancing the budget, reducing and eliminating inflation, stimulating the creation of jobs, and reducing the tax burden?

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And, if they haven't, are they suggesting we can continue on the present course without coming to a day of reckoning?

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: If we don't do this, inflation and the growing tax burden will put an end to everything we believe in and our dreams for the future.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We don't have an option of living with inflation and its attendant tragedy, millions of productive people willing and able to work but unable to find a buyer for their work in the job market.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We have an alternative, and that is the program for economic recovery.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: True, it'll take time for the favorable effects of our proposal to be felt.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: So, we must begin now.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The people are watching and waiting.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: They don't demand miracles.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: They do expect us to act.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Let us act together.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Thank you, and good night.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Mr. Speaker, Mr. President, Distinguished Members of the Congress, honored guests and fellow citizens: Today marks my first State of the Union address to you, a constitutional duty as old as our republic itself.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: finally staked on the experiment entrusted to the hands of the American people.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: For our friends in the press, who place a high premium on accuracy, let me say: I did not actually hear George Washington say that, but it is a matter of historic record.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: But from this podium, Winston Churchill asked the free world to stand together against the onslaught of aggression.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Franklin Delano Roosevelt spoke of a day of infamy and summoned a nation to arms.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And Douglas MacArthur made an unforgettable farewell to a country he had loved and served so well.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Dwight Eisenhower reminded us that peace was purchased only at the price of strength and John F.Kennedy spoke of the burden and glory that is freedom.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: When I visited this chamber last year as a newcomer to Washington, critical of past policies which I believe had failed, I proposed a new spirit of partnership between this Congress and this Administration and between Washington and our state and local governments.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: In forging this new partnership for America we could achieve the oldest hopes of our republic prosperity for our nation, peace for the world, and the blessings of individual liberty for our children and, someday, for all of humanity.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: It's my duty to report to you tonight on the progress that we have made in our relations with other nations, on the foundation we've carefully laid for our economic recovery and, finally, on a bold and spirited initiative that I believe can change the face of American government and make it again the servant of the people.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Seldom have the stakes been higher for America.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: What we do and say here will make all the difference to auto workers in Detroit, lumberjacks in the Northwest, steelworkers in Steubenville who are in the unemployment lines, to black teen-agers in Newark and Chicago;

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: to hard-pressed farmers and small businessmen and to millions of everyday Americans who harbor the simple wish of a safe and financially secure future for their children.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: To understand the State of the Union, we must look not only at where we are and where we're going but where we've been.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The situation at this time last year was truly ominous.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The last decade has seen a series of recessions.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: There was a recession in 1970, in 1974, and again in the spring of 1980.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Each time, unemployment increased and inflation soon turned up again.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: to describe this.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Government's response to these recessions was to pump up the money supply and increase spending.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: In the last six months of 1980, as an example, the money supply increased at the fastest rate in postwar history 13 percent.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Inflation remained in double digits and Government spending increased at an annual rate of 17 percent.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Interest rates reached a staggering 21 1/2 percent.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: There were eight million unemployed.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Late in 1981, we sank into the present recession largely because continued high interest rates hurt the auto industry and construction.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And there was a drop in productivity and the already high unemployment increased.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: This time, however, things are different.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We have an economic program in place completely different from the artificial quick-fixes of the past.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: It calls for a reduction of the rate of increase in Government spending, and already that rate has been cut n early in half.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: But reduced spending alone isn't enough.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We've just implemented the first and smallest phase of a three-year tax-rate reduction designed to stimulate the economy and create jobs.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Already interest rates are down to 15 3/4 percent, but they must still go lower.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Inflation is down from 12.4 percent to 8.9, and for the month of December it was running at an annualized rate of 5.2 percent.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: If we had not acted as we did, things would be far worse for all Americans than they are today.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Inflation, taxes and interest rates would all be higher.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: A year ago, Americans' faith in their governmental process was steadily declining.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Six out of ten Americans were saying they were pessimistic about their future.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: A new kind of defeatism was heard.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Some said our domestic problems were uncontrollable that we had to learn to live with the-seemingly endless cycle of high inflation and high unemployment.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: There were also pessimistic predictions about the relationship between our Administration and this Congress.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: It was said we could never work together.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Well, those predictions were wrong.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The record is clear, and I believe that history will remember this as an era of American renewal, remember this Administration as an Administration of change and remember this Congress as a Congress of destiny.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Together, we not only cut the increase in Government spending nearly in half, we brought about the largest tax reductions and the most sweeping changes in our tax structure since the beginning of this century.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And because we indexed future taxes to the r ate of inflation, we took away Government's built-in profit on inflation and its hidden incentive to grow larger at the expense of American workers.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Together, after 50 years of taking power away from the hands of the people in their states and local communities we have started returning power and resources to them.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Together, we have cut the growth of new Federal regulations nearly in half.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: In 1981, there were 23,000 fewer pages in the Federal Register, which lists new regulations, than there were in 1980.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: By deregulating oil, we've come closer to achieving energy independence and help bring down the costs of gasoline and heating fuel.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Together, we have created an effective Federal strike force to combat waste and fraud in Government.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: In just six months it has saved the taxpayers more than $2 billion, and it's only getting started.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Together, we've begun to mobilize the private sector not to duplicate wasteful and discredited Government programs but to bring thousands of Americans into a volunteer effort to help solve many of America's social problems.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Together, we've begun to restore that margin of military safety that insures peace.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Our country's uniform is being worn once again with pride.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Together we have made a new beginning, but we have only begun.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: No one pretends that the way ahead will be easy.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: ills we suffer have come upon us over several decades.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: They will not go away in days, weeks or months, but they will go away

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The economy will face difficult moments in the months ahead.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: But, the program for economic recovery that is in place will pull the economy out of its slump and put us on the road to prosperity and stable growth by the latter half of this year.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: That is why I can report to you tonight that in the near future the State of the Union and the economy will be better much better if we summon the strength to continue on the course that we've charted.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And so the question: If the fundamentals are in place, what now?

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Two things: First, we must understand what's happening at the moment to the economy.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Our current problems are not the product of the recovery program that's only just now getting under way, as some would have you believe;

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: they are the inheritance of decades of tax and tax, and spend

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Second, because our economic problems are deeply rooted and will not respond to quick political fixes, we must stick to our carefully integrated plan for recovery.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And that plan is based on four common-sense fundamentals: continued reduction of the growth in Federal spending, preserving the individual and business tax deductions that will stimulate saving and investment, removing unnecessary Federal regulations to spark productivity and maintaining a healthy dollar and a stable monetary policy the latter a responsibility of the Federal Reserve System.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The only alternative being offered to this economic program is a return to the policies that gave us a trillion-dollar debt, runaway inflation, runaway interest rates and unemployment.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The doubters would have us turn back the clock with tax increases that would offset the personal tax-rate reductions already passed by this Congress.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Raise present taxes to cut future deficits, they tell us.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Well, I don't believe we should buy that argument.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: There are too many imponderables for anyone to predict deficits or surpluses several years ahead with any degree of accuracy.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The budget in place when I took office had been projected as balanced.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: It turned out to have one of the biggest deficits in history.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Another example of the imponderables that can make deficit projections highly questionable: A change of only one percentage point in unemployment can alter a deficit up or down by some $25 billion.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: As it now stands, our forecasts, which we're required by law to make, will show major deficits, starting at less than $100 billion and declining, but still too high.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: More important, we are making progress with the three keys to reducing deficits: economic growth, lower interest rates and spending control.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The policies we have in place will reduce the deficit steadily, surely and, in time, completely.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Higher taxes would not mean lower deficits.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: If they did, how would we explain tax revenues more than doubled just since 1976, yet in that same six-year period we ran the largest series of deficits in our history.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: In 1980 tax revenues increased by $54 billion, and in 1980 we had one of our all-time biggest deficits.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Raising taxes won't balance the budget.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: It will encourage more Government spending and less private investment.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Raising taxes will slow economic growth, reduce production and destroy future jobs, making it more difficult for those without jobs to find them and more likely that those who now have jobs could lose them.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: So I will not ask you to try to balance the budget on the backs of the American taxpayers.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I will seek no tax increases this year and I have no intention of retreating from our basic program of tax relief.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I promised the American people to bring their tax rates down and keep them down to provide them incentives to rebuild our economy, to save, to invest in America's future.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I will stand by my word.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Tonight I'm urging the American people: Seize these new opportunities to produce, to save, to invest, and together we'll make this economy a mighty engine of freedom, hope and prosperity again.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Now the budget deficit this year will exceed our earlier expectations.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The recession did that.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: It lowered revenues and increased costs.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: To some extent, we're also victims of our own success.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We've brought inflation down faster than we thought we could an d in doing this we've deprived Government of those hidden revenues that occur when inflation pushes people into higher income tax brackets.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And the continued high interest rates last year cost the Government about $5 billion more than anticipated.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We must cut out more nonessential Government spending and root out more waste, and we will continue our efforts to reduce the number of employees in the Federal work force by 75,000.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The budget plan I submit to you on Feb. 8 will realize major savings by dismantling the Departments of Energy and Education, and by eliminating ineffective subsidies for business.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We will continue to redirect our resources to our two highest budget priorities: a strong national defense to keep America free and at peace and a reliable safety net of social programs for those who have contributed and those who are in need.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Contrary to some of the wild charges you may have heard, this Administration has not and will not turn its back on America's elderly or America's poor.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Under the new budget, funding for social insurance programs will be more than double the amount spent only six years ago.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: But it would be foolish to pretend that these or any programs cannot be made more efficient and economical.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The entitlement programs that make up our safety net for the truly needy have worthy goals and many deserving recipients.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We will protect them.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: But there's only one way to see to it that these programs really help those whom they were designed to help, and that is to bring their spiraling costs under control.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: and a large part of this goes to entitlement programs.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Committee after committee of this Congress has heard witness after witness describe many of these programs as poorly administered and rife with waste and fraud.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Virtually every American who shops in a local supermarket is aware of the daily abuses that take place in the food stamp program, which has grown by 16,000 percent in the last 15 years.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Another example is Medicare and Medicaid, programs with worthy goals but whose costs have increased from 11.2 billion to almost 60 billion, more than five times a s much, in just 10 years.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Waste and fraud are serious problems.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: corruption has permeated virtually every area of the Medicare and Medicaid health care industry.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: One official said many of the people who are cheating the system were very confident that nothing was going to happen to them.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Well, something is going to happen.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Not only the taxpayers are defrauded the people with real dependency on these programs are deprived of what they need because available resources are going not to the needy but to the greedy.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The time has come to control the uncontrollable.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: In August we made a start.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I signed a bill to reduce the growth of these programs by $44 billion over the next three years, while at the same time preserving essential services for the truly needy.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Shortly you will receive from me a message on further re forms we intend to install some new, but others long recommended by our own Congressional committees.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I ask you to help make these savings for the American taxpayer.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The savings we propose in entitlement programs will total some $63 billion over four years and will, without affecting Social Security, go a long way toward bringing Federal spending under control.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: But don't be fooled by those who proclaim that spending cuts will deprive the elderly, the needy and the helpless.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The Federal Government will still subsidize 95 million meals every day.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: That's one out of seven of all the meals served in America.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Head St art, senior nutrition programs, and child welfare programs will not be cut from the levels we proposed last year.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: More than one-half billion dollars has been proposed for minority business assistance.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And research at the National Institutes of Health will be increased by over $100 million.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: While meeting all these needs, we intend to plug unwarranted tax loopholes and strengthen the law which requires all large corporations to pay a minimum tax.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I am confident the economic program we've put into operation will protect the needy while it triggers a recovery that will benefit all Americans.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: It will stimulate the economy, result in increased savings and provide capital for expansion, mortgages for home building and jobs for the unemployed.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Now that the essentials of that program are in place, our next major undertaking must be a program just as bold, just as innovative to make government again accountable to the people, to make our system of federalism work again.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Our citizens feel they've lost control of even the most basic decisions made about the essential services of Government, such as schools, welfare, roads and even garbage collection.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And they're right.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: A maze of interlocking jurisdictions and levels of Government confronts average citizens in trying to solve even the simplest of problems.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: They don't know where to turn for answers, who to hold accountable, who to praise, who to blame, who to vote for or against.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The main reason for this is the overpowering growth of Federal grants-in-aid programs during the past few decades.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: In 1960, the Federal Government had 132 categorical grant programs, costing $7 billion.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: When I took office, there were approximately 500, costing nearly $100 billion 13 programs for energy, 36 for pollution control, 66 for social services, 90 for education.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The list goes on and on.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And here in the Congress, it takes at least 166 committees just to try to keep track of them.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: You know and I know that neither the President nor the Congress can properly oversee this jungle of grants-in-aid;

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: indeed, the growth of these grants had led to the distortion in the vital functions of Government.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: arms control not potholes.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The growth the growth in these Federal programs has in the words of one intergovernmental commission made the Federal Government more pervasive, more intrusive, more unmanageable, more ineffective and costly, and above all more accountable.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Well, let's solve this problem with a single, bold stroke the return of some $47 billion in Federal programs to state and local government, together with the means to finance them and a transition period of nearly 10 years to avoid unnecessary disruption .

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I will shortly send this Congress a message describing this program.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I want to emphasize, however, that its full details will have been worked out only after close consultation with Congressional, state and local officials.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Starting in fiscal 1984, the Federal Government will assume full responsibility for the cost of the rapidly growing Medicaid program to go along with its existing responsibility for Medicare.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: As part of a financially equal swap, the states will simultaneously take full responsibility for Aid to Families With Dependent Children and food stamps.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: This will make welfare less costly and more responsive to genuine need because it will be designed and administered closer to the grass roots and the people it serves.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: In 1984, the Federal Government will apply the full proceeds from certain excise taxes to a grass roots trust fund that will belong, in fair shares, to the 50 states.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The total amount flowing into this fund will be $28 billion a year.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Over the next four years, the states can use this money in either of two ways.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: If they want to continue receiving Federal grants in such areas as transportation, education and social services, they can use their trust fund money to pay for the grants or, to the extent they choose to forgo the Federal grant programs, they can use their trust fund money on their own, for those or other purposes.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: There will be a mandatory pass-through of part of these funds to local governments.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: By 1988, the states will be in complete control of over 40 Federal grant programs.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The trust fund will start to phase out, eventually to disappear, and the excise taxes will be turned over to the states.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: They can then preserve, lower or raise taxes on their own and fund and manage these programs as they see fit.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: In a single stroke, we will be accomplishing a real realignment that will end cumbersome administration and spiraling costs at the Federal level while we insure these programs will be more responsive to both the people they're meant to help and the people who pay for them.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Hand in hand with this program to strengthen the discretion and flexibility of state and local governments, we're proposing legislation for an experimental effort to improve and develop our depressed urban areas in the 1980's and 1990's.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: This legislation will permit states and localities to apply to the Federal Government for designation as urban enterprise zones.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: A broad range of special economic incentives in the zones will help attract new business, new jobs, new opportunity to America's inner cities and rural towns.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Some will say our mission is to save free enterprise.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Well, I say we must free enterprise so that, together, we can save America.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Some will also say our states and local communities are not up to the challenge of a new and creative partnership.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Well, that might have been true 20 years ago before reforms like reapportionment and the Voting Rights Act, the 10-year extension of which I strongly support.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: It's no longer true today.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: This Administration has faith in state and local governments and the constitutional balance envisioned by the Founding Fathers.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We also believe in the integrity, decency and sound good sense of grass roots Americans.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Our faith in the American people is reflected in another major endeavor.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Our private sector initiatives task force is seeking out successful community models of school, church, business, union, foundation and civic programs that help community needs.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Such groups are almost invariably far more efficient than government in running social programs.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We're not asking them to replace discarded and often discredited Government programs dollar for dollar, service for service.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We just want to help them perform the good works they choose, and help others to profit by their example.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Three hundred eighty-five thousand corporations and private organizations are already working on social programs ranging from drug rehabilitation to job training, and thousands more Americans have written us asking how they can help.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The volunteer spirit is still alive and well in America.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Our nation's long journey towards civil rights for all our citizens once a source of discord, now a source of pride must continue with no back sliding or slowing down.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We must and shall see that those basic laws that guarantee equal rights are preserved and, when necessary, strengthened.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Our concern for equal rights for women is firm and unshakable.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We launched a new Task Force on Legal Equity for Women, and a 50-states project that will examine state laws for discriminatory language.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And for the first time in our history a woman sits on the highest court in the land.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: So, too, the problem of crime one as real and deadly serious as any in America today it demands that we seek transformation of our legal system, which overly protects the rights of criminals while it leaves society and the innocent victims of crime without justice.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We look forward to the enactment of a responsible Clean Air Act to increase jobs while continuing to improve the quality of our air.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We are encouraged by the bipartisan initiative of the House and are hopeful of further progress as the Senate continues its deliberations.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: So far I have concentrated largely now on domestic matters.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: To view the State of the Union in perspective, we must not ignore the rest of the world.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: There isn't time tonight for a lengthy treatment of social or of foreign policy, I should say a subject I intend to address in detail in the near future.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: A few words, however, are in order on the progress we've made over the past year re-establishing respect for our nation around the globe and some of the challenges and goals that we will approach in the year ahead.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: At Ottawa and Cancun, I met with leaders of the major industrial powers and developing nations.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Now some of those I met with were a little surprised I didn't apologize for America's wealth.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Instead I spoke of the strength of the free marketplace system and how that system could help them realize their aspirations for economic development and political freedom.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I believe lasting friendships were made and the foundation was laid for future cooperation.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: In the vital region of the Caribbean Basin, we're developing a program of aid, trade and investment incentives to promote self-sustaining growth and a better, more secure life for our neighbors to the south.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Toward those who would export terrorism and subversion in the Caribbean and elsewhere, especially Cuba and Libya, we will act with firmness.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Our foreign policy is a policy of strength, fairness and balance.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: By restoring America's military credibility, by pursuing peace at the negotiating table wherever both sides are willing to sit down in good faith, and by regaining the respect of America's allies and adversaries alike, we have strengthened our country's position as a force for peace and progress in the world.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: When action is called for, we're taking it.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: with the forces of oppression.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: If the events in Poland continue to deteriorate, further measures will follow.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Now let me also note that private American groups have taken the lead in making Jan. 30 a day of solidarity with the people of Poland so, too, the European Parliament has called for March 21 to be an international day of support for Afghanistan.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Well, I urge all peace-loving peoples to join together on those days, to raise their voices, to speak and pray for freedom.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Meanwhile, we're working for reduction of arms and military activities.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: As I announced in my address to the nation last Nov. 18, we have proposed to the Soviet Union a far-reaching agenda for mutual reduction of military forces and have already initiated negotiations with them in Geneva on intermediate-range nuclear forces.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: In those talks it is essential that we negotiate from a position of strength.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: There must be a real incentive for the Soviets to take these talks seriously.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: This requires that we rebuild our defenses.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: In the last decade, while we sought the moderation of Soviet power through a process of restraint and accommodation, the Soviets engaged in an unrelenting buildup of their military forces.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The protection of our national security has required that we undertake a substantial program to enhance our military forces.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We have not neglected to strengthen our traditional alliances in Europe and Asia, or to develop key relationships with our partners in the Middle East and other countries.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Building a more peaceful world requires a sound strategy and the national resolve to back it up.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: When radical forces threaten our friends, when economic misfortune creates conditions of instability, when strategically vital parts of the world fall under the shadow of Soviet power, our response can make the difference between peaceful change or disorder and violence.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: That's why we've laid such stress not only on our own defense, but on our vital foreign assistance program.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Your recent passage of the foreign assistance act sent a signal to the world that America will not shrink from making the investments necessary for both peace and security.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Our foreign policy must be rooted in realism, not naivete or self-delusion.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: A recognition of what the Soviet empire is about is the starting point.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Winston Churchill, in negotiating with the Soviets, observed that they respect only strength and resolve in their dealings with other nations.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: That's why we've moved to reconstruct our national defenses.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We intend to keep the peace we will also keep our freedom.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We have made pledges of a new frankness in our public statements and worldwide broadcasts.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: In the face of a climate of falsehood and misinformation, we've promised the world a season of truth the truth of our great civilized ideas: individual liberty, representative government, the rule of law under God.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We've never needed walls, or mine fields or barbwire to keep our people in.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Nor do we declare martial law to keep our people from voting for the kind of Government they want.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Yes, we have our problems;

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: yes, we're in a time of recession.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And it's true, there's no quick fix, as I said, to instantly end the tragic pain of unemployment.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: But we will end it the process has already begun and we'll see its effect as the year goes on.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We speak with pride and admiration of that little band of Americans who overcame insuperable odds to set this nation on course 200 years ago.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: But our glory didn't end with them Americans ever since have emulated their deeds.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We don't have to turn to our history books for heroes.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: They're all around us.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: One who sits among you here tonight epitomized that heroism at the end of the longest imprisonment ever inflicted on men of our armed forces.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Who will ever forget that night when we waited for television to bring us the scene of that first plane landing at Clark Field in the Philippines bringing our P.O.W.'s home.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The plane door opened and Jeremiah Denton came slowly down the ramp.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: and then thanked us for bringing him home.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Just two weeks ago, in the midst of a terrible tragedy on the Potomac, we saw again the spirit of American heroism at its finest the heroism of dedicated rescue workers saving crash victims from icy waters.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And we saw the heroism of one of our young Government employees, Lenny Skutnik, who, when he saw a woman lose her grip on the helicopter line, dived into the water and dragged her to safety.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: And then there are countless quiet, everyday heroes of American life parents who sacrifice long and hard so their children will know a better life than they've known;

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: church and civic volunteers who help to feed, clothe, nurse and teach the needy;

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: millions who've made our nation, and our nation's destiny, so very special unsung heroes who may not have realized their own dreams themselves but then who reinvest those dreams in their children.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Don't let anyone tell that America's best days are behind her that the American spirit has been vanquished.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We've seen it triumph too often in our lives to stop believing in it now.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: One hundred and one hundred and twenty years ago the greatest of all our Presidents delivered his second State of the Union Message in this chamber.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We cannot escape history, Abraham Lincoln warned.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We of this Congress and this Administration will be remembered in spite of ourselves.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The trial through which we pass will light us down in honor or dishonor to the latest generation.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Well, that President and that Congress did not fail the American people.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Together, they weathered the storm and preserved the union.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Let it be said of us that we, too did not fail;

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: that we, too, worked together to bring America through difficult times.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Let us so conduct ourselves that two centuries from now, another Congress and another President, meeting in this chamber as we're meeting, will speak of us with pride, saying that we met the test and preserved for them in their day the sacred flame of liberty this last, best hope of man on Earth.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: This solemn occasion marks the 196th time that a President of the United States has reported on the State of the Union since George Washington first did so in 1790.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: That's a lot of reports, but there's no shortage of new things to say about the State of the Union.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: The very key to our success has been our ability, foremost among nations, to preserve our lasting values by making change work for us rather than against us.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I would like to talk with you this evening about what we can do together-- not as Republicans and Democrats, but as Americans-- to make tomorrow's America happy and prosperous at home, strong and respected abroad, and at peace in the world.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: As we gather here tonight, the state of our Union is strong, but our economy is troubled.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: For too many of our fellow citizens-- farmers, steel and auto workers, lumbermen, black teenagers, working mothers-- this is a painful period.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We must all do everything in our power to bring their ordeal to an end.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: It has fallen to us, in our time, to undo damage that was a long time in the making, and to begin the hard but necessary task of building a better future for ourselves and our children.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: We have a long way to go, but thanks to the courage, patience, and strength of our people, America is on the mend.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: But let me give you just one important reason why I believe this-- it involves many members of this body.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Just 10 days ago, after months of debate and deadlock, the bipartisan Commission on Social Security accomplished the seemingly impossible.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Social Security, as some of us had warned for so long, faced disaster.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: I, myself, have been talking about this problem for almost 30 years.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: As 1983 began, the system stood on the brink of bankruptcy, a double victim of our economic ills.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: First, a decade of rampant inflation drained its reserves as we tried to protect beneficiaries from the spiraling cost of living.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Then the recession and the sudden end of inflation withered the expanding wage base and increasing revenues the system needs to support the 36 million Americans who depend on it.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: When the Speaker of the House, the Senate majority leader, and I performed the bipartisan-- or formed the bipartisan Commission on Social Security, pundits and experts predicted that party divisions and conflicting interests would prevent the Commission from agreeing on a plan to save Social Security.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
text: Well, sometimes, even here in Washington, the cynics are wrong.

speaker: Ronald W. Reagan
